Erin Patterson is set to find out if she could face a longer prison sentence or a new trial, as Victoria’s highest court hands down its decision on two appeals regarding her triple murder case.
The court of appeal is set to rule on the two appeals from 10am on Friday, after justices Lesley Taylor, Stephen McLeish and Peter Kidd heard arguments from her legal team and prosecutors in August.
Patterson, 52, is not expected to attend the appeal decision in person.
She was last year sentenced to life imprisonment, with a non-parole period of 33 years, for the murders of her estranged husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt Heather Wilkinson, after she hosted them for lunch.
Patterson was also convicted of the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived the beef wellington laced with death cap mushrooms after spending weeks in hospital.
She has appealed against her convictions, while the director of public prosecutions appealed against Patterson’s sentence, arguing that it was manifestly inadequate.
In August, the court heard Patterson should have been given no possibility of ever being released from prison, or a non-parole period so lengthy that she was likely to die behind bars.
Her lawyers argued seven grounds for her appeal, including that allowing jurors to stay in the same hotel as police and the prosecution while they deliberated over their verdicts in the triple murder trial represented a “catastrophic” failure of the justice system.
Richard Edney, for Patterson, said the failure to properly separate the jury during their deliberations was a fundamental irregularity that had denied her a fair trial.
“What we say has occurred here in the applicant’s trial was an inexplicable and perhaps still unexplained failure of a process,” Edney told the court in August.
They also argued that the trial judge Christopher Beale erred in ruling that photos and videos related to mushrooms and found on an SD card in Patterson’s home was inadmissible, as it tended to support her evidence that she foraged for mushrooms.
During the hearings, Brendan Kissane KC, the DPP, said that even though Patterson would be aged in her 80s by the time she was eligible for parole, her sentence was still too lenient.
When asked whether a longer non-parole period would essentially damn Patterson to dying behind bars, and had “some artifice of it being life with life”, Kissane told the court: “It has its harsh aspect to it, of course, we accept that.”
“But in our submission that is not a matter that is outweighed by the seriousness of the offending.”
There are several possible outcomes to Patterson’s appeal: leave to appeal is not granted; leave to appeal is granted, but her appeal dismissed; leave to appeal is granted, her appeal upheld and a retrial ordered; or her leave to appeal is granted, the appeal upheld, and acquittal entered.
If either of the final two decisions are handed down, there will be no need to rule on the DPP’s sentence appeal.
If not, either the appeal fails, or it succeeds and Patterson is resentenced by the court of appeal.

క్లెయిమ్: ఫ్రాన్స్లో నిరసనకారులను అడ్డుకునేందుకు పోలీసులు ‘పిగ్ స్క్వాడ్’ను సిద్ధం చేయడాన్ని చూపుతున్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఇది కృత్రిమ మేధ (AI)తో సృష్టించిన ఫేక్ వీడియో. ఫ్రెంచ్ పోలీసులు అలాంటి స్క్వాడ్ను ఏర్పాటు చేసినట్లు ఆధారాలు లేవు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, ఈ విషయం గురించి ఇంటర్నెట్లో వెతకగా, నిరసనల కోసం ఫ్రెంచ్ పోలీసులు ఇటువంటి పిగ్ స్క్వాడ్ను సిద్ధం చేయడం గురించి ఎటువంటి విశ్వసనీయ వార్తా కథనాలు లభించలేదు.
ఇక వైరల్ వీడియోను పరిశీలించగా, ఇందులో ఉన్న మనుషుల ముఖాలు, అక్షరాలు అస్పష్టంగా, అసహజంగా ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. దీని ఆధారంగా, ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోని కృత్రిమ మేధ (AI) ఉపయోగించి సృష్టించి ఉండొచ్చని తెలుస్తోంది.
దీని ఆధారంగా, ఈ వీడియోను AI వీడియో డిటెక్షన్ టూల్స్తో(ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) పరీక్షించగా, ఈ వీడియోను ఏఐతో రూపొందించినట్లు స్పష్టమైంది.
అలాగే, ఈ వీడియోను ముందుగా ‘Jaranor films’ అనే ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ పేజీ అప్లోడ్ (ఆర్కైవ్) చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియో AI ద్వారా చేయబడిందనే లేబుల్ ఇందులో ఉంది. ఈ పేజీ వివిధ ఏఐ వీడియోలను రూపొందిస్తుంది. గతంలో కూడా ఈ పేజీలో అప్లోడ్ చేసిన ఈఫిల్ టవర్పై పాలస్తీనా జెండా వీడియో గురించి మేము రాసిన ఫాక్ట్-చెక్ కథనాన్ని ఇక్కడ చూడవచ్చు.
చివరిగా, నిరసనకారులను ఎదుర్కోవడానికి ఫ్రెంచ్ పోలీసులు పిగ్ స్క్వాడ్ను సిద్ధం చేస్తున్నారంటూ ఒక AI వీడియోను షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of trying to 'delegitimise' election
- Published
The main Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and Arab-led party leaders have denounced Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleging foreign interference following the election which saw his coalition lose its majority.
Netanyahu's Likud accused Israel's Arab-led parties of "stealing" the election. Home security agency Shin Bet is investigating whether they received illegal funding from Qatar and Turkey.
Qatar's foreign ministry denied the "ridiculous and dangerous" allegations and accused Israeli politicians of conducting a disinformation campaign against Doha.
Final results confirmed that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition had won a majority in parliament.
The two Arab party lists - The Joint List and the Ra'am - defied expectations to win a record 19 seats in the 120-seat Knesset following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That positions them as potential kingmakers, with Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats and his rival Gadi Eisenkot's bloc securing 48.
On Thursday Likud alleged that voters had been "bribed" to vote for Arab parties, after the head of the Central Elections Committee (CEC) asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate "serious suspicions" of foreign interference.
Both Arab parties strongly rejected the claim, with the Arab-majority Joint List alliance saying it was baseless.
The row is being seen by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to delegitimise the Arab parties, thereby making it politically impossible for Eisenkot to join forces with them - which is currently his bloc's only route to power.
Israeli media reported that the CEC had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's Foreign Ministry "categorically" denied the claims.
Netanyahu and his Likud Party framed the allegations as a "political earthquake" and an "an attack on democracy", aimed at removing their right-wing government.
But the Shin Bet later clarified that their investigation did not implicate an entire community who had voted legally, while acting CEC Director General Dean Livne said there was "no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity."
Eisenkot, who was briefed on the investigation, said "it is too early to determine what happened, or if anything happened at all," and accused Netanyahu of running "an orchestrated and organized campaign to delegitimize the election results".
Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, who is part of the Joint List, dismissed the allegation, saying: "The losing side is constructing a racist blood libel and calling on the security agencies to use force in order to overturn the election results."
Netanyahu's attacks on Arab voters and parties have been ongoing for days. He spent much of election day posting on social media that high Arab turnout is an "emergency" and a "matter of life or death" for the Israeli right. He also shared AI-generated images of Arab voters at polling stations, in an attempt to encourage right-wingers to get out and vote.
Arab Israelis, many of whom refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up about one fifth of the country.
For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout on Tuesday was inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, led by Netanyahu.
The final results offer only three plausible options for a government to be formed: a national unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.
Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but speculation has swirled in recent days that an agreement could yet be reached.
A snap poll conducted by Hebrew University showed that the most popular option for voters from every party in the opposition bloc was for Eisenkot to form a minority government with Ra'am, and supported from outside by the Joint List.

“Please have at least 125 miles of range left when we pick it up.” That request from the people who look after the Cadillac press cars wasn’t going to be hard to honor. The electric Escalade IQ arrived with an indicated range of 440 miles (708 km), and with a full week of work to squeeze in, getting anywhere close to needing to recharge it seemed unlikely. With more than 200 kWh of lithium-ion battery between its axles, range is one thing the big electric Caddy needn’t worry about.
Designed and debuted during a time of greater EV optimism, the Escalade is Cadillac’s statement that swapping out a V8 for a pair of powerful electric motors is no compromise to its ambitions, even if the brand’s future will now include a mix of electric and combustion cars beyond 2030. It shares a battery pack and much else with other full-size GM EVs we’ve tested: the Chevrolet Silverado EV, the GMC Sierra EV, and of course the divisive Hummer EVs. And like those trucks and SUVs, the Escalade is large and heavy—just small enough to fit into a standard parking space, with a curb weight sufficient to push it into the Class 3 truck category.
So, the side mirrors are flat, and there’s no formal EPA range—Cadillac says it achieves 460 miles (740 km) on the EPA test cycle—but there are plenty of airbags, even though the 9,046 lb (4,103 kg) curb weight does not require them. Yes, you did read that right, it does weigh 4 tons. And yes, the electric Escalade does weigh a third more than the last gas-powered one we tested.

Behind the wheel
However, it drives better. Like many a modern luxury EV, the Escalade IQ is held up by air suspension. Controlled by computers, air suspension is remarkably effective at concealing a car’s mass, although here it has been tuned for a rather floaty ride. In lesser electric SUVs—ones that weigh a mere 3 tons or less—you can often forget that curb weight entirely until it’s time to brake. Here, you just need to drive over something, like a recessed utility hole cover on the road, for the transient shock that makes its way into the cabin to remind you.
From behind the wheel, I find it slightly sobering, perhaps no bad thing when taking responsibility on the road. It’s easier to drive than one might expect, particularly at low speeds where the rear-wheel steering gives the car a shorter effective wheelbase than its actual 136.2 inches (3,460 mm). It might fill a parking space, but it’s not hard work getting it in or out. Forward visibility is good, but I found the passenger mirror less than completely effective and was glad for the blindspot monitoring camera that appeared when I used the turn signals, even if the camera quality was just the right side of potato.
At highway speeds, the rear wheels steer with the front wheels to effectively lengthen the wheelbase and thus increase straight-line stability. Nominal power and torque are 680 hp (505 kW) and 615 lb-ft (834 Nm), which you can increase to 750 hp (560 KW) and 785 lb-ft (1,064 Nm) with the V button on the steering wheel—this engages Velocity Max mode. It’s not ever going to ripple the tarmac like that electric Porsche Cayenne, but you can still hit 60 mph (97 km/h) from a standstill in less than 5 seconds should you need to.

Super Cruise is standard and works well on its premapped roads. The one-pedal driving calibration is, as always on GM EVs, very well-calibrated on its highest setting. It’s very effective for city driving, as you quickly adjust to its rate of deceleration to judge stops perfectly. There’s also a paddle on the steering wheel that will add regenerative braking on demand, should you wish to slow more but don’t feel like using the brake pedal.
The 460-mile range estimate is entirely believable, even with little attention given to driving efficiently. As you’ll note from the photos, on shorter trips the Escalade IQ reported efficiencies that wouldn’t be out of place in something like an Ioniq 5. But at highway speeds, you don’t get to recuperate nearly as much energy, and once it all averages out, the answer is close to 2.1 miles/kWh (29.6 kWh/100 km). Cadillac doesn’t provide a 10–80 percent fast charging time for the Escalade IQ—only that it can add 100 miles in 10 minutes—and by the end of the week, I was still at 65 percent state of charge, so a full DC fast-charge time remains a mystery. (But at least the car had plenty of range when it was collected.)
A tech-filled experience
Even if the Escalade IQ isn’t Cadillac’s flagship EV—that’s the hand-built $300,000 Celestiq sedan—the automaker has still packed in as much technology as it could. In front of the driver is a 55-inch display that encompasses touch-sensitive panels either side of the main instrument display and stretches across the width of the dash. On the left are the trip computer and lights, and to the right of the instrument display is the main infotainment touchscreen, which runs Android Automotive OS.

The dial controller on the center console allows you to interact with the infotainment, so you don’t need to use the touchscreen or try voice commands, something that worked here with moderate success. I would expect a slightly better scroll action considering the $153,490 sticker price for our Escalade IQ Premium Sport, but like the 55-inch display, the hardware is shared across the Cadillac EVrange. Climate controls are on a separate touchscreen, this one ahead of the center console and below the infotainment.
Another touchscreen serves the front-seat passenger, plus a pair for the middle row (the optional $1,995 rear-seat entertainment system). These stream video from a wide range of platforms—the industry mostly adopting Android Automotive OS has meant plenty of app support—and the screen for the front passenger has a filter that prevents the driver from seeing what’s being displayed while the vehicle is in motion. You can use your phone as an input controller, either as a keyboard or to play games, although it’s a little kludgy.
It is roomy in the back, and the middle row moves fore and aft. This can give the third row more than enough legroom for long journeys, although the lack of vertical space to put legs means that sitting back there involves knees next to faces.
I can see the appeal of the Escalade IQ as an alternative to the traditionally powered Escalade. It might not be very efficient for an EV, but 2.1 miles/kWh is still the equivalent of more than 70 mpg (3.3 L/100 km), whereas a standard V8 version only manages 16 mpg (14.7 L/100 km) combined. And you have to stop and fill that one up with gas almost 80 miles (129 km) before the electric one runs out of range.

California lawmakers began a discussion Thursday about removing the cap on the state’s $750 million incentive for film and TV production, while acknowledging that such a move would face budget hurdles.
At an Assembly committee hearing in North Hollywood, a handful of state lawmakers heard testimony from union leaders and industry advocates who argued that the program — which was doubled last year — is not enough to stop the outflow of production jobs.
Betsy Beers, the creative partner of Shonda Rhimes, told the committee that she had hoped to shoot a new “Grey’s Anatomy” spinoff in Santa Clarita. But the show, which is set in West Texas, did not get a California tax credit.
“We lost a lot of time, and a lot of money, and now we are filming in Albuquerque,” Beers said. “We want to be here.”
Because the state incentive is capped, projects must apply during periodic windows and then compete with other shows on a “jobs ratio” score. Beers said the show lost out initially because it didn’t get score highly enough. When ABC tried again in the fall, the program was already oversubscribed and was no longer taking applications.
“The program is still not competitive or predicable enough to address the loss of production to other regions,” said Arlen Valdivia, vice president of state government affairs at the Motion Picture Association. “There needs to be more done to make California competitive.”
FilmLA, the permitting agency, reported last week that production volume continues to fall in the Los Angeles area, even as the share of scripted TV shows receiving a state subsidy has nearly doubled. Several speakers at Thursday’s hearing called for eliminating the $750 million cap entirely — saying the limit leaves producers uncertain about whether they will get the credit.
Georgia’s credit has no limit and New York’s allows the state to pull from allocations for future years — amounting to an uncapped credit. Rick Chavez Zbur, who chairs the Assembly Select Committee on Growing and Retaining the Creative Economy in California, said he expects to make improvements in the next legislative session.
“I want to try to do our best to make whatever changes we can, and I think either increasing the cap or eliminating it,” Zbur said after the hearing. “But you know that is a heavy lift. But we’re going to try this year to make as much progress as we can.”
Lawmakers are also dealing with a structural deficit and deep cuts to Medicaid — which has intensified competition for tax dollars.
During the hearing, Zbur floated the idea of “dynamic scoring” — suggesting that the state should account for the benefit from the film credit instead just looking at the headline cost. That idea, he said, would be key to persuading lawmakers that an unlimited credit is a worthwhile investment.
“The way we’re looking at the return needs to be what we’re focused on,” said John Harabedian, another member of the committee. “It becomes a regional fight. It becomes a best-use-of-a-dollar fight… The numbers are going to convince our colleagues that don’t necessarily live in L.A.”
Rowan Isaaks, an economist with the state Legislative Analyst’s Office, cited research showing that film credits return 20-50 cents for every dollar invested by the state. He also expressed skepticism about dynamic scoring. “It’s subject to a lot of uncertainty,” he said.
Stephen Cheung, the president of the Los Angeles Economic Development Committee, cited his own group’s research, which found a return of $1.07 to state and local coffers. That report was funded by the MPA.
Assemblyman Nick Schultz floated the idea of extending the expiration date of the state program, which is currently set to sunset in 2030, as a way of offering greater certainty to productions. He and other also suggested providing a subsidy for above-the-line costs — salaries for actors, directors, etc. — and opening up eligibility for the program to commercials and game shows.
“Why should we be picking and choosing?” he asked. “Why should we be picking winners and losers? Let’s incentivize all of it to stay.”
The state raised the base credit from 20% to 35% last year, while increasing the overall cap from $330 million to $750 million.
“The higher credit might mean fewer projects overall,” Isaaks noted. “There’s a possibility that the more generous our credit is, the fewer productions we can fund in total.”
Since Gov. Gavin Newsom expanded the state incentive last year, lawmakers have added additional measures to bolster it. The Legislature created a $10 million incentive for post-production and passed a bill to expedite studio rebates and exempt credits for independent films from a $5 million credit cap.
While Congress is considering a 20% nationwide incentive, several speakers argued that even if that passes, California will still face stiff competition from other states.
“We should not assume the work will return because federal policy changes,” said Lindsay Dougherty, leader of the Hollywood Teamsters.

Gujarat court sentences 3 to life for cow slaughter, cites Manusmriti
Gujarat Deputy CM Harsh Sanghavi hailed the verdict, calling it a clear message that the law will never spare those who commit cow slaughter in the state.
A court in Gujarat's Gandhinagar district has sentenced three persons to life imprisonment in a cow slaughter case after they were found in possession of 277 kg of beef, citing Hindu scriptures to underscore the religious significance of the cow.
Gujarat Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghavi hailed the verdict, calling it a clear message that the law will never spare those who commit cow slaughter in the state.
In his judgment on Monday, Additional Sessions Judge BR Rajput also imposed a fine of ₹3 lakh on the convicts, Vasim Qureshi, Mohammad Rafiq Qureshi, and Asfaq Bahelim.
Quoting the Manusmriti, an ancient Sanskrit text, the court observed that the cow is not merely an animal but is regarded as a pillar of material prosperity and 'dharma' (righteousness).
"Sage Manu entrusted the primary responsibility for the protection and care of cattle to the 'Vaishya' class. Furthermore, in the context of 'Arsha Vivaha' (a traditional form of Vedic marriage), the pair -- a cow and a bull -- holds special significance," the judge said.
Further quoting the Vedas and other Hindu scriptures, the court said that when drops of 'amrita' (nectar) fell to the earth through the power of penance, the divine cow Kamadhenu emerged and came to be regarded as the progenitor of all bovine species on earth.

"The cow is regarded as the 'mother of the world', serving as an abode for 33 crore deities. Her four legs are symbolic of the four Vedas, the court said.
According to the prosecution, six persons were arrested with 277 kg of beef and weapons allegedly used to slaughter cows and a vehicle meant to transport the meat after a raid on a house in Jamla village of Gandhinagar district on August 22, 2024.
The prosecution said a father-son duo would purchase weak or non-lactating buffaloes. They would then bring four individuals from Ahmedabad to their home and have the animals slaughtered in a cruel manner for beef, all for the sake of financial gain.
Citing the investigation, the prosecution said the accused intended to sell the beef to one Ghulam Moin. After the trial, the court found three of the six men guilty. The prosecution produced 54 witnesses and 18 pieces of documentary evidence to establish the charges.
Gujarat Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghavi congratulated the Gandhinagar police and the prosecution for the "accurate investigation and presenting strong evidence" that led to the sentencing.
"This verdict under the Gujarat Animal Preservation Act is a clear message that the law will never spare those who commit cow slaughter in Gujarat. Protecting the cow mother is Gujarat's unwavering resolve. Congratulations to the Gandhinagar Police and the government side for the accurate investigation and presenting strong evidence," he said.
Through a 2017 amendment to the Gujarat Animal Preservation Act, 1954, the Gujarat government had enhanced punishment for those found guilty of cow slaughter to life imprisonment, making it the first state in the country to make cow slaughter punishable with such a sentence.
The Gujarat Animal Preservation (Amendment) Bill approved by the legislative assembly has a provision for ten years' imprisonment for transportation, storage or sale of beef.
In 2011, when Narendra Modi was the chief minister of Gujarat, the state government had imposed a complete ban on slaughter of cows, transportation and selling of cow meat by amending the said Act.

The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) will launch its much-anticipated navigation satellite NVS-03 aboard a Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) rocket on October 30, the space agency said on Wednesday. The GSLV-F18/NVS-03 mission is scheduled to lift off at 11:51 PM on Friday, from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh. NVS-03 is the third satellite in India's next-generation navigation satellite system, designed to ensure continuity of services under the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS). The satellite is equipped with an indigenous atomic clock, alongside procured atomic clocks. It also features the L1 frequency band in addition to the existing L5 and S bands, which provide positioning and location-related information, according to PTI. The navigation system is designed to cover India's landmass and an area extending up to 1,500 km beyond the country's geopolitical boundaries. ISRO's GSLV-F15 rocket, marking the space agency's 100th launch, successfully placed the 2,250-kg NVS-02 satellite into its intended initial elliptical transfer orbit of 170 km x 37,785 km on January 29, 2025. The satellite's solar panels also deployed successfully after launch. However, NVS-02 could not reach its final circular operational orbit because its onboard liquid-fuelled engine failed to ignite during the orbit-raising manoeuvre. An investigation by an ISRO Apex Committee, based on telemetry analysis, identified a failure in the electrical signal reaching the pyro valve. This valve uses an explosive-triggered mechanism to open the fuel and oxidiser lines required to fire the engine. The committee found that at least one contact in each of the main and redundant electrical connector paths had disengaged. This disrupted the electrical circuit and prevented the engine-firing mechanism from functioning, despite the satellite having built-in backup systems. ISRO plans to deploy five second-generation NavIC satellites — NVS-01, NVS-02, NVS-03, NVS-04 and NVS-05 — to strengthen the existing satellite constellation and ensure uninterrupted navigation services with improved capabilities. The NVS series introduces signals in the L1 frequency band in addition to the existing bands, expanding the range of navigation services offered by the system. NVS-01, the first satellite in this second-generation series, was launched aboard the GSLV-F12 rocket on May 29, 2023. The mission also marked the first time an indigenous atomic clock was carried onboard an Indian navigation satellite. Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC) is India's independent regional satellite navigation system. It is designed to provide users with accurate Position, Velocity and Timing (PVT) information across India and an area extending approximately 1,500 km beyond the country's landmass. NavIC offers two types of services: Standard Positioning Service (SPS), available to civilian users, and Restricted Service (RS), an encrypted service intended for authorised users. Panos Panay, Amazon's senior vice president of Devices and Alexa, says a couple hundred million people now use Alexa+, the revamped version of the decade-old voice assistant, on its Echo devices. He says people talk to Alexa+ two to three times more than before its AI glow-up, cook with it five times more, listen to music three times more, and create routines twice as much.
To keep that momentum going, Amazon has new Echo products to deliver a richer Alexa+ experience, including minor refreshes on existing hardware and entirely new categories. Announced Wednesday and available for purchase now, they include the Echo Dot ($100), Echo Studio With Home Camera ($250), Echo Show 16 ($500), Echo Time ($200), and the first Alexa Photo Frame ($200).
“I don't think anyone's really doing AI at all in the home, and if they are, they aren't doing it well,” Panay says at an intimate media-only event in New York City. As people have “deeper” conversations with Alexa+, Panay says devices need to be in premium shape—a strategy Amazon has been focusing on after announcing more premium Kindles and Alexa Tablets in early October.
You can see that premiumization in the hardware pricing: The Echo Dot—once the affordable, entry-level $50 smart speaker—now starts at $100. That's higher than the marked-up prices on existing Amazon devices from this summer, which the company blamed on the memory shortage.
Echo Dot
Panay says Amazon has sold more than 100 million Echo Dots, and in 2026 alone, people spent more than a trillion minutes listening to music on the diminutive orb. So, the main goal for the new Dot? Boost the sound. The full-range driver reportedly delivers 50 percent stronger bass performance and crisper vocals.
With four beamforming microphones (up from three) and Amazon's AZ3 chip, Alexa can isolate your voice in a noisy environment and track your commands more effectively. It also has Omnisense like last year's Echo Dot Max, which can sense the environment to, say, detect when you walk into the home and turn on the lights.
The Dot now supports the Matter standard and works as a Thread border router, turning it into a hub for setting up and controlling smart home devices. If you have an Eero router, it can also turn into a Wi-Fi extender.
It comes in four colors, three of which are calming pastels. Amazon's design head Chris Green tells WIRED that's intentional to evoke a calm, softer aesthetic, citing recent data showing nearly half of US adults are stressed once a week. Alternatively, you can buy the Kids Echo Dot, which has the same hardware but in fun designs, plus Amazon Kids+ for age-appropriate content.
Echo Studio With Home Camera
The new Echo Studio is the first Amazon smart speaker with a camera—a feature once limited to Amazon's Echo Show smart displays—allowing Alexa to identify the person making the command (along with voice recognition) for more personalized responses. That's especially important these days as Alexa+ can connect to email or calendar apps and needs to verify who's speaking before divulging personal information.
It also lets you use Live View to check in on your home and monitor pets, or video call friends and family. With no display on the Echo Studio, you'll need to pair it with a Fire TV or use your smartphone to view the camera feed of the person you're calling—as seen in the picture above when Panay used the Studio to Drop In on his dad. This “Drop In” feature will arrive later through a software update.
The camera enables what Amazon calls “Advanced Room Adaptation,” which tunes the sound to the room. Even if you move around the space, the volume will stay consistent. And it can also be used for visual intelligence—just like how you might use your phone to identify an object with Google Lens, you can pick up an object and show it to Alexa through the camera, and it can identify it and answer questions. For example, show a board game you've decided to play and ask Alexa to explain the rules.
While no privacy shutter physically blocks the camera, you can press a button to turn off the mics and camera, and an LED lights up when the camera is on and in use. If you don't want yet another camera in your home, Amazon says you can buy the standard Echo Studio. The speaker is otherwise very similar to the 2025 model and is meant to be the top-end option for folks who want even better audio quality.
Alexa Photo Frame
Digital photo frames are a well-established category now, with companies like Aura and Skylight leading the market. Now Amazon's entering the fray with the Alexa Photo Frame. Yes, you can still talk to Alexa just like any other Echo device, but the 10-inch display will always show your photos—nothing else. The bottom edge lights up when Alexa activates, and you can ask it the weather or to show you pictures of your dog last Halloween.
The caveat is that you need to use Amazon Photos. Once your images are in Amazon Photos, you can choose who and what appears on the frame—even newly captured photos so Mom can see the latest pics from your vacation before she even asks. The display is a semi-matte, anti-glare touchscreen that adjusts brightness based on the room's ambient light, and you can swipe the screen to see more images. Tap an image to play a voice note tied to the picture—that's something you can add in the Amazon Photos app, but a future update will let users add voice notes to images straight on the Alexa Photo Frame.
Smart curation happens in the background to choose the best photos. For example, if you have a lot of vertical images, it will stack them side by side and group familiar faces together. Maybe that means a pic of your kid when they were 8 years old, and the pic on the right of when they're 14. (Though Google has been doing this for years on its smart displays.) Alexa knows to choose pictures of people smiling, and understands timing—you'll be served last year's Halloween pictures around this time of year.
Amazon says it's easy to set up for someone else—like your grandparents—and the frame comes in three styles: black, birch, or walnut.
Echo Time
The other entirely new product is the Echo Time. It's similar in size and sound to the Echo Dot, but with a digital clock screen. No cameras here—it's designed for the bedside table, after all—and the 3.2-inch circular display can dim as low as 0.3 nits (the same as Apple's new HomeView).
It's hardly the first time Amazon has dabbled with clocks on an Echo (see the Echo Spot), and Amazon even sold a bedside sleep tracker before discontinuing it barely a year later.
The Echo Time doesn't track your sleep, but it can help you start a bedtime routine as you wind down. The embedded ultrasonic transducer can detect your breathing to identify when you're in a light sleep stage and gently wake you up within 10 to 60 minutes of your alarm, rather than forcing you out of deep sleep. These “Smart Alarms” are increasingly common on fitness trackers, like Google's Fitbit Air, but the pitch here is that you don't need a gadget on your wrist. Sadly, these features work only for the person closest to the Echo Time; with two people in bed, you'll need two Echo Time units—one on each nightstand.
You can choose from hundreds of clock faces, set up alarms with Alexa+, and ask the assistant to remind you about certain things when it wakes you up—like grabbing lunch from the fridge before heading out. Alexa can play soothing soundscapes to lull you to sleep like a sound machine. And when you wake up, you can tap the top of the device to snooze it (up to four times).
There's a Kids Echo Time with wacky designs and more limited features constrained to Amazon's Kids+ service. Kids can set their own alarms, ask for the weather forecast, and customize clock faces, but the main highlight is Sleep Studio. This connects to content from apps like Calm, Headspace, and Moshi to help kids wind down and fall asleep.
Echo Show 16
Finally, there's the Echo Show 16. Yes, it's a bigger smart display, but Panay says Amazon has redesigned the entire experience from the ground up. This specific model is designed to be wall-mounted, though you can buy a kickstand if you'd prefer. It starts at $500, but Amazon has introductory pricing of $400; the version with the Nanomatte anti-glare display (like the one on the Alexa Tablet Pro 12) costs $550.
It has slimmer bezels, a thinner frame, and an entirely new audio system with eight woofers and two tweeters. The 13-megapixel camera can supposedly identify people from up to 17 feet away, so you won't have to walk really close to the screen to see your personalized information. It also supports night vision, so you can use Live View to check in on your home and still see in the dark.
A full built-in Fire TV experience lets you watch as much content as you want while cooking, or follow along with recipes with Alexa. One big focus of the redesign was letting users prioritize the features they use the most. Want to use it as a smart home controller? There's a dashboard that shows all your controls as your primary “Screen Style.” Parents who prefer to use it as a calendar can set the “Family Organizer” screen as the main display. Or just let it turn into a digital photo frame with the Photos Screen Style.
More unique is the AI-generated interface Amazon is debuting with Alexa+ called “Neo.” Instead of a basic chat transcript like most other chatbots, Alexa+ will create charts, generate images, and offer other visuals to zhuzh up its responses during more complex conversations. (That's something Google and OpenAI have also played up with recent updates to Search and ChatGPT.) These “Cards" will also appear in your Alexa app so you can revisit them at any time.
A Reuters report earlier this year revealed details that Amazon was working on a smartphone, codenamed Transformer, with Alexa+ as the focus of the experience and a generative user interface. “Neo” on the Echo Show 16 gives us a first glimpse of what that might look like, and paired with many of the Alexa+ features introduced on the recent Alexa Tablet Pro 12, it feels like the Amazon smartphone is closer than ever.
I asked Panay point-blank whether Amazon was making a phone, and while he said there was “no intent," he pointed out that all of the new software experiences are “scalable.” He then asked to look at the iPhone Duo I was holding and remarked that it was similar in size to the Surface Duo, which Panay helmed at Microsoft. There may be “no intent” on paper, but it sure seems like he wants to make a phone again.

The US Army general fired by defence secretary 
Pete Hegseth
 admitted to leaking classified information about the wars in Iran and Ukraine to journalists over a period of roughly a year, according to an internal investigation report reviewed by Axios.
Lt Gen Brett Sylvia, who headed the Joint Chiefs of Staff’s Strategy, Plans and Policy Directorate, known as the J5, acknowledged sharing classified information with two reporters from separate media outlets, according to the report. A US official told Axios that Sylvia made the admissions on video after failing multiple polygraph tests during the investigation.
Sylvia was dismissed by Hegseth on Wednesday over what the Pentagon described as severe misconduct. The investigation, which has been referred to the Department of Justice for further action, remains ongoing.
According to the report, the disclosures began as early as June 2025 and continued after the Pentagon tightened restrictions on media access. Sylvia allegedly communicated with reporters through the encrypted messaging application Signal and also met one journalist in person at a Silver Diner in Arlington, Virginia.
The report said the diner meeting took place after the journalist’s access to the Pentagon had been revoked. During the meeting, Sylvia relied on notes he had made while reviewing a classified report to orally share information about US assistance to Ukraine. The journalist was working on a book and met Sylvia twice, the report said. Sylvia did not coordinate the meetings with the Pentagon’s public affairs office or seek clearance before sharing the information.
Investigation points to deleted messages
The investigation also raised questions about Sylvia’s handling of communications with one of the reporters. According to the report, he received a Signal message sometime in June or July that he believed concerned Iran. Sylvia said he could not recall its precise contents and claimed he had deleted the message, believing he had accidentally erased the entire conversation thread. This also removed Signal messages and calls that could otherwise have been recovered from his personal phone.
US officials suspect Sylvia deliberately deleted the communications and presented the action as accidental. The report also said he admitted to being one of 20 officials cited in a media story critical of Pentagon leadership.
Another US official told Axios that Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle and his office had lobbied the Joint Staff to issue a statement supporting Sylvia in an effort to limit the damage from any future allegations of leaks. The Joint Staff later withdrew the statement after someone in the Defence Department informed it of the reasons behind Sylvia’s dismissal.
US president Donald Trump, asked about the firing on Thursday, said Sylvia had “big problems” and that the administration was “very much looking for leakers”. Trump appeared to refer to Sylvia using female pronouns.
Separately to the Axios report, a defence department official also confirmed to Al Jazeera that Sylvia was under investigation for leaking classified information concerning the Iran war, Russia’s war against Ukraine and other matters. The official said he had failed three polygraph tests and accused him of putting national security at risk. The official also stressed that Sylvia was not a central planner for the Iran war, saying that responsibility rested with Centcom and its commander, Adm Brad Cooper.
Hegseth’s wider crackdown on leaks
Sylvia’s dismissal is the latest action in Hegseth’s campaign against unauthorised disclosures to the media. In July, the Pentagon announced a joint task force with the Justice Department to identify leakers and directed its Office of General Counsel to prioritise prosecutions over the unauthorised release of classified information.
The Pentagon had also introduced restrictive rules governing journalists’ access and reporting in October 2025, prompting several news organisations and defence reporters to surrender their press credentials.
Sylvia is the second officer to be removed from the J5 position under Hegseth. His predecessor, Lt Gen Joseph McGee, was forced into retirement in October last year.
No immediate replacement has been named for Sylvia, according to an official cited by The Associated Press.

Bus users have pointed out that the Telangana State Road Transport Corporation’s (TGSRTC) bus tracking app, Gamyam, has not been as effective as they had hoped, with concerns over live tracking, route information and the punctuality of services.
Sharing his experience, Prithvi Raj, a student and bus user, said there had been some occasions when he was unable to track in real time the bus he intended to board .
“RTC should ensure that Gamyam should not be limited to displaying bus locations. Data should be used to monitor whether buses are adhering to timetables, identify consistently delayed services, and improve punctuality. Another concern is that some buses are skipping designated bus stops and operating like express services instead of ordinary services. Such behaviour should be monitored through the app, and action should be taken,” he said.
The concerns come even as the TGSRTC has sanctioned ₹19.21 crore for the vehicle tracking and passenger information system, according to a response to a Right to Information (RTI) request filed by Kareem Ansari through the portal YOURTI.in.
According to the letter of award, the negotiated rate for the vehicle tracking and passenger information system is ₹375 per bus per month, excluding GST.
The rollout initially covered 4,170 buses and was subsequently extended. The corporation listed a total of 9,320 vehicles till March.
Transport researchers familiar with the system said the TGSRTC needed to ensure that route information was updated promptly to improve the app’s effectiveness. The corporation should inform the vendor of new routes on the day operations commence and ensure that these are reflected in the app, they added. Routes that are no longer operational should also be removed.
“The corporation should ensure that buses are mapped to the correct schedules before they leave the depot. Often, some buses are shown on a particular route but are operating on a different route,” a transport expert told The Hindu.
The expert also pointed out that route codes should be distinct even when a service terminates short of its usual destination or is extended by just one stop.
“For example, 195W terminating at JNTU cannot be coded as 195W. It should be coded as 195J,” he said.
Apart from improving the accuracy of route information, users said the app could be made more useful by introducing features to help passengers plan journeys involving transfers between buses.
“The app does not allow filtering by route direction when searching by route. Both directions are displayed simultaneously, which confuses passengers,” said Md. Shoaib, a media professional.

I am scheduled to die on August 10, 2060, at the age of 74.
So says my iPhone screen, where Death Clock, an AI-powered longevity app that predicts life expectancy based on your medical habits and lifestyle, has produced an image of a smiling grim reaper to celebrate my expiration date. There he was one September morning, looking especially thrilled about the reveal, gesturing with a peace sign as he reclined in a doughnut-shaped pool inflatable under that giant number: 74.
I have never resented getting older, but I suppose that’s younger than I’d like to be when my time is up. In the last four years—years that brought the passing of my grandmother and aunt within 18 months—I’ve become hyperaware of how finite my days are. Since turning 40 in January, I’ve also experienced daily reminders of aging: inexplicable pains that rotate between my back, neck, and hips. Spiritually, I feel young; physically, my body screams otherwise. Aging is natural, but I had a creeping suspicion I could buy myself more time.
Our collective obsession with life extension has given rise to a multitrillion-dollar longevity industry, bolstered by wannabe prophets like Bryan Johnson. Threats like climate change and AI doomerism only seem to have intensified existential fears, even as LLMs promise a new era of personalized medicine to address any health issue. Track enough pieces of data, the thinking goes, and algorithms can help you hack your own demise.
All of which led me to Death Clock, an app launched in 2024 aimed at tracking users’ health habits in an attempt to prolong their lives. In February, the company announced a new feature that lets you order biomarker panels. For a $69 subscription, you can get a basic blood panel that measures things like cholesterol, blood sugars, inflammation, vitamin D, and blood and organ health. There are also nine additional tests—assessing everything from hormones and micronutrients to your thyroid—that, altogether, cost $780. I opted for the routine blood panel and added the “stress” test ($29). Maybe some new insight could help me get a handle on it.
In an attempt to be more than another morbid countdown gimmick, Death Clock says it’s trained its AI on 1,200 longevity studies, actuarial data from life insurance companies, and life expectancy tables. Based on your results, its algorithms create a detailed prevention plan intended to help extend the time you have left.
Frankly, I was skeptical that anything meaningful would actually come from this. I was also, I can admit, a little fearful that I’d learn something I didn’t want to, a fact that might dissolve the little sanity I had left in a year that had already brought its share of unexpected problems.
After filling out an initial health questionnaire, a notification buzzed, forewarning my demise. There are three ways I will likely perish, it said: cardiovascular disease, a sleep disorder, or cancer (it doesn’t specify which type). This means, according to the app, I have already “completed” more than half of my existence on this mortal plane. A few days later, when I noted that my family has a mild history of diabetes, the app updated my age of death from 74 to 73.
And just like that, I lost a year.
I know I won’t live to be 100; people in my family generally croak in their early eighties. But was it possible to extend my lifespan by 10, even 15 years, with a hyperpersonalized plan? “You have two paths,” a message from the app exclaimed. “We are here to help you achieve the longer one.” I made an appointment with Quest Diagnostics, one of the two labs the company has partnered with, and willingly gave Death Clock my blood.
There’s no shortage of products that aim to reshape our relationship to our bodies. My inbox overflows with emails from longevity zealots pitching the latest anti-aging fads: salmon sperm scalp injections, a platelet-rich plasma treatment “Hailey Bieber swears by.” It’s almost too much, this urge to cheat the natural order of time.
“That’s a fool errand,” Death Clock CEO Brent Franson tells me one afternoon. He says advocates like Johnson—whose mantra “Don’t Die” reads more like a rejected Nike slogan than a wellness-oriented affirmation—“have to be really careful about inferring immortality when you have something to sell. That’s a dangerous place to be. The reality is we’re all going to die. It’s a question of when.”
Over Zoom, all I can think about is what Franson is trying to sell me.
The longevity market is projected to reach $8 trillion by 2030, meaning the future of health care may be shaped less by traditional treatment and more by personalized AI health services. With Doctronic, a HIPAA-compliant platform that works like a personal AI doctor, people can refill prescriptions without the need to see a human physician, while apps like Superpower and Lifeforce (similar to Death Clock) offer membership-based health insights and clinician-reviewed recommendations. Twin Health purports to create an AI replica, whatever that means, of a person’s metabolism. All of it is meant to help us live a little longer, though it’s unclear exactly how and at what cost.
Mike Ludkovski, a professor of statistics and applied probability at UC Santa Barbara whose research focuses on longevity analysis, says mortality awareness platforms like Death Clock “sell the illusion that individual lifespan is a linear process” that can be hacked. A 2024 Aging Cell study likewise suggested that an aging clock shouldn’t be treated as a measure of someone’s overall biological age. “Ultimately, individual-level triggers precipitating death are inherently random and will never be truly forecastable,” Ludkovski says.
I ask Franson if we’re actually getting healthier or just growing more anxious about being unhealthy. “I think both,” he says. “There’s a very unhealthy obsession with self-optimization—tracking everything, trying to control everything.”
Wasn’t Death Clock, in part, also guilty of that?
When the blood panels returned a week after I gave my sample, the results were mostly what my doctor had warned me about earlier this year. I’ve got borderline high cholesterol and blood sugar levels “creeping toward prediabetic range.” Shockingly, I have “optimal liver health” and normal cortisol levels. Videos from so-called wellness influencers had convinced me that a string of recent sleepless nights were the result of high cortisol, but, it turns out, the algorithm isn’t always right.
Based on my results, the app kept feeding me more tasks. Increase my vitamin D3! Schedule a DEXA scan for bone density! Discuss a prostate-specific antigen screening with a specialist! Despite Franson’s claim that he wants Death Clock to eventually be a replacement for primary care physicians, the app kept nudging me to discuss my results with a doctor.
Ultimately, I started to realize, tracking health data can only do so much. There is a belief, says Gretchen Terry-Leonard, author of Your Second Prime: Does Aging Suck, or Do We Suck at Aging?, that being able to measure something means it can also be managed. Death doesn’t work that way, she says, “so the measuring starts to serve a different need: the need to feel less afraid.”
Terry-Leonard is also the cofounder of the Center for Deeply Human Leadership, an independent research institute studying AI’s effect on brain health. She’s skeptical that consumer-facing longevity apps can lead to positive behavioral shifts on their own. “Facts don’t change minds,” she says. People understand that certain activities are unhealthy, but they do them anyway.
Keeping death in view is one of the oldest practices we have, and what seems to matter is whether a person feels they have the personal agency to make the necessary adjustments in their life. Researchers who study how thoughts of death shape health choices find that people move toward healthier behavior when they also have the confidence and resources to act, which not everyone does. “And without those,” Terry-Leonard tells me, “the anxiety tends to go into protecting how we feel about ourselves rather than into our health.”
While researching her book, Terry-Leonard found that older adults with more positive attitudes about aging lived an average of seven and a half years longer than those with negative outlooks. An app with a death countdown “can quietly teach us that aging is loss,” hindering longevity rather than promoting it.
In the month that I used Death Clock, this was the fact I couldn’t completely escape. I became a meticulous steward of my bodily functions, logging “daily habits” with the verve of an accountant manically calculating numbers just before tax deadline. In a single day I added 5.8 years to my life by earmarking that I’d completed at least 30 minutes of strength training, abstained from alcohol, brushed and flossed my teeth, gotten consistent sleep, spent time in the sauna, and drank more than eight glasses of water. But even as I labored to improve my death date, the clock was always there, counting down. It was an albatross that moved in a single, uniform direction: tick, tick, tick. Time became a burden I was being forced to optimize.
It makes sense that people are preoccupied with the very thing they are trying to escape. The need for control is addictive. But instead of assuaging my anxieties and questions about the great beyond, Death Clock only seemed to amplify them.
As the image of the life I want to build sharpens in my mind, a life that has already unfolded in deliciously unforeseen ways, I realize it has less to do with how I will make things happen and has everything to do with who I want them to happen with. Life isn’t about adding more time, but making it count when we can. I silenced Death Clock’s notifications on my phone and texted a friend: “Let’s meet at 7.”

India’s T-Series has boarded “The Pride of Bharat – Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj,” Sandeep Singh’s historical epic starring “Kantara” actor Rishab Shetty as the Maratha king.
The project will now be made in two parts, and filming begins in early 2027.
Bhushan Kumar and Krishan Kumar will produce for T-Series Films, and Shetty also comes on as a co-producer. To mark the partnership, Bhushan Kumar presented Shetty with a century-old painting of the Maratha ruler.
Shetty wrote, directed and starred in “Kantara,” the 2022 Kannada-language hit that won him the Indian National Film Award for best actor. Its prequel, “Kantara: Chapter 1,” was released in 2025 and grossed more than $91 million worldwide.
Shetty and Singh first announced the film in December 2024.
Across the two films, the saga will follow Shivaji Maharaj through his major battles and victories, the sacrifices that came with them and episodes from his life that are less widely known. The story centers on his skill as a military strategist, his leadership and his idea of Swarajya.
The production will have a large ensemble cast. Its creative team combines talent from India and abroad.
“Maharashtra and Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj have given us a legacy to be proud of, and I believe it is our responsibility to honor that legacy through cinema and share it with the world,” Bhushan Kumar said. “When Sandeep Singh narrated ‘The Pride of Bharat – Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj,’ I felt a deep sense of responsibility to bring this extraordinary story to the big screen.”
Kumar cited Shetty’s screen presence and his ability to bring legendary figures to life, adding that he believes the team is the right combination “to bring the courage, vision and spirit of Swarajya to audiences across generations. For T-Series, this is more than a film; it is a tribute to Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj and his timeless legacy.”
Shivaji founded the Maratha kingdom in 17th-century western India and spent much of his life fighting the Mughal Empire. He is revered in Maharashtra and a frequent subject for Indian filmmakers. Recent films about him and his circle include “Tanhaji: The Unsung Warrior” (2020), the Marathi film “Har Har Mahadev” (2022) and “Chhaava” (2025), which centered on his son Sambhaji. In May, Riteish Deshmukh directed “Raja Shivaji” and starred in it as the king. Released in the Hindi and Marathi languages, it became the highest-grossing Marathi film of all time.
Pre-production is under way ahead of the 2027 shoot.
Singh co-wrote the film with Rishi Virmani. Gulshan Kumar and T-Series Films present the project, which Legend Studios produces alongside T-Series Films. Shiv Chanana and Kabiir Sadanand join Shetty as co-producers.

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

Quick Answer
Apple’s new iPad mini features IP67 water resistance, an Acoustic Display with no grilles, a lighter body, and an 8.5-inch 60Hz OLED display with nano-texture options. Powered by the A20 Pro chip, it adds a landscape front camera, fast charging, and Pencil support. However, it lacks ProMotion, starts at $699/Rs 82,990, and comes in only two colors.
Apple has taken the wraps off a new iPad. This one is an iPad mini, and it comes with perhaps the most radical overhaul of Apple’s smaller tablet. The new iPad mini – which is being referred to as the iPad mini (A20 Pro) – comes with a truckload of new features, some of which have never been seen on any other iPad (including the Pros). Of course, it is also more expensive than ever before (such are the expensive memory times we live in), but is it worth sinking bucks in? Here are twelve things we think you should know about Apple’s new smaller iPad:
Table of Contents
First iPad with IP67 rating
Dust and water resistance have finally – FINALLY – come to the iPad. The new iPad mini comes with IP67 dust and water resistance, making this the first Apple tablet that can survive a spell in the rain or even a fall in the water. The iPad just got pool and beach friendly!
First iPad with an “Acoustic Display”: Look ma, no speaker grilles!
The new iPad mini is also the first to come with no speaker grilles at all. Apple says that its latest tablet has an Acoustic Display, which has specially designed woofers that are “paired through the display” for better bass and volume. There are also tweeters between the glass and aluminum enclosure for better highs. That’s some very impressive audio tech right there. What’s more, it comes with a sealed enclosure that enables the iPad mini to be dust- and water-resistant. Not many openings on this one!
The biggest display on an iPad mini – and the first OLED display on a non-Pro iPad
The new iPad mini comes with an 8.5-inch display, which is the largest seen on an iPad mini. The earlier generations of the tablet had 7.9-inch displays, while more recent ones had larger, 8.3-inch displays. It also comes with a higher resolution, 2316 x 1512, as compared to 2266 x 1488 of the previous iPad mini, although both have the same pixel density (326 ppi). The new iPad mini is also the first non-Pro iPad to sport an OLED display. In the past, the iPad Pros had what Apple calls a Tandem OLED display. That said, the display on the iPad mini is different from those on the Pros – the iPad Pros have an Ultra Retina XDR display, while the new iPad mini has what Apple has termed a Super Retina XDR display.
First iPad mini with TWO display options (and a “polishing cloth” in the box too!)
The new iPad mini actually gives consumers two display options. While the base 128 GB storage option has a “regular” display, the 256 GB and 512 GB variants also come with a “nano texture display glass” option, similar to those seen on the iPad Pro models. What’s more, those who go with this option will also get a “polishing cloth”. Such perks.
Not ProMoted to ProMotion: Bigger, brighter display…but STILL with a 60 Hz refresh rate
The iPad mini comes with a larger and brighter (600 nits) display than on the previous iPad mini (500 nits) and even the iPad Air M4 (500 nits), but, surprisingly, comes with the same 60 Hz refresh rate display that is seen in most non-Pro iPads. The new iPad mini does not come with a ProMotion display, which enables higher and lower refresh rates. No ProMotion for the new tablet in this regard. Pun intended.
Bigger display, but still smaller and lighter than the previous iPad mini (only slightly heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max)
Rather remarkably, even though the new iPad mini comes with a larger display than the previous iPad mini, it is actually more compact and even lighter as compared to its predecessor. It is slightly shorter (195.3 mm vs 195.4 mm), less wide (132.6 mm vs 134.8 mm) and slimmer (5.4 mm vs 6.3 mm) as compared to the previous iPad mini. Making this possible are incredibly thin bezels – 24 percent thinner than on its predecessor. At 255 grams, the new iPad mini is also the lightest iPad ever (the previous mini was 293 grams) and is only a feather heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max (249 grams) and even the iPhone Duo (255 grams). This is the easiest iPad to carry, by a mile, for miles (pun intended).
Driven by the latest iPhone chip, with differences across storage models
The iPad mini runs on the same processor that we have seen on the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the iPhone Duo – the A20 Pro. Interestingly, however, there are subtle differences between the processors on different storage variants. The 128 GB and 256 GB storage variants come with a chip with a 5-core CPU and 3 efficiency cores, while the 512 GB variant has a 6-core CPU and 4 efficiency cores. The processor on the 128 GB and 256 GB variants also has a 16-core Neural Engine, while the 512 GB one has a dual 16-core Neural Engine. We are not too sure what difference those make in everyday performance, but if you are a spec and high-performance chaser, then the 512 GB iPad mini might be the one for you.
A better front camera, and now on the landscape side
The new iPad mini has a similar rear camera to that of the previous one – a 12-megapixel camera with f/1.8 aperture – but the front-facing camera, or “selfie and video call” camera, is very different. While it has the same megapixel count (12) as its predecessor, it has a larger aperture (f/2.0 as compared to f/2.4) and, most interestingly of all, is now on the landscape edge rather than the portrait one. Apple has almost always shown the iPad mini being used in portrait mode (apart from when gaming), so this is a significant change.
Compatible with both Apple Pencils
The new iPad mini plays fine with both Apple Pencils, the Apple Pencil (USB-C) and the Apple Pencil Pro, making this pretty much a proper sketching, scribbling tab.
No smart connector, so don’t expect Apple keyboard covers
The new iPad mini has no smart connectors (those tiny metallic dots) on its side or back, so in spite of the bigger display and powerful specs, we do not expect to see keyboard covers from Apple for this one.
Fast charging comes to a non-Pro iPad (but the bundled adapter is a slow one)
While its battery life remains at the classic “up to 10 hours of surfing the web on Wi-Fi or watching video”– that is an iPad standard, the new iPad mini comes with support for fast charging. This enables it to get charged up to 50 percent in about half an hour with a 35W or higher adapter. Mind you, you will need to shell out extra bucks for that adapter, as the one that comes in the box is a 20W USB-C Power Adapter.
Also Read: Apple iPad mini (A20 Pro) vs Apple iPad mini (A17 Pro)
Kinda pricey: Priced close to the iPad Air 11 (M4)
The new iPad mini is the most expensive iPad mini ever released by Apple. The iPad mini (A17 Pro) started at USD 499 (Rs 49,900 in India), but the new iPad mini starts at a much higher USD 699 (Rs 82,900 in India). That places it incredibly close to the iPad Air (M4), which comes with a bigger display, a desktop-level processor, and an official price tag of USD 749 ( Rs 89,900 in India), but which is often available at lower prices.
And one more thing…ONLY TWO COLORS
The iPad Mini has generally had a wide range of color options. The 2021 iPad mini and the iPad mini (A17 Pro) had four color options each – space grey, blue and starlight, as well as blue for the A17 Pro and pink for the 2021 edition. The new iPad mini has, however, trimmed the product color palette – it is available in just two shades: midnight and starlight. Hopefully more colors will come along soon!

Approach African GP with humility, says Hamilton
- Published
Lewis Hamilton has addressed concerns on human rights grounds about holding an African Grand Prix in Rwanda by saying people should "approach it with humility".
Formula 1 has signed a 10-year deal with the central-east African country starting in the early 2030s.
Briton Hamilton, who has campaigned for a race in Africa for many years, said: "I don't get to choose where we go. Naturally, there are problems all over the world today, so I've seen many of the stories. But I think we really have to approach it with humility.
"There's a lot that we don't know. Growing up in England, they never taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum. A lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism and the West intervening."
Rwanda's east-central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.

And the DRC's Minister for Foreign Affairs Therese Kayikwamba Wagner said in a statement last week that "giving (Rwanda President) Paul Kagame this platform would help polish the image of an authoritarian leader whose government has helped fuel a devastating war in our country".
She pointed out that the US had sanctioned the Rwandan army and four senior officers for their role in destabilising the region, conducting military operations inside the DRC and supporting, training and fighting alongside the M23 rebel group.
She added that F1 "should require credible, independent guarantees that no money used to host the race comes from conflict-linked minerals or the exploitation of Congolese resources".
Hamilton, who will be 42 in January and has a contract until 2027, has suggested he could prolong his career in order to race in Rwanda.
"I'm now forced to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa, and that's been my dream, to be able to race in Africa," Hamilton said.
"I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we'll keep it going.
"Africa is a place that deserves to have a grand prix. It's about more than just one country. It's about the continent itself, and there are so many beautiful countries within it.
"The people are so lovely. The culture is so rich, and I think it's important that we get to show that to the world. We get to do that with our sport. We get to go to all these different countries, and people see some of these countries they didn't really know too much about.
"All of a sudden, it becomes something that's on the screen, and kids are talking about it. They go to school talking about it. So, I'm really, really hopeful for that grand prix."
However, the Ferrari driver added: "Going there doesn't mean that you neglect the things that are happening there.
"So hopefully many people start to educate themselves a little bit more about what is happening there and what has happened there for hundreds of years. I hope that does spark the conversation.
"And then I guess I'll finish it off with this: I think we need to make sure we're pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there's a lot of peace that I'm hoping we get to at some stage."
