Hong Kong’s leader has apologised for government shortcomings that contributed to a fire that killed 168 people in the city last year, a rare sign of public contrition that nevertheless failed to impress some victims’ families.
The chief executive, John Lee, and seven other officials bowed in apology at the release of a report that pointed to “decades of failure” by government bodies.
Four departments “should bear part of the responsibility” for the high casualties, the report said. So far one official, housing secretary Winnie Ho, has resigned.
Last November, a small fire probably started by a cigarette grew into an inferno that enveloped seven of the eight towers in Wang Fuk Court, a housing complex that was shrouded in bamboo scaffolding and netting for renovations.
Former residents and victims’ families have been waiting to see how the government will address who is to blame for the ignored warnings, substandard building materials and disabled fire alarms that made the fire the world’s deadliest in a residential building since 1980.
Authorities have filed charges, including manslaughter, against seven individuals and two companies over their roles in the fire. At least 35 people have been arrested.
The independent report released on Thursday found the “main culprits” of the fire were private contractors but also accused officials of “lax enforcement”.
Had the four departments better recognised the risks and acted accordingly, “there was a real possibility that the misconduct of the private-sector parties and the fire hazards in WF Court could have been rectified or removed before the fire”, it said.
Lee said a three-month investigation would now begin into the government’s role.
“I am deeply saddened. I would like to apologise to the affected residents and the general public,” Lee said on Thursday, adding that housing minister Ho should “bear political responsibility”.
But Yip Ka-kui, who lost his wife and home in the fire, told reporters he did not consider the government’s acceptance of accountability adequate. “All the secretaries for the departments named should step down,” he said, according to AFP news agency. “Administrative responsibility falls short” and political accountability even more so, Yip added.
Phyllis Lo, whose mother died in the fire, told AP news agency that progress had been made but that justice had yet to be served.
She added the officials’ apology was late, though it was better than nothing.
Hong Kong’s government has previously been accused by critics of being more concerned with clamping down on criticism than addressing the causes of the disaster.
Since a national security law was imposed on the city in 2020 by Beijing, the city’s once vibrant civil society groups and political opposition have been all but quashed.
In the weeks after the fire, authorities warned against crimes that “exploit the tragedy” and reportedly arrested at least three people for sedition.
China’s national security agency in Hong Kong also summoned international media representatives, saying they had smeared the government in their reports on the fire.
On Thursday Lee promised that “similar incidents will never be allowed to happen again”.
Some observers had called for a more legally powerful inquiry commission to be set up, rather than the judge-led independent review committee that compiled Thursday’s report.
Lee told reporters that authorities had proposed “systematic reforms”, including criminalising bid-rigging and overhauling the complaints system.
The report stated: “The fire has been put out, but the reform has only just begun.”

Crypto giant Binance freezes $2.5bn of assets over suspected hack
- Published
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that it has frozen digital assets worth more than $2.5bn (£1.87bn) to prevent them from being stolen while it investigates a security issue.
The company said as part of a series of alerts online that all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while its teams conduct security checks and that the firm will "cover all losses".
"It does look like a hack on Binance," said Binance's former boss Changpeng Zhao, who remains a majority shareholder of the firm.
Zhao added that two other crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, have also frozen around $1.7bn in stolen assets.
Circle chief executive Jeremy Allaire said the firm is "closely tracking reports of a potential exploit involving Binance" and that his company has frozen more than $800m in assets linked to the incident.
Circle is the issuer and co-creator of the USDC, one of the world's largest US dollar-backed cryptocurrencies.
Tether did not immediately respond to queries from the BBC.
Binance said the amount of funds frozen may continue to increase as its teams work closely with law enforcement and other partners to trace and seize additional assets.
"We are working around the clock and will share a full post-mortem once the investigation is complete. Please rely only on official Binance channels for updates," it said, adding that users' funds are safe.
Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes.
Bitcoin dropped by around 5% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply.

Laptops with OLED screens aren’t particularly special. They’ve been around for a decade. You can currently buy a touchscreen OLED machine for as little as $700, and even the iPad Pro has had an OLED screen since 2024.
So, why did Apple wait over a decade to release its own touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro? The simple answer for the long wait is that the company wanted to do it “the Apple way.” But in this case, “the Apple way” involves somehow cranking up the display to 2,000 nits, solving both the brightness and glare problems that OLED laptops have always suffered from.
Having seen the thing with my own eyes at a media event today in Los Angeles, I can tell you that this screen is the real deal.
Like No Other OLED
Apple is using a tandem OLED panel, the same layer-stacking technology used in the OLED iPad Pro. The real innovation here, however, is that the panel has been optimized to hit a new peak brightness of 2,000 nits, and that’s a result that matters.
That big number is meaningless on its own, but here’s the context. Nits are the standard measure of screen brightness used across the consumer tech industry. A cheap OLED laptop maxes out around 300 nits. A higher-end OLED laptop might get you up to 1,000 nits of brightness—but only in brighter and more colorful High Dynamic Range content like specific streaming apps, YouTube videos, and games. In other words, the vast majority of the time you’re using an OLED, it’ll feel like a dimmer screen than normal. The iPad Pro can get up to 1,600 nits for HDR content, and 1,000 nits for the less bright, less colorful Standard Dynamic Range content. That’s closer.
But this MacBook Pro’s screen is on an entirely different level. It’s a ground-up redesign of the tandem OLED layer arrangement in the iPad Pro, even down to the manufacturing process. And the result is that it can blast your eyes with 2,000 nits of brightness both in SDR and HDR. That means whether you’re looking at some generic wallpaper, a website, or a HDR-compatible movie, you’ll feel that extra brightness. That’s why, I assume, Apple gave it the name of PROLED XDR. In a world where the words “OLED” and “HDR” don’t necessarily indicate how good the experience is, more weighty jargon is needed.
As with all tech, bigger numbers don’t always add up to a noticeable difference for the user. But when it comes to HDR performance, we’ve been waiting a long time for OLED to catch up.
HDR, or High Dynamic Range, serves as a measure of color depth, brightness, and contrast—and in the past, this has always involved a trade-off. An OLED screen can turn each individual pixel any color, and it can turn off individual pixels in the display. This allows OLED to have great color control and unbeatable contrast, since when you turn a pixel off, it renders absolutely black.
But OLEDs couldn’t get super bright, and other screen tech like Mini-LED could get much brighter, which is why Apple stuck with Mini-LED for years, using it on the MacBook Pro and Studio Display XDR. This technology allowed Apple to have the laptops with the best HDR performance out there.
With the 2026 MacBook Pro, that compromise no longer exists. This OLED screen has both the brightness and contrast in its pocket, and you can see it.
An OLED panel has lots of more benefits over conventional backlighting beyond just contrast. Mini-LED struggles with an effect called blooming, where bright parts of images bleed light to the surrounding area, which is where lots of detail is lost in the image. OLED completely fixes that, giving each pixel a much wider range of control (up to completely turning off). As part of the Apple event I attended, we were shown a selection of HDR images with lots of contrast, a number of which had fields of darkness at the edges that made it look like the image simply disappeared into the bezel. Very pretty. We also watched a darker scene in the show Widow’s Bay in HDR, which was an excellent showcase of the range of detail this screen can show.
The new screen helps this MacBook stay exceedingly light, as well. Much of the savings in weight comes from the OLED design, since the screen uses thinner and lighter materials than screens past. Despite the computer using the same aluminum chassis as the previous MacBook Pro, the new 14-inch MacBook Pro weighs just three pounds, which is 12 percent lighter than before.
To put the new screen into context, we were also shown a comparison between Apple’s OLED and the OLED of a high-end competitive Windows laptop. The difference was striking, especially in off-axis viewing. At its worst, there were visible rainbow effects on the Windows machine’s screen.
There’s a catch, though. While Apple’s screen can get up to 2,000 nits, it’s normally capped at 1,000 nits. When the laptop’s built-in adaptive brightness sensor thinks you need a boost, the screen’s brightens increases up to 2,000 nits. So the brightness only hits the high end when you’re outside or working under really harsh lighting conditions. The previous-gen MacBook Pros also did this, but to a lesser degree. With this machine, you’re getting 400 more nits of SDR brightness right out of the box, with the ability to crank it up to twice as much.
Glare is another issue with conventional, low-brightness OLED laptops that the MacBook Pro improves. When deeper blacks are rendered on the screen, it often results in harsher reflections. Sometimes it can get so bad, it feels like you’re looking into a mirror. The brightness alone on the MacBook Pro goes a long way toward overpowering glare and reflections, but Apple is also using what it claims is a “state-of-the-art” anti-reflective coating. Almost every laptop screen uses some kind antireflective coating, so one can hope that Apple’s “state-of-the-art” coating is at least on par with those, but I can attest that this is the very best I’ve seen.
The ultimate solution to cutting glare and reflections is still the option for a nano-texture display, where the anti-reflective pattern is actually etched into the screen itself rather than layered on top. That’s available as an upgrade on both the 14-inch and 16-inch models.
Reach Out and Touch It
The other major innovation happening with the MacBook Pro’s screen is the introduction of touch. Like OLED itself, this is a feature we’ve seen on many other laptops for well over a decade. I came in hoping Apple would swing for the fences here, but its use of touch interaction feels much more modest. (Let us quickly forget the failure of the Touch Bar from 2016.)
The implementation itself is impressive. Interacting with elements on the screen feels every bit as fluid as it does on an iPad. The screen also supports many of the familiar trackpad gestures, such as pinch to zoom or a three-fingered swipe to switch Spaces.
The most natural feeling touch optimizations have been lifted directly from iPadOS. If you tap in the top left windows controls, they zoom in to let you select more precisely. You can even grab a window and flick it to the side to quickly get into Split View. My favorite optimization is the ability to tap, hold, and slide down to select an item within the Menu Bar. Very clever. And yet, I was still hoping for a stronger commitment on the software side. You can’t use an Apple Pencil on this screen, and nothing in the hardware of the MacBook Pro has been adjusted to make touching the screen feel any more ergonomic.
The bigger issue is with third-party apps though. While touch-to-click will work on all apps automatically, it’s up to developers to do any more than that. Even the third-party apps we were shown during demos had varying degrees of touch optimization.
The 3D modeling application ZBrush was a good example. While certain aspects were touch-enabled, none of the controls or menus had the useful optimizations that Apple’s first-party apps had. Hopefully this touch option will become more widely adopted, but I can foresee a future in which these fingers-first interactions are mostly forgotten outside of occasionally scrolling down a webpage with your thumb. And let me be clear: All of this is more than what Microsoft has ever done to optimize Windows 11 for touch. (And Microsoft even has Windows 2-in-1 tablets to support!)
With the 2026 MacBook Pro, Apple is doubling down on what’s working well for it: Leading the way in high-end hardware. There’s plenty more testing to do on the MacBook Pro in the coming weeks, but this OLED screen already looks like the one the entire industry will be chasing for years to come.

NEW DELHI: Arab parties emerge as kingmakers in Israel's next government after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc fell short of a parliamentary majority, with their combined 19 seats potentially offering the opposition a path to power.
However, disagreements within the opposition and uncertainty over cooperation with Arab factions could complicate efforts to form an alternative government.
-
Israel's final election results confirmed that Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc secured 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while the four main opposition parties won 48. The remaining 19 seats went to Arab factions, leaving all sides short of the 61 seats required for a majority.
Israel Election Results 2026 Live Updates
Likud emerged as the largest party with 27 seats, while opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar secured 21. The Joint List won 11 seats and Mansour Abbas's Ra'am secured eight, taking the combined strength of the Arab parties to 19.
The results have put Arab parties at the centre of coalition negotiations, with their support potentially determining whether Netanyahu retains power or the opposition manages to form an alternative government.
What are Arab parties likely to do?
The two Arab political groupings have different approaches to participating in the next government, making their support far from guaranteed.
Ra'am, led by Mansour Abbas, has previously participated in a governing coalition. The party joined the Bennett-Lapid government in 2021 and is seen as a potential partner in another arrangement that could keep Netanyahu out of power.
Also read-Israel election results: Netanyahu's bloc wins 53 seats, falls short of majority as coalition talks loom
The Joint List, comprising Hadash, Ta'al and Balad, has indicated that it could support an alternative government from outside the coalition rather than necessarily joining it. Its support could help an opposition-led minority government survive parliamentary votes.
-
However, Abbas has expressed doubts about the possibility of forming a minority government under Eisenkot with outside support from Arab parties. According to Channel 12 News, as cited by The Times of Israel, he told party members that such an arrangement was unlikely or impossible.
Opposition divided over partnership with Arab parties
The opposition's ability to secure Arab support is also complicated by differences among its own leaders.
Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Lieberman, whose party won seven seats, has reportedly opposed both joining a government with Arab parties and supporting a minority administration dependent on their backing.
Meanwhile, Yair Golan, chairman of The Democrats, has supported cooperation with Arab parties to form a government without Netanyahu. He met Ra'am chief Mansour Abbas on Thursday to discuss a possible political partnership.
Eisenkot also met B'Yachad chairman Naftali Bennett and Golan as opposition leaders began exploring possible coalition arrangements.
The political uncertainty has also prompted demonstrations outside Eisenkot's residence in Herzliya. Protesters urged him to cooperate with Arab parties to prevent Netanyahu from returning to power, chanting, "There is no change without partnership."
Amir Badran, deputy mayor of Tel Aviv-Jaffa, was among those attending the demonstration and expressed support for a partnership between the opposition and Arab parties.
What are Netanyahu's options?
Despite falling short of a majority, Netanyahu remains in contention to form the next government. His Likud is the largest party in the Knesset, and his bloc has 53 seats, leaving it eight short of the majority mark.
Netanyahu and finance minister Bezalel Smotrich, who leads Religious Zionism, have reportedly met to coordinate their efforts following the election.
The opposition could also explore a broader unity government involving Likud, Yashar, Bennett's B'Yachad and Lieberman's Yisrael Beytenu. Together, these parties could command 66 seats, although such an arrangement appears difficult given the opposition's campaign pledge to remove Netanyahu from power.
The final results will be submitted to President Isaac Herzog on November 4. He is expected to consult political parties before assigning a candidate the mandate to form a government. The newly elected Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on November 10.
If the government formation process fails within the stipulated timeframe, Israel could face another election.

Scientists are on the verge of confirming the discovery of another member of the solar system, a potential dwarf planet. Astronomers at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile located the object, provisionally named 2026 ED138.
The prospective planet measures somewhere between 600 and 1,500 kilometers in diameter and is located about 46 astronomical units from the sun (an astronomical unit being Earth’s approximate distance from the sun). For comparison, Pluto—which is also now considered a dwarf planet—orbits at an average distance of 40 astronomical units. Based on its location, ED138 belongs to the population of trans-Neptunian objects. According to its discoverers, it could be one of the brightest known objects of this type and also among the largest.
The difference between a planet and a dwarf planet is largely their environment. While both orbit the sun and have sufficient gravity to assume a nearly spherical shape, a planet has cleared its orbit of other bodies of comparable size. Dwarf planets, on the other hand, coexist with other objects in the region of the solar system they traverse. This is the main reason why Pluto ceased to be considered a planet in 2006 and was reclassified as a dwarf planet.
Matthew Holman, a researcher at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics and a member of the observatory’s operations team, identified the object on October 13 while analyzing data collected by Rubin in 2026. A more thorough search allowed the team to locate additional observations in archived records dating back to 2016. Thanks to this set of images, the team was able to reconstruct more than a decade of the object’s trajectory.
Astronomers explain that ED138 had managed to “hide” from us because its position in the night sky is against the disk of the Milky Way, which we usually see as a thick band of millions of stars. This concentrated brightness makes it difficult to distinguish fainter objects, but the Rubin Observatory’s enormous amounts of data made it possible to identify the object amid that sea of light.
Though ED138 appears to have the right characteristics, astronomers have yet to confirm whether it is a dwarf planet. For now, astronomers know it is a trans-Neptunian object, but they need to determine its size more precisely to establish whether its own gravity is sufficient to give it a nearly spherical shape. If it meets the requirements, ED138 would join the group of five dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, and Eris.
It is also not the only celestial body awaiting possible classification as a dwarf planet. Astronomers have identified dozens of objects in the outer solar system that, based on their size and other characteristics, could meet the criteria. Among the best-known candidates are Gonggong, Quaoar, Sedna, and Orcus. Experts acknowledge that the list could be even longer.
Confirming them as dwarf planets is no easy task. The enormous distance at which they lie makes it difficult to directly measure their size and mass and, above all, to determine whether their own gravity has given them a nearly spherical shape. To obtain high-resolution images of Pluto, for example, the New Horizons probe had to be sent to its vicinity—a journey that took nearly nine and a half years from its launch in 2006 to its flyby in 2015. Three years later, it reached the object Arrokoth, a small planetesimal even farther away.
The solar system is often depicted as a star surrounded by eight planets, but in reality it is a much more extensive and populous structure. In addition to planets and moons, it contains dwarf planets, asteroids, comets, and a vast number of small bodies that extend far beyond Neptune. The Kuiper Belt extends to approximately 50 astronomical units, while the scattered disk reaches nearly 1,000. Much farther out lies the Oort Cloud, a region we have never directly observed and that could extend up to about 100,000 astronomical units from the sun.

'I cannot teach you integrity': How employee theft is hurting small businesses in Africa
- Published
When popular Kenyan food creator That Girl Boina took a two-week holiday to Europe, she expected to relax. A week into the trip, an Instagram direct message exposed a problem that would ultimately lead to the closure of her business.
"I was at your studio, I liked everything. The only problem was that I was asked to send money to a different number. It wasn't the number on the wall," a customer wrote to her.
Boina had opened Waxaholic Studio, a waxing and hydrafacial parlour in Nairobi's central business district, on 1 September 2024. A year later, she had hired a receptionist and two specialists and felt confident enough to take a two-week holiday, her first international trip of the year.
"I trusted them. It's two rooms and a reception - how do you mess that up?" she recalls thinking.
"It never occurred to me that maybe I was getting clients and someone else was stealing from me," she tells the BBC.
The discovery prompted Boina to examine the business more closely. Although the business had made a profit in the first few months, revenue began to fall in early 2025. She initially dismissed the decline as a seasonal slump but then realised there was a problem.
"Everyone around was making money apart from me," she says in hindsight.
She had already considered closing because it was not making a profit, but her initial investment, three employees depending on the business and her vision for it kept her going. The customer's message became the turning-point.
"If I am not making money and I am willing to wait and see where this goes and you guys are not giving me the same energy, then why are we still open?"
Rather than confront the employees, Boina decided to close the studio. That weekend, she put it up for sale but found no buyer. She sold some of the equipment and took others, including decorations, home. Waxaholic Studio closed in October 2025.
"I remember my friend taking me to a restaurant, and I started crying. We were both silent."
"What else would we do?"
Boina describes the experience as the worst feeling she has ever felt. The closure was not just a financial setback, but the loss of something she had built to secure her future.
In September, nearly a year after the business closed, Boina shared a video on TikTok recounting the experience, explaining that she had needed time to heal before speaking publicly about what happened.
The video went viral after being reposted on X, formerly Twitter, garnering close to one million views. It drew responses from many Kenyan business owners who described how theft, ranging from payment diversion to stock theft and the sale of expensive equipment, had pushed their businesses to the brink, forcing them to fire staff, sell their businesses or shut down.
"Although I have recovered emotionally, I am yet to recoup the money I invested in setting up and running the studio," says Boina.
The reaction to her story showed that employee theft is a huge problem for many small businesses owners in Africa, where a handful of employees may control payments, stock and supplier transactions, often with limited oversight.
A 2022 survey by PwC, one of the world's biggest consultancy firms, found that 63% of respondents in East Africa said their organisations had experienced economic crime, compared to a global figure of 46%.
The risks are not confined to small businesses. Some of East Africa's biggest supermarkets have also reported significant losses linked to employee fraud and stock theft. Tuskys and Nakumatt have both collapsed this decade amid wider financial and operational problems partly attributed to employee theft.
At its peak, Tuskys had more than 6,000 employees and over 60 branches across Kenya and Uganda. In 2015, the retailer hired loss-prevention firm Hipora Business Solutions East Africa to help tackle fraud. An audit found that Tuskys was losing more than 100m Kenya shillings (£581,000; $770,000) a month to employee theft, Business Daily reported. The alleged schemes included cashiers pocketing money, manipulating till transactions, and colluding with suppliers over goods received.
Nakumatt also suffered significant stock losses attributed to employee theft before going under, with a Kenyan policy firm reporting that more than $100m (£75m) worth of stock was unaccounted for.
Hipora, which works with businesses across East and Southern Africa, says employee theft is a huge problem, estimating that it accounts for more than 60% of losses recorded by small businesses.
Employee theft has evolved over the years, Hipora boss John Wanjohi tells the BBC. "Employees are like a cartel that colludes with clients and suppliers to perpetuate theft."
Employee theft does not always involve money being diverted to an employee's phone. It can sometimes take subtle forms, making it harder for business owners to detect.
For Cris Njoki, founder of IKOJN, a Kenyan ready-to-wear clothes brand, the problem lay further up the supply chain.
"I found out that one of my staff was asking our suppliers to quote higher for some of the raw materials we were getting from them," she says.
The employee allegedly colluded with a supplier to inflate prices, with the two sharing the excess money after the company paid the invoices. Njoki investigated the scheme and confronted the employee with the evidence. The employee subsequently left the company.
Since then, Njoki has tightened her firm's procurement controls.
"We have now centralised the procurement process and created a paper trail. Finance speaks to the supplier and then makes payment," she tells the BBC.
Across the continent in Accra, Ghana, employee theft came close to bringing Muftawu Nabila's business to an end.
The Joy News sports journalist says he was robbed by two different employees in the four years he has run his electronics shop. But theft by a third employee, he says, nearly forced him to close it altogether.
His first employee was let off with a warning. The second tripled monthly sales but left when her university semester resumed.
Before traveling to the United States to cover the Fifa World Cup in June 2026, Nabila hired a third attendant, leaving the business with little supervision.
"She almost collapsed my shop," he says.
While other employees had taken smaller amounts, sometimes as little as 50 cedis ($4; £3) at a time, the third attendant was operating on a larger scale, he says.
"Assuming we are making a sale of $200 (£150) a day, she could take up to $30," he says.
The theft continued for two months. When Nabila tried to restock the shop, he realised the money coming in was not enough to replenish his shelves. He began counting his stock every morning.
When he confronted the employee, she denied the allegations. But a stock count she conducted herself revealed a significant gap between inventory and sales receipts.
"I just told her: 'If you go home today, don't come back,'" he says.
His salary from his journalism job allowed him to rebuild the business.
For him, the shop is a way of creating jobs, making the theft particularly frustrating.
"We have to generate the money from the shop for me to pay you. So if I pay you, pay electricity bills, shop rent and you steal some, where am I expected to generate money?"
Theft happens in businesses around the world, but its consequences can be particularly severe for small businesses in Africa.
Many operate on tight margins, with limited access to finance, high borrowing costs and unpredictable tax environments.
Purchasing power is also lower in many African markets, limiting how much businesses can recover through sales or pass on to customers.
This is especially significant in a continent where the informal economy accounts for a large share of employment and economic activity.
For businesses without much of a financial cushion, the loss of cash, stock or equipment can threaten their ability to pay staff, restock or keep operating.
What might be a manageable loss for a larger company can push a small business to the wall.
Wanjohi says many small businesses lack proper safeguards to prevent theft.
At one struggling pharmacy branch, his team tightened controls over cash handling, stock movements, and cashier operations. Wanjohi says daily sales subsequently increased from 80,000 Kenya shillings to 200,000 after the changes.
Wanjohi says many businesses seek help from loss-control specialists only after the problem has become serious.
Detecting suspected theft, however, is only part of the challenge. Employers must also follow the law when investigating allegations and deciding whether to dismiss an employee.
Judith Guserwa, an advocate, says employers must investigate suspected theft, gather evidence and allow employees to respond before taking disciplinary action.
If employees admit to theft and choose to repay, let it be in writing: "If they don't, you terminate with a valid reason and press charges," she says.
The experience has changed how Boina approaches hiring.
She says she will now be slow to hire and quick to fire.
"I cannot teach you integrity," she concludes.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

There’s a new Reencle composter in town, and of all the features I thought I might miss from the trailblazing original Reencle Prime, I didn't think it would be the auto-close lid.
The overly sensitive opening sensor annoyed me at first, but I ended up not giving the Prime’s lid another thought during my nearly 1.5 years of use. In hindsight, this is a testament to its convenience. It even has a setting for it to auto-open. Walk over to the receptacle, it opens; dump your scraps in, it closes. Buttons and lids remain clean and untouched by dirty, slimy hands.
Reencle’s brand-new, lower-cost unit, the Essential, is pretty much the same as the Prime (which is still available), with a few small tweaks—updated looks, a larger shovel, and a lid you have to manually close and a button you have to press to open. The button and lid already dirty after only three weeks, but my family consistently forgets to push the lid closed, having grown used to the auto-close lids of both our trash can and our old Prime. At least a few days a week, I will be caught off guard by a constant beeping—the Essential letting us know its lid is still open.
Aside from that, the Essential delivers the same user-friendly, close-to-compost-producing experience as its older sibling, but for $150 less.
Compost in Progress
You may have heard of kitchen composters before, whether the Lomi, FoodCycler, or the original Reencle Prime. It’s a compelling fantasy: Food scraps go in the bin, and out comes ready-to-use compost.
Unfortunately, for all of these machines, it’s just that: a fantasy. Many of them (like Lomi and FoodCycler) simply grind and dry the scraps to create a material that looks kind of like dirt. Sure, it’s odorless and shelf-stable, but if you want to use it in your garden, you’ll need to mix it into potting soil at a very low ratio—like 1:10, or even 1:20 if you’re processing a lot of meat and dairy.
Reencle, meanwhile, actually uses thermophilic bacteria (including Bacillus and Actinomycetes) to break down the waste, resulting in a biologically active material that, while not ready-to-use compost, is at least part of the way there. There are a couple of other machines that also do this, and I’ve tried them, but they’re bulkier, pricier, and louder than Reencle—don’t discount the noise-polluting effects of an audible fan running 24/7, especially if you live in a small space. (Reencle’s large-capacity Gravity model was—and remains—the only food recycler/composter I’ve ever tested that was truly silent at all times.)

All Phantom Blade Zero ‘The Gold-Masked One’ Locations

Some of the health harms of climate change grew faster in the decade since the Paris Agreement entered into force (2016-2025) than in the previous decade (2006-2015) as climate action fails to keep pace, according to the 10th Lancet Countdown Report on Health and Climate Change.
The report, which was released on Wednesday, said the annual average heat-related deaths rose by nearly 36% globally after the Paris Agreement was introduced.
"In 2023 alone, heat was linked to a record 710,000 deaths with more than 70 per cent of that toll attributable to human-caused climate change," it said.
The analysis represents the work of 146 multidisciplinary researchers from more than 100 institutions across more than 30 countries. It tracks 54 indicators of the health impacts of climate change and the health effects of climate action.
The report highlights that cleaner energy, more resilient health systems, more health-protecting legislation and growing scientific evidence have brought real health benefits to local communities since the Paris Agreement, but these gains are still too slow, too insufficient, and too inconsistent to offset the growing risks.
"Rising overall energy demand and slow system change means fossil fuels still supply over 80% of the world's energy, and climate-heating emissions reached a record high in 2024," it said.
The report added that despite gains in some countries, fossil-fuel air pollution still kills an estimated 2.8 million people a year worldwide.
Moreover, adaptation funding is falling far short of what's needed.
According to the report, the health adaptation needs quantified so far by developing countries put the minimum cost at $3.3 billion a year, based on data from only 48 of the 79 countries that have completed these estimates.
However, only around a third of this declared need, $1.1 billion, was committed in 2024.
"This substantial financing gap is reflected in countries' ability to translate adaptation priorities into action, with finance and human resourcing identified as the top barriers to implementation of Health National Adaptation Plans," said the report.

Carney says Canada is working to become an 'associate member' as he hosts EU leaders in Montreal
Some members of the bloc object to the title, while promoting deeper ties with Canada
Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada is working to become an "associate member" as he hosts European Union leaders in Montreal, although it remains unclear what that would look like and how viable the pitch really is.
"We share a common mission. We're in the process of forging a new alliance — alliance for the future — with Canada as an associate member," Carney said ahead of a roundtable with Canadian and European business leaders on Thursday afternoon, wading into an ongoing back and forth about how to describe the new partnership both sides are seeking.
Carney has, until Thursday, largely stayed away from using the associate member title, instead arguing the nomenclature doesn't matter.
CBC News has requested clarity from his office about his associate member comment.
Making Canada the first associate member of the EU is something European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen first championed last month, but the move faces some objection within the 27-member bloc. The status currently does not exist.
Von der Leyen renewed her calls to carve out a special place for Canada within the union during a keynote speech hours earlier in Montreal, where she told a crowd she wants a partnership with Canada "that comes closer to membership than anything we've done before."
Von der Leyen and other European Union delegates are in Montreal for a two-day summit aimed at forging a new phase in the Canada-EU relationship, as they both seek to lessen dependence on the United States under an unpredictable and protectionist President Donald Trump.
"In a world of growing rivalries, sovereignty and independence are no longer just the freedom to act alone — it is the capacity to act together. And this is why we will build an alliance for the future," she said.
"And we start with Canada."
What to call that alliance has overshadowed the gathering and caused confusion.
The day before von der Leyen's speech, it was revealed the words "associate membership" were removed from the draft of a joint statement expected to be published on Friday and replaced with a commitment to an "ever closer association," as objections within the bloc persist.
- Why none of the EU's existing partnerships are the right fit for Canada
- EU dropping associate membership title for its closer alliance with Canada
However, von der Leyen marched on with her vision in her Thursday speech.
"It is an association without accession," she said.
The leader said becoming an associate member would see a close alignment on policies, including AI, climate, energy, security and governance.
"It means more work shared by the European Commission and the Canadian government," von der Leyen said, suggesting that could mean "parliament to parliament" and "court to court" co-operation.
As European Commission president, von der Leyen can advocate for policies but it's up to the bloc to decide what happens next.
Sources speaking to CBC News said Germany in particular opposes the "associate member" term, calling it a red line.
Earlier in the day, Carney said the name of the alliance "doesn't matter."
"This new alliance is not a marketing exercise," he told reporters during a news conference.
"What matters to Canadians ultimately from this new alliance is going to be affordability, it's going to be opportunity. Opportunity for young Canadians, to live, travel, study. Opportunities for our researchers to plug into one of the most advanced research networks across a wide range of domains."
Former ambo calls debate a 'distraction'
David Plunkett, the former Canadian ambassador to the European Union, said the title is a tricky issue for the Europeans — pointing to their relations with other countries who also want to join.
"Since this thing first came up, I have thought it was an unnecessary distraction to spend a lot of time on this empty label," Plunkett said.
"I think it's far more important that the two sides continue to work on developing the broadest and deepest package of substance that they can get and at the end, once they've got everything put together, they figure out what they want to call it."
Trump has threatened retaliation
Talk of making Canada an associate member has irked Trump, who previously said if he interpreted the move as a "hostile act," he might stop trading with Europe "on many things."
It raises the question of whether the president will look unkindly at this week's gathering in Montreal.
Asked Wednesday about the possibility of retaliation from Trump, a senior Canadian government official, speaking on background, told reporters the summit isn't directed against anyone but reflected deep interests between Canada and the EU.
Carney government invests $1.6B in AI company
Over the course of the summit, the two sides are expected to continue talks on deepening trade, investment and security partnerships.
In their Thursday speeches both von der Leyen and Carney stressed the importance of collaborating on artificial intelligence. On the sidelines of the summit, the prime minister announced plans to invest up to $1.6 billion in Cohere, the Toronto-based company specializing in generative AI.
"We're not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don't know or by whom we don't trust," said Carney.
The version of the EU-Canada statement seen by CBC News also commits to reinforcing "a predictable trade environment," deepening collaboration in the Arctic, countering foreign information manipulation and interference and continued support for Ukraine.
Both sides are also promising to launch negotiations toward deeper participation in Erasmus, the European Union's student and youth exchange program.
A source speaking to CBC News on the condition they not be named says this statement is now finalized by EU member countries, but Canada could still ask for changes before the summit wraps on Friday.
Canada's Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre called the summit a "grand theatrical meeting to sign a bunch of meaningless declarations filled with big words."
"No one's mortgage or grocery bill will come down," he posted on social media.
"Get EU countries to let our beef into the continent and cancel their planned carbon tariff on Canada. Otherwise stop wasting your time and our money. Both are running out."

Sony has a collection of colorful, translucent cosmetics for its PlayStation consoles and controllers. Announced Wednesday, the Prism collection brings three new, gorgeous color options that conjure a nostalgic, transparent tech feel.
They come in Flare Orange, Emerald Green, and Graphite Gray. (Based on the pictures, the gray looks more like a blue to me.) You can get Sony’s DualSense PlayStation 5 controllers in the Prism design or opt for PS5 console covers. On the controllers, translucent plastic wraps around almost the entire device’s frame, letting you view the components inside. On the console cover version, the transparency is more limited—you can see only the fan and a few other components.
The Prism Collection DualSense wireless controllers cost $85, while the console covers cost $75. Preorders start on November 10, but the collection won’t ship until February 4. Those are roughly the same prices as existing controllers and covers, though on the higher end. Basic color controllers start at $74 on the PlayStation website. Covers start around $59. The more colorful options on both products go up from there.
Apple’s original iMac largely popularized translucent, colorful tech that lets you see inside the machine. The look was en vogue for a while in seminal devices like the PlayStation 2 and Nintendo’s Game Boy Color.
That see-through aesthetic was a signature in the early 2000s. (My first CD player had a translucent top, and you could see the disc spinning around the whole time.) Twenty-some years later, it’s being revived as nostalgia bait in a transparent tech renaissance. You can find the transparent look in everything from gaming handhelds to a Theragun. Sony also has a transparent pair of earbuds.
Reminiscing about the good ol’ days might also remind you that Sony’s old consoles used to have disc drives. In July, Sony made a controversial decision to end production of physical game discs starting in 2028. Ownership advocates have decried the choice, noting that Sony’s own terms of service state that buying a digital copy of a game does not mean the customer owns it. It’s yet another move toward the end of physical media.
Still, the Prism collection sure looks pretty.

The Fitbit Edge is a $179.99 fitness tracker with a 1.34-inch AMOLED display, built-in GPS, ECG, replaceable battery, and up to seven days of battery life. It also offers Google Maps navigation, Gemini-powered coaching, advanced health tracking, and a special Stephen Curry edition.
The fitness world may be in a “to screen or not to screen” state, with fitness bands without screens gaining popularity, but Google is clearly keeping its Fitbit feet in both screen and screenless fitness trackers. Days after launching its Fitbit Air screenless tracker in India, the Search giant has launched the Fitbit Edge, a fitness tracker with a display that sits right in the middle of the Fitbit Air and the Pixel Watch 5, both in terms of pricing (it starts at USD 179.99, well above the USD 99.99 of the Fitbit Air but well below the USD 399.99 of the Pixel Watch 5) and display size. Only time will tell whether it will hit the golden middle ground between “lots of display” and “no display at all,” but while we wait for the Fitbit Edge to hit stores later this month (and indeed, hopefully arrive in India soon), here are twelve points worth noting about the latest Fitbit in fitness town:
Table of Contents
A big display in an increasingly no-display zone
In a fitness band world that seems to be aiming to become more and more screen-less, the Fitbit Edge comes with a big-gish display for a fitness tracker. It has a 1.34-inch AMOLED, always-on display, which is 46 percent bigger than the one on the Charge 6, its predecessor. It is also much brighter and has Gorilla Glass 3 protection. Fitbit actually claims it is the brightest and biggest display on a Fitbit fitness tracker. Should the Fitbit Air be jealous?
Wear it without Wear OS: Fitbit OS onboard
It comes from Google and also has a display on board like the Pixel Watch 5, which has led many to assume that the Fitbit Edge must be running on Wear OS, but that is not the case. The Fitbit Edge actually runs on Fitbit OS. And like all Google fitness devices, it also uses the Google Health app to keep track of your data and give you fitness inputs. While this means you get relatively less distraction and only basic notifications, it also means you do not get access to third-party apps on the device.
Bye bye Haptic, Hello real button!
One of the biggest headaches of the Fitbit Charge 6 was its pressure-sensitive, haptic touch button, which many of us struggled to use (it almost had a vibe of its own). Thankfully, the Fitbit Edge fixes that and brings a physical button on the side for controls. We couldn’t be more glad. The haptic control on the Charge 6 was a bit of a pain and messed up what was (and still is) a superb fitness tracker.
A battery that can be removed and replaced
Most modern devices have given up on the concept of a removable battery, which was sad because once the battery of a device died, it tended to render an otherwise perfectly good device useless, unless one went in for complex engineering. That, however, has been changing thanks to regulations from the EU, and the Fitbit Edge comes with a removable battery. Which means you can simply remove the battery and replace it if its health deteriorates, increasing the life of the fitness tracker.
Very Air-y battery life
In terms of battery life, the Fitbit Edge rather surprisingly has the same battery life as the display-less Fitbit Air – about a week. However, keeping the always-on-display feature on reduces this to a rather low two days.
Metal frames that can take an ECG…and save your life (in select countries)
The Fitbit Edge’s metal frame can be used to take a 30-second manual ECG. This can highlight heart rate irregularities and can also spot signs of AFib. The tracker also has an optical PPG heart rate sensor that continuously tracks one’s heart and pulse rate and alerts the user if their heart rate is unusually high or low. The catch is that the ECG is only available in select countries, but it is still great to see an ECG on a fitness tracker – a feature seen generally in premium smartwatches.
Take it swimming
Much like its screen-less sibling, the Fitbit Air, the Fitbit Edge too is pretty sturdy. The device comes with 5 ATM water resistance, which means you can easily take it along for your swim sessions. The device also features IP68 dust and water resistance, and as we mentioned earlier, Gorilla Glass 3 protection.
Comes with GPS and is stair-worthy
The Fitbit Edge has an improved and built-in GPS, something the Air lacks, so you do not need to carry your phone along to cover outdoor workouts and activities. It has multi-constellation support, which is paired with a new antenna and chip, making the device up to 40 percent better at tracking locations than the Charge 6. The Edge has another edge over the Air – an integrated altimeter, which can detect changes in altitude, and comes in handy not only while counting stairs but also during hikes and trekking, where you can accurately measure altitude change.
Get Google Maps directions on your wrist:
The Fitbit Edge might not have Google Wear, but it works in sync with Google Maps on your phone and can show you turn-by-turn directions on your wrist. The feature requires you to have an active Bluetooth connection between your phone and the Fitbit Edge, and directions will start popping up on your tracker screen when you start walking, running, cycling, or even driving. That big display really helps!
Quick Notifications, quicker actions but no call support:
The Edge has a mixed relationship with your smartphone. It is a few steps ahead of the Air in terms of notifications, or some might say behind it in terms of a distraction-free experience. You get basic call, message, and app notifications on the tracker, and also get quick reply and navigation access on it. However, you cannot use it to handle calls because the device does not have a mic or a speaker. You can accept a call from the tracker, but it will be directed to your smartphone.
Google Health Guardian’s on your wrist
Earlier limited to the more expensive Pixel Watches, Google’s Health Guardian is available on the Fitbit Edge. This comes with cardiovascular tracking and alerts, alerts for potential breathing and pulse issues, and tracking of trends in the background to create monthly reports on blood pressure and even insulin resistance. It also unlocks premium features of the Google Health app, like personalized coaching and deeper tracking and analysis.
Gemini present, but cannot be summoned:
The Fitbit Edge comes with personalized Gemini coaching to help you meet your health and fitness goals. But complete access to all of Gemini’s features requires a subscription, and you cannot summon the AI assistant on your tracker – you have to use your phone for it.
And one more thing: There is a Stephen Curry edition:
The Google Fitbit Edge comes with a special edition, designed in collaboration with 4-time NBA champion Stephen Curry. It pairs the regular tracker with a Satin Pyrite aluminum case and also features a custom moisture-wicking, water-repellent, recycled polyester yarn band. Also on board are special basketball watchfaces. Mind you, all that extra goodness will set you back by an additional USD 40 – the Stephen Curry edition starts at USD 219.99.

US sanctions Rwanda's defence ministry over DR Congo conflict
- Published
The United States has imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry over its alleged support for the M23 rebel group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, increasing pressure on Kigali to withdraw its troops and halt support for the rebels.
"Rwanda must halt its support for M23 and withdraw its troops from eastern DRC," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
The sanctions come months after Rwanda and DR Congo signed a US-brokered peace agreement aimed at ending the conflict.
Fighting has continued in eastern DR Congo since early 2025, when M23 seized the cities of Goma and Bukavu. Rwanda denies backing M23.
The US Treasury says Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training.
The M23 has seized mineral-rich areas, including gold-mining sites in South Kivu and Rubaya, a major coltan-producing area in North Kivu. Washington says minerals from rebel-held territory enter Rwanda's supply chains, alleging that Rwanda exports more minerals than it produces.
- Inside the Congolese mine vital to mobile phones, as rebels give BBC rare access 
  - Published13 July 2025
- The evidence that shows Rwanda is backing rebels in DR Congo 
  - Published29 January 2025
The sanctions are intended to reinforce the Washington Accords, signed by the Congolese and Rwandan presidents in December 2025 under US mediation. The deal aimed to end the conflict and expand regional trade and investment, but fighting has continued.
On 24 October, ahead of the sanctions announcement, DR Congo President Félix Tshisekedi urged the international community to increase pressure on Rwanda.
"We must firmly demand that the international community impose concrete sanctions against Rwanda and exert increased pressure, so that we may finally secure a lasting peace in our country," he said.
In a statement to Reuters, DR Congo foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions and urged Rwanda to honour its commitments under the Washington Accords, respect the UN Charter and withdraw its troops from Congolese territory.
"The Washington Accords contain clear commitments regarding Rwanda's security, specifically the neutralization of the DR Congo-sponsored FDLR genocidal militia, which are wholly unmet, and with no accountability," Rwandan government spokesperson Yolande Makolo told the BBC.
The FDLR is a militia linked to perpetrators of Rwanda's 1994 genocide. Kigali considers it a security threat and cites its presence in eastern DR Congo to justify its military posture.
"Rwanda remains ready to fully implement the Washington Accords, concurrently with the willingness of the DRC to fulfill those commitments, and with the mediator holding all parties accountable," she said.
The US also sanctioned Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a popular bank and financial institution serving Rwanda's security services.
Washington alleges it facilitated tens of millions of dollars in transactions for M23 and its political wing, the Congo River Alliance, helped pay for military equipment for Rwandan forces from China and enabled gold to be transported from rebel-controlled areas to Kigali.
The sanctions freeze the designated entities' assets under US jurisdiction and generally prohibit US individuals and businesses from conducting transactions with them, unless authorised or exempt. Violations can result in penalties for US and foreign parties.
The measures follow earlier US sanctions against Rwanda's army and four senior military commanders in March 2026. The US imposed further sanctions on Gasabo gold refinery and three mining companies accused of smuggling conflict minerals in June 2026.
Pressure is also mounting over Rwanda's international sports partnerships. Two US senators have urged the National Basketball Association (NBA) to reconsider its commercial relations with Kigali, questioning whether it aligns with the league's stated commitment to human rights.
In a letter sent to NBA commissioner Adam Silver on 23 October, senators Jeff Merkley and Marsha Blackburn questioned the league's continued partnership with Rwanda amid allegations of human rights abuses.
The NBA has yet to issue a substantive response to the letter.
Rwanda has used sports high-profile sports sponsorship to raise its international profile. Early this month, it secured a 10-year deal to host Formula 1's African Grand Prix in the early 2030s.
The country's sponsorship of Arsenal ended in 2026, while Bayern Munich has also ended its commercial partnership with Visit Rwanda.
The M23 has recently joined a new rebel coalition, known as the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) and led by former Congolese President Joseph Kabila, which wants to oust Tshisekedi's government.

Delhi and the National Capital Region (NCR) saw a cool Friday morning after overnight rain swept across the city, lowering temperatures and bringing a noticeable chill to the air, signalling the early onset of winter. The sudden spell of showers on Thursday prompted a noticeable drop in temperatures across the region, setting the stage for the winter chill to settle over Delhi-NCR. On Thursday, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued a yellow alert for Delhi and its adjoining NCR, forecasting spells of rain and thunderstorms over the region in the next 24 to 48 hours, followed by clear weather heading into early November. According to the Regional Meteorological Centre in New Delhi, widespread weather activity is likely across Delhi, Noida, Ghaziabad, Gurugram and Faridabad. The forecast also predicts generally cloudy skies with one or two spells of light to moderate rainfall, along with thunderstorms and lightning across several parts of the city. It also expects isolated pockets of the region to experience heavy rain during the night. The rain is likely to continue on Friday, with light showers forecast in several areas and isolated moderate rain possible from morning to forenoon. The maximum temperature for Friday is likely to be between 26 and 28 degrees Celsius, while the minimum temperature is expected to be between 16 and 18 degrees Celsius. The weather agency expects minor traffic disruptions on roads today and warns of an increased chance of vehicle accidents and water accumulation in low-lying areas and on roads. It also suggests checking for traffic congestion on your route before leaving for your destination. Follow any traffic advisories issued in this regard. Avoid going to areas that are often prone to waterlogging. Dark clouds hung over Delhi since morning, and the city recorded trace rainfall in the last 24 hours. The maximum temperature at Safdarjung, Delhi's base weather station, settled at 25.4 degrees Celsius, 5.6 degrees below normal. It was the lowest October high since October 8, 2022, when the maximum temperature was 23.4 degrees Celsius. Maximum temperatures ranged from 20.6 degrees Celsius in Haryana's Karnal to 27.4 degrees Celsius in Punjab's Patiala, with Delhi's base weather station, Safdarjung, recording 25.4 degrees Celsius, about 5.6 degrees below normal. Meanwhile, states in central and eastern India face intense precipitation due to the remnant cyclonic circulation, along with isolated extremely heavy rainfall forecast over north Bihar on Friday and parts of Chhattisgarh and Odisha. Additionally, widespread heavy to very heavy downpours are also expected in Jharkhand, Sub-Himalayan West Bengal, Sikkim and East Uttar Pradesh. A low-to-moderate flash flood risk has also been flagged till Friday across several vulnerable watersheds in Chhattisgarh, including Korba, Surguja and Balrampur; Odisha, including Sundargarh, Keonjhar and Sambalpur; Jharkhand, including Palamu and Simdega; Bihar, including East and West Champaran, Rohtas and Bhojpur; and East Uttar Pradesh, including Sonbhadra, Ghazipur and Ballia. A legal motion from the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia also referred to Omar as "llhan Nur Said Elmi."
- Snopes found that the claims lack evidence because they appear to be entirely circumstantial and unsubstantiated. Having possibly similar names does not prove that Omar is related to Leila Nur Said or Ahmed Elmi. Additionally, the claims did not confirm Ahmed Elmi's parentage or his relationship to Leila Nur Said. The claims also ignore Somali naming conventions in which children receive first names tied to their paternal lineage.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have reached out to Omar, the U.S. attorney's office and an individual believed to be Ahmed Elmi, and are waiting for responses.
For years, U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has been the subject of claims that she committed immigration fraud by marrying her brother, which Snopes has determined were unfounded. In October, President Donald Trump's administration reopened an investigation against Omar in which it claimed to have more evidence about her family history and alleged she had committed identity fraud, leading to federal agents raiding her home in Washington, D.C.
Following this development, Snopes readers asked us to once again determine whether Omar married her brother to commit immigration fraud and whether the U.S. government had DNA evidence to substantiate that claim.
The accusations continued to claim that Omar had married her brother, a man named Ahmed Elmi. New reporting from The New York Post claimed Omar's father's name was actually Nur Said Elmi, not Nur Omar Mohamed. According to the Post, a U.K. marriage certificate showed that Omar's ex-husband lived in London with a woman named Leila Nur Said, who was believed to be Omar's sister and whose father's name also also Nur Said Elmi.
A Fox News story, citing anonymous sources, claimed Omar's real name is Ilhan Nur Said Elmi. Motions filed by Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, related to the search warrant also referred to Omar as "Congresswoman Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar."
In an X post, responding to allegations about her name, Omar wrote: "So let's make it crystal clear. My name has always been Ilhan Omar."
A NewsNation report claimed the federal agents went through Omar's garbage in the hopes of obtaining DNA samples during the raid on her house. Omar told MSNOW that she did not believe they had taken DNA samples, nor was she asked to provide any. Without DNA testing Elmi and Omar, there is no definitive proof they are siblings.
In an interview with MSNOW, asked directly whether she was related to Elmi in any way, Omar said, "Not to my knowledge."
We found that this was not evidence enough to support the claim she married her brother or committed immigration fraud. We have reached out to Omar's office for a response to the above allegations, as well as to Pirro's office, and will update this report accordingly.
Below, we break down all the claims about Omar's past marriages, her father's name and her alleged sister:
What is the timeline of Omar's marriages?
As we have reported previously, Omar was married twice before her current marriage to Tim Mynett: to Ahmed Hirsi (who was Ahmed Aden before he gained U.S. citizenship) and to a U.K. citizen, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi — the subject of the above claims.
According to a statement Omar released in 2016, she and Hirsi applied for a marriage license in 2002. The couple married in an Islamic ceremony but never completed the process for a civil marriage, according to Hirsi. By 2008, Hirsi and Omar had separated (per Islamic custom). After that relationship ended, Omar had a civil marriage with Elmi in 2009. When that relationship ended, Elmi moved to England and they divorced per Islamic practice in 2011, but without receiving a legal divorce.
Omar and Hirsi reconciled in 2011 and remarried in an Islamic ceremony, according to her statement. In 2017, Omar formally petitioned for divorce from Elmi, and legally wed Hirsi in 2018. Minnesota court records show Omar and Elmi's marriage was legally dissolved on Dec. 4, 2017. Minnesota court records show Hirsi and Omar legally divorced on Nov. 22, 2019. Hirsi and Omar have three children together, according to court documents.
Who is Omar's father?
Nur Omar Mohamed died in 2020 from COVID-19 complications, according to a report in Sahan Journal, a Minnesotan news organization focusing on immigrant communities. The obituary described him as a prominent Somali military officer during the late-1970s Somalia-Ethiopia war.
The report noted Mohamed was a colonel during the dictatorship of Mohammed Siad Barre, who was removed from power in 1991, after which the country descended into civil war. Mohamed and his family subsequently became refugees.
In a statement announcing his death, Omar referred to her father as Nur Omar Mohamed. However, in a deleted 2013 tweet about Father's Day, Omar referred to her father as "Nur Said." Many jumped on this as evidence that Omar's father could also be the father of her ex-husband Ahmed Nur Said Elmi.
In 2019, after Omar's account deleted the tweet about her father, Omar's spokesperson said (archived):
When people write vile things on posts about people she loves—including posting disturbing doctored images of her father—she takes them down. Nur Said means 'Happy Light' and it's been her dad's nickname since he was a kid. He has a public page with the same name. She isn't deleting it for the disturbing and hateful reasons that are being implied by conspiracy theorists.
According to the Defense Language Institute Foreign Language Center, part of the Defense Department, Somalis have names with three or more components and don't commonly use hereditary surnames. A Somali often receives a personal first name at birth, followed by their father's first name, and then their grandfather's first time. So most children, male or female, share their father's and grandfather's first names. However, many Somalis also have additional names based on their lineages or clans. The institute noted, "Because all three names come from a shared pool of personal names, many Somalis have names that are the same or similar."
Omar's tweet referring to her father as "Nur Said" on its own does not establish that Ahmed Nur Said Elmi was her brother. The names Said, Nur, and Elmi are extremely common among Somali Muslims. Further, according to a 2016 profile of Omar, her paternal grandfather's name was Abukar.
Snopes was unable to find Mohamed's original Facebook account. It is likely the account has been deleted.
Is Omar related to Leila Nur Said?
The New York Post connected Omar's father's Facebook account to Leila Nur Said, saying she frequently left "hearts" on his pictures. Snopes was unable to locate either account and thus cannot independently verify this connection.
The Post's pool of evidence that established these connections is flimsy. A U.K. marriage certificate obtained by the Post for Leila Nur Said lists Nur Said Elmi, a military officer, as her father. Ahmed Elmi is not mentioned on this certificate. The Post reported: "Elmi's parentage is not known, but he lived in London with Leila Nur Said, a Somali woman who is thought to be Omar's sister, who possibly raised him."
Neither the Facebook connection to Omar's father, nor the marriage certificate, can effectively establish Ahmed Elmi's relationship with Leila Nur Said.
Media reports claim Elmi is a doctoral researcher at the University of Bristol. We reached out through an email listed on the university website and will update this post accordingly.
Our previous coverage
As we reported before, Omar showed a reporter from the Minnesota Star Tribune photos of documents from her family's entry into the U.S. after fleeing the civil war. She did not provide the reporter with copies of these papers but showed that they listed her father and showed her as the youngest of seven children. There was no one named Ahmed Nur Said Elmi listed in the documents.
We previously noted that Omar and her siblings all arrived in U.S. with refugee statuses. Omar was a minor when she became a naturalized U.S. citizen. How one sibling could end up with a completely different immigration status from the others remains unexplained by the claims.
According to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services policy, immigrants can apply for permanent residency status (opening the pathway to naturalization) if they are siblings of a U.S. citizen, or if they are married to a citizen. Any sibling of Omar would not have to marry her in order to secure a path to citizenship. If Elmi desperately wanted U.S. citizenship, he would not have immediately returned to England after his split with Omar.
In sum …
There is not enough evidence establishing familial ties between Elmi and Omar. Media reports are relying on similar names to establish connections — disregarding Somali naming conventions in which unrelated people can share common names. Until we know more, we leave this claim unrated.
For further reading, we are have reported on numerous rumors about Omar, including that she allegedly fled to Morocco after the raid on her home and that she changed her birth year in official records.

In 1904, two scientists, Henry Wheeler and Treat Johnson, synthesised a variant of cytosine, one of the building blocks of DNA, in the laboratory.
The variant they synthesised contained a chemical tag called a methyl group (-CH3) attached to cytosine, so they called it 5-methylcytosine. Their motivation for doing so was based on the observation that two other building blocks of DNA and its chemical cousin RNA, called thymine and uracil, differed only by the presence of a methyl group.
So Wheeler and Johnson figured that a methylated version of cytosine might also exist in nature.
In 1925, Johnson, while working with another scientist named Robert Coghill, finally discovered 5-methyl-cytosine in the DNA of the bacterium that causes tuberculosis. Two more decades later, Rollin Hotchkiss found 5-methyl-cytosine in the DNA of cows. Soon, scientists found that it existed in nearly all animals.
However, nobody knew why it existed — or why some of the cytosines in DNA were methylated while others were not.
Genes on and off
That insight came in 1975, when Robin Holliday and John Pugh proposed that the methylation of the cytosine could be a way for the body to use the information stored in DNA.
DNA is segmented into genes, and each gene contains the information necessary to make a particular protein. These proteins perform their specific functions in the cells. Since every cell in the body has two copies — one from each parent — of all human DNA, all cells technically have the blueprint to make a whole organism.
However, cells also have specialised functions. A brain cell will not need the genes for the proteins used to digest food. So Holliday and Pugh suggested that chemical modifications such as the methylation of cytosine could help establish and activate genes that a cell wants while silencing those it does not.
This idea, that cells could use chemical tags on DNA to control which genes were active, has come to be called epigenetics. (The British biologist Conrad Waddington had actually coined the term in 1942 itself.) Soon, scientists found enzymes that could add and remove these chemical tags to and from DNA.
Today, we know that cells use many other chemical tags, not only on DNA itself but also on the proteins around which DNA is wrapped like a vine around a stick.
Together, all these chemical marks help control which genes are switched on or off. Problems in this system can lead to changes in gene activity, which in turn can lead to diseases like cancers.
Functional cure
Now, according to a paper that appeared in Nature Biomedical Engineering on September 21, scientists have used this epigenetic control to treat a hepatitis B infection.
This is a remarkable development because, instead of targeting the virus directly, the work silenced the viral DNA. This is promising because current treatments rarely eliminate the DNA, which allows the virus to rebound. By silencing this residue, the treatment could offer a path to a lasting functional cure for hepatitis B.
The hepatitis B virus mainly infects liver cells. After entering a cell, the virus’s DNA serves as the template to make new viral particles. In many people, the immune system clears the infection, but if it does not, the viral DNA can persist for years or even decades in the host’s liver.
In this time, the virus can remain silent, meaning the viral DNA is still present in the cell but its genes are not active to produce new viruses. This allows the virus to ‘hide’ from the immune system. Then, at a later point, the virus can activate again and produce new virus particles.
And studies have shown that one of the mechanisms by which the virus stays silent is by methylating the cytosines.
Locator and effector
The authors of the new study have reported a new experimental therapy called CRMA-1001, which, they have claimed, can silence the DNA of the hepatitis B virus by selectively adding methylation marks to the viral genome.
The study is innovative because it uses several different technologies to overcome three major challenges. To epigenetically silence viral DNA, scientists first need to be able to target the virus’s DNA without methylating any of the cytosines in the host’s DNA. Then, the silencing mechanism must switch off the virus’s DNA effectively. Finally, all of this should happen without causing any unwanted side-effects to the host.
The study authors solved the first two problems by combining two substances called a ‘locator’ and an ‘effector’. The locator used the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing tool to find and bind to a specific DNA sequence: in this case, that was a sequence within the viral DNA. This allowed the CRISPR system to take the ‘effector’, the methylation machinery, to the correct location. The effector had proteins that could add methyl groups to nearby cytosines in the viral DNA and proteins that help switch off genes.
Finally, the researchers packed the entire system and delivered it on an mRNA platform (similar to the mRNA vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic). This made the system transient: once a cell had read the instructions to make the required proteins, it degraded them, stopping the production of those proteins too.
Novel therapy
The researchers gave mice infected with hepatitis B virus either a single dose of CRMA-1001 or three doses, one month apart, and regularly tested them for six months for the signs of infection. They reported that after one dose, the levels of several hepatitis B virus markers, including the viral DNA and two viral proteins called HBsAg and HBeAg, dropped significantly. When they tested the viral DNA, they found new methyl groups, suggesting that the treatment was working as intended. The effect was even stronger after three doses: six months after the first dose, as many as 90% of the animals had less viral DNA than could be detected.
CRMA-1001 is not a cure in the traditional sense of the word. The hepatitis B virus DNA is still present in the liver cells. Instead, the study demonstrated a functional cure: when the virus is not necessarily eliminated but is kept so thoroughly suppressed that, for all intents and purposes, the patient has no active signs of disease.
In this study, the team followed up with the mice for six months after treatment, and the researchers found sustained suppression of the virus in that period. However, the study did not establish whether the virus could eventually become active again after those six months, since the viral DNA was still present.
Further studies are needed to examine the long-term effects of CRMA-1001, including whether the silencing effect can persist over many years and whether the virus can ever become active again after treatment. An ongoing phase I/II clinical trial includes these among other questions.
If CRMA-1001 is eventually approved as a therapy for the market, it will represent a novel way to tackle a viral infection: where instead of fighting the threat, the cell ignores it.
Arun Panchapakesan is an assistant professor at the Y.R. Gaitonde Centre for AIDS Research and Education, Chennai.
