Bucking the age-old trend of films, both big- and mid-budget, relying heavily on weekend collections, several recent titles with positive word-of-mouth have managed to draw significant audiences through the working week, according to theatre owners and trade experts.
While big films such as Dhurandhar: The Revenge and Border 2 have shown that large-scale cinema can continue to perform exceptionally well on weekdays, mid-budget Hindi films such as Welcome To The Jungle, Bhooth Bangla and Main Vaapas Aaunga have also seen steady weekday footfalls across multiplexes.
Theatre owners say audiences are becoming more selective about what brings them to cinemas. Films that earn their trust can sustain footfalls rather than rely solely on a strong opening. Cinemas, meanwhile, are increasingly treating weekdays as a distinct opportunity rather than simply an extension of the weekend. Weekday pricing, food and beverage (F&B) combos and loyalty offers are being designed to make a Tuesday or Wednesday outing more compelling. Showtimes and screen allocation are also becoming more dynamic, with cinemas responding to actual demand through the week rather than relying only on opening-day performance.
“We are seeing a very encouraging shift in the way audiences are coming to cinemas beyond the Friday-to-Sunday weekend. They are no longer deciding purely on opening-day hype. When a film connects, word-of-mouth takes over and gives it a much longer and healthier theatrical life,” said Sanjeev Kumar Bijli, executive director, PVR INOX Ltd.
“The biggest change is that audiences have become more deliberate about the films they choose. The opening weekend is often driven by star power, marketing and the initial excitement around a release. But the weekday audience is driven much more by whether people genuinely enjoyed the film and what they are hearing from others. That word-of-mouth brings in working professionals and families who may prefer a quieter weekday evening over the weekend rush,” Bijli added.
The company is closely tracking weekday demand and using it to fine-tune screen allocation and show timings, Bijli said. The weekday has become the real test of a film, he added, as it shows whether the initial buzz can translate into genuine audience connection.
The trend has played out across regional cinema as well, with Tamil films Gatta Kusthi: 2nd Round and Idhayam Murali, Punjabi film Carry On Jatta 4 and Malayalam film I, Nobody showing strong weekday holds.
Rohit Dalmia, chairman and managing director of entertainment financing platform CineNow, said Main Vaapas Aaunga actually grew through its first Wednesday and Thursday after a modest opening, while Telugu film Lenin also held strongly during the week. The trend remains title-specific, but good word-of-mouth is giving smaller and regional films longer theatrical runs, he added.
Sameer Munshi, chief operating officer, Miraj Entertainment Ltd, said theatre operators are moving away from a one-size-fits-all weekday strategy towards a more location- and city-specific approach to pricing, programming and showtimes.
“We use local audience behaviour, advance bookings and occupancy data to optimize shows and respond quickly to films showing stronger weekday legs,” Munshi added.
Agreeing that films which open small and then build through the weekdays are no longer the exception, Ashish Misra, head of commercialization, Cinépolis India, said the way films are marketed has also changed. The marketing push no longer stops on the day of release. Production houses now sustain their social media campaigns well beyond opening day, leaning into audience reactions as they come in and allowing that momentum to carry into the second and third week.
Pricing is another lever, according to Misra. The company's Blockbuster Tuesday ticket offering is designed to address this, taking the price question off the table on Tuesdays.
“Weekend ticket prices can be quite high, so many viewers, especially middle-class families and working professionals, prefer a Tuesday or Wednesday show when it is more affordable. People are also more careful about what they spend on now. They often wait for the first reviews and audience reactions before deciding if a film is worth watching in a theatre,” said film producer Anand Pandit.
At the same time, filmmakers are making more genre-specific films for particular audiences instead of trying to please everyone. Such films may start slowly but pick up as the right audience finds them, Pandit added.
“I do think we are seeing signs of greater staying power among certain films, although I wouldn’t call it a uniform trend just yet. What is particularly encouraging is that some of the strongest examples are coming from mid-sized, story-driven films, suggesting that sustained audience interest isn’t necessarily limited to big Hindi or pan-India tentpoles,” said Ashish Saksena, chief operating officer - cinemas, BookMyShow.
The platform is seeing audiences plan theatrical outings around their individual schedules, with working professionals, college students and families increasingly finding weekday slots that work for them, Saksena added. This creates an opportunity for films with strong audience appeal to build steadily across the week, even after the initial marketing-led hype has died down.

'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next
- Published
The Ukrainian city of Kherson has known its first two days of quiet after many years, as a US-brokered temporary ceasefire has allowed residents rare moments of respite from the constant Russian aerial attacks that plague the front line region.
Videos posted on social media showed people strolling down streets covered in anti-drone nets and gathering in the city's squares - ordinary activities that usually mean keeping one eye on the sky and one ear out for incoming drones.
"Ever since the ceasefire was announced, there's been total silence," said Olga, 42, speaking by phone from Kherson. "We are all, of course, overjoyed."
"I don't even know what to call it," she added, her smile coming through in her voice. "It's as if everything has finally come to an end."
Since Tuesday, Kherson has "literally come back to life," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
"People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. What for some is ordinary everyday life, for residents of the Kherson region today is the greatest desire."
The temporary pause in hostilities - due to end on Sunday - is the result of efforts by US First Lady Melania Trump to broker a safe passage out of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which lies on the other side of the Dnipro river from Kherson.
For several days, Russian forces have been working to clear the road of mines, ahead of a planned evacuation of Oleshky's civilians on Friday.
But there are fears that, alongside carrying out the well-publicised "humanitarian operation" – which some American journalists will be invited to witness – the Russians are using the truce to bolster their forces in the area ahead of a renewed onslaught of Kherson from next week.
"They are... using this lull to strengthen their positions, bring in more military supplies, weapons, ammunition, and drones, and carry out some redeployment of their forces," an anonymous source working in local government told the BBC.
Petro Andriushchenko, Director of Ukraine's Center for Studying the Occupation, says Kherson locals have told him that they witnessed a military build-up around Radensk, some 20km (12 miles) from Oleshky.
Its residents will be saved but "we are simultaneously giving the enemy an opportunity to exploit the ceasefire for its own military purposes," he said. Once the ceasefire ends, the situation may be "worse than we saw before, because Russia's units will be stronger. They have enough time to prepare to prolong this action."
Though Kherson residents are clear-eyed about what lies ahead, for a brief period this week the city caught its breath.
No violations have been reported on either side since Tuesday. There have been other ceasefires in the past, but these were generally not respected, Kherson resident Dima said.
"This is the first time the shelling has stopped, people don't quite believe it," he told the BBC. "They are going to the shops, drinking coffee, walking around... The city is alive."
On social media, a woman named Yulia wrote about her unusually uneventful trip to the supermarket with an edge of disbelief. For once, she said, she returned home from the shops "whole and calm, not as usual - scared, sweating from the horror and with a lump in my throat."
This week, dozens of people were also able to access their belongings and homes in the so-called "red zone" of Kherson – an area so exposed to drones and artillery attacks that it has become unlivable.
"Some are venturing into places where nobody has dared to go for years, filming areas where simply being present has meant - and will once again mean - almost certain death," said Denisa Bohackova, a Czech volunteer who lives in Kherson.
Dima described scenes of "girls, boys, parents, grandmothers" walking down the streets of the red zone carrying suitcases and bags, returning to their flats to see what they could retrieve.
Some of those who returned to the red zone found buildings reduced to charred, empty shells; in other cases, homes had been looted. The scale of destruction in some of these places, Bohackova said, is "breathtaking".
Others were rushing back for reasons beyond material concerns. Angela Dobrovolska's husband Serhiy was killed two years ago by a grenade dropped by a piloted Russian drone - an instance of a "human safari" attack of the kind that Kherson has become sadly infamous for.
On Thursday, Angela headed back from Kyiv to Kherson to visit his grave for the first time in months. "They say that all the people have rushed to Kherson," she said. "And I'll be going to the cemetery to my husband."
The population of Kherson has dwindled from over 250,000 to about 65,000 since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which will enter its sixth year in February.
Though civilian life in the city never stopped, Bohackova said, it also carried on under the conditions of an active battlefield, with schools, theatres, kindergartens and hospitals moved underground.
"An ordinary civilian from Kherson has experienced more of this war than many soldiers," Bohackova said.
Olga, who is raising two children, described regular blackouts, mines dropped by drones and concealed by fallen leaves, drone fragments ricocheting, and a city that typically shuts by the afternoon.
But since silence fell on the city, Olga has been able to live a normal life. She drove to a different town and took the bus to another district to visit her grandmother with her son. Around her, the shops were full, as were the cafes. After years of quiet streets, "there was even a small traffic jam," she smiled.
But the clock is ticking.
The evacuation of nearby Oleshky is due to be completed by Sunday, after which the ceasefire will be over. "The concern is that, starting Monday, things could turn truly chaotic," Olga said.
"We know the strikes will resume, and that they will increase," said Dima, as he and his wife prepared to visit their flat in the red zone for the first time in several months.
"These few days showed us how it could be if it all finally ended."

The 56th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu examines early-onset Alzheimer’s disease, concerns about the reliability of cancer research and challenges in accessing treatment for children with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA).
Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu, discuss how Alzheimer’s disease can affect younger people, the implications of unreliable cancer research, and concerns raised by families over a generic SMA drug.
The episode begins with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease and how the condition can present differently in younger people. The discussion looks at changes in memory, behaviour and everyday functioning, and the challenges of recognising the disease when symptoms appear earlier in life.
Another segment examines cancer research articles flagged for suspected links to paper mills. These businesses produce and sell research papers, sometimes using fabricated data, manipulated images or other questionable research practices. The discussion looks at how unreliable publications can undermine scientific progress, affect future research and complicate efforts to assess the evidence behind medical findings. It also highlights the need for careful investigation, as an article being flagged for suspected links to a paper mill does not, by itself, establish research misconduct.
The episode also looks at concerns raised by families of children living with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) in Keralam over a generic drug used to treat the rare genetic condition. The concerns have brought questions about the safety, quality and effectiveness of medicines into focus. The discussion examines the importance of reliable information about treatment, regulatory oversight and the challenges families face in accessing medicines for rare diseases, where treatment costs can be a significant barrier.
The final segment revisits the history of Alzheimer’s disease through the case of Auguste Deter. In 1901, German psychiatrist Alois Alzheimer began documenting the symptoms of Deter, a 51-year-old woman who experienced changes in memory, behaviour and her ability to carry out everyday activities. Her symptoms differed from cases he had typically encountered. After her death in 1906, Alzheimer examined her brain and identified changes that contributed to the understanding of the condition later named after him. The segment explores Deter’s experience and the role of clinical observation and patient documentation in the history of medical research.

India's largest share sale could end cheap mobile internet for millions
- Published
India's biggest telecom giant, the Meta and Google-backed Jio Platforms, is set to make its stock market debut on Wednesday.
Despite a bruising spell for Indian markets, its historic $3.2bn initial public offering (IPO) - the country's largest ever - has drawn overwhelming demand from top global fund managers, domestic institutions and mom-and-pop retail investors.
Bids outstripped the shares on offer within hours of subscriptions opening on 21 October.
Owned by Asia's richest man, Mukesh Ambani, Jio is one of India's most consequential companies, with half a billion people subscribing to its cheap mobile data. But its meteoric rise has also been dogged by controversy.
The company burst onto India's crowded telecom scene in 2016, offering throwaway tariffs that got millions of Indians hooked to the internet.
But its launch led to a huge disruption in the telecom sector. A market once crowded with 17 operators shrunk to an oligopoly of just three, with critics accusing the deep-pocketed company of waging a price war that pushed rivals out of business.
More recently, Elon Musk criticised Ambani, calling him the "real boss of India", suggesting that Jio was trying to thwart Starlink's entry into India. Reliance dismissed the allegations saying it welcomed competition from Musk.
For all the scrutiny it has faced over the last decade, Jio's discounted data plans have been a bedrock of India's digital revolution, spawning a huge digital economy and democratising online payments, food delivery and e-commerce in Asia's third-biggest economy.
Within three years of its launch, customer data usage rose fifty-fold and data prices crashed.
This aggressive discounting helped Jio rapidly amass some 553 million mobile subscribers by 2026. It also cemented its dominance in other segments, capturing 50% of the wireless broadband market and more than 40% of fixed broadband.
Jio also carries 60% of India's wireless data traffic and boasts of the largest 5G subscriber base outside China, according to brokerage Emkay Global, which has described the company as the "digital engine of India".
But analysts say its stock market debut - which will see its promoters dilute their shareholding by about 3% - could mark a turning point in Jio's pricing strategy, potentially bringing an end to years of ultra-cheap tariffs.
"The era of Jio using cheap tariffs as a market-share weapon is drawing to a close," said Nitya Shah, co-founder of KamayaKya Wealth Management.
"A listed Jio must answer to minority shareholders… which structurally reduces its incentive to keep pricing suppressed."
Jio's future growth will no longer be driven primarily by adding subscribers through discounted plans. Instead, it will depend on "earning more per subscriber - through the migration to 5G, successive tariff revisions, and the extension of fixed wireless broadband into homes fibre has never reached", brokerage company Motilal Oswal said in a note.
The listing could also pave the way for Jio's competitors to raise prices, as fears of being undercut by a cheaper rival begin to recede.
"The biggest beneficiary of this shift could be Vodafone Idea," says Shah. "It is a moment the sector's weakest balance sheet gets its strongest tailwind".
For Indian consumers, any further increases would come on the heels of an industry-wide tariff hike a few years ago. Analysts say another round of price rises could trigger a fresh churn in the market as price-sensitive customers switch to the cheapest plans available.
While consumers may have to brace for higher bills, Jio's IPO offers investors a bet on India's seemingly insatiable appetite for data - and the growing ecosystem of digital services the company offers across entertainment, cloud computing, gaming and financial services.
India has emerged as the second-largest consumer of mobile data in the world, driven by lower tariffs and rising penetration of smartphones.
Jio's monthly data use per customer has climbed from 28.7 GB in 2024 to 42.3 GB in 2026 - up by 52% in two years. As per some estimates, usage is expected to surge further to 65GB by the end of this decade as disposable incomes rise.
All of this will give a tailwind for Jio to drive long-term growth in average revenue per user.
"Penetration of most digital services remains well below China and the US, which leaves significant headroom [for growth]," according to Emkay Global.
The listing is also likely to enhance transparency and provide investors with a "clearer market valuation" for the company, according to Moody's rating agency, as Jio is currently part of Reliance Industries, which has businesses spanning oil refining and retail.
But as much as its central and growing role in India's economy has excited investors, the buzz about the IPO also comes from the fact that this is the first share sale from the Reliance conglomerate in over two decades.
The company - which started as a small spice and polyester yarn trading venture in 1958 before expanding into textiles, petrochemicals, refining and eventually to retail, telecom and digital services - is known for its track record of long-term wealth creation, and enjoys legendary status among mom-and-pop investors.
Dhirubhai Ambani, the founder of the Reliance empire, is said to have played a foundational role in popularising equity investing and taking it beyond the preserve of traders and wealthy families in the 1980s and 90s.
In its early years, Reliance built a vast base of individual shareholders by turning its annual general meetings into grand spectacles of big announcements, dividend payouts and celebrations of public share ownership. Over time, this helped forge a fiercely loyal investor base, many of whom developed a deep emotional bond with the company.
And while Reliance Industries' stock has fallen nearly 20% over the past year, its longer-term track record continues to inspire confidence.
"The company has given average annualised returns of around 30% consistently for thirty years," Kranthi Bathini of Mumbai-based WealthMills Securities told the BBC.
"That's why there's anticipation that the same magic can be replicated with the Jio IPO."

Trump approval rating is historically low for a president heading into the midterms
The last time a sitting president faced approval ratings this low heading into a midterm election was Harry Truman in 1946

Republicans are facing a difficult political environment ahead of November’s midterm elections, driven in large part by President Donald Trump’s historically low approval ratings.
With the pivotal elections approaching, Trump’s approval rating dropped to 30 percent earlier this month, according to polling from the Pew Research Center. The slump marks the lowest point of his second term and represents the lowest level any sitting president has reached heading into the midterms since Harry Truman in 1946, as reported by TIME.
“This is historically low approval ratings for a president,” Peter Enns, a professor in the department of government at Cornell University and co-founder of the survey research company Verasight, told TIME.
Data indicates that much of the public discontent with the administration stems from economic performance. An Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll released earlier this month found that only 26 percent of U.S. adults approved of how Trump was tackling the economy, and just 17 percent approved of his handling of the cost of living.
Foreign policy has generated similar pushback. The same AP-NORC poll showed that only 28 percent of respondents expressed support for Trump’s handling of the war in Iran.
“Part of the reason Trump’s approval ratings are so low is he’s pushing policies and pushing positions that are very unpopular, and so the conflict in Iran is a great example; the public understands that this was Trump’s decision, and they understand this connects to extremely high gas prices,” Enns told TIME. “It’s very unusual for a President to position himself on the side of so many unpopular positions.”
These voter priorities could prove decisive at the ballot box. Pew Research data shows that 84 percent of registered voters rank the economy as a “very important issue” heading into the midterms, while 57 percent say foreign policy is “very important” to their vote.
Midterm elections are routinely difficult for the party controlling the White House, as voters frequently express frustration with the sitting administration. This dynamic is a “well-known phenomenon” resulting from dissatisfaction among both opposition voters and a president's supporters who feel policy progress has lagged, Enns told TIME.
“That doesn’t mean everybody’s changing their vote,” Enns said. “It just means the backlash, the tides, are working against the incumbent president.”
Costas Panagopoulos, a professor of political science at Northeastern University, told the magazine that voters often sought “partisan balance in Washington,” particularly when one party held unified control over the executive and legislative branches.
“There’s simply nobody else to blame for government actions and current policies if voters are unhappy with those besides the Republican Party [right now],” Panagopoulos said. “It’s very easy for [voters] to point the finger to the Republicans if they’re not happy with what they’re seeing.”
Though historical precedents usually favor the opposition party, rare exceptions have occurred. Following the September 11 terrorist attacks, President George W. Bush maintained a 63 percent approval rating, allowing Republicans to gain seats in both the House and Senate during the 2002 midterms.
Current polling metrics favor Democrats in voter engagement. A recent PBS News/NPR/Marist poll showed that 91 percent of Democrats expressed enthusiasm about voting in the midterms, compared to 86 percent of Republicans. Democrats have also shown strength in competitive state races, including in Texas, where Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico holds a narrow lead in polls over Republican candidate Ken Paxton.
“I think we can expect Republicans to be facing an uphill battle at the polls,” Panagopoulos said. “We can expect that they will likely lose seats in the House and also the Senate. And the question is, will they lose enough seats to lose the majority in either or both those chambers?”

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Thursday that $2.54 billion worth of crypto assets had been frozen as it investigated a possible security breach. Stablecoin issuers Circle and Tether also froze assets linked to the incident, news agency Reuters reported.
"Binance will cover all 
hacking
 losses," Binance co-founder Yi He said.
The exchange said the amount frozen could increase as it worked with law enforcement agencies, token issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and other industry partners to trace and freeze more assets.
Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao, who no longer runs the company, said in a post on X that the incident "looked like a hack."
Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.
Binance said it was carrying out security checks and would resume withdrawals once the issue was fully resolved. It also assured users that their funds remained safe and said its teams were reviewing the incident. The exchange temporarily suspended trading on its Binance Alpha platform as a precaution.
World Liberty Financial, a cryptocurrency company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it had worked with crypto custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.
Yi He said $27 million in stablecoins and around $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.
Crypto firm Ripple also froze around $200 million in funds, Yi said. Jack McDonald, senior vice president of stablecoins at Ripple, said the company was closely monitoring reports of a possible security breach involving Binance. He added that Ripple was freezing affected funds and coordinating with relevant parties.
Miguel Morel, CEO of blockchain intelligence firm Arkham, said data suggested that billions of dollars may have been stolen from Binance by an unknown attacker. However, the exact cause of the incident had not been confirmed.
Morel said the incident began around 4:30 pm EST and appeared to be ongoing.
The incident adds to a series of cryptocurrency thefts. Attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency in nearly 150 attacks last year, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
In September, cryptocurrency exchange Bitget said around $350 million worth of crypto had been stolen from its platform, highlighting the security risks facing the industry.
Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move money across borders outside the traditional financial system.
Binance allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets. It has more than 300 million registered users globally and around $160 billion in assets under custody, according to the exchange's 2024 annual report.
Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident. Coinbase also said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation.
In a separate incident on Thursday, prediction market operator Polymarket temporarily halted trading following a security issue involving a third-party provider. Trading later resumed, and the company said it would fully reimburse affected traders.

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.
Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.
"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

A federal judge on Thursday rejected the federal government’s new definition of “medical frailty” and ruled that states did not have adequate time or resources to overhaul their eligibility systems, injecting new uncertainty into the imminent rollout of Medicaid work requirements across the country.
Judge Richard D. Stearns of the U.S. District Court of Massachusetts ruled that federal regarding who is considered too sick to work was overly restrictive, and said that the suit from over two dozen states successfully demonstrated that implementation of the Medicaid work requirements, as written, would cause “irreparable harm.”
“Because enforcement of an unlawful definition of ‘medically frail’ may lead to the disenrollment of otherwise eligible vulnerable individuals relying on Medicaid coverage for continuity of care, the States (and public) face potential for great hardship in the absence of an injunction,” Stearns wrote in his order.

A six-year-old boy from Burhanpur in Madhya Pradesh has won a Toyota Fortuner worth around ₹50 lakh in a lucky draw after his grandmother purchased a coupon for just ₹200 at a Garba event.
Medansh Raikwar, a resident of Seelampura, won the first prize in a lucky draw organised at Shri Sarkar Dham in Abhapuri. His grandmother, Kiran Raikwar, had purchased the coupon nearly a year ago and entered her grandson’s name in the draw.
According to the family, Kiran bought the coupon when she attended a Garba event at the venue last year. The family had little idea that the small investment would eventually win them a luxury SUV.
When the lucky draw results were announced in 2026, Medansh’s name was selected for the first prize, leaving his family delighted.
The announcement triggered celebrations in the neighbourhood, with residents gathering to congratulate the young winner.
Medansh received a grand welcome amid the sound of drums as the news of his win spread. The family also performed a puja and offered prayers to seek blessings after receiving the car.
For the family, the prize marks a memorable milestone and brings them closer to fulfilling their long-held dream of owning a car.
The unusual win also generated considerable interest on social media, where users expressed surprise that a ₹200 coupon had secured a vehicle worth around ₹50 lakh. Many congratulated the family on its good fortune.

The Fortuner is available with 2.7-litre petrol and 2.8-litre diesel engine options, paired with manual or automatic transmissions, depending on the variant. Its combination of space, performance and rugged design has made it a prominent offering in India’s premium SUV segment.

For people living with peripheral artery disease (PAD), walking even short distances or doing routine household tasks can become difficult because of leg pain. The condition develops when arteries supplying blood to the legs become narrow, usually because fatty deposits build up along their walls. With less blood reaching the muscles, walking can cause pain, cramps or heaviness that ease with rest. In advanced cases, pain may persist even when a person is sitting or lying down, and poor circulation can lead to wounds that do not heal.
Treatment can be challenging too because movement is an important part of managing PAD, while pain makes it difficult to stay active. Structured exercise, medicines and control of risk factors such as smoking, diabetes and high blood pressure can help manage the condition. When blood flow is severely reduced, procedures may be needed to prevent damage to the feet and legs. PAD can also affect overall cardiovascular health, increasing the risk of heart attack and stroke.
Managing pain
Pain, cramps, heaviness in the calf or thigh that develop during walking and ease with rest are known as intermittent claudication. This happens when narrowed arteries cannot supply enough blood to meet the muscles’ increased needs during activity.
Venu S., consultant vascular surgeon, Prashanth Hospitals, Chennai, says structured walking programmes can help patients gradually increase the distance they can walk. Patients are generally advised to walk until the discomfort becomes moderate, rest until it settles and then resume walking. Sessions commonly last 30 to 45 minutes and take place several times a week, with supervision where possible.
He says patients who follow a structured programme for about three months may be able to walk twice as far, or more, before pain begins. The pace and duration should suit each patient’s ability. Those who find walking difficult may need an adapted exercise programme under medical supervision.
Balaji V., senior consultant, vascular surgery, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai, says quitting smoking, eating a healthy diet, staying physically active and controlling blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol are also important parts of treatment.
Exercise should not mean pushing through severe pain. Pain that does not settle with rest needs medical assessment. Pain in the feet or toes while resting, particularly at night, can indicate a serious reduction in blood flow and requires prompt medical attention.
Diagnosis and treatment
Diagnosis usually begins with a review of symptoms and medical history, followed by an examination of the legs and feet, including checking the pulses. Doctors may measure the ankle-brachial index (ABI), which compares blood pressure at the ankle with that in the arm, to assess blood flow. A Doppler ultrasound scan can help identify narrowed arteries and assess circulation. In patients with severe symptoms or wounds that do not heal, a CT angiogram may be needed to locate the blockage and plan treatment.
Medicines aim to relieve symptoms, slow the progression of arterial disease and reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke. Antiplatelet medicines such as aspirin or clopidogrel help prevent blood clots. Statins lower cholesterol and help stabilise fatty deposits in artery walls. Medicines to control blood pressure and diabetes are also important. Cilostazol can help some patients with walking-related pain walk farther before symptoms begin, but it is not suitable for people with heart failure. Select patients may need additional medicines to reduce cardiovascular and limb-related risks.
Experts say treatment often needs to continue long term, even when symptoms improve. Patients should not stop or change prescribed medicines without consulting their doctor.
Diabetes can damage nerves and reduce sensation in the feet, allowing cuts and wounds to go unnoticed. It can also affect smaller arteries, making some blockages harder to treat. High blood pressure and cholesterol contribute to arterial damage and the build-up of fatty deposits. Kidney disease can cause calcium to build up in artery walls and delay wound healing. Heart disease can occur alongside PAD because both may result from the same underlying process.
During follow-up, doctors assess changes in walking distance and symptoms and may repeat ABI measurements or Doppler scans to check blood flow. Blood tests can help monitor cholesterol, blood sugar and kidney function.
Preventing complications
When symptoms remain disabling despite medicines and exercise, doctors may consider a procedure to widen the narrowed artery. The decision depends on the location and extent of the blockage, the severity of symptoms and the patient’s overall health.
Angioplasty uses a small balloon to widen a narrowed artery. A stent may be placed to help keep it open. Experts say newer techniques can also help treat complex blockages.
Intravascular lithotripsy uses shock waves delivered through a specialised balloon to modify heavy calcium deposits in the artery, making it easier to widen the vessel. Atherectomy devices can remove fatty deposits in selected cases, while thrombectomy devices are used to remove blood clots. The appropriate method depends on the type and location of the blockage.
For extensive disease, bypass surgery creates an alternative route for blood to reach the affected part of the leg. The choice between a procedure performed through a blood vessel and surgery depends on the blockage, the patient’s condition and the likely benefits and risks.
Pain at rest, wounds that do not heal or gangrene can indicate that the leg is at risk and require urgent medical assessment. A wound that has not healed within two weeks, a cold or discoloured foot, or a black patch on a toe or heel should not be ignored. Sudden, severe leg pain accompanied by paleness, coldness, numbness or weakness is a medical emergency because it may indicate a sudden blockage of an artery.
Regular foot checks are particularly important for people with diabetes, who may not feel an injury developing. Recognising worsening symptoms and seeking timely care can help preserve mobility and prevent serious damage to the feet and legs.

The federal government’s anti-semitism envoy has proposed an “external independent ombudsman” to monitor ABC and SBS coverage of the war in Gaza, as well as codes for arts organisations to limit “personal political or ideological activism”.
In an updated plan released on Friday, Jillian Segal said Australia’s two public broadcasters should be subjected to greater oversight.
“Given the extent and seriousness of concerns about subjective, inaccurate and disproportionate reporting in accordance with its own standards, it would be in the public interest for the public broadcasters’ coverage and approach to be the subject of more detailed analysis and independent review,” Segal wrote in the new ASECA Priorities plan.
It suggests a government-appointed panel review the public broadcasters’ previous reporting and states the government should consider “transferring” responsibilities from the ABC and SBS ombudsmen. Those powers would be transferred to an “external independent ombudsman consistent with other sectors such as telecommunications and banking”.
“Many in the Jewish community remain concerned that coverage they perceive as one-directional may contribute to a negative – and even hostile – view by audiences of those who support Israel, or have sympathy for it,” Segal writes.
“Jewish Australians have reported being abused, harassed and accused of being ‘baby killers’ or supporters of ‘genocide’ simply for their belief in the right of Israel to exist.
“That perception of a link between coverage and hostility is itself a matter of public importance.”
Segal said she had received “many expressions of concern from the Australian Jewish community” about ABC and SBS reporting that was perceived to be “disproportionate, misleading or inaccurate on issues relating to Israel and the conflict in the Middle East”.
The special envoy to combat antisemitism’s initial plan, released in mid-2025, said the envoy would “work with the publicly funded broadcasters to encourage them to develop programs that add to social cohesion”.
Segal then told the royal commission into antisemtism in mid-2026 she wanted a new “oversight” committee that could give ABC and SBS coverage a “tick” or “guidance”.
The broadcasters rejected calls for external oversight.
The royal commission was established in response to the Bondi beach massacre in December when 15 people were killed during a Hanukah celebration.
Segal appeared before Senate estimates this week, telling senators she held concerns about “the tone [and] the frequency of reporting about Gaza from the ABC”.
Friday’s report argues publicly funded arts organisations should be able to impose “enforceable conditions” on artists and terminate grants if they promoted antisemitism.
Segal states that all arts organisations – private and public – should develop policies to govern the use of their venues, festivals, and stages “or artists’ personal political or ideological activism outside the scope of the advertised show, performance or exhibition”.
Similarly for universities, the envoy’s updated plan proposes allowing grant authorities to impose enforceable conditions on academics, allowing “for the termination of grant funding … where the recipient engages in antisemitic speech or conduct”.
Segal said the proposals outlined in the plan were “not about silencing criticism of Israel”.
The report argues that “modern ‘progressive’ antisemitism” was the most pervasive form of the prejudice in Australia today.
“It takes the hostility of Islamic extremism and far-left antisemitism, together with traditional antisemitic tropes, and gives it a respectable face through the language of social justice and human rights”.
Segal said Islamic extremism, far-left and far-right antisemitism were still prevalent “and they require vigilance and laws that are properly enforced”.
“But the form that is leaving Jewish Australians increasingly anxious and excluded is the one that has taken root in influential institutions, where Jewish Australians are being discriminated against, blamed and vilified for the actions of the government of the state of Israel.”
The release of the envoy’s updated plan comes two days after Segal appeared at Senate estimates.
She defended evidence she gave to the royal commission into antisemitism, during which she criticised SBS for quoting death toll figures provided by the Gaza Ministry of Health, saying those figures failed to distinguish combatants from civilians, were “grossly inflated” and their inflation was “well known and even accepted by the United Nations”.
A spokesperson for the UN secretary general responded at the time: “For us [the UN] the Ministry of Health in Gaza is a source we, and many others, often cite. Independent validation of subsets of the data has found no significant discrepancies in their numbers.”
Segal told the estimates hearing this week: “I note the United Nations views. I accept the United Nations views because they are the United Nations but that does not detract from the concerns of the Jewish community as conveyed to me about the way in which the reporting had been done.”

It is officially the flu season with winter and monsoon seasons creeping in on large parts of the world. There is a need to take precautions and be aware of the risks of the season, particularly at a time when we are hearing of old viruses resurging, or new, never-before heard pathogens rearing their heads, even known microorganisms that cause disease among humans, after a zoonotic spillover.
As in the case of the Shamonda virus. Last week France reported the first human Shamonda virus case, a virus usually circulating amongst livestock. The severely immunocompromised patient died, spurring global public health concerns. While France said there was no health risk as a result of this, there are definitely problems when a new pathogen crosses the barrier. For everything we currently know about the Shamonda virus, read Athira Elssa Johnson’s explainer, here.
She also writes on Melioidosis in India: a potentially deadly infection that may be going undetected. Melioidosis caused by B. pseudomallei which is found in soil and water in tropical and subtropical regions, can cause pneumonia, bloodstream infection, skin and soft-tissue infections, abscesses in organs such as the liver and spleen, septic arthritis and bone infections. It can also affect the kidneys, muscles and prostate.
Meanwhile, as the second patient in Nigeria, a relative of the first case of death from Ebola in the nation, also died of Ebola, some hopeful news came from DR Congo where the Ebola vaccine trial began for the Bundibugyo strain.
In the U.S., where an early U.S. flu season has set in, doctors warned that the current strain may signal a higher risk for younger people; and urged them to get shots.
Talking of the weather, it is also time to discuss pollution and climate-related health effects. Nikhil M. Babu writes that air pollution in Delhi-NCR has come ahead of winter.
In Mumbai, Yohaan Varghese says another crisis is brewing, as attention remains on the northern States. Mumbai recorded 231 days of ‘good’ or ‘satisfactory’ air quality in 2026. The BMC has been forced to unveil a winter pollution action plan.
Geetha Srimathi interprets a global report that claims: Extreme weather, harmful chemicals escalating health risks among food workers.
As a bellwether State for healthcare in the country, what happens in Kerala affects the entire nation, in some way. The Spinal Muscular Atrophy controversy, currently brewing in the southern State too could contain lessons for the nation.
First do read C. Maya’s explainer on what this controversy is all about, here. After the government switched the drug in its SMA programme from branded to generic, parents of children living with SMA have been asking for a switch back to the branded version; meanwhile the label on a drug bottle has sparked concerns, and political parties have now latched on to the issue.
Meanwhile, experts have opined that the Row over SMA drug distribution in Keralam is unwarranted and a hospital rejected charges of ‘clinical trial drugs’ given to children. Further a doctor at SAT Hospital said Parents were actually counselled about the generic drug that was to be used ahead of administration.
We are sure to be following up this story until it reaches its logical conclusion.
Further on the regulation scenario in the health care/medical sector, the issue of prices of drugs was top of the agenda after the recent Supreme Court judgement. Devyanshi Bihani looked at data and found that ₹8,447 crore in medicine overcharging claims remain outstanding as SC seeks wider price controls.
Bindu Shajan Perappadan wrote on the concerns over the National Medical Commission withdrawing the 2023 Rules on medical education standards. While the government claims this has been done to eliminate duplication and multiple overlaps, it has raised questions about how violations by medical colleges will be penalised, and how compliance with prescribed standards will be verified under the remaining regulatory framework.
She also recorded the disability lobby’s demand that the Centre classify communication aids as essential products.
Dr. C. Aravinda explained what the National Medical Commission’s new guidelines say about advertising in medicine, while Afshan Yasmeen reported a Lancet review that called for clinical assessment over routine scans for back pain.
It may no longer be an overstatement to say ‘diet is everything’ when it comes to staying on the good side of health. Studies have proven, increasingly, the impact of a diet over the body’s ability to handle disease, fight various conditions and stay on the path of good health.
This recent UK-Chennai collaborative study showed that good-quality diets are associated with better cholesterol levels even among those with a genetic predisposition.
Jacob Koshy wrote about a study that claimed Plant-based meat yielded a higher share of absorbable protein than traditional meat, and on the side of plants, still, Vasudevan Mukunth asked if theCentre’s new fortified potato variety the Centrecan address India’s hidden hunger or undernutrition problem.

The private space tourism era looked so very promising five years ago. Blue Origin and Virgin Galactic had begun flying customers—real people with zero space experience—on suborbital missions. And at about the same time, private citizens were going to orbit for days at a time aboard SpaceX’s Crew Dragon.
But that was then. Consider the state of play today:
- It has been 10 months since Blue Origin’s New Shepard spacecraft flew its last mission in January. The program was subsequently “paused,” but let’s be real. Blue Origin has moved on. New Shepard’s engineering teams are now supporting the New Glenn rocket and Blue Moon lander programs.
- SpaceX flew its final free-flyer mission on Dragon, Fram2, in April 2025. A handful of non-NASA missions bound for space stations remain on the spacecraft’s manifest, but all are likely to carry at least one government astronaut. Then Dragon will be retired. There is no credible timeline for SpaceX’s Starship to fly humans into space from Earth.
- As for Virgin Galactic, the company flew its final suborbital mission on the VSS Unity spacecraft more than two years ago, in June 2024.
So we are now 10 months, and counting, without a space tourism mission in the United States.
Hello Apeiron, you shiny object
At the time of Unity‘s final flight, Virgin Galactic said it was moving on to the second generation of its suborbital spacecraft. It planned to bring two of these Delta-class ships into service by the year 2026. Of course, it is now 2026, and there are no Delta-class ships in service.
But apparently we are getting closer to that goal. On Wednesday, the first Delta-class ship received a name: Apeiron. According to Virgin Galactic’s news release, the name is drawn from the ancient Greek concept of the boundless, which is an interesting choice for a vehicle that will forever be bound by Earth’s gravity. It was chosen through a public vote.

A three-year long study in Bengaluru of over 10,000 frontline workers has brought to light reduced lung function among BMTC bus drivers, traffic police, pourakarmikas and construction workers — sections most exposed to polluted air.
The study, done by the VAAYU Occupational & Environmental Respiratory Illness Clinic (VOERIC), screened 4,517 BMTC drivers, 3,285 traffic police personnel, 2,169 construction workers and 379 pourakarmikas.
Vulnerable sections face highest health risk
All the groups that were screened showed higher-than-normal prevalence of early lung-function abnormalities.
Among the occupations, pourakarmikas were found to have the highest proportion of workers with the PRISm pattern, an indication of reduced lung capacity. Around 45% of them showed indications of reduced lung function.
BMTC workers and traffic police followed, with 29.5% and 28%, respectively, showing reduced lung function. Among construction workers, 15% showed a PRISm pattern.
Around 2.6% of BMTC drivers, 2.3% pourakarmikas, 2.1% construction workers, and 1% traffic police personnel reported signs of obstructive airflow.
The survey also found that 88.2% of the BMTC drivers never used a mask, as was the case with 55% traffic police, 37.9% construction workers, and 16.3% pourakarmikas.
Comorbidities
The subjects were also analysed for comorbidities, and the results revealed a grim situation, with high levels of obesity reported among the sections.
Pourakarmikas had the highest proportion at 62%, closely followed by BMTC drivers, 60.7% of whom were found to be obese/overweight. For traffic police, the figure stood at 51.3%.
The figures are much higher than the India reference figure of 28.6%.
The study also flags that diabetes prevalence among BMTC drivers was 18.2%, higher than the Indian average of 11.4%. Among traffic police personnel, the prevalence was 14%.
The physically active nature of the work and the relatively young demography among the construction workers translated to lower prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases. The average age of construction workers was found to be 31.3± 10, 98.3% of whom worked for more than 8 hours daily.
The concerns with higher incidences of diabetes, uncontrolled blood pressure, overweight and obesity across occupational groups has reinforced the need for a comprehensive approach to worker health including cardiometabolic screening
“While the findings demonstrate a significant burden of health abnormalities, further longitudinal research is required to establish the extent to which occupational exposures contribute to specific respiratory and cardiovascular outcomes. VOERIC plans to start this as cohort along with government support,” a statement from VOERIC said.
“Air pollution is considered the new tobacco. It is an emerging risk-enhancing factor for heart attack and brain stroke,” said C.N. Manjunath, leading cardiologist and Bengaluru Rural MP, at a round table where the results from the study were published.
Speaking about the importance of reducing traffic congestion, scientific garbage disposal and adoption of necessary measures during road construction to reduce dust, in tackling air pollution, he acknowledged the importance of policy intervention backed by data.

Kenya's Health Ministry announced the country's second Ebola death on Friday (October 23, 2026), saying a 65-year-old woman who was a close relative of the first patient died after developing symptoms while in quarantine.
The woman began showing symptoms 10 days ago and began receiving supportive care at an infectious disease unit in the capital, Nairobi.
The Ministry said medical personnel "did everything possible to save her life", but she died on Friday (October 23) evening.
Her family was notified, and the Ministry said it would arrange a safe and dignified burial in consultation with relatives.
The remaining seven Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities. No new infections were reported.
Kenya announced its first ever Ebola case on October 6 after a 40-year-old Kenyan man who was living in Congo travelled to Kenya via Uganda, arriving on October 3. He was driven by a relative to Nairobi Hospital, where he tested positive for Ebola on October 5 and died the same day.
Authorities have identified some 135 contacts of the first patient, placing 118 in quarantine. Eight tested positive while in quarantine, including four health workers and four close family members.
The Health Ministry said some contacts who completed the 21-day quarantine period without developing symptoms would be released starting Saturday (October 24).
'Nigerian patient did not travel to Congo'
In Nigeria, authorities said on Friday (October 23) that they were yet to verify how the country's first Ebola patient contracted the disease. The woman tested positive for the virus upon her return to Nigeria's capital of Abuja from Uganda.
The woman — married to a Swiss diplomat in Nigeria whom she had been travelling with — did not visit Congo and "is believed to have contracted the virus whilst travelling to Uganda", Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, or FDFA, told The Associated Press on Friday (October 23).
Her husband has not shown any symptoms and remains in isolation, the FDFA added.
Nigeria's Health Minister Muhammad Pate told reporters on Friday (October 23) that the Nigerian patient "appears to be closely related" to the first case in Kenya in terms of the nature of their infection. "That may or may not change the understanding of the route of transmission given that the virus itself takes time to change," Mr. Pate said.
The Africa CDC earlier said the first patients in Nigeria and Kenya had travelled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport on October 3.
U.S. introduces new protocol for all travellers
United States health officials this week said that all passengers boarding an international flight to the U.S. — no matter from where — must sign a statement attesting that they have not been in Congo in the previous 21 days. The US has been screening travellers from Ebola-affected countries during the current outbreak.
Travellers who were in Congo in the three weeks leading to their trip will not be allowed to board flights with U.S. destinations, including Americans, the U.S. CDC said on Thursday (October 22).
Ebola is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, including blood and vomit, or through contact with contaminated materials and surfaces, such as bedding and clothing. Congo is experiencing its deadliest outbreak, with at least 4,000 deaths since May.

The Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (KSSP) has supported the Kerala Health Department’s decision to provide a low-cost generic version of the drug Risdiplam to patients afflicted with Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), a rare and threatening genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness.
In a statement, KSSP president C. Ramakrishnan and general secretary V. Manoj Kumar said that access to this medication is crucial for improving the quality of life and life expectancy of patients.
The statement from the pro-Left people’s science movement comes close on the heels of public health experts such as B. Ekbal, K.P. Aravindan, and V. Ramankutty endorsing the government’s stand.
The KSSP functionaries pointed out that Natco Pharma is an Indian pharmaceutical company that plays a key role in making affordable cancer treatments more accessible to the general public, both in India and in international markets. They claimed that the department’s decision is not merely aimed at saving public funds. It is a humanitarian responsibility to ensure that life-saving treatment is accessible to more SMA patients, they added.

Rather than directly converting photons into electricity, concentrated solar energy uses mirrors to turn sunlight into heat, which can then be used to drive traditional generating turbines. Up to about a decade ago, there was a case to be made that concentrated solar energy had a bright future, as improvements in heat storage had turned it into a way to generate power around the clock.
It wasn’t to be. While concentrated solar costs fell enough to compete with nuclear power, the price of photovoltaics plunged, making solar panels the cheapest source of power in most locations. Currently, if you have a good site to generate solar power, then the economics of PV panels are hard to beat.
That has left us needing to build a mixture of other facilities—typically batteries and natural gas facilities—to handle overnight needs or weather-driven shortfalls. But a small company is promising that it can help avoid the need to build a separate facility. Its version of concentrated solar is designed so that a fossil-fueled backup system shares most of the generating hardware with the solar side.
Back to the future?
Concentrated solar, also called solar thermal, is pretty simple in principle. Most of the site is covered with heliostats, devices that incorporate mirrors and a motorized tracking system that can keep their focus on a single point as the Sun moves across the sky. The point of focus is in a tower, where sunlight heats a working fluid. The hot fluid can then be used to power a traditional steam turbine, or its heat can be stored and used to generate power overnight.
There are many potential variations, however: different working fluids and methods of heat storage, trough-shaped mirrors that eliminate the need for a tower, and so on. All of those variants are meant to reduce some of the issues inherent to solar thermal: lots of moving parts, potentially corrosive fluids, and so on. Those issues and the lack of standardization have helped ensure that the costs of these plants haven’t come close to keeping pace with photovoltaics.

B.C. NDP caucus taps Jennifer Whiteside to be new interim leader
David Eby stepped down as leader after Saturday's election loss
The B.C. NDP caucus has announced Jennifer Whiteside as its choice for the party's new interim leader.
The caucus recommended Whiteside after David Eby resigned as party leader when his snap election call resulted in a resounding defeat of the NDP at the polls.
Eby's majority government fell from 47 seats in the legislature to 28, according to the initial count.
At a caucus meeting Thursday, Mike Farnworth was named house leader and Niki Sharma was named caucus chair.
- Wounded B.C. NDP caucus meets after humbling election defeat
- Analysis 5 reasons why Lorne Doerkson is the next premier of British Columbia
Whiteside said it was a unanimous recommendation.
The B.C. NDP's constitution requires its provincial council to vote on the interim leader after considering the recommendations of the caucus.
Eby wasn't at the in-person caucus meeting, nor was he present virtually, Whiteside said.
Whiteside said she was humbled by the caucus's recommendation.
"It is not an outcome I was necessarily expecting," she said.
She said she's looking forward to using her advocacy skills in the role.
Whiteside, MLA-elect for New Westminster-Coquitlam, previously worked as chief spokesperson and lead negotiator for the Hospital Employees' Union.
She said the caucus meeting included discussions on what the community needs.
"We are very focused on making sure that British Columbians understand that we are standing for them, that we have their backs, and we will continue to do that work in the opposition caucus."
The B.C. NDP will serve as Official Opposition to Lorne Doerkson's B.C. Conservative Party, which won 63 seats.

How Kane defied doubters to become world's best
- Published
Harry Kane has taken the scenic route to the Ballon d'Or - a road littered with doubts and diversions, but one that eventually led to the ultimate destination: being crowned as the world's best player.
The 33-year-old's glory at the London Palladium on Monday is fitting reward for an exemplary career that has seen records fall at his feet for England, Tottenham Hotspur and Bayern Munich.
Kane is England's top goalscorer with 91 goals. He has 125 England caps, joint-highest with Peter Shilton. He is Spurs' record scorer with 280 goals in 435 appearances. He scored a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for Bayern Munich and England during the 2025–26 season.
This is the Kane of recent vintage, the world-class striker and complete footballer who beat Real Madrid and France striker Kylian Mbappe, as well as Spain's teenage Barcelona forward Lamine Yamal, to the sport's biggest personal honour.
Kane's humility has seen him described as an 'anti-superstar' and his achievement has been commended both inside and outside the football world.
One post on social media from Kane as he celebrated the greatest moment of his career said it all: "Work hard in silence. Let success be your noise."
And yet, Kane's journey was not always smooth.
It was one that started with loan moves around the lower divisions with Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City before he developed into a great for club and country.
The same Kane sat on the bench on loan at Leicester City – alongside future England team-mate Jamie Vardy – when the Foxes lost a dramatic Championship play-off at Watford in May 2013.
Kane went through hard schools and hard times away from his more familiar environment at Spurs, joining Orient on loan as a 17-year-old in January 2011, playing 18 games with nine starts and scoring five goals.
He joined Millwall in similar circumstances a year later, with some behind the scenes at Spurs fearing the traditionally hostile atmosphere at the New Den might intimidate the teenager, but he acquitted himself well, scoring nine goals in 24 starts.
Former Spurs manager Tim Sherwood said: "I used to watch Harry a lot at Millwall and it was an intimidating atmosphere. I remember overhearing one of our scouts come and talk to Harry Redknapp - who was Spurs manager at the time - and say: 'We need to get Harry Kane out of Millwall, it's no good for him there'.
"I went straight in and said: 'This is the perfect atmosphere for him'."
Kane made his Spurs debut in August 2012 before a spell at Norwich City, where he failed to score in three starts and suffered a serious foot injury.
It was an unhappy time but Chris Hughton, the former Spurs defender who was manager at Carrow Road, said: "What I saw in him was a desire to do well. Did I see him having the mobility and flexibility he has in his game now? Probably not. He was a very good finisher. He would stay out after training for half an hour every day, left foot, right foot."
Next stop was Leicester City between February and May 2013, when he made five starts and scored two goals, a stint best remembered for that dramatic Championship play-off game when Troy Deeney scored for Watford to send them to Wembley seconds after Anthony Knockaert's penalty was saved by Manuel Almunia.
Kane was not even selected in Leicester's starting line-up, only being sent on after 61 minutes. And who was alongside him on the bench? Vardy, who later won the Premier league with the Foxes and played alongside Kane for England.
He later admitted this was a time of self-doubt, saying: "That was probably the time in my career where it was the hardest - I was 19 and I was thinking, 'If I can't play for Norwich or for Leicester, even in the Championship, then how I am going to get back and play for Tottenham?'"
- Ranking England's Ballon d'Or winners - how does Kane compare? 
  - Published7 hours ago
- Quiz: Kane and who else? Name every men's Ballon d'Or winner 
  - Published4 hours ago
It is testimony to Kane's strength of character, even as a youngster, that he not only returned to Spurs but left for Bayern Munich in August 2023 as one of their greatest ever players.
Even at Spurs, Kane's superb record always carried the qualification that he never won a trophy, a stick used to unfairly beat a player whose remarkable consistency and approach marked him down as the consummate professional.
Kane has put that right spectacularly at Bayern, winning the Bundesliga twice, the move propelling him to the level of global superstar, giving him the profile and platform to win the Ballon d'Or - the first English player to win the trophy since Michael Owen in 2001 and the fifth overall.
Former England midfielder Danny Murphy told BBC Sport recently: "He's a born goalscorer. He's a super professional. He's technically brilliant. He's been an absolute credit to himself and his family in the way he's conducted himself and the longevity he's had in his career."
There is still that one space on his roll of honour, namely success with England after losses in two Euros finals and two World Cup semi-final defeats, but who would bet against Kane being fit and motivated enough to have one last crack at Euro 2028 in the UK and Ireland.
Kane is now at the peak of his powers and fitness, not just a goalscoring machine but the complete player capable of dropping deep into midfield to play the sort of breathtaking defence splitting pass exemplified by Alphonso Davies' goal against Arsenal in the recent Champions League game.
One of Kane's illustrious predecessors in England's number nine shirt, Alan Shearer, told BBC Radio 5 Live: "It was so well deserved because he hasn't had things all his own way. He's had to go round it the hard way. He had to start off the hard way by someone telling him, 'You're not quite good enough, you're going to have to work a lot harder to get to where you want to'.
"He did that. He went out on loan and worked harder than anyone else. He's got to the very, very top and now he's the best player in the world and that's what dedication does for you. It's a message to everyone.
"Harry said it in his speech - that if you're told you're not good enough, then go and try again and work harder. He did that and look where he is now. He's been scoring goals at a phenomenal rate for so many years now and he deserved it."
Shearer added: "I think the best thing for me is how humble Harry is. Footballers are like movie stars nowadays. You see them walking down the red carpet and some of them are in sunglasses when it's pitch black and eight o'clock at night. Harry is just normal, as normal as they come."
Once the celebrations die down, it will be back to business for the humble superstar, with Bayern playing Magdeburg in the German DFB Pokal second round on Wednesday before the big home fixture against Borussia Dortmund on Saturday evening.
Kane's career has not been without its obstacles but he remains as focused as ever to conquer whatever is placed in front of him by Bayern Munich and England.

DoorDash acquires Instacart in $17 billion delivery service merger
The deal combines the two largest grocery delivery platforms in the US.
DoorDash has struck a deal to acquire rival Instacart in a deal valued at $17 billion. The purchase will combine the two biggest grocery delivery services in the US, assuming it isn't stymied by antitrust scrutiny.
DoorDash gained popularity as a restaurant and takeout option, but it does also offer other shopping services, including grocery delivery. The integration of Instacart's network could help further bolster those features. The Instacart acquisition isn't DoorDash's only recent expansion. Earlier this year, the company began testing a drone delivery program.
Multiple advanced reports, including from The Information and The Wall Street Journal, had recently suggested that Instacart was exploring options for a sale. In addition to DoorDash, at some point Uber was also reportedly a potential buyer.
Today's announcement isn't the first time DoorDash had made a pitch for Instacart; it had been in talks that placed Instacart at a higher valuation back in 2021, but those negotiations reportedly ended due to concerns over price and possible antitrust regulation.

Words were misinterpreted: Karnataka minister clarifies SIR stand after backing it
Satish Jarkiholi clarified that his Karnataka SIR remarks concerned Congress efforts against alleged Form 7 voter deletions. The intervention followed Priyank Kharge's questions and came before the INDIA bloc's Delhi rally.
Karnataka Minister Satish Jarkiholi on Friday clarified his remarks on the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, saying his statement had been misinterpreted.
He said he was referring to the Congress's efforts to counter attempts to delete the names of eligible voters through Form 7 applications and had not endorsed the SIR process itself.
In a statement posted on X, Jarkiholi said his remarks were intended to highlight how attempts to remove the names of Congress-supporting voters from electoral rolls in Karnataka had been thwarted through the efforts of Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and under the guidance of Deputy Chief Minister DK Shivakumar.
"Compared to other states, the BJP's conspiracy to delete names of Congress-supporting voters from the electoral rolls in Karnataka through Form-7 has been foiled through the struggle of our national leader Shri Rahul Gandhi and under the guidance of Hon'ble Deputy Chief Minister Shri D.K. Shivakumar — this was the intention of my statement," he said.
He added that he had not intended to suggest that the SIR process was correct or valid.
Jarkiholi said the resistance against attempts to delete eligible voters' names had begun in Belagavi district. Reiterating his position, he said he opposed any move to deprive eligible voters of their voting rights and supported Rahul Gandhi's efforts to protect democratic values.
"My stand against any attempt to snatch away the rights of eligible voters has been firm from the beginning. I strongly oppose attempts to illegally remove names of eligible voters from the voters' list," he said.
