North Korea's Kim calls for rapid expansion of drone technology and observes weapons tests
North Korea says that leader Kim Jong Un has called for rapidly expanding drone technology and observed tests of various weapons
SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for rapidly expanding the country's drone technology and observed tests of various weapons, state media reported Friday, as his nation remains embroiled in a standoff with rival South Korea along their heavily fortified border.
Acquiring advanced drones is a top priority for Kim, who now wants to beef up both conventional and nuclear capabilities. Experts say his troops dispatched to Russia to support its war against Ukraine have likely gained valuable expertise on drone warfare from Russian forces and related battlefield experiences.
The North's official Korean Central News Agency said that Kim on Thursday visited an exhibition of a variety of attack and other drones that show recent achievements in the field of unmanned aeronautical technology.
In a speech at the exhibition, Kim stressed the need to seize “the absolute superiority in the drone technology” and announced unspecified steps needed to “rapidly expand and strengthen the unmanned aeronautical technology,” KCNA said.
South Korea’s Unification Ministry said it would monitor North Korean moves. The ministry said it was the first time that North Korea has held an exhibition exclusively dedicated to drone technology.
To mark the event, KCNA said that North Korea conducted test-launches of various drones, missiles and weapons from the 600 mm-caliber ultra-precision multiple rocket launchers. KCNA photos showed Kim watching soaring weapons or him clenching his fist while his teenage daughter was clapping her hands beside him. South Korea's spy agency assesses that the girl, reportedly about 13, is likely Kim's heir.
South Korea's military earlier said it detected the launches of about 10 short-range ballistic missiles off the North's east coast on Thursday. They were North Korea's first ballistic weapons firings in 17 days.
Tensions between the two Koreas are running high since last month's land mine blasts at their border that wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of burying the mines south of the military demarcation line and demanded an apology. But Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked.
Last week, North Korea threatened to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and place new weapons systems along the border.
North Korea's Defense Ministry on Friday slammed an ongoing U.S.-South Korea combined aerial exercise as “provocative" and warned it was increasing the danger of an armed conflict. South Korea's military earlier said the two-week biannual Freedom Flag drill was to run until Nov. 6 and was meant to improve combined operational capabilities. It said aerial assets like fighter jets, helicopters and drones would be mobilized.
North Korea has pulled out of talks with the U.S. and South Korea after Kim's high-stakes diplomacy with U.S. President Donald Trump collapsed in 2019. In recent weeks, North Korea has dialed up weapons testing activities in a likely attempt to boost its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after Trump expressed his eagerness to restore talks with Kim.
On Saturday, Kim made a surprise visit to a Chinese border town via a newly opened bridge and vowed to develop bilateral ties. Kim has recently taken steps to cement ties with China, North Korea's economic pipeline, after years of prioritizing ties with Russia, including by supplying thousands of troops and ammunitions likely in return for economic and military assistance.
Meanwhile, Switzerland’s Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis arrived in North Korea on Thursday to see the reopening of Switzerland’s diplomatic office in Pyongyang and meet North Korean officials. He is travel on to South Korea on Friday.

Girl seriously injured after being attacked by wolf in Germany
The girl was in a park that houses brown bears, lynx, and grey and arctic wolves

An eight-year-old girl has been airlifted to hospital by after being seriously injured in a wolf attack at a German wildlife park, police said.
The attack happened in Baruth/Mark, a town south of Berlin. Neither the employee nor the other children were injured.
The incident happened inside an animal enclosure at Johannismühle that offers small group tours. The child was with a staff member and two other children.
Police said: "The girl was attacked and seriously injured by at least one wolf within an animal enclosure while she was there with two other children and a staff member."
They added in a statement that "the precise circumstances of the incident are the subject of an ongoing police investigation".
The park houses brown bears, lynx, and grey and arctic wolves, its website states. It has temporarily closed without providing further details.
In March this year a wolf bit a woman in a shopping area in Hamburg, in what is believed to be the first such attack since wolves returned to the country in 1998. Emergency services at the time said that the woman was taken to a Hamburg hospital after the unusual encounter. The attack took place in a shopping area near the Altona station, west of the city center.
The latest incident in Germany comes after a number of other animal attacks at zoos and wildlife parks across Europe in recent weeks.
A keeper at a Dutch zoo died after being mauled by a leopard. The woman, whose name has been withheld in accordance with Dutch privacy law, passed away on Tuesday, the park in the southern Dutch town of Hilvarenbeek said.
She had suffered serious wounds to her head and neck on Saturday while working in an enclosure with two male Persian leopards. The woman began working at the zoo when she was 17.
In Yorkshire a man was killed by a tiger at Wildlife Park earlier this month. The man was seen wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in.
City of Doncaster Council launched a health and safety investigation into the death.

Grieving Spain demands answers for latest rail disaster that killed 69 people
The accident happened on a key line linking Madrid to the southern city of Seville, which was also the scene of a collision in January that killed 46 people.
TOLEDO: Spain began demanding answers on Thursday (Oct 29) after its second high-speed train collision this year killed 69 people and injured scores, with distraught relatives desperately seeking news about their loved ones.
One of Europe's deadliest rail disasters this century struck south of Madrid on Wednesday morning when a service by state operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo.
Manuel San Emeterio, whose 54-year-old brother Pepe is missing, came to the central city of Toledo to provide DNA samples to the Civil Guard.
"The uncertainty is the worst thing that you deal with, everyone is dealing with it," he said. "But I think there's something that counters it, which is hope ... we must never lose it."
Toledo has received 52 of the corpses, overwhelming its morgue's capacity of 30 and forcing the army to set up an improvised facility.
Forensics experts in green jackets, a black funeral car and army vehicles moved in and out of the site, equipped with red marquees and refrigerated containers, an AFP reporter saw.
Sniffer dogs and thermal drones were searching for bodies at the crash site outside the central village of Urda, around 130km south of Madrid.
The toll rose from 68 to 69 on Thursday, according to regional authorities. Among the victims was Fatima Banez, a former labour minister for the main conservative Popular Party (PP).
"NERVOUS AND DESPERATE" RELATIVES
Jose Miguel Fernandez, a parish priest in Urda, joined the emergency services in offering support to families still waiting to learn the fate of their loved ones.
"Many of them were calm, others were nervous and desperate. They wanted to know straight away and get news" of their loved ones, he told AFP.
Flags flew at half-mast on public buildings with official ceremonies and public events cancelled or scaled back on the first of three days of national mourning.
A minute of silence was observed up and down the country, including at Spain's busiest train station Atocha in Madrid, where some mourners shed tears.
Wednesday's accident happened on a key line linking Madrid to the southern city of Seville, which was also the scene of a collision in January that killed 46 people.
It has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain's high-speed rail network, the second-largest in the world after China's.
Toledo resident Marcos Ibanez, who works in tourism, told AFP he had avoided high-speed trains "for a long time because of this".
"I've gone through the place where the accident happened several times ... and you never know when it might be your turn," the 28-year-old said. "Most people are pretty fed up."
During a visit to the disaster site, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who faces a general election on Nov 29, pledged "to establish every last detail of this tragedy and strengthen safety measures to ensure it never happens again".
King Felipe VI also intervened in the debate after visiting the injured in Toledo, calling for measures "to ensure this does not happen again".
"SEARCHING FOR CULPRITS"
Transport Minister Oscar Puente said on Wednesday that an automatic control system went down on 69 kilometres of track, causing all trains there to be stopped.
But the control centre decided to "resume traffic in circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable", Puente said, with the Renfe train travelling 25km before striking the Iryo.
The control centre "had more than enough time to verify the error, and they did not fix it", he added.
Sanchez's main rival, PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo, accused Puente of "frivolity" by trying to pin the blame on one control centre operator.
"Political responsibilities cannot wait for an investigation," Feijoo said.
The head of train driver union Semaf, Diego Martin, said "attention is wrongly being focused on searching for culprits" when workers were using "degraded systems".
Renfe train drivers on Thursday maintained a strike that Semaf had called before the accident "to defend rail safety", saying previous commitments on the issue had been broken.
Renfe reported "a major impact" on its minimum service requirements as 26.6 per cent of the staff concerned joined the industrial action.
The Madrid region's sprawling commuter network suffered the most disruption, with 81 per cent of its planned services cancelled.

Meta is testing 'Threads Friends' for sharing posts with smaller groups
Twitter Circle, anyone?
Threads is experimenting with a way to more privately share posts with smaller groups of followers. The app said it's testing "Threads Friends" in Ireland, Italy and Japan.The feature is basically like a "close friends" list for Threads. It allows people to opt to share posts with up to 50 friends (or "Thriends" as the app also calls it) without making it visible to anyone else on the platform.
If that sounds familiar, it's also remarkably similar to a feature Twitter introduced back in 2022 called "Circles." Twitter's version of the feature allowed users to limit posts to groups of up to 150. The company killed Circles about a year later.
It seems that Meta is helping users create their initial friends list. The app will automatically suggest followers that you frequently engage with, a Meta spokesperson shared, though the list is customizable. Once a friend list is set up, users are then able to tap a green bubble at the top of their feed to see "Friends' posts that have been shared in the last 24 hours.
The company hasn't shared detailed images of the feature yet, but Laura Javier, product design director for Threads, did show a little preview of what a friends-only post will look like. She also showed off an Easter egg that will change "Threads Friends" to simply "Thriends."
It's not clear if or when Meta plans to expand the initial test, so most users in the US won't have access to it for now. However, if you know someone in one of the test countries, you will be able to see their friends-only posts if they add you to their list.

The 5G Use Case Lab at the Visvesvaraya Technological University (VTU) Centre for Post Graduate Studies in Kalaburagi has been recognised as the best-performing 5G laboratory in Karnataka by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT), securing an ‘Excellent’ grading with a score of 143.
The recognition was conveyed in a letter dated October 23, by Shreenivas S. Galgali, Deputy Director General (Technology), Karnataka to VTU Vice-Chancellor S. Vidyashankar. The assessment was based on the monthly 5G Lab Gradation Framework for the period up to September 2026.
Addressing a press conference at the regional centre on October 29, Shubhangi D.C., Director of the VTU Regional Centre, and Professor Basavaraj Gadgay shared details of the recognition and the laboratory’s performance.
“The 5G laboratory at the VTU Regional Centre in Kalaburagi was among the 100 laboratories established across India, including eight in Karnataka, in 2023 and inaugurated through video-conferencing by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on October 27 that year. The lab at VTU Regional Centre in Kalaburagi is now among the top-performing facilities in the country,” Mr. Gadgay said.
The other seven institutions that got the 5G Lab in Karnataka were Indian institute of Science in Bengaluru. NIT-K Surathkal, IIIT Dharwad, SIT Tumakuru, BMS College of Engineering, MS Ramaiah Institute of Technology, and MIT Manipal.
Ms. Shubhangi said that the laboratory was recognised for its contribution to international journals and standardisation bodies, the development of functional 5G products and use cases, and the active participation of students and faculty in academic and research projects.
“Professor S. Vidyashankar, Vice-Chancellor, Visvesvaraya Technological University, Belagavi, and Professor Gadgay, were instrumental in getting the 5G lab for VTU Kalaburagi Regional Centre,” she said, thanking them for their efforts and the support.
The Department of Telecommunications commended the efforts of ms. Shubhangi, the nodal officer of the 5G laboratory, and her project team for their dedication and proactive approach in promoting 5G innovation and technological advancement in the region.
The recognition is expected to encourage the university to further strengthen research and innovation through the laboratory, with a focus on generating patents, commercialising technologies, and developing indigenous 5G solutions.

Lewis Hamilton: Ferrari driver says he 'is built differently' amid defiance over extending his F1 career into 2030s
Lewis Hamilton insists the idea of him continuing his F1 career into the 2030 is realistic; the 41-year-old wants to compete in F1's first race in Rwanda; watch every session of the Mexico City GP with Friday's practice sessions at 6.30pm and 10pm, live on Sky Sports F1
Thursday 29 October 2026 23:48, UK
Lewis Hamilton insisted he "is built differently" as he continued to rule out extending his Formula 1 career into the 2030s.
Following the announcement earlier in October that Africa will return to the F1 calendar at some point in the 2030s with a race in Rwanda, Hamilton had said he hoped he would be able to compete in the first grand prix on the continent since 1993.
Given Hamilton turns 42 in January and will be 45 at the start of the 2030 F1 season, at which point it is far from certain the circuit in Rwanda will be ready, it was initially unclear how seriously his comments should be taken.

But quizzed on the topic on Thursday ahead of this weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix, the seven-time world champion said: "I mean, firstly, you've never had anyone like me here in the 70 years [of the sport's history], so I feel that I'm built differently.
"Of course, there are challenges up ahead that I can't foresee that come with age. But along this way, along this journey, there have been so many preconceived ideas about the fact that your reaction time drops off.
"Did you see my reaction in the last race? My reaction is faster than some of the youngest people here. There are lots of tools that you can utilise to continue to keep yourself, your mind sharp.
"I guess as long as you're willing to sacrifice everything, which I am right now, I can't say in four years whether I want to continue to do what I'm doing. But I love what I'm doing still now. I'm still all in, and I will be for the foreseeable future."
Hamilton's current contract with Ferrari is understood to run until the end of the 2027 season, with the Brit holding an option to extend for a further year should he wish to do so.
After a blockbuster move from Mercedes to Ferrari for the 2025 season, Hamilton's performances during his first year in red raised doubts, at times from the driver himself himself, over whether his skills were declining, but he has bounced back with a much-improved 2026 campaign, which included a memorable victory in Barcelona.
Hamilton continued: "Whether or not I can compete at 44 with a 20-year-old, who knows? But at 41, I can compete with a 20-year-old. So, time will tell whether I'm here in the 2030s, we'll see.
"But I never want to overstay my welcome in the sense of still not having the performance. I don't want to be driving around with that really dropped off.
"My reaction has dropped off, my driving has dropped off, and my pace has dropped off, which everyone assumed last year. But I've proved everyone wrong with that, and I'll continue to try to do so."
Hamilton's focus on Constructors', not Drivers' Championship
While Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli is set to seal the Drivers' Championship this weekend with four races to spare, Hamilton is part of an extremely tight four-way battle for second place in the standings.
Antonelli's team-mate George Russell is in second, a point ahead of Hamilton, with Red Bull's Max Verstappen five points further back and the other Ferrari of Charles Leclerc three more points adrift.
Hamilton insists his focus is on ensuring Ferrari seal second in the Constructors' Championship, in which they hold a 119-point over Red Bull and McLaren, with Mercedes 133 points clear out front.
"I'm not going to say it [second in the Drivers' Championship] doesn't mean anything, but it's not something I focus on," Hamilton said. "Winning the championship is the only thing any of us really care about.
"Maybe some people do care about the other positions, but for me, my sole focus is on making sure that we secure second in the Constructors' Championship because the team deserve it.
"It's a huge boost from last year and it really is something we can build on for next year.
"In terms of finishing second, third, fourth, you want to finish first."
'The car should be good here'
Hamilton is hopeful Ferrari can deliver a strong weekend in Mexico, where many believe the turbo element of their engine, which is smaller than their rivals', could be an advantage at high altitude.
Asked about Ferrari's chances, Hamilton said: "Someone just said that it should be good for our car, and I really have no idea.
"I mean, everyone's going to be maximum downforce here. It would be an unusual experience for us all, because it's like 25 or 30 per cent less downforce than we had the last time we drove here.
"So, whether we can get the tyres switched on... the car should be good here.
"And being that we have high altitude, hopefully straight-line speed won't be as affected as it is in some of the other places where at sea level the drag is significant.
"So, I'm hoping that we are able to continue on from the strong performance we had last year and bring it into this weekend."

Halloween is that time of year when you can be anyone you want, and if you’re a Fortnite fan, there are plenty of costumes to choose from in 2026. While there’s very little time to get your cosplay in order, here are some of the 10 best Fortnite costumes you can get for Halloween at the very last minute.
Peelverine
Introduced in Fortnite Chapter 5 Season 4, Peelverine is a variant of Peely that’s based on none other than Marvel’s Wolverine. Epic Games first showcased this version of the character at Disney D23 in 2024 to promote the new Fortnite Season. It was a hit with fans and became an instant comic relief.
Peelverine has remained popular to this day, with many users cosplaying him in-game every time there’s a new Marvel collab in Fortnite. Cutting to the chase, if you want to wear this Fortnite costume for Halloween 2026, you need to make it from scratch.
- How to DIY: Get a regular Peely costume, add a superhero utility belt with an X-logo, blue shoulder guards, blue gauntlets, and blue boots (X-Men suits). Get Wolverine’s iconic helmet wings (can be made from cardboard and painted black). Lastly, get Wolverine claws and paint them to look like banana slices.
Drift
Drift has been in Fortnite since the OG days of Season 5. He’s arguably the first human to be rifted to the Fortnite island. Although we’re now in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4, Drift’s popularity has never ‘drifted,’ and as such, it’s a solid Halloween costume to use in 2026.
Unlike the aforementioned Peelverine costume, which has to be made using Peely as the base, you can outright purchase Drift. There are several options to choose from, and depending on your budget, you can either get a replica of Drift as a Fortnite Halloween costume. Or you can choose one that’s less expensive, and while not an exact copy, it resembles Drift very closely.
Dark Voyager
Dark Voyager, not to be confused with Dark Voyager (Reality Redacted) from Chapter 7 Season 3 Battle Pass, is a great choice for a Halloween costume for Fortnitemares 2026. Much like Drift, the Dark Voyager is an OG character and has been popular ever since being added to Fortnite in OG Season.
Unlike the newer version of the character, Dark Voyager played no role in the storyline, nor will he in any time soon. Nevertheless, given how iconic he is, it’s always worthwhile cosplaying as him when given the chance. To that end, there are several options to purchase this Fortnite Halloween costume in 2026.
Raven Team Leader
Raven Team Leader is by far one of the best Fortnite Halloween costumes you can have in 2026. The character is a brilliant ‘remix’ of two very popular Fortnite skins: Raven and Cuddle Team Leader. It goes without saying that this amalgamated ‘dark’ version of the Team Leader is perfect for Fortnitemares 2026.
There’s just one problem when it comes to costumes, which is that you cannot purchase it online. This is a labor of love and has to be made from scratch. We suggest you either get someone to help you craft it, or you can cosplay as someone else.
- How to DIY: Purchase the Raven Team Leader suit design on Etsy to craft the entire costume. This includes the hood, bodysuit, and greaves. With the base done, you then need to add other elements such as color, feathers, and the all-important hood. To replicate Raven Team Leader’s face, you need to get a Bluetooth-enabled LED screen mask. This can be programmed, allowing you to get her exact facial features.
Midas
Midas, often called the “Golden Mischef Maker,” is not just a character, but part of Fortnite’s history. While the name and the legend originate in Greek and Roman mythology, Epic Games has somehow managed to make Midas their own. To that end, he’s one of the most easily recognizable characters, and dressing up as Midas for Halloween 2026 is a great idea.
Unlike other Fortnite costumes on this list, recreating Midas’ look is very easy. There’s no complexity involved, nor do you need to spend a lot of money on accessories. If you have a formal suit, you’re halfway there. To add some flair, you can create a tiny Fortnite pirate treasure chest to carry as a reference to the upcoming Mini Season.
- How to DIY: Buy a white shirt, black pants, black leather shoes, black vest, black tie, gold gloves, and a shoulder holster. This is the base of the entire Midas Fortnite Halloween costume for Fortnitemares 2026. To complete the look, buy a few toy pistols (Deagle is a must-have) and paint them gold. For the finishing touches, get temporary tattoos of your choice and cover your forearms.
Funk Ops
Bringing the ‘boogie’ to Halloween 2026, Funk Ops has been one of the most popular costumes over the years. What makes the character stand out is that it features a disco-themed 1970s outfit that’s mixed with tactical military gear to create something unique. While not being one of the rarest Fortnite skins to exist in-game, it has OG status due to being released in Season 3.
Coming to the costume, creating Funk Ops is going to take a bit of work. There’s no crafting involved per se, but there are numerous elements that need to work together. If nothing else, it’s a great DIY project that you can complete in a day or two.
- How to DIY: First off, you’re going to need a sparkly, sequined, or metallic button-down or V-neck disco shirt. It doesn’t have to be from the 70s; it just needs to be era-accurate. Next, you want chrome, metallic, or sparkly disco pants. Red fingerless gloves and chunky retro sneakers. Or combat boots if you want a more military design. A harness crossing the chest and waist is optional, but will complete the look. If you find a Boogie Bomb, you can add it as a prop. You will also need an afro wig and a colorful bandana for a headpiece.
Boxer
Getting straight to the point, Boxer is a DIY Fortnite Halloween costume that you should definitely try to make for Fortnitemares 2026. What’s great about Boxer is that the character concept was created keeping in mind that it could be replicated easily. To elaborate, Boxer is essentially a human being who’s wearing cardboard boxes.
Despite there being only three styles for Boxer, you can create any style you want since the signature aspect of the costume is the cardboard boxes. You can even attach some Fortnite One Piece Wanted Posters to the cardboard to give it some flair. Whatever you choose to wear underneath has no relevance.
- How to DIY: Get a long-sleeve or short-sleeve top and a pair of pants in a dark or grey color. Get full gloves and boots. Get black duct tape and wrap it around the sleeves of the top and the pants. Use the tape to also tape cardboard greaves to your arms and legs (you can also use string to make it look more interesting). Get a large enough cardboard box, which you can wear as a suit of armor for the upper torso. Lastly, get a cardboard box large enough to cover your head. Cut out eye sockets and a mouth to give you some room to breathe. With that, your Boxer Fortnite Halloween costume is done; if you want to spruce it up a bit more, you can color or paint over the cardboard to make it more interesting.
Five Nights at Freddy’s
Fortnite FNAF skins are all the rage in Fortniteamares 2026, and for that reason, it’s the best time to dress up as one of the characters for Halloween. There are many options to choose from in the FNAF franchise, but looking at the collab in Fortnite, the choice is narrowed down to just four characters: Freddy, Bonnie, Chica, and Foxy.
Since the designs are very intricate, unless you plan on wearing a T-shirt of the same color alongside a mask to represent one of the characters, costumes are the only option. To that end, they can be expensive, and given how popular the franchise is, you need to move fast to get yourself a FNAF Fortnite Halloween costume.
Skull Trooper
Skull Trooper is Fortnite’s most iconic skin that’s on this list. The character is as old as the Battle Royale mode, being introduced in Fortnite OG Season 1. It’s hard to confuse him with anyone else, and with five different styles to choose from, there’s no need to look further for your Halloween costume this year.
To that end, we recommend that you try to make the costume yourself, using basic materials such as a jumper, fabric color, and a mask that can be painted. However, if you would rather purchase a licensed Fortnite Halloween costume for Skull Trooper, that option is there, too.
Punk
With a new Gold Punk Fortnite skin available until the end of Fortnitemares 2026, this is a great time to whip out the Punk Halloween costume. Introduced in Chapter 2 Season 4 towards the end of Fortnitemares, Punk was an instant hit with the fanbase.
The character design is simple, and yet it makes a statement that’s loud enough to resonate with many players. The unique selling point of Punk is that he has a pumpkin for a head. The rest of the costume is run-of-the-mill and rather ordinary.
That’s our pick for the 10 best Fortnite Halloween costumes to buy in 2026, and if you decide to cosplay as someone from the list, that’s fine, too. Let us know in the comments which Fortnite Halloween costume you plan on using this year!

The EU has backed away from its offer to Canada to start talks on becoming an “associate member” after disagreements between members states just as an EU-Canada summit was set to begin in Montreal.
A draft of a joint statement to be issued after the end of the summit, which runs Thursday and Friday, showed a watered-down version offering “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself”.
The issue was triggered after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, surprised nearly everyone by announcing in last month’s state of the union address that the EU would consider “associate membership” for Canada.
The declaration had been hailed as a landmark in EU history, offering a non-EU country such close ties to the bloc, which has not allowed any state membership since Croatia joined in 2013.
It was also seen as a sign that the call by Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, at the Davos summit in January for “middle powers” to work together was paying off.
But instead of announcing a work programme on developing “associate membership”, the draft communique, seen by the Guardian, states the two sides would “work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself, to reflect, through this even closer association, our common endeavour and cooperation towards our shared goals of prosperity, economic security and strategic autonomy”.
Associate membership had been mooted, and rejected, previously for countries such as Ukraine.
Von der Leyen’s declaration caught EU capitals by surprise and led to pushback politically and legally. Given “associate status” has no definition, diplomats wondered about such issues as whether Canada could join the European Council, legislative bodies or decision-making processes without a vote.
At a meeting on Monday, ambassadors in the EU raised concerns about the dramatic offer, but vowed to make efforts to seek a diplomatic path to rescinding the offer of “associate” membership without embarrassing Von der Leyen. It is understood that Italy suggested “associate membership as proposed by the commission”, with the definition to be thrashed out later by member states.
Germany walked back further, suggesting the wording “an ever closer association of Canada” to the EU.
“Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [Von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem. Many member states, including Germany, were not happy. This is all about fixing the plane while it is flying,” said one diplomat.
Germany had argued that “associate membership” should be reserved as an interim step for prospective candidate countries, such as Ukraine or Montenegro, noting that the status has no formal grounding in current EU treaties.
Donald Trump, the US president, previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable”, and said if he interpreted the move as a “hostile act” the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things”.
A bitter trade war with the US, a longtime ally, has seen Carney seek out new trading partnerships around the world. Ahead of the summit in Montreal, one of Canada’s largest banks released a report suggesting there was “meaningful” upside for Canada if it were to deepen economic ties with Europe. Tens of billions of dollars in additional trade would be possible if barriers were removed in areas of overlapping interest such as defence, energy, critical minerals and digital markets, TD Economics said.
Carney has spoken specifically about the need to lessen reliance on Elon Musk‘s Starlink satellite network, following a decision to throttle its usage over Ukraine.
Earlier this week, Carney posted on social media that Canada would join the popular music competition Eurovision. But despite fears raised by political rivals, Carney has said Canada has no interest in formally joining the EU. Changing Canadian laws to bring it in line with European nations would probably prove unpopular, despite public support for stronger ties.
Carney told reporters on Tuesday that the summit this week was the launch of further formal negotiations that will take place another year.
“The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”
A previous draft statement had included at least two references to Canada as an “associate member”, including an acknowledgment that defining the term would take another year.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

The European Union plans to create the first subsea Internet cable directly connecting Europe to Greenland. The Pan-Arctic Cable project could also extend to Canada and eventually link with Japan and South Korea, notably bypassing the United States.
The Pan-Arctic Cable is described as a European Union flagship project in a European Commission joint communication published on October 20, 2026. The policy document describes a new European strategy for the Arctic that supports “a sovereign, secure and resilient submarine cable connection linking Greenland directly to the EU,” while also suggesting that “like-minded partners like Canada” could provide a stepping stone for future cable expansion toward Asia.
“It is interesting that this project is even being considered, because five years ago it would have seemed like not a particularly commercially attractive proposition,” Elisabeth Braw, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads the Threats to the Global Maritime Order Initiative, told Ars. “But the fact that it’s being considered is very much on trend and a sign of our times.”
The project has gained official support after repeated Trump administration attempts to claim Greenland were finally settled through a trilateral security agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark in September 2026. The agreement preserves Greenland’s autonomous territory status within the Kingdom of Denmark while expanding US military access. But relations have grown increasingly strained between the United States and its allies in Europe and Canada since President Trump initiated trade wars with multiple countries and has taken an increasingly pro-Russia stance on the war in Ukraine.
Europe has also been eyeing new Internet cable routes to Asia because more than 90 percent of communications between Europe and Asia run through undersea cables in the Red Sea, according to TeleGeography. Maintaining such cables has become riskier since open warfare resumed between the Yemeni government and Houthi faction this year, with Houthi forces having fired missiles and drones at commercial ships in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait chokepoint and the broader Red Sea.

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

CBSE revises Class 9 scheme 6th time in 7 months; drops 3 planned curricular components
In nearly seven months between April 2 and October 29, the board has issued multiple circulars, notifications and clarifications, including successive changes to its three-language policy
The dropping of three planned curricular components for students currently in Class 9 on Thursday is the latest in a series of changes to the Central Board of Secondary Education’s (CBSE) scheme of studies since the 2026-27 academic year began on April 1.
In nearly seven months between April 2 and October 29, the board has issued multiple circulars, notifications and clarifications, including successive changes to its three-language policy introduced in line with the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020.
The latest move came six days after the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) released a 20-hour introductory module on computational thinking (CT) and artificial intelligence (AI) for Classes 9 to 12 on October 23.
In a circular dated October 29, CBSE said Individuals in Society and the CT and AI modules would not be part of the Class 9 curriculum in 2026-27, while Environmental Education would be excluded when the same batch moves to Class 10 in 2027-28. The changes do not apply to the current Class 10 batch.
The circular, signed by Dr Praggya M Singh, professor and director (academics), said the exclusions were intended “to align the introduction of this curricular area with the implementation schedule”. It did not specify when the components would be introduced for subsequent batches.
NCERT’s CT and AI module covers AI in everyday life, machine learning, misinformation, data privacy and responsible use of AI. The council is yet to release the Individuals in Society textbook; the Environmental Education textbook for Class 10 is expected next year.
Also Read:Supreme Court directs CBSE to extend 3rd language policy exemption to Class 6 students
CBSE did not respond to HT queries on the reasons for the changes, and the future implementation timeline. However, People familiar with the development said the latest circular was intended to clarify provisions for the current Class 9 batch as it progresses to Class 10.
“Our foremost priority is to safeguard students’ interests by clearly communicating the academic and examination-related provisions well in advance. The emphasis is on encouraging students to focus on meaningful learning rather than solely the examinations,” one of them said.
From phased language rollout to mid-session mandate
On April 2, CBSE released its revised scheme of studies for Classes 9 and 10, aligned with NEP 2020 and the National Curriculum Framework for School Education (NCF-SE) 2023. It proposed a phased rollout of the three-language formula, beginning with Class 6 in 2026-27 and reaching Class 10 by 2030-31. The scheme also planned advanced-level options in Mathematics and Science, vocational education, art education, physical education and well-being, and interdisciplinary learning.
Also Read: CBSE says no to Class 6 exemption from 3-language rule; SC suggests 2027 rollout
Under the original language framework, R1 referred to the first language, R2 to a second distinct language, and R3 to a third language. At least two of the three were to be native Indian languages. R1 and R2 would have board examinations, while R3 would be assessed internally. The initial rollout envisaged R3 progressing one grade each year.
On April 9, however, CBSE clarified that R3 would “not [be] applicable till the academic session 2029-30 at the class 9 level”. It also allowed an optional third language at the R1/R2 level until 2028-29.
Barely five weeks later, on May 15, the board mandated three languages for Class 9 from July 1, with at least two being Indian languages. Acknowledging the change, it said: “Given that the current academic session commenced in April 2026, CBSE has decided to adopt a transitional approach to align its Scheme of Studies with the NCERT syllabus.”
The circular directed schools to use Class 6 textbooks for R3 until dedicated material became available, citing a 75-80% overlap in core language competencies between the middle and secondary stages. It also suggested interim arrangements to address shortages of qualified language teachers.
On June 5, HT reported that the May directive appeared to contradict a recommendation ratified by CBSE’s governing body in December 2025 to continue the existing scheme, particularly for languages, until NCERT released graded textbooks.
On June 29, CBSE granted a one-time relaxation to students in Classes 7, 8 and 9 who had already chosen two non-native languages. They could continue studying those languages while adding an Indian language as their third. The board said: “No student shall be disadvantaged due to this alignment. The focus remains on joyful, meaningful language learning, not on examination.”
The board issued R3 assessment resources on July 2 and detailed implementation guidelines on July 10, retaining the transitional relief for existing batches.
Supreme Court flags implementation concerns
The language policy also became the subject of litigation. On July 15, the Supreme Court sought responses from the Centre on petitions challenging the revised policy, with parents citing shortages of textbooks and teachers. The next day, Justice BV Nagarathna questioned the decision to introduce a compulsory third language in Class 9, saying, “Don’t start a new language in 9th.”
In August, the court asked CBSE to consider transitional relief for the current Class 6 batch and address concerns over teachers and course material. On September 28, it directed CBSE to extend to Class 6 the relief already available to Classes 7 to 9, allowing students to study R3 without a mandatory Class 10 board examination in it.
Also Read: Schools as markers of class and aspirations
While retaining all the clarifications related to language policy till July 10 in its October 29 circular, CBSE has also provided a mechanism to replace a failed language in the Class 10 result. If a student scores less than 33% in either R1 or R2 but passes an additional optional language, the optional language may replace the failed language for result computation. The optional language must be selected from the 45 languages listed by the board and must be different from all three compulsory languages — R1, R2 and R3. This is separate from R3, which remains compulsory and is assessed internally. For subjects assessed through both internal assessment and the Board examination, students must secure at least 33% in the combined marks to pass.
Educationist Keshav Agarwal welcomed the objective of multilingual education, saying learning languages can improve communication, cultural understanding and cognitive flexibility.
“However, implementation will be crucial. Schools will need qualified language teachers, adequate instructional time and clarity regarding the languages available to students,” he said adding that R3 should promote meaningful communication rather than rote learning and examination pressure, while avoiding unnecessary burdens on students preparing for competitive entrance tests.
Nine subjects in Class 9; must pass 5 in Class 10
The October 29 circular requires the current Class 9 batch to study nine compulsory subjects: R1, R2, R3, Mathematics, Science, Social Science, Art Education, Physical Education and Well-being, and Vocational Education. Students may choose one optional subject from 57 listed options; an optional language must differ from R1, R2 and R3. Vocational education remains compulsory. Students can choose Kaushal Vikas, assessed internally by schools, or one of 22 skill subjects, which require a Class 10 board examination. Students passing a skill subject will also receive a certificate under the National Skills Qualifications Framework.
The board’s latest circular in its frequently asked questions (FAQs) also clarified the Class 10 examination and pass criteria. Students must secure at least 33% in each of the five compulsory board-exam subjects, R1, R2, Mathematics, Science and Social Science, calculated by combining internal assessment and board examination marks. A passed skill subject can replace a failed Mathematics, Science or Social Science subject in result computation, but this does not apply to Kaushal Vikas. A passed optional language can similarly replace a failed R1 or R2 language, provided it is different from all three compulsory languages.
Also Read:Bridge course mandatory for Classes 3, 4 and 6
The circular also provides flexibility for Children with Special Needs (CwSN), who must take one compulsory language with a board examination and can choose their remaining four board-examination subjects from a specified list. They may opt for up to two skill subjects, except Automotive; Information Technology, Computer Applications and AI cannot be taken together.
Sudha Acharya, principal of Delhi-based ITL School, said the changes could ease examination pressure.
“Having five compulsory Board-examination subjects in Class 10 can help reduce unnecessary examination pressure and allow students to focus more on learning rather than examinations alone.” She welcomed the flexibility to choose skill subjects and provisions for CwSN as steps towards a more inclusive scheme.

Anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy has unilaterally passed a rule that will allow specialty pharmacies to sell six specific peptide drugs, overruling scientists at the Food and Drug Administration.
The peptides are popular among members of Kennedy’s Make America Health Again movement and many prominent MAHA figures and Kennedy allies sell them. Kennedy said he uses some of the peptides and called himself a “big fan.” But FDA scientists continue to say there is insufficient evidence to show if they’re effective and they are potentially dangerous. In 2023, the safety concerns led the FDA to remove the six peptides from a list of drugs that can be made by specialty pharmacies called compounding pharmacies—which make customized formulations of drugs for patients, or, in cases such as this, specialty drugs in bulk.
Kennedy’s new rule sidesteps the need to formally undo that FDA action. The rule is titled “Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances” and was made available Wednesday on the Federal Register, with the final publication data set for October 30. The rule does not change the regulatory status of the peptide; instead, it states the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) will no longer take enforcement action against compounding pharmacies for making the peptides, essentially giving them a green light to freely produce and sell them. Kennedy had quietly proposed this rule earlier this month.
Questionable rationale
Along with the notice in the Federal Register, HHS also posted a more detailed explanation of the policy today that includes more of Kennedy’s rationale for easing enforcement of the six select peptides, which are: BPC-157, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax, and TB-500.

Abdul El-Sayed doesn’t make headlines as the Senate candidate who wrote a book on applying systems science to public health, or who worked to rebuild Detroit’s health system, or who researched the ways social circumstances can impact maternal mortality.
With six days left in his bruising, contentious campaign, El-Sayed is known for his comical social media videos, his advocacy of “Medicare for All” and his controversial stance on U.S. policy toward Israel. As the man Vice President JD Vance called “a little weasel.” As the Egyptian-American who President Trump has said would “open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas.”
But El-Sayed’s medical and public health background is likely to figure prominently if he is elected as a senator from Michigan. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) has pitched El-Sayed as the future standard-bearer for Medicare for All, the policy Sanders popularized in the American consciousness. He would be the first epidemiologist to make it to the upper house, and the first holder of a medical degree to represent the Democratic party in the Senate since 1969. He would also be the first Muslim senator.
And at a moment when there is no clear challenger to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s remaking of the agencies that are the bedrock of public health, he is the candidate many supporters hope will push back.
“Public health is really under attack now, and the situation really needs response. Currently there is almost no public health person in the administration,” said Alfredo Morabia, an epidemiologist at Columbia University who taught El-Sayed in a class on the history of public health while El-Sayed was earning his doctoral degree.
As a second-generation immigrant, a federally funded health equity researcher, a former local public health director, and an evangelist for single-payer health care, El-Sayed stands for much that is under siege by the Trump administration.
El-Sayed’s time in academia and health departments, and his description of himself as a doctor, have come under scrutiny during this race. His opponent, former FBI agent and Republican representative Mike Rogers, has repeatedly attacked El-Sayed for not being “a real doctor.” While El-Sayed has both a DPhil and an M.D., he never completed a medical residency, and cannot see patients. Rogers has also criticized El-Sayed’s Medicare for All proposal, saying it would force Americans to ration care while raising costs.
On Monday, at an event with Rogers, Kennedy said “there’s 500 million Arabs in the world and yet they don’t produce science.” He went on to say “they don’t win the Nobel Prize. They don’t win the Fields prize.” (The Fields Medal is awarded every four years to honor outstanding mathematical achievement.)
El-Sayed responded in an interview with STAT Wednesday that “it’s ironic to hear a guy who’s trafficked in eugenicist terms, who rejects science outright, come to Michigan to lecture voters about an Arab American scientist with two doctoral degrees who believes in science, like vaccines.”
He said he views Kennedy as “truly the most incompetent HHS secretary we’ve ever had.”
Beyond advocating Medicare for All legislation, El-Sayed has said he would seek an assignment to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, which sets budgets for the Department of Health and Human Services.
From that position, El-Sayed has said, he “can’t wait to sit across [from] RFK Jr. and actually grill him.” He told STAT he is “looking forward to sitting down with public health leaders and scientists and researchers … and being ready with a package on day one in 2029 for the next Democratic administration to start building what we need.”
In the meantime, he said he would be holding the Trump administration “accountable for all of the failures.”
But El-Sayed also shares some priorities with the current administration. His platform includes capping overhead costs for universities receiving federal research funding and finding ways to incentivize high-risk, high-impact scientific research.
If there is a silver lining in the Trump administration’s remaking of the federal health agencies, El-Sayed told STAT, it’s that “we get an opportunity, I think, right now, to build what we need.”
At the National Institutes of Health, he said, that means ensuring that funding goes to projects that are responsive to the needs of Americans, rewarding new ideas, and shoring up training programs. At the Food and Drug Administration, FDA, he wants to speed up drug approvals. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, El-Sayed said, must be “more responsive to the future.”
Many who knew El-Sayed in academia in the 2010s sensed his frustration with the pace at which research can help those most in need. That pushed El-Sayed toward the centers of power, where he believed he could have more impact, though some of his critics have questioned how much he changed in his short time leading public health departments.
El-Sayed ran the Detroit health department for nearly two years before launching a failed bid for governor of Michigan in 2018. He later led the separate public health agency in Wayne County, which encompasses Detroit and some of its suburbs, until again leaving to pursue his political ambitions. His allies hope 2026 can be his moment.
“This guy, man, he just has this energy about him that just gets people around him excited,” said Katelyn Jetelina, the founder and CEO of Your Local Epidemiologist, who joined El-Sayed as a co-host on his podcast, “America, Dissected,” at the end of 2024. Part of his appeal, she said, is that he envisions an improved public health system, rather than one that simply attempts to walk back changes the Trump administration has enacted.
“He’s not just complaining, but coming up with solutions,” Jetelina said.
Shaped by his immigrant identity
El-Sayed was born in Rochester Hills, Mich., in 1984 to two Egyptian immigrants. His father came to the United States to attend graduate school at Wayne State University and then became an engineer, while his mother worked as a nurse practitioner.
El-Sayed often recounts visiting his teta, or grandmother, in Kardasah, Egypt, where he was exposed to some of the inequities he would later try to address. “You can imagine me walking into that apartment, my hat backward with my American kid swagger,” El-Sayed said at a campaign event in Kalamazoo, Mich., in September 2025. “You can imagine her pointing to one of my cousins, ‘That one is smarter than you.’ Points to the next one: ‘I don’t have to tell you, is taller and better looking.’ Points to a third one: ‘Nicer, kinder-hearted. Fourth one is more athletic, fifth one works harder than you.’”
“By the end of this, I am like ‘Teta, what do I have going for me?’ and she’s like, ‘Habibi, [my beloved, in Arabic] you have the best thing of all.’ And I am like ‘What’s that?’ She goes ‘You get to go back to America at the end of the summer.”
In his memoir, “Healing Politics,” El-Sayed refers to this as a “matched-pair epidemiological study of sorts.” The difference between him and his cousins, he writes, is privilege: clean water, political rights, and life in a high-income country. Being able to witness what poverty looks like, and having the ability to address it, he said, is something he viewed as a “profound responsibility.”
His identity would also spark his foray into academic research. Like many Muslim-Americans, El-Sayed saw the 9/11 terror attacks change his reception in the predominantly white suburb where he lived. A high school student at the time, he endured racial slurs, was bullied by other students on the football field and told to “go back to your own country.” It’s a line of attack that has extended to the current campaign.
His opponent, Rogers, wrote in a statement the day after the Aug. 10 Democratic primary that “never in a million years did I think that I would be running against someone who believes America deserved 9/11.” There is no record of El-Sayed saying that.
By his senior year at the University of Michigan in 2007, El-Sayed would be named valedictorian of his class, and was bound for medical school in Ann Arbor. He hoped to combine his growing interest in politics with academic training in the medical sciences.
The path to merging those two passions seemingly presented itself after El-Sayed sat down with Sandro Galea, a professor of epidemiology at the school who studied the ways social factors impacted health outcomes. El-Sayed asked to volunteer in Galea’s lab to learn the ropes of social science research. Unfortunately, Galea told El-Sayed, he didn’t take volunteers and didn’t have funding for another research assistant.
El-Sayed was undeterred. He showed up the next morning to Galea’s lab and told him, “I’m ready to work.” The two went on to collaborate for years, and two decades later, Galea is still a mentor.
“I think everything he’s done has been evidence of his hard work, strategic hard work,” said Galea, who now leads the Bursky School of Public Health at Washington University in St. Louis.
Early in El-Sayed’s apprenticeship in Galea’s lab, he read a paper on the effect of intensified Islamophobia on birth outcomes in the wake of 9/11 in California, which found that the risks for preterm birth and low birth weight infants increased for women of Arabic descent, but had not for any other group.
“In that paper, science, social science, and my own life experiences collided in a way I had never known was possible. It was exhilarating and devastating at the same time,” El-Sayed wrote of the study in his memoir.
In 2008, El-Sayed was chosen for the prestigious Rhodes Scholarship, which would take him to England’s University of Oxford for two years of research. While there, he worked on using AI-based modeling to simulate the many social factors that created racial disparities in rates of obesity in England.
El-Sayed then made his way to New York, where he began the clinical side of his program to become a clinician-scientist. He figured out how to navigate the emergency room where he worked, but often felt at odds with a system that perpetuated the disparities he wanted to work toward ending.
His breaking point was watching the treatment of Martha, as he refers to her in his memoir, who had slipped and hit her head in a subway station. His colleagues had not ordered a CT scan, which should have been the first step in assessing the unhoused woman, and were preparing to discharge her. He spent two weeks caring for Martha, learning that she was also HIV positive and a person with alcoholism and diabetes who had been in and out of the medical system, and arranging for her to go to a rehabilitation facility.
Instead, she went to live with her daughter. Several weeks later, as El-Sayed was boarding a subway, he found Martha sleeping there. Feeling that he, and the medical system, had failed her, he pulled his residency application that day.
“Practicing medicine wasn’t the path to solving the problems I cared about, as scared as I was to admit it after so many years of training,” he wrote.
As a professor of epidemiology at Columbia University, El-Sayed focused his academic work largely on health disparities, with an emphasis on maternal mortality. He also studied the health of Arab Americans.
One paper that found Arab mothers had better birth outcomes when the father was also Arab was labeled as “racist” by Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz. “Scary stuff,” he wrote on X. That paper had not received much attention from the scientific community before that criticism, but El-Sayed’s work on Arab Americans was seen by some as pioneering.
“I think he brought this population into the health disparities literature in a way that many folks before him had trouble doing,” said Nadia Abuelezam, an epidemiologist at Michigan State University who has worked with El-Sayed. Before working with him, doing research on Arab populations had been “very discouraged at my institution because there wasn’t a lot of funding for it and folks didn’t see it as a priority population.”
In a 2011 study, El-Sayed, working with Galea, found that marriage was not as protective against poor birth outcomes as many had thought. Galea said the study illustrated El-Sayed’s research approach: “A searching mind, one that is not willing to accept that things are static, and that we should be always thinking about our world and how it may be shifting.”
Katherine Keyes, a former Columbia colleague who published several papers with El-Sayed on infant mortality and on the public health impacts of incarceration, agreed. “He thought of the idea, he located the data, he analyzed the data, he brought together experts who knew how to interpret the data,” she said. “Every step of the way was Abdul creating something out of nothing, some knowledge that didn’t exist before.”
Lofty ideas and political realities
To those close to him at Columbia, it was obvious El-Sayed was destined for bigger things. Some wondered whether he would lead a university or school of public health. The answer came a little over a year after he became a professor there. He was tapped by the mayor of Detroit for a homecoming of sorts, leading the Detroit Health Department.
To his colleagues, it seemed like an obvious transition. El-Sayed was frequently frustrated at the slow speed by which academia can make a difference in people’s lives. Academics “are much more ready to study than to act as a rule, and that’s been true for generations. I think Abdul was uncomfortable with that,” said Steven Mooney, an epidemiologist at the University of Washington who previously worked with El-Sayed.
In taking the job, El-Sayed was facing an uphill battle. In what was the poorest major city in America, he was tasked with rebuilding the health agency after a prior administration had privatized it. He had lofty ideas: He launched a program to provide up to 5,000 children with free eyeglasses, increased testing for lead in water following the water crisis in nearby Flint, and launched an initiative to help residents pay off their medical debt, which has paid off over $95 million in debt, according to a local government dashboard. (El-Sayed has claimed on the campaign trail it has paid for $700 million).
But the progress he was able to make didn’t feel like enough. Mooney recalls El-Sayed’s dissatisfaction with a project studying the potential impact of building demolitions on blood lead levels of children living nearby. It was a difficult problem. “We couldn’t say the demolitions weren’t a problem for kids, but we couldn’t say they were either,” Mooney said “You could feel him being disappointed in that result.” The data were not compelling enough to spur action.
That frustration grew with the election of Donald Trump in 2016.
“So many of the programs that we had instituted were funded, directly or indirectly, by federal grant programs,” El-Sayed wrote in his memoir. “Those programs would likely face cuts or consolidations that would likely hurt the poor Black communities like Detroit that Trump would characterize as ‘American carnage’ in his inauguration.”
A few months later, he submitted his resignation and launched a campaign for governor.
“As an appointed public official,” El-Sayed told STAT, “you sit behind an elected politician who gets to set that frame of the debate. I think it’s just really important, as a scientist and public health leader, to be able to engage in the conversation about what that public mandate ought to be, about where public health ought to go.”
He said he hopes to embolden public health leaders to “pick broad, righteous fights” with private corporations that have been “hurting people.” The hesitation to do so, he believes, has harmed trust in the field.
During the Covid pandemic, he recalled, there was a “gentleman who was like, ‘Look, man, I’m going to take this vaccine. I get it, but you’re asking me to take a vaccine that didn’t exist a year ago for a disease that didn’t exist a year ago, but … I can’t afford my insulin, which is a medication that’s existed for 100 years for a disease I had my whole life.’
“We’re not standing up to the paywall that sits in front of a lot of the incredible things that science can produce for people,” he said.
‘Carefully analyzed the health care system’
El-Sayed garnered national attention as the possible first Muslim governor in the U.S., but lost in a primary to Gretchen Whitmer. He would remain a fixture on the national stage.
While campaigning, El-Sayed had appeared on the popular, left-leaning podcast, “Pod Save America.” Believing there were few forums left for discussion of public health, El-Sayed flew out to Los Angeles and pitched the same network on the idea of a public health-focused podcast. He did 10 episodes about what he saw as the most pressing issues.
Plans for what was to be a limited series changed as news of a novel coronavirus spread across the globe. El-Sayed was asked to do a biweekly show. He also campaigned with Sanders, who was running for the Democratic nomination for president.
He has incorporated Sanders’ Medicare for All initiative as one of the policy pillars of his Senate campaign. The proposal remains an uphill battle. But the public may be increasingly receptive to the idea: Support is at its highest since Sanders introduced it in 2016, according to a recent KFF poll. Two-thirds of respondents said they back a national health plan, with support higher among Democrats and independents.
That figure is likely the result of growing concerns about the affordability of health care, said Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at KFF. “I would not interpret our poll as some indication that the public is knowledgeable about Medicare for All,” he said. The poll also found that support dropped when people were told Medicare for All would eliminate private health insurance, lead to delays in treatments, and require higher taxes.
Joel Zinberg, director of the public health and American well-being initiative at Paragon Health Institute, a free market health policy think tank, and a critic of the proposal, said El-Sayed “relies very heavily on the idea that there’s going to be these tremendous administrative savings, you’re getting rid of complexity, whereas in fact, that’s sort of an illusion.”
Allies of El-Sayed, however, hope that as someone who has written a book on Medicare for All and has seen many sides of the health care system, El-Sayed can legitimize the discussion around the proposal.
“A common critique of Medicare for All folks is that it’s just a slogan. It’s not serious, not rigorous on the policy. For Abdul that’s certainly not the case,” said Hayden Rooke-Ley, a friend of El-Sayed’s and a professor of health services policy and practice at Brown University.
“He’s somebody who has carefully analyzed the health care system, and asked what is the most efficient, just, and democratically accountable way to finance it and insure people,” he said. “And he’s concluded, I think correctly, that it would be to expand Medicare to everybody.”
