US and Japan agree to establish a Japanese facility for joint missile production
CEBU, Philippines — The United States and Japan have agreed to establish a Japanese facility for the joint production of advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles, the Japanese defense chief said.
It is the latest move by the allies, which have repeatedly expressed alarm over China's growing assertiveness in Asia.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi made the announcement in a news conference Wednesday night in the central Philippine province of Cebu, where he met U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the sidelines of an annual meeting of Southeast Asian defense chiefs and their major Asian and Western counterparts.
Koizumi renews concern over China's naval activity
Koizumi raised concern Thursday about China's increasing naval activity in southwestern Japan. He said that three Chinese destroyers and a coast guard ship together crossed the Osumi Strait south of the southern main island of Kyushu and headed east to the Pacific Ocean this week. It was the first such fleet configuration his ministry has spotted, he said.
Koizumi said he cited the incident as "an example illustrating the challenging security environment in the region" in his remark at a session Thursday. His ministry will keep watching the Chinese activity with high level of interest, he said. Japan has been accelerating military buildup in southwestern Japan to deter China.
The annual meetings aim to avert a major regional conflict and strengthen defense cooperation. On the sidelines of the meetings, however, the U.S. and China and their allies have often traded criticisms.
Japan, US to bolster joint missile production capacity
The missiles that will be produced as part of a joint effort called "Operation Supercharge" are essential for the F-35 fighter jets, Koizumi said. The two sides agreed to build a final assembly and inspection plant for the Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, or AMRAAM, in Japan, he said. The U.S.-made F-35s are one of the world's most advanced aircraft and are also used by the Japanese military.
During his brief meeting with Hegseth in Cebu, Koizumi said he "shared a sense of crisis … regarding the increasingly severe regional situation and we agreed to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-U.S. alliance with greater speed and intensity than ever before."
"We reaffirmed the importance of a free and open international order based on the rule of law, which rejects any attempts to unilaterally alter the status quo through the use of force, coercion or other means," Koizumi said.
Hegseth reassures US engagement in the region
Hegseth renewed the Trump administration's repeated assurances of commitment to help deter aggression in the region in a separate meeting on Wednesday with ASEAN defense ministers, who were led by the host, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. Like Koizumi, Hegseth did not mention China by name in expressing his security concerns in the region.
"The approach we're taking, we describe as strong, quiet and clear," Hegseth told the ASEAN defense chiefs. "Strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics to let our actions speak for themselves."
His message is "clear enough that our friends, our partners and potential adversaries understand precisely where the United States stands and that we will defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners," Hegseth said.
Hegseth has assured the Philippines, the oldest treaty ally of Washington in Asia, that the Trump administration will build a robust deterrence against China's increasingly aggressive actions in the disputed South China Sea. Beijing claims the busy waterway, a key global trade route, virtually in its entirety.
Australia shows commitment to defend the rule of law in the Pacific
Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles said his country's forces, along with allies like the U.S., will press on with efforts to defend the rule of law despite China's increasing assertiveness, including in the South China Sea. Australia protested last year after a Chinese J-16 fighter aircraft released flares and passed within 30 meters (100 feet) of an Australian P-8 Poseidon surveillance jet over the disputed waters.
"That doesn't deter us from doing what we need to do and that's essentially asserting the rules-based order here in the end of the Pacific," Marles told The Associated Press in Cebu on Wednesday. "Freedom of navigation on the high seas is profoundly important for Australia."
The Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei, all ASEAN member states, along with Taiwan, also have overlapping claims in the South China Sea. Confrontations have particularly escalated between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and navy vessels in disputed shoals and outlying waters.
Washington has warned that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces, ships and aircraft come under an armed attack, including in the South China Sea.
Beijing and Tokyo have a separate dispute over tiny Japanese-controlled islands in the East China Sea, with both sides often accusing the other of infringing on their maritime territory.

Domestic worker gets jail for punching non-verbal autistic child at least 23 times
The 29-year-old woman also recorded videos of the family’s three children naked in the toilet and sent them to her husband “to show him how mischievous the victims were”.
SINGAPORE: A domestic worker was sentenced to three years’ jail on Friday (Oct 30) for repeatedly abusing a four-year-old autistic child in her care, including punching him at least 23 times.
She was also punished for recording obscene videos of the family’s three children, including the boy’s seven-year-old sister and one-year-old brother, and sending them to her husband.
The 29-year-old woman, who cannot be named to protect the identity of her victims, kicked the four-year-old boy’s head twice in a separate incident.
About a month after she started working for the family, she also used a handheld shower head to spray water directly onto the one-year-old boy’s face for 16 seconds, causing him to flinch and cry.
The woman was arrested in March after her employer found videos and photographs of the abuse and his naked children on her phone.
Investigations uncovered four videos and two still images of the children naked in the unit’s toilet.
She had sent two of the videos and both images to her husband “to show him how mischievous the victims were”, the court heard.
The Indonesian national started working for the household in January. According to court documents, she abused the boy because she was feeling tired and frustrated from caring for him.
Deputy Public Prosecutor Mohamed Riasudeen asked for 35 to 41 months’ jail for the woman, highlighting that she repeatedly punched the boy even as he was trying to shield himself.
She removed his hands to continue the assault and the video she recorded showed that she was using a considerable amount of force, he said.
The boy was non-verbal and “entirely unable” to seek help or report the abuse to his parents, which made him "more defenceless" than another child his age, the prosecution stressed.
The woman's decision to record the abuse demonstrated a “chilling indifference” to the victim's pain and suffering, Mr Riasudeen said. 
Feeling tired and frustrated from caring for the boy did not justify her actions, he added.
While the prosecution and defence agreed that the videos of the naked children were not taken with any intention for sexual gratification, Mr Riasudeen argued that the fact that the woman's position as their caregiver was an aggravating factor.
He also noted that her husband could have forwarded the videos to other people.
The woman’s lawyer, Mr Ariffin Sha, who represented her pro bono under the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme, argued for two years and 10.5 months' jail for her.
He did not dispute the prosecution’s sentencing arguments for the abuse charges, but argued that her obscene videos of the children were not the “archetypal offence” for sexual gratification.
Mr Ariffin, of Shehzhadee Law Corporation, said the woman wanted to place her unqualified apology to the victims and their family on record.
Despite the stress and her two requests to transfer out of the job before these incidents, the woman recognised that these factors do not excuse her actions, he added.
Laying out the woman’s sentence, District Judge Sharmila Sripathy-Shanaz highlighted that the child was non-verbal – he could not speak for himself, ask for help, or tell others about the abuse.
“There are few betrayals of trust more disturbing than the abuse of a child by the very person entrusted with his care,” she said, noting that this case was particularly troubling because the main victim was a child with special needs.
The judge acknowledged the physical and emotional demands of caregiving but stressed that such difficulties could never justify abusing a child.
“Stress is not a license for violence nor is frustration an excuse for cruelty,” she said.
The sentence would have been “considerably higher” if there were evidence of physical injury to the victims, the judge added.

BreakingUS bans Chinese labs from testing electronics ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
The FCC measure targets testing facilities with alleged PLA ties, giving US labs until December 2028 to expand capacity
The United States on Thursday banned all Chinese laboratories from testing electronic devices destined for the US market, just weeks before US President Donald Trump is due to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) voted to bar testing laboratories and certification bodies in China and other economies that lack a “mutual recognition agreement” or reciprocal trade agreement with the US.

Fan fiction website AO3 is down, and it could take weeks to recover
The site's data is reportedly intact, but the cause of the outage is still unknown.
Archive of Our Own (AO3), one of the best-known homes for people who read and write fan fiction online, is currently down for maintenance. The Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the nonprofit that founded AO3, took the site offline just after 3AM ET and originally planned to keep it down for only 12 hours, per its status page, but now says maintenance could take weeks.
"We estimate that service restoration for #AO3 will take around 2 weeks but it could be up to 4 weeks," the OTW says. "We are hopeful that we will be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state sooner. If that does happen, there may be times when the site has to be brought down temporarily until this is fully resolved. Please stay tuned for further info."
AO3 hosts millions of transformative fanworks based on existing books, movies, TV shows and more, and likely serves millions more readers who want to read stories about their favorite characters and worlds. The OTW has said the site's data is intact, according to a former AO3 volunteer who moderates r/AO3, which should mean those stories are safe. What's less clear is what caused this lengthy outage.
The OTW logged problems with email notifications, search, history and listings between October 23 and 24, but hasn't elaborated on what issues it's dealing with now. In the last two weeks, two major security vulnerabilities, one found in the PHP scripting language and another found in TLS certificates, have forced some websites to go offline to patch and protect themselves. That includes another OTW site, Fanlore, which was briefly shut down to deal with the PHP flaw. The nonprofit hasn't given any indication it's dealing with those same problems on AO3. Whatever the cause, though, the OTW's engineers are volunteers rather than paid staff, which might make fixes take longer to implement.
Engadget asked the OTW to comment on the outage and share what maintenance work is being done. We'll update this article if we hear back.

Strauss Zelnick is relentlessly focused on making "the best entertainment on earth." There's no confusion about that mission among his employees, he said.
"I have 13,000 colleagues," the Take-Two Interactive CEO said at Business Insider's The Long Play event in New York City on Thursday. "100% of them can and will tell you exactly what I just said."
His management philosophy — "establish a mission, establish a strategy, and promulgate collective culture" — is about to get its biggest test in years.
Take-Two is the publisher behind popular games like "Red Dead Redemption" and "NBA 2K," and, on November 19, they'll launch a new "Grand Theft Auto." The wildly popular series hasn't had a new mainline installment since 2013 and has delayed its launch twice in an effort to meet the studio's exacting standards. GTA 6 is central to Take-Two's forecast for at least $8 billion in net bookings for fiscal 2027.
Zelnick has run the company since 2007. To align employee incentives with Take-Two's big expectations, he believes compensation should be based on a formula aligned with the company's mission — not left to manager discretion.
"I personally believe that discretionary compensation programs are toxic," he said, adding that they create "politics and get you the wrong results, especially over time."
"So, we're all formulaic," he said. "You perform, the company performs — you get paid. You perform, the company doesn't perform — you don't get paid. Company performs, you don't perform — if you still have your job, you get paid."
Zelnick also said he has no chief of staff, is available on Slack 24/7, and shares his cellphone number with employees.
"If you're not president of the United States, you have no reason to have a chief of staff," he said.
That doesn't mean he will swoop in and override an employee's manager, said Zelnick, who considers himself an empathetic listener. He said workers should feel heard — and that he will try to help them solve a problem.
Still, he doesn't believe his formula at Take-Two is necessarily the right approach for every leader.
"Leadership comes in all flavors," he said. "You have to be your own kind of leader, and I don't think anyone should adopt my skills, because you're not me."

A few weeks ago, French company Mistral released an early version of its new artificial intelligence model, nicknamed Le Chonk. At the time, the company said it was the most advanced open-weight offering outside of China. After further refinement, Mistral now says Le Chonk is the “world’s best” open-weight model for automated coding and cybersecurity.
The advances, Mistral says, were made possible by feeding the model increasingly difficult cybersecurity and coding problems, which allowed the trillion-parameter Le Chonk to match or surpass models from leading Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Z.ai.
“It’s a pivotal moment in the global AI leadership race,” Pierre Stock, VP of science at Mistral, told reporters during a press briefing. “It offers frontier capabilities for enterprises and governments to defend against an increasing threat level in cyber.”
The finalized version of Le Chonk is now freely available for anybody to access. After a flurry of AI-related cybersecurity incidents, Mistral claims that it’s important for the West to have its own advanced open-weight models. “You have no guarantee that [Chinese models] won’t behave maliciously. They can be threat vectors,” Stock said.
The most high-profile episode occurred when one of OpenAI’s models broke loose from a testing sandbox and hacked into multiple companies over the summer. It sparked panic over the idea that AI could escape human oversight and be abused by threat actors to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. (One of the affected companies, Hugging Face, used an open-weight model from China to assess and defend against the attack.)
Since then, AI has unearthed security vulnerabilities in ubiquitous software, too. In October, a raft of websites were taken offline after an AI tool discovered serious flaws in a foundational piece of web technology.
Mistral pitches its open-weight models, like Le Chonk, as part of the solution. If AI is destined to become a central feature of both cyber offense and defense, the argument goes, businesses and governments will need to be equipped with models that are freely available and cannot be switched off remotely, unlike proprietary models from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.
“AI is going to be like electricity. You don’t want to live in a world in which your neighbor can cut off electricity from one day to another,” Stock said. “Once you open source the weights, they’re all over the internet. It’s impossible to cut off access.”
The trade-off, however, is that freely available models can also be downloaded and customized by threat actors.
“It’s clearly a dual-use technology,” Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “Anything that’s available to download and circulate unfettered has the ability to be abused as well as used for productive purposes.”
According to Pilling, though it’s possible a Chinese model with internet access could siphon away data, all advanced models are capable of going rogue without careful supervision—no matter their country of origin.
“The technical realities and the narrative—which often has a nationalistic leaning—are two different things,” he says.“It’s about having the right monitoring and controls in place to be confident that, even if the model was trying to be deceptive or nefarious, you might have some way of detecting it.”

Differences within Janata Dal (United) surfaced on Thursday (October 29, 2026) when party MLC Neeraj Kumar refused to seek the blessing of senior party leader and Union Minister Rajiv Ranjan alias Lalan Singh.
Mr. Neeraj who has registered victory for the fourth consecutive term in Patna Graduate constituency was speaking to reporters after meeting party’s president Sanjay Jha in Patna.
When reporters asked whether he will also go to seek the blessing of Lalan Singh, Neeraj replied, “Shawal hi paida nahi hota hai, akhir mera gunah kya tha ki inti pareshani jhelni padi (There is no question about it—what did I do wrong that I had to endure such trouble?).”
During the entire Legislative Council election, Mr. Singh did not even campaign in support of Neeraj, rather gave moral support to Anant Singh who was campaigning against Neeraj Kumar.
Making a direct attack on the Union Minister, Mr. Kumar said, “My parents and ancestors have given me this lesson that if you have ever taken a debt, make sure to pay it back, and I shall repay this political debt with interest.”
He further said, “Those who wish to offer congratulations are doing so—sending blessings through social media and through various other channels and I have received immense love from the party workers.”
Asked about any chance of a reconciliation, Mr. Kumar said, “I didn’t even make any attempt towards it, I was never in favour of one. However, everyone should fulfil their ‘party duty’ just as I had fulfilled my own party duty.”

When the conflict had started between Neeraj Kumar and Anant Singh, JD(U) Working President Sanjay Kumar Jha had said that Lalan Singh was deputed to resolve the issue. All three leaders belong to Bhumihar caste.
However, after meeting Anant Singh, the Union Minister had defended the Bahubali (strongman) MLA from Mokama and had pointed towards past actions of Neeraj Kumar, asserting that when Anant Singh was contesting the election (2025 Assembly election), some party leaders, including Neeraj Kumar had opposed him and party leadership failed to take action against Neeraj that time.
“Har kriya ki pratikriya hoti hai (every action is bound to have a reaction); it takes two hands to clap—both hands must come together. Lalan Singh indirectly gave moral support to Anant Singh, and after that, Anant Singh openly opposed JD(U) official candidate Neeraj and campaigned for Jan Suraaj Party (JSP) candidate Anuj Singh. After the victory, Neeraj Kumar met all the top leaders of JD(U) to seek their blessings, including former Chief Minister Nitish Kumar, Deputy Chief Minister Vijay Kumar Choudhary and Sanjay Jha. He also met Rashtriya Lok Morcha (RLM) President and Rajya Sabha member Upendra Kushwaha.

Sources in the party said that JD(U) leader and minister Ashok Choudhary is also on the radar of the party’s leadership, and action could be taken against him as well for secretly working against the party’s official candidate.
In Darbhanga Graduate constituency, RJD candidate Anil Jha defeated BJP’s Sarvesh Kumar. With this out of eight seats of Legislative Council, RJD and BJP won two seats each, JD(U) and JSP one seat each and two by Independent candidates.

Since 2020, under Walz and Flanagan's leadership, the state has awarded several grants to Southside Harm Reduction Services, a Minneapolis-based charity that operates several harm reduction programs, including boofing kits. The $8 million figure cited in examples of the claim is not the amount of money Southside spent on the boofing kits — it is the total amount of money granted to Southside for all purposes. (Though Snopes calculated that figure at $9.1 million, promised through 2030.)
A week before the 2024 U.S. presidential election, conservative investigative journalism outlet The Washington Free Beacon published a story saying Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz provided funding to an organization that gives drug users "booty bumping kits," allowing them to consume drugs through the rectum (a practice sometimes called "boofing").
The claim about the Democratic then-candidate for vice president spread on social media before fizzling out.
Two years later, The Washington Free Beacon published another story saying Walz and the state's Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan "Steered Millions To Pay for Disgusting 'Booty Bumping' Kits." Flanagan is currently running for U.S. Senate in the 2026 midterms.
Citing the outlet's 2026 report, social media users claimed in October that Walz and Flanagan have provided roughly $8 million to Southside Harm Reduction Services, a Minneapolis-based nonprofit organization that operates several harm reduction programs and supposedly provides the kits.
Snopes readers also contacted us for more information about this story.
We found that Walz and Flanagan's administration has provided funding to Southside since 2020. While The Washington Free Beacon claimed in October 2026 that the state government has promised roughly $8 million to the organization, Snopes calculated Southside has been promised $9.1 million in grants through 2030.
Southside does provide "booty bumping kits" to drug users. However, it was not possible to find evidence that the organization spent "millions" in state funding on such paraphernalia. The actual figure is likely to be significantly lower — not a seven-figure sum.
Snopes contacted Flanagan's campaign, the Minnesota state budget office and Southside Harm Reduction Services for comment on the story. None had replied prior to publication.
What's true?
In 2023, during Walz and Flanagan's time in office, the Minnesota State Legislature passed a budget that designated $100 million in funding to organizations that assist the state's homeless population. Southside Harm Reduction Services is directly named in the news release announcing the funding.
"[The charity provides] harm reduction services via outreach to people experiencing unsheltered homelessness who use drugs, primarily in or near Minneapolis and St. Paul," according to the news release. "Services include syringe exchange, naloxone distribution, education, rapid HIV testing and referrals to social services including housing."
Snopes reviewed contracts for active and expired grants between the state and Southside, confirming they are a recipient of funding and have been since 2020.
Turning to the nonprofit's social media sites and yearly reports shows the "booty bumping kit" in question and its accompanying mini-zine containing instructions and information about the paraphernalia.
In sum, Southside Harm Reduction Services does receive funding from the state government, and it does provide boofing kits.
Clarifying the figures
The $8 million figure does not represent the amount of money the state has spent on boofing kits, as some may have incorrectly inferred from the social media posts. The Washington Free Beacon says this figure is the total amount of money the state granted to Southside. The headline of the outlet's article could, however, lead some readers to incorrectly believe the nonprofit spent "millions" on the kits.
Using Minnesota's funding transparency database, Snopes calculated that The Washington Free Beacon's $8 million figure was previously correct but is now outdated. Our calculations showed the state's Health Department and Human Services Department have promised Southside approximately $9.3 million in total between 2020 and 2030 for all operational purposes. 
The grants function as monthly reimbursements from the state (Page 4, Section 3.2) rather than an up-front lump sum payment. In other words, if Southside does not spend the $9.3 million, the state does not pay anything.
This is noteworthy because budgeting documentation from multiple grants reveals that Southside sometimes, but not always, does not spend all its allocated money (see the table on Page 7). For instance, in an amendment to a grant worth $620,400 spanning a 42-month period, the organization budgeted $22,200 from the grant for "supplies" for the 2025 fiscal year (part of which would presumably have been used to fund the boofing kits). But, according to that grant amendment, Southside spent less than $6,000 of the grant on supplies that year. 
Other grants provide a more detailed breakdown of the organization's budgeting. Southside's largest active grant for a total of $2.5 million runs between October 2025 and June 2029. The budgeting documentation provided alongside that contract breaks down Southside's yearly budget for supplies — $84,378 for the 2026 fiscal year (PDF Page 29) — into individual components, including $37,000 for "Safer-use supplies for safer injection, smoking, and all works" (PDF Page 31).
Southside also spends the grant money on things like travel, benefits and salaries for personnel — not just supplies.
Given that boofing is a rather uncommon method of drug ingestion, that Southside does not always spend all of its granted money, and that the money gets spent in other areas, we conclude Southside is spending a a small fraction of the funding it receives from the Minnesota state government on the kits. 
Why offer these kits in the first place?
As its name suggests, Southside Harm Reduction Services provides harm reduction programs for the Minneapolis-Saint Paul metro area, according to its website. Though the kits may sound odd, they do qualify as harm reduction products.
According to the National Harm Reduction Coalition, harm reduction is a set of principles that aim to reduce the negative consequences that come with drug use, like HIV or hepatitis C infections. The principles are formed around the idea that humans will always choose to consume substances, both legally and illegally, and therefore it is worth minimizing the potential harm these substances can cause.
Well-known harm reduction programs are needle and syringe exchanges, which are called syringe service programs, or SSPs, in the United States. Since infections like HIV and hepatitis C can be spread through contact with blood, used needles and syringes can transmit the virus from person to person. SSPs reduce infections by approximately 50%, according to the U.S. government. These programs also help establish reliable lines of communication with drug users, which can be used to provide additional information on treatments for substance use disorders. (Boofing also requires a syringe, explaining why Southside offers the kits).
In addition to a syringe exchange, Southside's website notes it also helps give people access to both mental and physical care, including substance use programs, vaccinations, STI testing and more.

Kauvery Hospital, Alwarpet, Chennai, has treated a 63-year-old man with severe leakage in his aortic valve using a minimally invasive procedure called transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), the hospital said at a press conference. The patient had a hole in one of the leaflets of his aortic valve and had previously undergone mitral valve replacement.
Aortic regurgitation occurs when the aortic valve does not close properly, allowing blood to flow backwards into the heart. Treating this condition through a catheter-based procedure can be challenging because the valve may not have enough calcium deposits to help secure the replacement valve. The patient’s previous mitral valve replacement added to the complexity.
The HANCHOR valve has a frame that expands with a balloon and a special anchoring mechanism made of nitinol, a flexible metal alloy. This mechanism is designed to hold the replacement valve securely in place by gripping the existing valve leaflets.
The hospital said checks after the procedure showed no remaining leakage through or around the replacement valve and no abnormal narrowing. No significant problems with the heart’s electrical signals were reported. The patient was discharged three days later.
Rajaram Anantharaman, senior consultant interventional cardiologist said the valve’s anchoring mechanism helped address the challenges of positioning the replacement valve in this case.
Asik Ali, senior consultant and clinical lead, Cardiac Imaging Radiology; Mahesh Kumar K., medical superintendent; and Kamal Kanth, consultant cardiologist, were also present at the press conference.

The law firm that helped set up Elon Musk’s America PAC has created a new, nationwide “election integrity” organization aligned with Donald Trump’s false claims of election fraud, WIRED has learned.
The organization, a nonprofit called the Association of State and Local Election Officials, was established by a lawyer then at Lex Politica, the Musk-linked law firm founded by Chris Gober, who was chief counsel for America PAC in 2024 and is now running in Texas for a spot in the House of Representatives.
The board of directors, according to the nonprofit’s registration filing in Texas, boasts Florida secretary of state Cord Byrd, current and former state election officials in Georgia, a Michigan state representative, and the president of Cleta Mitchell’s Election Integrity Network, a Trump administration-aligned election denial group. Byrd announced his involvement with the group—which he said won’t begin until after the election—alongside Florida governor Ron DeSantis in September, as the pair touted its mission, which aims to bring what they call “election integrity” policies down to the state and local level nationwide.
It’s not clear if Musk is involved in the organization. Until now, Musk has simply been a funder of Republican candidates and causes, and a benefactor of government contracts. Musk’s financial involvement in the midterm elections has been extensive: Musk’s America PAC is financing a sprawling canvassing operation aimed at helping Republican candidates get out the vote in November, and Musk is the single largest donor to Republican candidates this election cycle, spending more than $445 million, targeting Senate races key to maintaining a Republican majority. Since July, Musk has spent nearly as much money—$276 million—to boost Republican candidates as he did during the entire 2024 presidential election cycle. These elections are crucial for Musk. If Democrats win majorities in the House and Senate, Musk and his companies could be the subject of congressional investigations.
The link between a law firm that has worked with Musk and officials involved in purported “election integrity” activities is not surprising. For years, Musk has pushed the racist great replacement theory, which posits that minorities are systematically replacing white people in the US and in Western countries around the world. Election denialism—rooted in the unfounded theory of widespread voting by undocumented immigrants—is part of that racist theory of demographic societal change.
Musk has continually pushed election conspiracies that align with Trump’s false claims of election fraud, and this year, he’s doubled down. Musk has been a major disseminator of election misinformation this cycle, and recently boosted the false story that Texas US senate candidate James Talarico had been committed to a psychiatric facility in Ohio. America PAC has also spread inaccurate information about mail-in ballots.
The Association of State and Local Election Officials was first registered on June 17 by Michael Garcar as a nonprofit in Texas. At the time, Garcar was an attorney at Lex Politica, which was expanded after its lead lawyer, Gober, helped launch Musk’s America PAC. Gober has represented Musk’s and America PAC’s political interests in court cases in Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.
On July 20, the Association of State and Local Election Officials was granted tax-exempt status by the IRS, according to an agency letter addressed to the organization at its Washington, DC, address. That address—a box in a UPS Store on Pennsylvania Avenue—is the same as the one Garcar listed on the organization’s Texas filing and belongs to Lex Politica, according to a US Supreme Court filing from one of the firm’s attorneys, Erin Hawley, wife of Senator Josh Hawley. The nonprofit’s Texas registration was first unearthed by True North Research, a non-partisan research group.
Garcar has since left Lex Politica and now works for Five Rings Law Group. The firm lists just two partners—both Lex Politica alums—and former Koch Industries lawyer Jenny Kim. Before launching Five Rings, Kim worked for Gober.
Garcar, Kim, and Gober did not respond to questions about Lex Politica’s ties to the Association of State and Local Election Officials.
At a September 24 press conference about the organization, Byrd and DeSantis announced their partnership with the nonprofit and said the Association of State and Local Election Officials will use Florida’s hard-line voting and election rules as a “blueprint” to enact similar policies across the country.
Byrd said the organization would “have state chapters to support, educate, and train local and state election officials on election integrity, because that’s something that the other side has been very good at.”
“They’re the ones going in and certifying and training people who run our elections, and not doing it in a way that we think comports with the law and voter trust,” Byrd said. The association “will be a national organization to promote election integrity, principles, and federal law and policy,” he added.
Under Byrd and DeSantis’ leadership, Florida has enacted rules and laws that voting rights advocates have criticized, including passing a state version of the federal SAVE Act that requires proof of citizenship at polling locations and prohibits the use of student IDs to vote beginning in 2027. “I’m very excited to head up that initiative and take what we’ve done in Florida as the blueprint, as the model for the nation, take it nationwide,” Byrd said in September.
The offices of Byrd and DeSantis did not respond to questions about their involvement with the organization.
The organization’s board is also staffed by Sharon Bemis, the president of Mitchell’s Election Integrity Network, the country’s most prominent election denial organization; Julie Adams, an election denier who is both a member of the Fulton County Board of Elections in Georgia and a regional coordinator for the Election Integrity Network; Janice Johnston, who recently left the MAGA-dominated Georgia State Election Board; and Michigan state house representative Ann Bollin, who has coordinated with the Election Integrity Network.
The organization’s board members did not respond to questions for this story, though Johnston and Bollin have both previously denied being election deniers. The organization’s Texas registration contains no information about its work, and the group does not appear to have a web presence.
But the presence of Johnston and Adams on the board is telling.
In Georgia, Adams has made a name for herself by pushing Trump’s conspiracies about widespread election fraud and has sued multiple times for access to voting records with the help of the Republican National Committee. She has refused to certify results without being allowed to inspect voting records.
Johnston recently left Georgia’s State Election Board for what she said were “family and personal responsibility” reasons, and her time there was marked by turmoil, partisanship, and legal battles based on false fraud claims. Under her direction, the election board pursued specious investigations of Fulton County, supported mass voter purges championed by election denial activists, and worked to effectively eliminate voting machines.
Adams and Johnston have long targeted Fulton County for supposed fraud, and gleefully celebrated when, in January, the FBI raided an elections warehouse there, seizing tens of thousands of ballots from the 2020 election. Johnston was one of the unnamed witnesses in the FBI affidavit that preceded the raid, providing information about alleged double-counted ballots to the agency that had already been investigated and proven to have had no effect on the outcome of the 2020 election.
The Justice Department briefly fought in court to keep her name hidden from public view, but described a witness in the affidavit as “a Republican-appointed member” of the State Election Board who previously “was an obstetrician,” which identified Johnston. As the raid was being carried out, Johnston went live on Steve Bannon’s War Room podcast from an SUV parked nearby.
When asked about Johnston’s presence on the board of the new Musk-linked election denial organization, Sara Tindall Ghazal, the lone Democrat on the Georgia State Election Board and Johnston’s former colleague, replied, “lol.”
“I mean this quite seriously, ‘lol.’ That’s my comment,” she tells WIRED.
And while Musk has quietly increased his political funding of Republicans, he has taken a bit of a step back from publicly discussing or posting about US politics and elections—with the exception of Talarico. His most recent post about voting is from September, when he responded to a question from Senator Mike Lee, a Republican from Utah. “Who benefits from noncitizen voting?” Lee asked on X.
“Democrats, which is why they push for open borders and noncitizen voting!” Musk responded. “Incentives explain behavior.”

Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
- Published
A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.
The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.
That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.
DR Congo
The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.
The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.
Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.
The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.
His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.
Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.
Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.
Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.
On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.
We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Uganda
However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.
But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.
Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.
The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.
But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.
It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.
Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.
Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.
Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.
Kenya
Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.
By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.
He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.
The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.
The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.
Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.
Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.
CDC advice
Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.
"When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said.
The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected.
The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist.

Spain reckons with 2nd deadly train crash of the year ahead of national election
URDA, Spain — Spain's second high-speed rail disaster this year, a crash in which one train struck another from behind, killing 68 people, has raised fresh concerns about the safety of the country's rail network.
Spain's network of high-speed rail has been considered one of the nation's crowning achievements. It ranks second to China in track mileage in the world. Until this year, it had not endured a deadly crash since coming into service over three decades ago.
The collision Wednesday that turned a sleepy stretch of rail lined by olive groves into a scene of carnage came just four weeks before the country votes in a national election.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez visited the crash site in the central province of Toledo after regional authorities confirmed that more than 60 people had died and dozens more were being treated at hospitals.
Only in January, 46 people had died when one train jumped the track and slammed into the side of another going the opposite way in southern Spain.
Sánchez pledged an investigation into the latest collision and improvements to prevent another tragedy like the two that have shaken trust in a rail system that carried 45 million travelers last year, including millions of tourists.
"It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail," Sánchez said. "It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year."
Sánchez's government declared three days of mourning starting Thursday.
Both deadly crashes this year involved a train operated by the state-owned RENFE company and one from the privately owned IRYO. Spain only liberalized its high-speed rail service in 2021, with the Italian IRYO starting service the following year.
Political implications for Sánchez ahead of election
Sánchez has weathered many crises since taking power in 2018, staying in power and winning reelection after the COVID-19 pandemic and the global rise in inflation.
But polls show he faces another uphill battle when voters cast ballots in Spain's first national election since 2023. The new rail disaster can't help the prospects of his Socialist party.
Sánchez and other progressive parties had hoped to leverage a wave of discontent over housing costs and high rents when he called for early elections earlier this month.
About an hour before news of Wednesday's crash spread, Sánchez had posted on X a message that "There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about this country."
Now it appears he will have to handle concerns over the state of Spain's rail service along with attacks from right-wing parties over his liberal migration policies and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which both he and his wife deny.
His transport minister, Óscar Puente, had to handle media questions over whether he would resign following a second major train wreck under his watch. His response was that he was fully focused on dealing with the collision, not his future.
Sánchez's main rival, Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, demanded a full investigation of the crash. The conservative leader said that in respect for the victims his party canceled its campaign events for the day.
"This is the moment to respect the dead, the injured and their families," Núñez Feijóo said. "That does not mean we will ignore the fact that Spaniards are asking tough questions that demand answers."
The far-right Vox leader, Santiago Abascal, who is likely hoping to enter a coalition government with the conservatives, did not show the same restraint.
"More dead. Another tragedy. More rage over being left to fend for ourselves, the despair and the betrayal that Spaniards are enduring," Abascal said just hours after the crash.
"I promise to work tirelessly until this government, which is a criminal organization, is sitting in a courtroom to answer for its crimes," he said.
Human error was behind the crash
Puente said that the crash was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command center for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. At that point the IRYO train was stopped near the town of Urda, while the RENFE train was 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) behind it.
But a few minutes later the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stationary IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Workers started to use cranes to move parts of the damaged trains late on Wednesday after a hectic day involving hundreds of emergency workers, firefighters, police and soldiers all pitching in to rescue survivors and recover bodies.

Ex-West Brom & Stoke striker Berahino retires at 33
- Published
Former Premier League striker Saido Berahino has retired from football at the age of 33 to concentrate on his role as a coach with Burundi's national team.
The Midlands-bred Burundi international made his name with boyhood club West Bromwich Albion, where he had one especially prolific season of 20 Premier League and cup goals in 2014-15 before joining Stoke City for £12m in January 2017.
But, having already faltered at Albion in his latter days under Tony Pulis, Berahino flopped badly for Stoke, who went on to suffer relegation from the Premier League in April 2018.
After being given a second chance by then Stoke boss Gary Rowett, he scored five times in 2018-19. But he soon fell out of favour again until he was released by mutual consent with still three years remaining on his contract.
Having left Stoke in August 2019 for Belgium, Berahino played at Waregem and Charleroi before being signed by former Baggies boss Darren Moore at Sheffield Wednesday in August 2021.
He has since played in Cyprus, India and Slovenia, as well as for his native country, having previously been capped by England at all age levels up to and including under-21.
Berahino was twice called up for England's full squad by then manager Roy Hodgson - but was not picked to play.
Berahino's 'Letter To The Game'
Berahino reserved special thanks for his first club, for whom he scored 36 goals in 121 appearances in all competition, including a hat-trick on his first start, as a 20-year-old, against Newport County in the EFL Cup in August 2013.
In a statement, entitled 'A Letter To The Game', posted on Instagram, Berahino wrote: "I want to thank West Bromwich Albion for believing in me when I was a boy.
"Those years at the club, the goals, the fans, the moments, they will always be special. There were highs and lows, mistakes and lessons. I learned that the game can lift you up and test you at the same time.
"The time has come to hang up the boots. My body and my heart are ready for the next chapter. I am proud and grateful to now serve the Burundi national team as a coach. Giving back to the country that made me, and helping the next generation, feels right.
"To my family - you have been my strength. To the fans who stayed with me through every chapter - I will never forget your support. This is not goodbye to football. It is simply the end of one story and the beginning of another.
"Football has given me everything. From the streets of Bujumbura to The Hawthorns, from the Premier League to places I never imagined I'd play - this game carried a young refugee kid through life."

Born into a small village in West Bengal, Shahida Fakir had always taken her vote for granted. That was, until it was suddenly taken away. She presented officials with her Indian birth certificate and family land documents from the village going back to 1962.
Both her parents had been on the electoral roll going back decades, so she showed proof of that too. But when the final revised voter list came out in April, Fakir was not on it.
The 38-year-old migrant worker, born into a poor Muslim family, was not alone. Since last year, 130 million names – more than the population of Japan – have been removed from India’s electoral roll through a process known as SIR, or special intensive revision. In the nearly eight decades since India’s independence, never have the voter rolls shrunk by such a huge amount over such a short time.
The Narendra Modi government has called SIR a legitimate exercise to clean up the electoral rolls. Overseen by the election commission, tens of millions of dead and duplicate names have been removed. Yet so have the names of millions of living Indian citizens.
Critics allege that the pledge to “purify” India’s voter roll of illegal immigrants has instead been used for more sinister purposes – disenfranchising tens of millions of Muslims, other minorities, and poor and lower caste communities, who are largely not BJP voters.
In a matter of weeks, nationwide anger at SIR has boiled up and spilled out on to the streets of India’s biggest cities, presenting a formidable challenge to the government. Over the weekend, Delhi was transformed into a high-security fortress of barricades, roadblocks and tens of thousands of police and paramilitaries who detained thousands of people, as they attempted to stop youth-led protests calling for the man who oversaw SIR, the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down immediately.
On Monday, opposition parties – who have decried SIR as a “weapon for vote theft” by the Modi government – drew tens of thousands of supporters as they marched through the capital and presented a petition to the supreme court, demanding Kumar’s resignation. The youth-led Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, who were behind the call for Saturday’s action, have vowed to “fight on” in their protests against SIR.
Opposition and civil society leaders allege that SIR has already given the BJP an electoral advantage in states such as Bihar and West Bengal, claims the party denied. Others say the exercise has had even more concerning implications: under changes to SIR unilaterally implemented by Kumar, the election commission has become the arbiter of Indian citizenship, a sweeping overreach of its remit.
The consequences are already playing out in West Bengal, where Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) recently came to power and began a crackdown on “illegal” immigrants, complete with several new detention centres. Civil society groups say Muslims excluded by SIR are being targeted.
Fakir was among them. Just three months after the voter list was published – and while her hearing to challenge her exclusion was pending – she was picked up by police and accused of being an illegal Bangladeshi immigrant.
In July she was pushed over the border to Bangladesh, a country she had never been to nor had any connection with, and remains stuck there. “I have all the documents to prove I am an Indian citizen,” she said in a tearful phone call from the Bangladesh border village where she has been sheltering. “I fell on their feet and begged the police not to send me to Bangladesh but they pushed me over the border.”
A Bangladesh border guard officer confirmed Fakir’s account. “We checked all her documents and are convinced that she is an Indian citizen,” they said. In September, her family submitted a petition to the supreme court challenging her deportation. The Indian government was given a month to respond.
“All I want is to return to my family and my home in India. I am waiting desperately for that day,” she said. The backlog of millions of voters in West Bengal challenging their exclusion means it could be years before Fakir’s case is heard.
Those across West Bengal who have been stripped of their votes speak of their terror of being accused of being an alien in their own land. Some have had benefits taken away. Mohammad Hedayet Ullah Siddiqui, 80, from the North 24 Parganas district, said his grandfather had been a freedom fighter for Indian independence and three generations of his family were on the voter rolls. Yet after SIR, Siddiqui described his “humiliation” on finding his name gone.
“With my name erased from the voter list, I am in constant terror. What if they send me to a detention camp?” he said. “I cannot bear to think about being separated from my children and grandchildren at this age, especially when all my ancestors have been buried in India.”
Critics say the problems began in 2023, when the Modi government changed the process for appointing the three-body election commission, giving majority control to the government for the first time. Within a matter of months, the Modi-led panel had appointed Kumar as the election commissioner in spite of opposition objections.
“For decades, the election commission was one of our more credible, independent bodies, but now that has been eroded,” said Ronojoy Sen, a senior fellow at the South Asian Studies Programme, National University of Singapore.
By the following year, the new election commission body had begun SIR, starting in Bihar, where it immediately raised concerns among human rights groups after more than 6 million names were removed. Not long after the revisions, the BJP won a landslide victory in the Bihar state elections.
Despite concerns over SIR rumbling on for months, it did not spark national protests until the Indian Express newspaper last month revealed that two members of the election commission had raised 14 objections to how voters were being excluded from the rolls, but they were unilaterally overruled by Kumar.
“India has always been a flawed democracy but at least citizens felt they had the right to vote and that elections were regular and fair,” said Sen. “SIR has taken away that right. From how it has been conducted, it’s difficult to see how the motive was anything other than to enhance the election prospects of the BJP.”
Three former election commissioners have openly criticised SIR as a “hostile exercise” that has undermined the sanctity of the country’s electoral rolls by focusing on the exclusion – rather than inclusion – of voters. OP Rawat, a former chief election commissioner, described changes to the voter registration form as “wrong and illegal”.
Ashok Lavasa, who was an election commissioner between 2018 and 2020, called for the SIR to be scrapped. “An unfair procedure has been imposed on millions of people in the country, and you have the judiciary which has validated that,” he said last month. “How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?”
None have been more vehement in their opposition than SY Qureshi, who was chief election commissioner between 2010 and 2012. “This is a national harassment exercise designed to throw Muslims off the electoral roll,” he claimed. “The only way to restore the credibility of India’s elections is to restore those deleted voters.”
The BJP has denied any political involvement or motive in the SIR process, accusing the opposition Congress party of “jealousy” over its recent electoral victories and saying any deleted voters can simply re-enrol. The BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi said the allegations were “disinformation” and part of an opposition campaign “being orchestrated to create an atmosphere of division and anarchy”.
Nonetheless, the election commission has appeared to accept some flaws in the process. Late last week, it belatedly put a cap on the number of voter deletion forms – which allow people to submit objections on behalf of others – after incidents in which people submitted thousands of forms targeting legitimate Muslim voters.
Public anger, meanwhile, has continued to build. In Delhi, where the SIR exercise left millions of people off the draft list, protests are expected to continue this week.
A Delhi resident for 30 years, Prashant Tandon, 60, said he could not believe it when a notice came to his door, questioning his life as a voter. “If someone doubts my citizenship, they should produce evidence against me,” he said furiously, adding that he would be protesting alongside the young people. “I should not have to prove that I am an Indian citizen.”
Additional reporting Aakash Hassan

Trump administration will allow pharmacies to make popular peptides
Unproven but popular peptides touted for wellness have been available on the gray market, despite an official ban. Now, the Department of Health and Human Services is looking to bring them out of the shadows.
HHS said in a new policy that it will exercise enforcement discretion for a half dozen peptides, essentially looking the other way when they're made by small compounding pharmacies.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been a vocal supporter of peptides, saying he has used some of them himself.
Peptides are strings of amino acids, shorter than proteins, that can exert powerful effects in the body. Some occur naturally and others are synthetic variations. Wellness influencers and some clinicians have promoted unproven peptides for a wide range of uses, though the evidence for their safety and effectiveness is sparse.
So even though these peptides have not been through the Food and Drug Administration's rigorous drug review and approval process, they could become easier to get. But the policy's focus on smaller producers may mean that pharmacists will have a tough time meeting demand.
In July, a panel of advisers to the FDA voted in favor of expanded access to six peptides through compounding pharmacies. However, at the same meeting the FDA's own scientists recommended against unwinding the existing restrictions on them.
The new policy says compounding is a safer alternative to illicit "research-use-only" peptides that are available online. They're often sourced from sketchy suppliers overseas.
The peptides, and some of their unproven uses, are:
- BPC-157, ulcerative colitis
- Epitalon, insomnia
- KPV, wound healing
- MOTS-c, metabolic health
- Semax, migraine
- TB-500, wound healing 
Joshua Fritzler, the president of Olympia and Wesley Pharmaceuticals in central Florida, says people have been asking about these peptides for years. But because they were illegal to compound, his company didn't make them.
The new policy doesn't change their legal status, but it does create a path for small compounders, called 503A compounding pharmacies. It doesn't apply to the larger ones, called 503Bs, that are outsourcing facilities producing higher volumes of medicines.
So at Fritzler's company, only its smaller compounding facility will be able to make the peptides – and only in small quantities, he says.
And that has implications for consumers.
"We won't be able to meet demand," he says, explaining that Olympia will likely only compound one of the six peptides and needs to get its facility ready first. "I don't think all the [503]As in the country could meet the demand."
The Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding's CEO Scott Brunner wrote in a statement that his group is pleased with the administration's decision to allow the peptides to be compounded because it offers a "more accountable alternative" for patients seeking gray market peptides.
"It also brings patients into a system where pharmacy standards, regulatory oversight, and serious adverse event reporting apply," he says.
Brunner warned, however, that it may take some time for compounding pharmacies to begin dispensing these products to patients. That's because ingredient suppliers need to make sure their active ingredients meet the policy's requirements — and pharmacies need to verify that, too.
Several consumer advocacy groups say the policy puts patients at risk, however. The nonprofit Public Citizen noted that Kennedy seems to have acted unilaterally rather than through the typical rulemaking process.
"By allowing unproven and potentially unsafe peptides to be manufactured, marketed and prescribed without concern about potential federal enforcement actions, Kennedy has undermined the FDA and threatened public health," Dr. Robert Steinbrook, Health Research Group Director at Public Citizen wrote in a statement. "All peptide substances should go through the standard FDA approval process for new drugs. The HHS Secretary should support, not sabotage, needed FDA enforcement actions to protect consumers."
Steinbrook advised clinicians to talk to their patients and tell them about the risk of contamination and other adverse effects.
The Partnership for Safe Medicines, which includes various pharmacy and pharmacist organizations around the country, filed a citizen petition last week, urging the FDA to ignore the recommendation from its advisory committee in July to allow compounding pharmacies to make the six peptides.
"Today's decision leaves Americans in a grey area as to whether peptides are safe or not, even though the FDA's own scientists recommended against voting in favor of these substances due to concerns with evidence," its executive director Shabbir Safda wrote in a statement.

Goodbye to the everyman who gatecrashed the greats
- Published
Whether through technique or toil, Stan Wawrinka has always been able to whip fans into a frenzy.
The ability to stir the emotions of a crowd never left him - even in what proved to be the final tour-level match of the 41-year-old Swiss star's glorious career.
Former world number three Wawrinka might have lost to Czech opponent Jiri Lehecka in front of passionate home support in Basel on Tuesday, but he did not wave farewell without showing the hallmarks of a stunning career that exceeded expectations.
The stylish one-handed backhand down the line. The finger pointing to the temple. The demand for more noise from the stands.
The roar of "Allez!" after winning a point he probably should not have won.
The temptation to snap his racquet over his knee after missing a shot he felt he should have made.
There were tears, too, of course.
Wawrinka, his family, and his team were dabbing their eyes once the reality of an honourable 7-5 7-6 (7-2) defeat dawned.
It meant a professional career spanning 23 years, 985 matches and three Grand Slam titles was over.
"All I wanted in my career was to give everything, have no regrets, to always fight, to always give 100% in every match - out of respect for myself, the opponent, the tournament, the fans, for everybody," Wawrinka told the ATP website., external
"That was always the most important thing for more than 20 years, and the only way you can leave the sport - without any regrets."
Wawrinka is loved by millions of fans because he is relatable - an everyman personality who reached the pinnacle of his sport by pushing himself to the limit.
So many talented players of his generation lamented the presence of Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic, believing the 'Big Three' to be a blockade preventing them from becoming a Grand Slam champion.
It did not stop Wawrinka. With explosive shot-making, relentless endurance and indomitable spirit, he barrelled past the trio of superstars on his way to winning his trio of majors.
Wawrinka had been a player whose career was ticking along steadily, rather than spectacularly, until he lifted one of the sport's biggest prizes at the age of 28.
Seeded eighth at the 2014 Australian Open, he saw off Djokovic in the quarter-finals before completing an unforeseen triumph against top seed Nadal.
"I never expected to win a Grand Slam because, for me, I was not good enough to beat those guys," Wawrinka admitted as he clutched the trophy in Melbourne.
In fact, he was more than good enough - proving it again and again.
At the 2015 French Open, Wawrinka brushed past Swiss compatriot Federer in the quarter-finals, then demolished Djokovic in the final with a display of unrelenting power - a performance which must be ranked among the greatest of his era.
His last major title arrived at the 2016 US Open, when he escaped from match point down against Britain's Dan Evans in the third round and went on to beat Djokovic for the title.
It is little wonder that 24-time major champion Djokovic - considered by many the greatest player of all-time - described Wawrinka as a "legend".
"Stan's had an incredible career. The competitor he is on court, talent, strength, power, precision - he had it all," said the 39-year-old Serb, who practised with Wawrinka in Basel.
Wawrinka was good enough to win majors, but he wasn't as consistently good as his illustrious rivals.
The 'Big Three' is often expanded to a 'Big Four' featuring Britain's three-time major champion Andy Murray, who soared to world number one, won two Olympic singles gold medals and lifted the ATP Finals trophy.
Wawrinka recognises he was "really far" from creating a 'Big Five' - and the evidence underlines that.
Spending 267 weeks in the top 10, winning one Masters 1,000 tournament and claiming 15 other tour-level titles is well below Federer, Nadal, Djokovic and Murray, but it is also more than most players can dream of achieving.

In early October, some social media posts spread the claim that an Israeli company manufactures 3D-printed salmon meat and sells it at U.S. grocery stores.
For example, a YouTube video (archived) claimed, "the first 3D-printed salmon just hit U.S. grocery shelves." It then explained the salmon was manufactured by an Israeli company called Steakholder Foods and that the product is not required to have a label indicating it was 3D-printed on its packaging. It also noted that the salmon contained a chemical used in laxatives.
Users also shared the claim on Facebook (archived) and Instagram (archived). Snopes readers sent emails asking whether it was true.
In short, on Sept. 3, Israeli company Steakholder Foods, which specializes in making 3D-printing technology for plant-based meats, announced the launch of its 3D-printed, plant-based meat and fish products, including salmon, in Northeastern U.S. retail stores under the brand name Perfecta.
Therefore, we're rating this claim true.
Snopes has already fact-checked a claim about Steakholder Foods' 3D-printed meat hitting grocery-store shelves. That claim and the claim about salmon came from the same product announcement and thus share much of the same research.
It's not clear which grocery stores or retailers have started selling or stocking the products. Snopes reached out to Steakholders Foods via a contact form on its website for more information. The company has not replied to Snopes' prior requests for information.
According to Steakholder Foods, the company uses plant-based ingredients and cultivates cells to create what ultimately becomes the 3D-printed meat.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service do regulate "lab-grown" meat and require a label for such products. However, this regulation is specifically for food made with cultured animal cells, not for food made with other kinds of cells, which is what Perfecta products consist of.
The FDA told Snopes in an email:
The product you are describing sounds like it is made from plant-based ingredients using a specific manufacturing process (3D printing). It does not appear to involve cultured cells of any type. The FDA generally does not approve finished foods or manufacturing processes. Although the FDA does not approve final food products, ingredients and additives must be demonstrated to be safe before they are used in food or in materials that contact food.
The FSIS told Snopes in an email that it regulates meat, poultry and egg products, and directed us to the FDA for more information.
Based on how the product boxes appear on the website, there doesn't seem to be any text identifying the food as 3D-printed or made with cultured cells. The boxes do clearly identify the meat as "premium plant meat" and "plant-based."
Manufacturers of plant-based meat products usually have to process their ingredient mixes in a way that allows them to mimic the texture of conventional meat. According to the Good Food Institute's Asia-Pacific website, the most common processing method requires putting shear stress on the ingredients to align them into a meatlike texture. There are several other methods of processing plant-based meats, including 3D printing.
Methylcellulose, the chemical used in laxatives, is included on the 3D-printed salmon's ingredient list. Methylcellulose is used in plant-based meats as a binder to keep the ingredients together and to replicate the texture of real meat.
The FDA has approved this kind of use of methylcellulose in food.

'No choice left but to look to increase fares': IndiGo CEO on 'very significant' rise in fuel bill
The warning comes as IndiGo’s parent company, InterGlobe Aviation Ltd, reported a loss for the third consecutive quarter.
IndiGo CEO Willie Walsh has said the airline has “no choice left but to look to increase fares” as it faces a “very significant” rise in its fuel bill. The warning comes as IndiGo’s parent company, InterGlobe Aviation Ltd, reported a loss for the third consecutive quarter, with surging fuel expenses offsetting the gains from higher fares.
The airline’s loss narrowed in the July-September quarter compared with a year earlier, but remained substantial despite an increase in revenue, Bloomberg reported. Walsh said the airline did not expect immediate relief from elevated fuel costs.
“We are looking at a period of elevated fuel cost for sometime,” he said, adding that IndiGo would continue to explore internal measures to absorb the increase. “We will continue to look at every measure that can be taken internally to offset the very significant increase in our prices,” he said.
IndiGo raises fuel charges
Jet fuel can account for around 40% of an airline's operating costs, leaving carriers vulnerable to sharp price increases and increasing the likelihood of higher ticket prices, as per Reuters. India’s largest airline has already revised fuel charges on domestic and international routes amid a sustained increase in jet fuel prices.
The latest revision, effective October 6, came after IndiGo said the month-on-month increase in ATF prices had exceeded 14%, taking costs to among their highest levels in the past decade, HT reported earlier.
Under the revised structure, IndiGo’s fuel charges on domestic flights range from ₹375 to ₹1,300, depending on the distance travelled. The charges were raised by ₹100 to ₹350 per sector.
For international flights, the revised charges vary by destination, ranging from ₹1,000 to ₹10,000. Flights to Europe attract a fuel charge of ₹10,000, while flights to Southeast Asia, the Gulf region and parts of East Asia attract a charge of ₹5,500.
IndiGo’s loss narrows, but fuel costs surge
According to Bloomberg, InterGlobe Aviation reported a net loss of ₹1,879 crore for the quarter ended September 30, lower than the loss recorded a year earlier and below the average analyst estimate of ₹2,063 crore in a Bloomberg survey.
Revenue increased 26% to ₹23,364 crore, exceeding analyst expectations. However, total costs rose to ₹26,188 crore, while fuel expenses surged 67% from a year earlier to nearly $1 billion, Bloomberg reported.
In its earnings statement, Walsh said the airline had faced unusually high fuel costs during the seasonally weaker September quarter, alongside continued geopolitical uncertainty.
“The seasonally soft September quarter saw exceptionally elevated fuel costs and continued geopolitical turmoil,” he said. He added that the steps taken by the airline had supported revenue but could only partly offset the increase in expenses.
The July-September period typically sees relatively subdued domestic air travel in India. Demand is expected to improve during the festival season, potentially providing some support to airlines as travel picks up.
Passenger numbers fall as airline cuts capacity
IndiGo carried 27.5 million passengers during the quarter, 4.5% fewer than a year earlier. It also reduced capacity by 1% as part of efforts to manage costs.
Passenger yield -- the average revenue earned per passenger -- increased 34% year-on-year, according to Bloomberg. However, the airline’s passenger load factor, which measures how much of its available seating capacity is occupied, declined to 80.3% from 82.5% a year earlier.
The company’s debt increased 7.1% from the preceding quarter to ₹87,303 crore, Bloomberg reported. IndiGo expects capacity growth in the December quarter to be in the low single digits.
Why rising fuel costs are pushing airfares higher
Aviation turbine fuel is one of the biggest expenses for airlines, accounting for a substantial share of their operating costs. Sharp increases in fuel prices can squeeze profit margins, particularly when airlines are unable to pass on the entire increase to passengers.
Fuel prices have remained volatile amid geopolitical tensions in West Asia. The impact on airlines is compounded by fluctuations in international oil prices and currency movements. IndiGo’s latest move follows an earlier revision of fuel charges in April. The airline has said it will continue to monitor fuel prices and make adjustments as required.
