Accurate color for movies, shows, and games. Affordable price for the RGB TV category. Nice low-latency gaming capability. Easy setup.
TIRED
Not as bright as some RGB models. Didn’t render some dark scenes in movies with enough contrast or clarity. Internal speakers were just average.
An array of brilliant colors is what you want from an RGB television, and on that front, the Hisense UR8 RGB MiniLED delivers. After having reviewed a number of the top RGB TVs, including the flagship Hisense UR9 RGB MiniLED and offerings from Samsung and LG, I can report that this UR8 is solidly good. It provides mini RGB tech at a lower price than the impressive UR9. As long as you can accept UR8's lacking contrast and brightness capabilities—at least compared to its high-performing sibling—the television's color accuracy stands to wow you.
What makes RGB models like the Hisense UR8 RGB MiniLED so interesting is that you can tweak the picture quality for more brilliant and accurate colors. While testing proved the UR9 has a brighter panel that performs at a higher caliber for movies, shows, games, and even displaying artwork, the UR8 is certainly colorful. But are the compromises of this more budget-friendly model worth the savings? That has less of a clear, black-and-white answer.
Setting Up Shop
The UR8 is a bit thicker than the UR9, but it is otherwise visually similar: They appear to have the same chassis and similarly feature a single pedestal. The stand snaps into place and requires some screws, but the assembly process is overall straightforward and quick. Installation couldn't be simpler: Just scan a QR code that connects to Google Home and move through the steps.
The left side of the TV houses all of the port inputs: an Ethernet port for reliable streaming, an optical audio port, a coaxial port, and one USB-A port for external storage or connecting an HD antenna. Like the UR9, this model supports Wi-Fi 6E for speedy and reliable streaming. For color accuracy, the UR8 meets 100 percent of the BT.2020 spec and is Pantone Validated, meaning it can showcase a broad selection of color variation.
Photograph: John Brandon
Now for the key differences in specs between the UR8 and UR9 RGB models: The UR8 is around 3,500 nits while the UR9 is 5,000 nits—a delta that made a big difference in my benchmarks, which I’ll cover in a bit. The UR8 has four HDMI 2.1 ports, while the UR9 only has three; however, the UR9 adds a USB-C port on the side for low-latency gaming, which didn't prove particularly impactful.
The UR8 also has less capable internal speakers than the UR9. It’s a 2.1.2 system (two main channels, one sub, and two height channels) compared to the 4.1.2 channel configuration on the UR9 (which adds a side channel). If you use a soundbar or an AV receiver, this won’t matter. Both models support Dolby Atmos and have an eARC passthrough audio port for surround sound.
The UR8 offers a 55-inch size, while the UR9’s smallest size is 65-inch. Otherwise, both are available in 75-inch, 85-inch, and 100-inch sizes.
Finally, the two share a remote control design, with a nicely centered Home button but a strangely hidden Mute on the lower right. I am not sure why there is a shortcut button for Kidoodle.TV, either, but I love that it’s backlit.
Diving Into the Benchmarks
Photograph: John Brandon
First, some background on micro and mini RGB televisions: Like traditional LED televisions, RGB models use LED backlights. But instead of shining white or blue lights through a color filter and LCD panel (as is the standard for an LED television), RGB TVs use red, green, and blue lights. The result is often strikingly realistic, even if you’re watching during the bright daylight.
To test the capabilities of the UR8, I watched scenes of the film Awake on Netflix that are so remarkably dark on many midrange televisions that it's nearly impossible to see what's happening. As with all RGB televisions I've tested, I could adjust the picture quality on the UR8 to help with contrast, but that function isn't a cure-all. Initially, a scene where the main character rides a bike was almost completely dark, especially while using Dolby Vision Reference mode and standard Dolby Vision modes. Switching to a custom Dolby Vision setting helped after I cranked up the brightness, but the picture still wasn’t overly clear.
Next, I watched an episode of House of the Dragon using the HBO Max app via Google Cast. During a scene with a dragon, the scales looked visible but not nearly as textured as they did when using the UR9. Whether the subtle difference is worth paying more for the higher model remains to be seen, but the differences are noticeable nonetheless.
In the movie The Creator on Fandango at Home, a beach landing looked a bit washed out and dark. During The Batman, gunfire looked bright enough in a dark hallway scene, but—similar to the aforementioned dragon scene—lacked rich detail.
The Super Mario Galaxy Movie on Peacock is tailor-made for testing colors: Stars floated around on the screen in a brilliant rainbow of colors, appearing bright and accurate, but some of them had too much blooming (aka a halo effect where bright tones bleed onto their darker surrounding colors). In all fairness, the UR9 also rendered this scene in a similar way.
Photograph: John Brandon
It’s not all bad news, though. In fact, in the movie Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 on Disney+, the RGB tech kicked into high gear. The color accuracy was ultrarealistic, showing bright blues, reds, and oranges in an opening scene. My only issue was that the contrast was not as tonally rich as it was on the UR9, and it also lacked some shadow detail. The LG Micro RGB Evo rendered this scene even brighter.
For benchmark tests using the Spears & Munsil discs, skin tones looked dimmer and less varied than the LG Micro RGB Evo or the Hisense UR9. The demo reel revealed a few other differences, too: White mist on a white mountain didn’t look as distinct as it did on the UR9, but (thanks again to the color accuracy) it did render green grass by a fence to a similar appearance as what the UR9 produced. A scene showing dark trees at night looked much clearer on the UR9 thanks to the higher nits rating. On the UR8, you could see the texture on the trees, and a red cactus and yellow flower also looked darker on the UR8.
Games People Play on RGB and More
This is a great TV for video games, as it can sense the game content, adjust for latency, and even help improve picture quality. Every time I started a game, the UR8 (similar to the UR9) automatically made key picture adjustments. Blacks looked a bit richer than expected, which was great for Resident Evil: Requiem, because it seemed the entire game took place in the dark. Here, the Hisense UR8 delivered an atmospheric look: dark and moody but not washed out. In fact, I didn’t notice much of a difference in latency compared to playing the same game on the UR9. (Indeed, Hisense reps told me the latency was roughly the same.)
Photograph: John Brandon
Senua's Saga: Hellblade II on the Xbox Series X looked vibrant on the UR8, despite its dark scenes by an ocean. Rocks in one scene reflected the ambient light in an ultrarealistic way that could make you feel as if you could pick one up. I also played NBA 2K27 with the DLSS 5 setting turned on and loved the clarity and crispness. Some players looked amazingly photorealistic, and colors popped so clearly.
Surround sound audio using the UR8's internal speakers was not as convincing as with the Hisense UR9, but the lower model still had a nice oomph during more explosive action movies.
Several features matched the caliber of the UR9, including Google Gemini suggesting movies and letting me create an AI-generated slideshow by voice. AI smoothing for motion worked well for games and movies, and both televisions did a good job adjusting for ambient light. I also loved how artwork (including a shipwreck painting) featured deep textures and luminance.
All in all, the Hisense UR8 RGB MiniLED performed as expected at this price—not as bright as the UR9, but certainly just as colorful. As long as you can accept that it's not the flagship model, the UR8 color accuracy is still a major perk.

The early years of a child’s life are critical for lifelong health, learning, emotional well-being, and social development. Inclusive early childhood development (iECD) seeks to ensure that every child, including those with developmental delays, disabilities, autism and other forms of neurodivergence, has equitable access to healthcare, nutrition, nurturing care, early learning, protection, and early intervention, Deepa Bhaskaran, Director, Child Development Centre (CDC), Thiruvananthapuram, said.
Speaking at a media workshop on inclusive early childhood development and the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for effective storytelling, organised by UNICEF India in association with the Press Information Bureau, Dr. Bhaskaran said early identification and interventions were vital to ensure that children with disabilities and developmental delays were included at home, in learning environments, and in their communities.
“We train and support medical staff and caregivers, improve early identification and intervention, and provide advanced disability inclusive services,” she said.
Amar Fettle, State Nodal Officer for Adolescent Health, speaking at the workshop, added that while medical infrastructure and personnel were geared towards clinical care, research, teaching, and community outreach, it was equally important to shape public understanding of children’s issues and government programmes.
“Families and the public should understand the services available and help reduce the stigma surrounding disability and developmental delays. The idea is to ensure that children are included in society,” Dr. Fettle said.
The workshop aimed to strengthen understanding of inclusive early childhood development, child rights and disability inclusion, promote ethical, child-sensitive and non-stigmatising reporting, and raise awareness of AI-related risks, including misinformation, deepfakes, bias, privacy violations, and fabricated content.
While reporting, subject matter expertise is essential, Muralikrishna Chinnadurai, trainer with the Google News Initiative India Network, said. Relying on a single AI prompt could produce unreliable information, Mr. Chinnadurai said.
“Humans must be in the loop. AI tools should be used ethically and in an environmentally responsible manner,” he said.

Cledith Arthur was never tried on the rape charge because he and Donna Arthur fled the state, and Cledith Arthur never returned to face the charges before his death in 2004. Without a conviction, Snopes cannot definitively confirm he raped Acton.
In October, less than a month before the U.S. 2026 midterm elections, Ohio's Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy released an advertisement featuring Donna Arthur, the mother of his opponent Dr. Amy Acton. In the advertisement, Arthur claimed that Acton "lies about her past." 
In response, Acton's campaign released a statement from her brother, Philip Stearns, noting that the two had been estranged from their mother for decades. Her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, raped Acton when she was 12, and both she and her brother were removed from Donna and Cledith Arthur's custody after his arrest, according to the statement. Stearns' statement further claimed that Donna Arthur "stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died" in 2004. 
Acton, the former state health department director, has been open when talking about her difficult childhood for years. A 2019 piece about Acton for Youngstown, Ohio's local newspaper The Vindicator described her as "abused, abandoned, neglected," and claimed she lived in "18 or so homes in her first 12 years," including a winter spent living in a tent at a Youngstown campground. That article also mentioned the sexual abuse she suffered at the hands of her stepfather.
Donna Arthur disputed the "living in a tent" claim directly in the pro-Ramaswamy advertisement, but did not mention the abuse allegations. (PolitiFact found she did claim Acton lied about being raped in a 2020 interview with Operation Rescue, an anti-abortion group.)
Ramaswamy has stood by the ad, and President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have said they support running it. Vance told Republicans to "stop whining" about the ad at a rally.
But the insinuation Acton was lying about her abusive childhood struck many as insensitive, including some Republicans. Ohio Sen. Jon Husted (who is running for reelection this year) said he would not have run the ad, and incumbent Gov. Mike DeWine (who is not running because he is term-limited) called for Ramaswamy to take it down.
Snopes received several requests from readers asking us to get to the truth of the matter — was Acton actually lying about her childhood, as her mother claimed?
We vetted the story. Court records show Acton's stepfather was charged with raping her, as she claimed. We also found evidence that Donna and Cledith Arthur remained married and lived together until Cledith Arthur's death in 2004.
In a response to Snopes' request for comment, the Acton campaign provided a comprehensive timeline of events and images of court documents documenting the rape charge filed against Cledith Arthur, Acton's stepfather, alongside several interviews in which she discussed her childhood. The Acton campaign also noted that Donna Arthur was found guilty of felony theft in 1996 and of animal neglect in 2021, and that Cledith Arthur was also indicted on an incest charge in 1974, before he and Donna married. (A note in The Youngstown Vindicator on March 22, 1974 — Page 25, at the bottom of the article titled "Trumbull Indicts 2 Mahoning Men for Shooting Deaths, clear third" — lists Arthur as both indicted and not indicted for incest. While this suggests he faced two separate charges and was only indicted for one, we were unable to definitively verify that was the case.)
We then requested the files for the rape charge against Arthur from the County Clerk in Mahoning County, Ohio (which can be viewed here), in order to confirm the legitimacy of the documents the Acton campaign provided.
Next, we searched the archives of local newspapers for Cledith Arthur's name, and found two brief articles in The Vindicator reporting on the rape charge in 1978.
To verify that Cledith and Donna Arthur remained married, we ran a background check on both, and found that both were using the same mailing address as late as 2003, suggesting they continued living together. We also searched the courts for divorce records and found none.
In sum, all of the information matched Acton's claims.
It's worth noting that because she was a minor at the time, Acton's name was redacted on the set of documents Snopes obtained via public records request.
The documents we received from the Acton campaign, meanwhile, were not redacted. In order to obtain those, someone personally involved with the case (likely Acton or her brother, Philip) would have needed to make the request.
It's also worth noting that while a grand jury indicted Arthur on rape charges (he pleaded not guilty, according to the court records viewed by Snopes), he was never tried because he and Donna Arthur moved out of state before the hearing. Cledith Arthur died in Pennsylvania in 2004, according to FindAGrave and the Acton campaign.
The timeline
According to the 2019 Vindicator profile, Acton's biological mother, Donna, and father divorced when she was 3, and her mother retained custody of the children. In 1975, according to the statement from Acton's campaign, Donna remarried Cledith Arthur. 
On July 13, 1978, Acton's biological father filed a formal complaint against Arthur, alleging he raped Acton between December 1976 and April 1978, when she was between the ages of 10 and 12.
The court documents viewed by Snopes listed Arthur's address as "Terrace Lake Park" on State Route 7 in Rogers, Ohio. Snopes found the property is now called Terrace Lakes Camp Ground.
Arthur was arrested the day after the complaint was filed, and he pleaded not guilty to the rape charge five days later. This fact was reported in The Vindicator on July 17. Acton and several police officers were subsequently subpoenaed as witnesses, according to court documents.
On Aug. 11, The Vindicator reported that Arthur would face a grand jury for the rape charge. The court documents showed Arthur testified before the grand jury in late September 1978, where he was indicted.
"In the courthouse after they were charged, I went to give her a kiss, and she just turned her cheek away," Acton said of her mother while speaking to The Vindicator in 2019. "That was the last time I ever saw her."
Cledith and Donna Arthur seemingly skipped town before Arthur's Oct. 13 hearing, and a judge issued a warrant for Arthur's arrest on Oct. 26. "It appears the Defendant has willfully vacated his last known address and has failed to provide any forwarding address and his present whereabouts are unknown," the order read.
The court issued an additional warrant against Arthur on Dec. 9, 1981, but, as previously stated, he was never found.
There was exactly one sticking point in the files — it was unclear exactly when the court officially transferred custody of Acton and her brother to their biological father. 
Snopes requested those files from both the Mahoning County Clerk and the Acton campaign. The Acton campaign did not have them available and the Mahoning County Clerk did not provide them alongside the file on Arthur's court case. The files are likely unavailable to third parties under Ohio law, but Snopes is awaiting confirmation from the County Clerk on this fact.

Careless dismissals give Australia route to series win
- Published
Third Test, Cape Town (day three of five)
South Africa 329 & 140-4: Ackerman 62; Starc 2-29
Australia 429: Inglis 102; Harmer 4-104
South Africa lead by 40 runs
Batters carelessly gifting wickets to Australia... we have been here before.
This time it was not England helping their opponents, although they will have taken note with a tour of South Africa to come this winter.
South Africa's attempt to fight back in the decisive third Test against Australia was hurt by two poor strokes on day three.
Having taken the last six Australian wickets for 99 runs in the morning despite Josh Inglis' second Test century, the Proteas began their second innings facing a deficit of exactly 100.
They needed runs from their experienced opener and number three. Neither Aiden Markram nor David Bedingham could deliver.
By the end, even captain Temba Bavuma had been tempted into a wild swipe to fall for 35. South Africa were 140-4, just 40 runs ahead, at the close.
Australia are closing in.
Weakness exposed by Australia
In isolation, Markram's drive off Mitchell Starc straight into the hands of mid-off for one appeared the most egregious.
The ball was the fullest of the six balls Markram faced but not there for him to play his trademark shot. Fielder Travis Head did not have to move.
Worse, though, was the dismissal of Bedingham, who showed he had not learned from the first innings.
Then, the right-hander top-edged a pull to Josh Hazlewood off the bowling of Starc. This time he repeated the shot, with Hazlewood the wicket-taking bowler.
"That is just absolutely soft from David Bedingham," said former South Africa bowler Vernon Philander.
"He knew they were going to target him in that zone. For the second time in the Test, he has fallen to the same ploy."
Given the prized position in South Africa's batting order on the back of strong domestic form for Durham in the County Championship and twin hundreds for Western Province in September, this score of 11 followed contributions of 49, 46 and 50 in his other four innings.
He has got in but has not made a match-winning contribution.
Batting in the key position of first drop, some would say that is more infuriating than not getting in at all.
His dismissal, again like in the first innings, came shortly after being hit by a bouncer, with Starc clattering one into his chest on this occasion.
When, after starting with two balls on a good length, Hazlewood went short again, Bedingham's eyes lit up.
Ollie Robinson, Jofra Archer and co should have been taking note. It was the fifth time he has been dismissed pulling in his 18 Tests.
On average he gets out playing that shot once every 13 deliveries.
"He never looks in the right position to play the pull or hook shot," former South Africa captain Graeme Smith said. "He is always off balance. He is never in a strong position.
"You think about best pullers in the game they have a strong base. He is pirouetting on one leg.
"[South Africa great] Hashim Amla just put the pull shot away for a phase.
"That is what a player like Bedingham needs to think about."

Cummins tweak brings Bavuma wicket
Bavuma, in contrast, dug in for 115 balls in which he hit only one boundary.
As he had in his 179 in the second-Test win in Gqeberha which set up this grand Cape Town finale, he showed his side the way in a partnership lasting 17.3 overs with Matthew Breetzke after opener Marques Ackerman had briskly made 65 before being bounced out by Starc.
But with four minutes to go in the day, Australia captain Pat Cummins tweaked his field for spinner Nathan Lyon.
Bavuma had pushed and driven outside off stump to that point but, with a silly point now in place, he was dragged from his crease and tried to force through mid-wicket.
Australia's celebrations suggested they believe that was the crucial wicket.
The vicious turn Lyon found means any chase over 200 would not be straightforward for Australia. South Africa's spinner Simon Harmer dismissed Inglis and Alex Carey (80) earlier in the day on his way to figures of 4-104.
The Proteas have Breetzke and Ryan Rickelton at the crease - and Test triple-centurion Wiaan Mulder to come, before in-form all-rounder Marco Jansen and the tail.
This still appears a tall order, however.
As on day one and two, Australia have held firm and their opponents faltered. England know that feeling too.

'Like cutting up a Picasso': AI microdrama edit of Neighbours worries actors and crew
- Published
Former Neighbours actors and crew have raised concerns about plans to use AI to help re-edit old footage and make mini episodes for mobile phone viewers.
Fremantle, producer of the now-defunct Australian TV soap opera, has partnered with US-based RoseBerry Media for the project that will use AI to "scan decades of episodes" to help make short vertical videos.
Footage of Margot Robbie, who played Donna Freedman from 2008 to 2011, will be the initial focus of the micro-drama.
Both companies say the move will bring the show - which aired its final episode last year - to new audiences. But some actors and crew say they have not consented to their images, voice or work to be re-purposed.
Robbie has yet to respond publicly. The BBC has contacted her agency for comment.
In a statement, the companies behind the project said the AI-assisted technology will "scan decades of episodes to map character arcs, storylines and standout moments, helping editors quickly identify the strongest material".
The micro-drama episodes will use "original, previously broadcast footage, dialogue and performances", according to Fremantle spokesman.
"It does not generate new scenes or performances, alter actors' faces or likenesses, or use synthetic voices," he said, adding that a human editor would be "reviewing and approving every stage of the editing process".
The mini episodes will likely feature Matt Werkmeister, 34, who joined the set of Neighbours in 2005 when he was 13 years old. He played a regular character, Zeke Kinski and shared many scenes with Robbie's character.
Now a Melbourne-based producer and director, Werkmeister says he hasn't been approached by the companies behind the micro-drama and is concerned what the episodes will feature.
"If they're creating a new micro-drama out of something that already exists, I feel there needs to be consent for using our image and voice as well as the writers," he said.
Robbie is "obviously a big draw card" and "it's nice to watch old clips from shows you used to watch," Werkmeister said, but when he signed his contract two decades ago, "streaming didn't even exist as a platform" so he's unsure of what his rights are.
That uncertainty is also at the forefront of Sam Clark's mind. He played Ringo Brown on Neighbours from 2006 to 2010, a character who later marries Robbie's fictional character.
Speaking from Los Angeles, Clark – now working as a producer and voice actor - said he hadn't heard about the micro-drama until a friend sent him an article.
"I don't have a negative view of the work that we did all those years ago getting a second life as long as it's not being manipulated into new storylines," Clark, 39, said.
"AI and social media obviously wasn't a thing when I signed my contract 20 years ago so I'm still trying to understand exactly what those parameters are."
Sound recordist Bruce Findlay, 68, has worked in the TV industry for close to five decades and Neighbours has a "special place" in his heart, having worked on the show from episode one.
Using AI to help make short episodes from old footage was "like cutting up a Picasso and rebuilding it".
"We worked so hard to get this product out… and now they're chopping it up into little tiny pieces, throwing it up in the air and putting it back together again using AI - it belittles the process".
Guy Hameiri, head of RoseBerry Media, said the project is the first time the company will use its in-house AI tool to sift through Neighbours footage - there are more than 9,300 episodes - to make "premium vertical television".
The project will "reimagine" the material, giving it "new audiences, new relevance and new value," he said.
The head of Fremantle's commercial and international arm, Jens Richter, has called the project "an exciting example of how technology and creative thinking can unlock new value" from their catalogue.
It's understood that Fremantle is in discussions with two unions on the issue and that residuals - ongoing payments for actors and writers when their work is re-aired or syndicated - will be paid, but this does not apply to crew.
The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance, one of the unions, confirmed the talks.
"Workers should be consulted before their likeness or expertise is used in a way they could never had envisioned when they signed contracts decades ago," said MEAA's acting CEO Adam Portelli.

The students had also been seeking the announcement of a definite timeline for student union elections. The JMISU was dissolved following recurrent incidents of violent clashes, attacks on teachers and the occasional disruption of classes during that period. The administration also claimed that student representatives had begun interfering in administrative matters and that the union’s activities were affecting the academic environment. Most people worldwide could be categorised as having a high genetic risk for three of 28 common conditions, including diabetes, cardiovascular disease and schizophrenia, even if they might not develop them, a new study has found.
Researchers, led by the UK's University of Exeter, described the 'average' human genome, finding that everyone, regardless of their current health status, could be considered at risk for numerous conditions based on their genetics alone.
Every person's genome, or the average human genome, contains around five million variants, or DNA locations that differ between individuals, the findings published in the journal Genome Medicine reveal.
The locations include around 10,000 variants that alter gene sequences, which can have positive or negative effect, ranging from lactose intolerance to drug response, though are often biologically neutral, they show.
Each person also carries between one and three rare variants previously shown to cause serious genetic diseases, and another 50 rare variants that are currently of uncertain clinical relevance, the researchers found.
The team analysed data from two major population biobanks -- the UK Biobank and the US' All of Us -- that include whole genome sequencing, covering nearly one million individuals.
Senior author Caroline Wright, from the University of Exeter, said, "Whole genome sequencing has become such an important tool in diagnosing genetic disease, and we're increasingly moving towards genetic screening for predicting disease."
"Yet most people are unaware of just how much genetic variation is present in every genome. Actually, variation is the norm. For the first time, our study outlines what to expect in the average human genome, which can benefit clinicians and patients across the word in understanding, interpreting and contextualising genomics," Wright said.
The researchers also analysed numerous polygenic risk scores, which consider all known genetic factors to calculate a person's future risk of developing a disease.
"... applying polygenic scores (PGS) for 28 common diseases within UKB (UK Biobank), we estimate that the average person is in the top 10 per cent for (nearly) three conditions, and around one in five people are in the top one per cent for at least one PGS," the authors wrote.
"Importantly, we found that everyone carries a small number of genetic variants linked to disease, although many of these will not actually cause disease in that individual," Wright said.
The senior author added, "It is therefore crucial to consider context when interpreting findings from genetic testing, including symptoms or family history of disease as well as other clinical and environmental risk factors. Our findings also provide important context for professionals who are interpreting genetic testing results or commissioning genetic screening programmes."
Although the studies are large, participation is skewed towards people of Western European origin, and the researchers acknowledged the need for data from more diverse populations to further improve understanding and impact.

‘Orders becoming a mockery’: Supreme Court pulls up Delhi govt over firecracker curbs
A bench questioned the authorities over the lack of concrete data on enforcement and the impact of measures taken to curb pollution in Delhi-NCR.
The Supreme Court on Thursday criticised the Delhi government and the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) for failing to enforce its firecracker rules during festivals. Repeated violations made its orders seem “academic” and amounted to a “mockery”, the top court reportedly said.
The apex court was hearing the impact of firecrackers on Delhi-NCR’s air quality. A bench of Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale questioned the authorities over the lack of concrete data on enforcement and the impact of measures taken to curb pollution in the region.
“What did you actually do? Unless you can tell us what you have done, what is the point of passing orders? It becomes a mockery then,” the bench asked Delhi government, as per news agency ANI. Additional solicitor general Aishwarya Singh Bhati, appearing for the Union government, told the bench that an enforcement mechanism was in place but had not been presented to the court.
Deep Dive
The top court reportedly asked whether enforcement teams had visited the identified areas, when they went and what data they collected. It also sought data comparing areas where the AQI rose with those where it did not.
“Next year you will make a similar submission when we will not be there, to another bench,” the court observed, asking the authorities to “think now at a higher level”. The bench said that air pollution was not an adversarial issue but one that affected “every living being”.
The court-appointed adviser said authorities had not properly assessed the impact of last year’s relaxation of firecracker rules. Despite permission for green crackers, banned firecrackers were allegedly used, while enforcement teams failed to provide clear data on violations. The bench said bursting firecrackers would inevitably worsen air pollution.

“Obviously when you burn crackers it goes without saying, it’s going to happen,” the judges said. When the amicus curiae raised concerns about violations, the court asked whether the submission implied that firecrackers should be completely banned. “So what you’re saying is it should be closed (a compete ban on firecrackers)?” the court asked.
SC seeks balance between celebrations and public health
The Supreme Court said it wanted to balance religious sentiments with public health concerns, clarifying that it was not seeking a complete ban on firecrackers but wanted to curb pollution.
“We are not for absolute ban, we have been trying to balance it,” the court said, asking authorities to monitor compliance on the two days when firecrackers were permitted.
“Obviously as a trader, they will always go with supply and demand. They’ll do maximum business as possible,” the bench said, questioning whether regulating sales alone was enough. It suggested involving prominent public figures and celebrities to discourage people from bursting firecrackers. The bench said authorities should focus on implementing its orders rather than prosecuting people celebrating festivals.

“We also understand sentiment of the public. We are not on religion. But we are on the logical thing. How will we actually celebrate a festival without causing any harm to anybody?” the court said.
“It’s a festival of light. It was not there originally a problem. Problem came when firecrackers came. Otherwise we used to light lamps and it was beautiful. Ultimately problem is fire, not light,” the bench observed.
It also suggested using prominent personalities to spread awareness. “In an attempt, use prominent personality, somebody like Virat Kohli, to spread awareness,” it said.
Court questions pollution-control measures
The authorities presented measures for the coming winter pollution season, including 608 anti-smog guns, EV charging infrastructure, greening initiatives and enhanced monitoring. Additional solicitor general Aishwarya Bhati told the court that the Delhi government had prepared an action plan for the pollution season, ANI reported.
The bench, though, cited a report saying that only nine of CAQM’s 29 units were functioning. It also questioned the lack of reports showing whether the authorities had followed its directions and whether their measures had reduced pollution.

Separate bench to hear Diwali firecracker issue
The Supreme Court has taken up Delhi's air pollution issue through suo motu proceedings arising from a petition filed by advocate MC Mehta. A separate petition filed in 2015 by three toddlers sought a complete ban on firecrackers, citing their harmful effects on children, older people and those with health conditions, HT reported earlier.
Last year, the court allowed a limited window for the sale and use of firecrackers during Diwali in an attempt to balance public health concerns with religious and festive sentiments.
Firecracker retailers have sought a similar arrangement this year, asking the court to permit sales and regulate the use of fireworks on specified dates and during designated hours. A separate bench will consider the firecracker issue.
Earlier this month, the court called for a “practical and pragmatic” approach that balances public health concerns with religious sentiments. The Centre has also submitted formulations for less-polluting firecrackers developed with scientific and regulatory agencies.

Waking early, I put a small jar of my sauerkraut into my messenger bag, hop on my bicycle, ride to Seattle's King Street Station, and board a train heading to the Portland Fermentation Festival, the yearly gathering affectionately nicknamed “Stinkfest.”
Usually the sheer existence of a festival like this is enough to get people revved up to come together and talk about their favorite ferments, but in an interesting twist, fermented foods are enjoying a popularity boost from a different crowd. The MAHA movement, and particularly the Donald Trump cabinet, are big into fermented food, eating meat, usually steak, with fermented sides like kimchi or sauerkraut at every meal.
I've come to Portland, Oregon, wondering if there was going to be any overlap in the Venn diagram between festival attendees and the MAHA steak-and-ferment crowd. I mentioned this to my cousin-in-law Erick, who's been part of the Portland food scene for years, and he laughed out loud.
“It'll be more like a Venn dumbbell,” he said, making a pair of thumb-and-forefinger circles and tracing a line in the air between them. “No overlap, but food will be the bridge.”
Still, I was curious. I’d check.
The festival is almost exactly what the fermentation-friendly might hope to find. Right inside the main door next to the check-in desk is a bacterial petting zoo—a common thing at this sort of event—and a table where attendees can drop off their own ferments to share. Further on, lining every wall of the main room, are exhibitors who have paid a grand total of 25 bucks for a table, handing out free samples of fermented foods.
The space quickly fills up–several hundred people flow through over the course of the evening–and it appears that there's both a line in front of each exhibitor and perhaps a more organic continuous line with people flowing clockwise from one exhibitor to the next. People are notably excited and happy. There's a kid walking around with a tray of handmade pickle pins he's giving people to wear and there's a collective gasp when 20 or 30 minutes in, Dillon T. Pickle, the mascot of the Portland Pickles West Coast League baseball team, walks into the room. At one point, a big baby crawls across most of the main floor, unhindered and happy.
In the middle of it all is festival co-organizer, journalist, and cookbook author Liz Crain. She explains that the Fest, now in its 14th installment, was started in 2009 by friends who love to ferment. There were members of a little company called Pickleopolis and a club called The Kraut Collective, and, with some help from author and fermentation rockstar Sandor Katz, they launched a Portland tradition.
When I ask how the festival has evolved since its first year, she gets a little philosophical.
“Cheap. Portland. Weird. People get excited,” she says in a tone where several punctuation options would be in the spirit of the festival. “People lined up on the sidewalk all the way around the building for the first one. I poured hard cider that I made from a tree in my backyard.”
“There's nothing for sale, and that gives it a potluck-y party style. Most big festivals have consumers and purveyors, but without those distinctions here, it makes conversations a bit deeper, a bit more personal,” she says. “There's no gatekeeping, no secret recipes. It's always been wacky and fun.”
She isn't sure how much MAHA crossover I'll encounter, but she has an openness to it.
“RFK is certainly infatuated with sauerkraut and steak. There's some good to be found in the overall MAHA tenets, but so much of it has been muddied by the anti-vax stance and ludicrous conspiracy theories,” she says, though she believes it's important to “look closely and critically at pesticides and favor less-processed foods.”
“But a diet that's based solely on meat, particularly beef, animal fats, and sauerkraut … well that's not a very diverse diet,” she says. “Let's just say I wouldn't want to sit next to that person on a plane or be stuck in an elevator with them.”
I pick up on these ideas with Chris Curtin, a fermentation microbiology researcher at Oregon State University.
“Historically, everything has shown that narrowing the scope of your diet misses some things. They don't turn out to be the best in the long run,” he says. An Australian living in the US for the last decade, he can clearly see the way trends are moving and notes that registered dietitians have consistently put fermented foods at the top of their superfood lists for the past decade.
Curtin describes his work as caring about what happens when we mess around with microbes to see what happens to the raw material. As he puts it, "I'm interested in tinkering if it involves microbe wrangling." He also gets the festival's popularity among those who ferment.
“Fermenting is such a readily accessible scientific experiment that you can do in your kitchen. People go, find foods they like and want to make in their own kitchens. It's accessible and tactile.”
This plays out at the festival as I begin to sample the merchandise. The first thing I taste is an “orange whey Julius” that includes whey and OJ and is pleasingly reminiscent of the Orange Julius I'd get as a treat as a kid at the Mall of New Hampshire.
Next to that is Nat West's booth with Peruvian corn beer called chicha. West has run a cider company, dabbled in politics, driven a TriMet city bus in Portland, and now runs the Vancouver, Washington, farmers’ market. In a chicha, the fermentation starts by the brewer chewing ground field corn. At the festival, attendees are drinking what West has chewed. As people in line joke about drinking this guy's spit, or at least the byproducts of it, West interjects, “nobody's died yet!”
“The ptyalin enzymes in the saliva kickstart the starch-to-sugar process,” he explains as I take a sip and gaze longingly at the draft beer in the hands of someone who's wandered into the show from the Hotlips pizza next door.
Further along, Portland's Jorinji Miso has a double booth with samples of miso soup with bonito flakes along with koji (rice fermented with Aspergillus oryzae spores) and amazake, a koji-based drink.
The couple who run Maypop Wine Co. have their hands full at the Fest. The company’s cofounder Vince Kelsea explains that they make “anything but pinot” in the Willamette Valley—a lush north-south valley in Oregon renowned for its pinot noir. Making unfiltered, low-intervention wines like Maypop in a region famous for its pinot sounds like they're making things hard for themselves, but the attendees maintain a several-deep line at the booth all night long.
In one corner is Kiyomi Hasagewa, a third-generation Japanese bean purveyor. She’s sharing tastes of a 15-year-old miso she dehydrated and ground so she could bring it from Hokkaido to the festival. She sprinkles it over the rice and tops it with a wedge of sun-dried daikon which her elderly mother fermented in a mashed pumpkin paste. It is easily the most interesting bite in the room.
Back in the entry hall are my personal favorites, the ferments that attendees have brought to share. Liz Crain has brought along plum and dandelion wines, pickle brine, a blackberry-blueberry-lemon water kefir, and a monster jar of sour dills. I note with pride that the jar of sauerkraut I brought is next to Liz’s pickles, near-empty. Nearby is another giant jar of “fermented carrot coins, cherry bomb, garlic, ginger, horseradish,” which I anticipate as a pleasant assault on my senses, but it's really just pleasant. A garlic blast for sure, but one with all of the harsh edges smoothed by time and beneficial bacteria into something lovely.
Also at the community table are Portland occupational therapist Eva Ortega and her fermentation buddy Letti Kittel who drove down from Seattle.
“I've only made unsuccessful ferments so far,” says Ortega, undeterred. “I'm here to learn.”
Kittel says she's been nerding out on fermenting for about a year and has brought a kombucha starter with its bacteria-and-yeast scoby for others to bring home and try. And while both of them have no comment about the MAHA connection, Ortega puts some of Kittel's starter in a little jar and drops it into her purse.
I'm expecting another round of “no comment” when the MAHA diet comes up with three other fermenting friends, Megan Andricos, Josh Monifi, and Desiré Demarest, but Andricos, aka DJ Sappho, followed a similar diet 20 years ago in what they call their “fermented-pickled food and protein phase,” which consisted of “mostly kimchi and meat.”
They're off that diet now, but they liked being on it. “Kimchi evens out my gut biome. I felt better. Not superhuman, but better.”
Also on the community table is something called “Higgins Kraut,” made with Napa cabbage, carrots, garlic, and ginger, which, with a lovely melding of flavors, won my personal Best-in-Show award.
Turns out it's made by one of the show’s other founders, George Winborn, who was involved for the first 10 years. He'd been farming in Dallas when he moved to Portland, to a place that had no yard and nowhere to farm.
“Doing the Fest helped scratch the itch,” he says. He's now getting Wellspring Farm in Gresham, Oregon, off the ground and noted how the festival has become a bit more commercial, a bit less homemade. But all that's relative, considering we're standing here over our jars of sauerkraut, and the exhibitors are very small businesses, if they're businesses at all.
“I still love the DIY and starter tables,” he says. “It reminds you that everyone can do this.”

Rivian reported its third quarter earnings of 2026, providing us a closer look at the company’s financial health as it ramps up production of its all-important R2 electric vehicle — which is now, for the first time, outselling all of Rivian’s other EVs.
Rivian’s R2 is officially its best-selling vehicle
The mass-market R2 has quickly become the company’s top seller by volume, but high-margin software deals and the Volkswagen partnership are the real forces keeping the automaker in good financial health.
Rivian said it brought in $2.155 billion in revenue, a 38 percent increase compared to the $1.558 billion in Q3 2025. Of that amount, $1.55 billion came from automotive revenue, which is up 36 percent year over year. Comparatively, the company reported $605 million from software and subscription services, a 45 percent increase year over year. As EV sales slow down, the company is seeking to make more money from its digital products, including the Autonomy Plus package.
Automotive gross profits were on an upward trajectory, a sign that the company’s finances were improving as it delivered more vehicles. Rivian made $176 million in gross profit this quarter, a $152 million improvement compared to the same time last year. The company still lost $80 million in Q3 automotive gross profits, which is much better than the $130 million loss a year ago.
In other words, Rivian is losing less than it did a year ago because they sold more cars and made more money per vehicle. (Also, the company continued to sell pollution credits to other carmakers, and also received a tariff refund from the government — all of which was recorded as revenue.)
Rivian is losing less than it did a year ago because they sold more cars and made more money per vehicle.
Rivian brought in $256 million in profit in software and services, up $102 million from last year, with a strong 42 percent profit margin. Most of this cash came from licensing their tech to Volkswagen, alongside customer subscriptions for Rivian’s Autonomy Plus driving features. In many ways, Rivian’s tech partnership with Volkswagen and software sales are currently paying the bills, keeping the company profitable overall while it absorbs a lot of heavy upfront costs from launching the R2.
Earlier this month, Rivian reported a record sales quarter, with 19,751 vehicles produced and 19,248 delivered. That represents an 85 percent year-over-year increase in production and a 45 percent jump in deliveries. (For a direct-to-consumer automaker like Rivian, deliveries serve as a proxy for sales.)
Rivian doesn’t break down sales by model, so we don’t exactly how many R2s have reached customers so far. But the company said that the R2 is now the “best-selling Rivian vehicle by volume,” outselling the R1T and R1S, as well as the Electric Delivery Van (EDV).
“We had great results with R2 becoming our best selling vehicle by volume in the third quarter,” Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe said in a statement, ahead of the company’s earnings call this afternoon. “Customer and media feedback on R2 has been exceptional.”
The R2 was designed from the ground up to be Rivian’s higher-volume, mass-market offering — and by overtaking the company’s more expensive, lower-volume legacy vehicles, it seems to be doing just that. Still, the R2 isn’t bringing in the bulk of the revenue yet, as indicated by Rivian’s use of the phrase “by volume.” Most of the money is still coming from the VW partnership and its software division.
But that could change once Rivian starts shipping the more affordable versions of the R2, like the $55,485 Premium trim (coming in late 2026), the $49,985 Standard Long-Range (early 2027), and the $46,495 Standard (late 2027).

The Pentagon inspector general’s office declined a request from US senators to investigate restrictions recently imposed on the Ukraine military’s use of SpaceX’s satellite network.
Ukraine, which uses SpaceX’s Starlink service and the military version known as Starshield, said earlier this month that military drones lost satellite connectivity when traveling above 161 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour). The limit was removed after about 10 days.
Five Democratic and four Republican senators sent an October 15 letter to Department of Defense Inspector General Platte Moring, asking for a probe into the reported disruptions of Starlink and Starshield. The letter asked, among other things, “whether any restrictions on Starlink or Starshield services were directed, authorized, or implemented by SpaceX, the Department of Defense, or other US government entities; whether such restrictions were consistent with applicable US government contracts, and what actions, if any, the Department of Defense took in response.”
Platte told the senators in a letter Tuesday that the questions should be directed to the US Air Force and Space Force, according to CNN. “They are better suited to address the matters raised in your letter and to coordinate any Department responses to your questions,” Moring wrote.
A spokesperson for the Pentagon inspector general’s office told Ars today, “The Department of War Office of Inspector General (The DoW OIG) answered recent correspondence from members of Congress regarding Starlink… We carefully considered the congressional request and determined that the matters raised were best addressed by the DOW. Should new information come to light, we may reconsider.”
We asked the Department of Defense whether it plans to investigate and will update this article if it responds.
Democrats and Republicans want answers
The satellite problems “were discovered after the administration threatened to withhold intelligence to Kyiv over its strikes on Russian refineries and after President Donald Trump made a deal to buy Russian diesel and ease sanctions on Moscow,” CNN wrote.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Baramulla, Oct 29: The absence of reflective markers on concrete road dividers installed at several locations in north Kashmir has emerged as a road safety concern, with residents warning that poorly visible barriers, particularly during night hours, could lead to serious accidents.
The authorities have installed concrete dividers at various stretches to streamline traffic movement and ease congestion in busy areas.
However, the absence of reflectors on these structures has raised concerns among commuters, who say the dividers become difficult to spot after dark, increasing the risk of vehicles crashing into them.
Residents said several road mishaps had occurred in Baramulla town in the past, allegedly due to the poor visibility of these dividers.
Such accidents have resulted in injuries to vehicle occupants and damage to vehicles, with some incidents reportedly causing serious injuries.
In one such incident about a year ago, a car travelling from Srinagar towards Baramulla rammed into a concrete divider near Nanak Bhawan.
The collision left the occupants with severe head injuries and caused extensive damage to the vehicle.
Locals said the absence of reflective markers makes the dividers particularly hazardous at night, when drivers have limited visibility of the road ahead.
The problem becomes more acute during power outages, when inadequate street lighting leaves the concrete structures barely visible to approaching motorists.
They said drivers unfamiliar with the area are especially vulnerable, as they may fail to notice the dividers in time to manoeuvre their vehicles safely.
“Installing reflectors would cost only a few thousand rupees, but it could help save lives. The authorities must pay attention to this issue before another accident occurs,” said Mushtaq Ahmad, a local resident.
Residents said that while installing concrete dividers may help regulate traffic and prevent vehicles from entering the wrong lane, ensuring their visibility is equally important for road safety.
They urged the concerned departments to conduct an assessment of dividers installed across Baramulla and other parts of north Kashmir and equip them with reflective markers or other suitable visibility aids.
They also called for adequate street lighting at vulnerable stretches, particularly along busy roads and at locations where dividers are difficult to distinguish from the road surface.
Residents said relatively inexpensive safety measures could help reduce the risk of collisions and prevent avoidable injuries and loss of life.
They urged the authorities to address the issue on priority, particularly as traffic movement increases on busy roads.

How talking about Man Utd's cycle of doom became an industry
- Published
Manchester United. More a high-volume content farm than a football club these days.
Michael Carrick's starring role in what has become one of the nation's favourite soap operas has been extended for at least another week, with the 45-year-old set to be in charge for Saturday's visit to Chelsea.
Good news - you'd think - for Carrick. But even better news for Amazon's All or Nothing camera crews, who have been given "unprecedented" access to document the behind-the-scenes goings-on at Old Trafford this season.
United fans will presumably be relieved when the football resumes on Saturday, if only to break up the constant stream of opinion for 90 minutes.
But while the wall-to-wall reporting of one of the world's biggest football clubs is hardly new, the unrelenting coverage from former players is a growing phenomenon.
It is easier to name the Manchester United legends who don't have a platform from which they scrutinise the club's every move than those that do - and it begs the question whether the club's demise has been industrialised into a content-creating machine.
'It doesn't really help in any way'
Whether supporters feel comments from ex-players are damaging or not differs from fan to fan, but what cannot be denied is how difficult it is to escape their views.
Sky Sports pundit Gary Neville provided scathing on-air commentary during United's 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth last Sunday, before conducting a post-match podcast in the Old Trafford gantry in which he accused some of their players of being unprofessional.
"There's a couple of them... I live in Manchester and they're not that professional, some of them," Neville stated.
"I've got no time for them. There's a few of them that don't go to bed at the right time. Don't eat the right things. Don't think about Manchester United every single minute of every single day."
But it's digital and streaming platforms that are re-defining a new age of analysis.
Neville launched The Overlap in 2021, and its success across video and podcast platforms has seen the channel become one of the most influential outlets in sports media.
On Tuesday, Wayne Rooney appeared on Neville's Manchester United-dedicated YouTube channel 'Stick to United' where he said Carrick's players "need a firework up their a***".
Neville has since hosted his own The Overlap show where he said managers sometimes need to be sacked "for their own good", while ex-United captain Roy Keane said Carrick and his backroom staff are "lucky boys" to still be in jobs.
Neville acquired a network of YouTube channels from United influencer Mark Goldbridge last summer, which has significantly increased the channel's coverage of the club.
Largely known for viral clips of his expletive-laden rants during streamed 'watchalongs' of their matches, Goldbridge's YouTube channels had amassed more than 3.7million subscribers.
Goldbridge - whose real name is Brent di Cesare - now co-hosts the 'Stick to United' show with Rooney, the club's record goalscorer.
But Neville, Rooney and Keane are far from the only ones setting the agenda.
Class of '92 pair Paul Scholes and Nicky Butt co-host their own podcast called 'The Good, The Bad & The Football'.
Before last season's Manchester derby at Old Trafford - Carrick's first home game in charge - Butt said City striker Erling Haaland would "pick Lisandro Martinez up and run with him", while Scholes said the Norway forward would "throw him in the net" after scoring.
United won the game 2-0, with Martinez putting in a stellar performance.
Asked about Scholes' comments after the match, the Argentine defender said: "Honestly, he can say whatever he wants. I told him already, if he wants to say something to me, he can come to wherever he wants. To my house, wherever. I don't care."
Asked during Thursday's news conference how he deals with the 'noise' from former team-mates and ex-players, Carrick said he avoids it as best he can.
"I don't see it really. I see the things that I need to see," he added.
"I don't look for it - it doesn't really help in any way.
"I've said it before, I care about what the supporters think. I care about what it feels like in the stadium, and them travelling to games for us, to come and see us and support us. I care about what we give them, and what we offer them, and what they see. I genuinely don't take any notice of anything else."
- How Lineker and Neville became rival media moguls 
  - Published24 April
- 'Fully committed' Fernandes to remain Man Utd captain 
  - Published15 hours ago
- Sometimes managers need sacking for own good - Neville 
  - Published19 hours ago
'Unhelpful' or standard-bearers?
Where once a low rating in a newspaper could anger players, they now have to deal with days of debate after a bad result or below-par performance.
Former manager Erik ten Hag recently alluded to the difficulty his Manchester United squad had dealing with the opinions of people like Neville and Rio Ferdinand, and said former players could be "more helpful" to the club.
"I did nice interviews with them both [Neville and Ferdinand], so it didn't hurt me. Of course, they have podcasts, they have their models," Ten Hag told The Athletic, external.
"Sometimes it's difficult for players. Some of them get affected by it, get annoyed by it.
"They achieved massive successes. But also, they can help the club more, help the players more. There should be two ways that they support it. But I think always the thing you most love, you most criticise."
It is a point Neville agrees with.
Speaking on Ferdinand's podcast, external last summer, it was put to Neville he had been overly critical when covering his boyhood club.
"It's a balance though Rio, isn't it?" he told his former United team-mate.
"It's like, do I want [Manchester] City to win the league? I absolutely don't want City anywhere near the league title."
And he insisted "United are the hardest games I do".
"People might think that I'm more critical of United when they don't play well. Sometimes, over the last maybe 10 years, the balance, maybe I've not got it right," admitted Neville.
But, having won 18 major honours in 19 years at Old Trafford, few are better placed to judge the club than Neville.
"There was a banner in the first half [against Bournemouth] that was held up in the Stretford End - 'standards'. They went a long time ago," he said last Sunday.
Like Neville, Butt also came through United's academy and said former players have the club's best interests at heart.
"When it goes bad, you can't cry and go, 'Oh, they're [ex-players] having a go at us'," explained Butt back in January.
"We love the football club. I've been a Manchester United fan since the age of six or seven, as long as I can remember. I'm not saying it to go, 'Let's stab everybody in the back'. I'm saying it because it is genuinely c**p."
'Hated, adored, never ignored'
While the club would rather be awash with positivity, negative coverage is consumed by a wider base that more regularly includes non-Manchester United fans.
It's difficult to apply a value to the club's popularity but United have remained one of the highest-grossing football clubs in world football since last winning the Premier League in 2013.
Much of their off-field success has been underscored by industry-leading commercial deals, as well as strong matchday revenue. Only Arsenal made more money from matchday revenue last season in the Premier League.
Former executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward angered supporters in 2018 when he said: "Playing performance doesn't really have a meaningful impact on what we can do on the commercial side of the business."
Being a constant source of attention is something that the club and supporters have regularly boasted about, too.
The 'hated, adored, never ignored' mantra regularly appears on banners at Old Trafford, while the club even released a clothing range that adorned the slogan.
It's fair to say, then, that the club are as guilty as anyone in capitalising on their global fame and ability to grab headlines.

WASHINGTON — The Department of Health and Human Services released a policy that will temporarily allow compounding pharmacies to manufacture some peptide products, increasing access to the experimental wellness therapies embraced by many in the Make America Healthy Again movement.
The policy states that HHS will use “enforcement discretion” to not take action against state-licensed pharmacies, federal facilities, or licensed physicians compounding the six peptides previously backed by a Food and Drug Administration advisory committee.
The proposal comes as the FDA continues to weigh whether to allow compounding pharmacies to manufacture peptides. In July, an FDA advisory panel voted to recommend that these pharmacies be cleared to manufacture six of these substances.

Where does Fleetwood beating Arsenal rank in biggest cup upsets?
- Published
Arsenal suffered a shock Carabao Cup exit at the home of Fleetwood Town, as the League Two side recorded one of the biggest upsets in the competition's history.
Mikel Arteta's Premier League champions lost 5-3 on penalties to a Fleetwood outfit ranked 84 places below them in the English football pyramid.
Following Fleetwood's victory, BBC Sport looks at some of the biggest shocks of all-time in the FA Cup and League Cup.
This isn't an exhaustive list, and you can leave your thoughts in the comments, rank the historic upsets and share your results.
Fleetwood 1-1 Arsenal (5-3 on pens, League Cup, 2026)
Fleetwood Town celebrated the biggest victory in the club's history as they stunned Champions League finalists Arsenal to reach the EFL Cup quarter-finals at Highbury Stadium.
The League Two club stunned the visitors when Aaron Loupalo-Bi gave Fleetwood, who sat 19th in English football's fourth tier, a 21st-minute lead.
Viktor Gyokeres pulled Arsenal level after the break - but they could not kick-on and were reduced to 10-men in the 86th minute when teenager Max Dowman kicked out following a challenge by Harrison Neal.
In the shootout, Fleetwood goalkeeper Jay Lynch saved Bruno Guimaraes' spot kick before Conor Haughey scored the winning penalty to spark scenes of ecstasy on the pitch and in the stands.
Grimsby 2-2 Man Utd (12-11 on pens, League Cup, 2025)
An upset as astonishing for its manner as it was for its proportions. Grimsby Town, a League Two side, beat top-flight Manchester United.
Not only did they win, but they were 2-0 up after 30 minutes following goals from Charles Vernam and Tyrell Warren.
The visitors pulled one back through Bryan Mbeumo with 15 minutes to go and United looked like they might squeeze through when Harry Maguire went on to level in the 89th minute.
But an incredible shootout followed, with Clarke Oduor for Grimsby and Matheus Cunha for Manchester United missing the only penalties as each side's 11 took one.
The players then went again and, after Darragh Burns scored to make it 12-11, Mbeumo struck his second spot-kick against the crossbar.
Plymouth 1-0 Liverpool (FA Cup, 2025)
Arne Slot made 10 changes to his Liverpool side after they had won an EFL Cup semi-final in their previous game and the Reds were made to pay.
Eight minutes after the interval, the Pilgrims were awarded a penalty after Harvey Elliott's handball and Ryan Hardie drilled home from the spot in emphatic fashion.
Hardie almost added a second shortly afterwards when his shot was turned on to the post by Liverpool keeper Caoimhin Kelleher.
The bottom club in the Championship held on, with Conor Hazard making crucial late saves, to beat a team who would go on to win the Premier League title.
Chelsea 2-4 Bradford City (FA Cup, 2015)
Bradford ranked 49 places below their opponents as they travelled to Stamford Bridge to take on Chelsea, who at that point were top of the Premier League.
Gary Cahill and Ramires netted to put the hosts 2-0 up and give Chelsea firm control of the fourth-round tie.
Bradford had other ideas, though, as Jon Stead pulled one back before Filipe Morais side-footed in an equaliser.
Andy Halliday then blasted the Bantams ahead before Mark Yeats slotted a fourth to inflict a crushing defeat on Jose Mourinho's side.
Oldham 3-2 Liverpool (FA Cup, 2013)
Premier League giants Liverpool had ample strength at Boundary Park, with the likes of Luis Suarez, Raheem Sterling and Daniel Sturridge all starting.
League One hosts Oldham were in the midst of financial problems but produced a spirited display against the odds, with Matt Smith nodding in a Youssouf M'Changama cross to open the scoring.
Suarez levelled, but Smith soon took advantage of an error from Liverpool goalkeeper Brad Jones before Reece Wabara netted a back-post header to give the Latics a 3-1 lead.
Joe Allen volleyed home to pull one back and Liverpool brought on Steven Gerrard, but it was not enough to avoid defeat.
Bradford City 1-1 Arsenal (3-2 on pens, League Cup, 2012)
A fourth-tier side against Premier League opposition in the quarter-finals of the league cup - Arsenal were clear favourites.
Bradford had already caused an upset in the tournament, beating Wigan on penalties in the round before.
Up for a fight at home to Arsene Wenger's Gunners, Garry Thompson volleyed the Bantams ahead before Thomas Vermaelen headed home a Santi Cazorla cross with just two minutes of normal time remaining.
Just as Mbeumo missed the decisive kick for United against Grimsby after scoring in normal time, the same happened for Vermaelen here as Bradford prevailed 3-2 on spot-kicks.
Liverpool 2-2 Northampton (2-4 on pens, League Cup, 2010)
Another surprise cup exit for Liverpool.
This one happened in the League Cup - at Anfield.
Milan Jovanovic fired in an opener for Liverpool but Billy McKay equalised and Michael Jacobs tapped in to give the Cobblers a lead early in extra time.
David Ngog scored from a late header to set up the penalty drama, but Northampton were the victors from the spot, with Abdul Osman keeping his cool to slot in the decisive spot-kick.
Man Utd 0-3 York City (League Cup, 1995)
Ruben Amorim is not the first Manchester United to suffer a shock in the League Cup - even Sir Alex Ferguson has faced the same.
The United boss didn't take the game lightly and made just four changes from the league game which they had played three days before, with the likes of David Beckham, Lee Sharpe and Ryan Giggs starting.
Paul Barnes, father of Newcastle winger Harvey Barnes, scored twice for Alan Little's visitors, including one from the penalty spot, before Tony Barras headed a third to inflict a crushing defeat at Old Trafford.
United put out another strong team at Bootham Crescent for the return leg two weeks later, with Eric Cantona in their squad, but despite getting two goals from Paul Scholes and another from Terry Cooke, the Minstermen went through 4-3 on aggregate thanks to a strike from Scott Jordan.
Wrexham 2-1 Arsenal (FA Cup, 1992)
Arsenal were reigning Premiership champions and second in the top flight.
Wrexham were 24th in the Third Division.
The Gunners made the trip to Wales as firm favourites and were just 10 minutes from securing a spot in the fourth round after Alan Smith's first-half opener.
But Mickey Thomas sent a 25-yard free kick past David Seaman before Steve Watkin's strike earned victory for Wrexham just two minutes later.
Sutton 2-1 Coventry (FA Cup, 1989)
Sutton United had a memorable cup run in 2016-17, beating three EFL teams - including Leeds United - before losing to Arsenal in the fifth round.
They have also produced one of the biggest shocks of all time.
The non-league side took on a Coventry team who were then in the First Division and had won the FA Cup in 1987.
The part-time side upset the odds at home, with Matthew Hanlan volleying home the winner just before the hour mark.
Hereford 2-1 Newcastle (FA Cup, 1972)
Top-flight Newcastle were beaten in the third round of the FA Cup by non-league opposition when they took on Hereford United in 1972.
Hereford took the tie to a replay after a 2-2 draw at St James' Park, but Newcastle looked destined to make it to the fourth round thanks to a late goal by Malcolm McDonald in the rematch.
However, the non-leaguers had other ideas and Ronnie Radford popped up to score the most famous 30-yard goal in FA Cup history to take the game into extra time.
Substitute Ricky George scored the winner - amid scenes of wild celebration at Edgar Street - as Hereford became the first non-league club to defeat a First Division side since 1949.
