On October 24, All India Students’ Association (AISA) president Neha Bora arrived at Delhi’s Mandir Marg police station in a Toyota Camry. Bora had been summoned to appear before the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) in connection with proceedings requiring her to furnish a peace bond following her participation in protests in the city, which Bora has denied signing.
Subsequently, several social media users began claiming that she owned the luxury car, questioning how a student could afford a vehicle reportedly worth Rs 60–70 lakh.
An X account, Tejash (@lord_geopolitic), shared an image showing the car’s registration number alongside a photograph of Neha. Calling the AISA president a “communist fraud”, the user questioned how Neha, a PhD student at JNU School of Arts and Aesthetics, could afford such an expensive vehicle and asked Grok about her source of income. The post garnered around 727,100 views and over 600 shares. (Archive)
Neha Bora is a communist fraud and a failed student who doesn’t have a job and only participates in protests, yet she is roaming around in a luxury car worth ₹60–70 lakh.
Hey @Grok, what’s her source of income? 🤔 https://t.co/5iCfUo6juP
— Tejash (@lord_geopolitic) October 24, 2026
Another X user, Monica Verma (@TrulyMonica) posted a video showing the car entering the police station, claiming that “Only in India would unemployed students travel in luxury cars.” The post similarly implied that Neha owned the vehicle. This post amassed around 380,000 views and over 3,000 shares. (Archive)
“Student Leader” Neha Bora is coming to police station in a ₹65 lakhs Toyota Camry Car. Only in India would unemployed students travel in luxury cars 🤡 https://t.co/t3iKqjCK2K
— Monica Verma (@TrulyMonica) October 24, 2026
Several other users circulated similar claims, questioning how Neha could afford to travel in a “luxury” car while being a student and participating in protests. Some posts even insinuated that student protesters were receiving funding from undisclosed sources to “abuse Modi and India”.
A few of the claims are shown in the gallery below:
Fact Check
Alt News contacted Neha to ask about the details of the car. She clarified that the car did not belong to her but is her lawyer Abhik Chimni’s. She further stated that she does not own any vehicle. “I don’t have a car or any form of vehicle of my own. That car belongs to my lawyer Abhik Chimni. He not only has a successful career allowing him to afford a car but is also generous enough to offer to escort me inside the Mandir Marg police station in it,” she said.
“The escorting was necessary because a mob was chanting ‘Neha Bora Murdabad’, ‘Desh Ke gaddaron ko, joote maaron saalon ko’ amongst other slogans outside the police station…The Delhi Police took no steps to disperse the crowd until Abhik specifically mentioned it to the Magistrate and requested him to take measures to handle the hostile and possibly violent atmosphere outside the police station,” Neha told Alt News.
In the video, the number plate is visible and it is: DL12CY3747. Alt News obtained the vehicle’s registration certificate (RC), which identifies the white Toyota Camry hybrid EV with the same number plate as belonging to Neha’s lawyer, Abhik Chimni.
Speaking to Alt News, N Sai Balaji, former AISA president, who accompanied Neha to the Mandir Marg police station on October 24, corroborated her account of the situation outside the station.
According to Balaji, him and Neha initially reached the location in a cab. However, they encountered around 40 people whom he described as Right-wing supporters, allegedly raising slogans against Neha and threatening her safety. He said that Chimni then raised concerns with the police about Neha’s security and requested that the entrance be cleared. The police suggested that Neha enter the premises in a private vehicle, offering to allow a car inside the police station under police escort.
After the incident, Neha took to Instagram to describe the situation, stating that about “50-60” goons had gathered around 100 meters away from the station, allegedly raising threatening slogans against her.
View this post on Instagram
To sum up, the claim that Neha owns a Toyota Camry reportedly worth Rs 60–70 lakh is false and misleading. Neha denied owning any vehicle and the car’s RC identifies her lawyer, Abhik Chimni, as its registered owner.

Narendra Modi’s heavy-handed crackdown on protests over electoral rights in Delhi appears to have backfired. Over the weekend, his government tried to crush demonstrations led by the gen Z Cockroach Janta party (CJP). It locked up thousands of young people, detained journalists and shut down the capital as if he had declared emergency rule. Abhijeet Dipke, who launched the CJP in May after India’s chief justice compared jobless youths to “cockroaches”, was detained with other leaders when he landed in Delhi. Those who did take to the Indian capital’s streets were roughed up by police or taken into custody. Even when the usually deferential supreme court ordered peaceful assembly be protected, Mr Modi’s government showed its authoritarian contempt for fundamental constitutional rights.
This was less a display of strength than a government showing its fear of voters it claims to represent. But the actions did not stop the protests. On Monday, thousands marched in Delhi, demanding the resignation of India’s election chief over reports that the names of more than 130 million voters were deleted from the electoral roll to benefit Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) in recent elections. It’s a charge that India’s election commission denies, although some commissioners have raised concerns over voters’ names being removed without their knowledge.
Demonstrators’ demands for electoral fairness deserve answers, not arrests and intimidation. The BJP won state elections in West Bengal, where Muslims make up roughly 27% of the 100m population, for the first time ever after 2.7 million voters had been officially struck off the rolls. In many seats won by the BJP, the number of deleted or disputed voters exceeded the margin of victory. The courts said that the missing voters could cast their ballots next time.
Mass voter deletions and a brutal crackdown are fuelling distrust. Daily protests by student organisations, political parties and the Cockroach movement have been taking place in the capital for weeks. The world’s largest democracy ought to be protecting constitutional rights and finding responses to its critics. A crisis is growing because of repeated cycles of government failure, official denial and resistance to accountability. The Cockroach movement was born of anger over indifference to exam leaks that benefit connected insiders. It has become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Clearly, many are now challenging a government that they say denies them opportunity and accountability. Repression risks hardening their frustration into wider resistance.
This latest episode reveals that Mr Modi has significantly weakened the public’s faith in independent institutions like the election commission and the courts. That may be by design. It’s hard not to think that India’s prime minster bets he can survive the public’s anger as long as the protesters cannot turn it into leverage over his government – and the institutions meant to hold power accountable refuse to act. But what happens when the state makes correcting mistakes impossible? Without a democratic release, the ire builds up to a potentially volatile confrontation.
There is still reason for hope in India. The Indian Express newspaper revealed officials had raised objections to scrubbing voter lists. The resulting political mobilisation has raised the cost of ignoring such dissent. Mr Modi can’t wave this issue away. In 2011, corruption scandals became evidence that the Congress-led government had lost its moral authority. Mr Modi rode the wave of public disgust into power three years later. Now, allegations about electoral rolls could unite people around the belief that Mr Modi has betrayed them. Silencing young people with martial law-like tactics only helps to dramatise the grievance.

The internet must be put out of its misery.
Any rational observer can admit that the current iteration of the web—and the social fabric woven there—is not what they signed up for. Symptoms of advanced cultural decay can no longer be ignored. This thing is eating itself.
Giants including Meta and Google have been forced to settle massive consumer lawsuits brought over privacy violations and mental health harms allegedly caused by the addictive mechanisms of their platforms. Schools are banning smartphones as multiple countries institute social media restrictions for under-16s. Parents are in a panic about their kids aspiring to careers as social media celebrities, losing themselves in a vast ecosystem of online casinos, or joining extremist movements.
Generative AI, briefly considered an amusing novelty, is now a turbocharged slop engine for the web, filling feeds and comment sections with useless, grotesque content. As humans scroll past headlines about AI taking their jobs, confusing fantasy for reality, and contributing to cognitive decline, any consumer appeal the technology might have is turning to anguish. The data centers that power it have become increasingly unpopular, and politically radioactive.
To be online, many now admit, is to be endlessly manipulated and exploited. In December, Oxford University Press declared rage bait to be the word of the year, noting that use of the term had tripled over the previous 12 months. The lexical spike represented a heightened awareness that monetized social accounts churn out bad-faith takes and extremist content, automating this abusive behavior with generative AI, simply to profit off hostile engagement. Billionaire oligarchs have opened the floodgates to such inauthentic activity, conspiracy-mongering, and hate speech by rolling back moderation.
In short, when you hang around online in 2026, you see little worth saving. Perhaps a decade ago, you felt that the glimmers of community and joy, of artistic and intellectual exchange, were enough to balance out the toxic junk. No longer.
It’s not necessarily that people have gotten worse. “Dead Internet Theory”—the proposition that a vast majority of the interactions on the web are fake, bots talking to other bots—has accrued more supporting evidence recently. One cybersecurity firm concluded this spring that agents already outnumber human users, their traffic surging by 8,000 percent through 2025. No wonder seemingly everyone has at some point caught themselves scrolling through a wasteland of brainrot and asked, “What the hell am I even looking at?” Underlying that question is another: “Is it always going to be like this?”
With this anxiety hammering at my prefrontal cortex day in and out, I was more than intrigued by the absolutist title of technologist and Pulitzer-winning journalist John West’s new book, The Internet Will Die, and So Will You: On Learning to Live in Our Digital Age. In his discerning treatise, West confirms what many have suspected for a good while now: The platforms once seen as enduring archives of knowledge and communication are being cannibalized by ideological warfare and basic greed.
But that’s not the whole story. For one, West argues, people misperceive the “vastness” of the internet, which really amounts to “a vanishing fraction, a rounding error, of the human experience.” Moreover, it is remarkably fragile—West opens with the story of how a 2001 train derailment in a Baltimore tunnel took out a major bundle of fiber-optic cables, leading to internet slowdowns nationwide—and continually undergoes cycles of death and rebirth as a result of this natural instability.
If the internet is much smaller and less solid than imagined, West’s book suggests, then it’s crucial to recognize the forces that determine how those deaths unfold, or which pieces are preserved while others crumble. Because the market has falsely sold us the web as a comprehensive library of accumulated wisdom, each transient phase of this global network comes to define the present, for better and worse. Today we witness a dismal paralysis brought on by algorithmic incentives to churn out inflammatory garbage: Full-time influencers are in a losing arms race for attention with low-effort, high-volume channels that streamline production by delegating the creative process to bleeding-edge software.
West draws a sharp contrast between this holographic environment of monetization and a passionate, personalized internet that spanned from the primordial GeoCities to Tumblr, describing how these innovative communities have been gradually erased. While some endure in half-dead and highly corrupted form, others are lost. In middle school, West maintained a web page devoted to his love of anime; later, he kept a blog documenting his college years. Looking back as an adult, he’s vexed by the fates that have befallen each.
“I really wanted to delete my anime site,” West tells WIRED. “I don't have access to the AOL account anymore, and I couldn't do it.” Instead, it lives on as a zombie page, cluttered with spam ads and dead-end links. As for the college blog, he had neglected to pay domain fees toward the end of his time writing it, and so the final year of posts disappeared. “I kind of got obsessed with this idea that the things we want to last really don't, and then oftentimes the things that we kind of wish would go away hang on for way too long,” West says.
These shifting sands are a far cry from the flawless, collective, permanent memory that internet users originally believed they were building. “‘Forever’ is such a strong word, and it's the wrong word,” West says. Online spaces are memento mori, the same as individuals who self-promote across them (and that includes certain longevity-obsessed biohackers). Sure, there was a time when a celebrity could be “canceled” for tasteless posts unearthed years later, but in 2026, it’s not so easy to surface specific messages when you go hunting for them in your AI-powered Gmail account. Zeitgeist-defining platforms like Vine can be vaporized in an instant, a fact reinforced in January 2025, when Americans posted farewell TikTok videos ahead of an expected US ban on the app.
This random ephemerality, West points out, has eroded any confidence in claims previously backed up by hypertext cross-references, and thus any kind of consensus truth. An analysis of hyperlinks in articles on The New York Times website between 1996 and mid-2019 found that 25 percent of all links were inaccessible. According to a 2016 study, “three out of four citations in scholarly articles have drifted—the websites they purport to cite no longer say what they once did,” he writes. “Over half of Wikipedia’s entries contain at least one link in its references section that goes nowhere, a Pew report found.”
The impulse to drive engagement spreads to users themselves: West noticed, for instance, that when he recently reread a favorite book, Marilynne Robinson’s Gilead, he had the nagging thought that while he loved returning to the novel for the fourth or fifth time, he wouldn’t be able to count it toward his annual Goodreads stats. West says this fixation on the internet’s hollow validations creates “the exact conditions for a space to be filled by something that isn't human.”
Wouldn’t it be liberating, then, to actually deny our attention to astroturfed outrage, engineered virality, and influencer sponcon? To let the mainstream digital economies propped up by AI-enabled surveillance finally fall to ruin? If what the titans of the industry have to offer us these days are “pervert glasses” and the suppression of ads for a probably unflattering documentary, why are we helping them stay in business? Leaving their platforms for dead might be the last lever of power available to the masses.
Doing so could free people to explore dormant corners. West notes that some of the most interesting parts of the internet are the ones that nobody sees, like web portals to streams of YouTube videos that have almost no views. “Some of it’s fucking weird and creepy, but a lot of it’s just people singing a song and having a blast,” he says. West also cites the bustling, zero-revenue, circulation of poetry in web journals as proof that “you can find meaning and make meaning online all the time,” provided there is no financial motivation.
When you eliminate what the platforms want you to fixate on, it’s clear what you’ve been missing, and how you were steered away from it. Your opinions are shaped in a bubble by avatars you’ve never met, weaponized against equally hermetic rival camps. The internet doesn’t really have winners, unless you count the few without the sense to stop chasing relevance at any cost. That’s why the main characters are so malleable in their beliefs; never afraid to pivot, betray, and discard what they once held to be the core of their identity. And that’s when they stood for anything to begin with.
Absent a sudden, lasting outage due to a fresh and severe catastrophe, the internet as it exists won’t perish anytime soon. There are, however, splintering cracks in its facade, which may create room for emergent and strangely evolved life-forms. There’s no reason to assume that the present tech empire will rule the century to come; the organic and anarchic web stands to mount a triumphant renaissance if (or when) it falls.
“Look, the internet is rotting,” West says. “The question is, where are we going to put our energy?” A metaphor he often turns to in his book is compost. “Compost is just rot harnessed for a purpose,” he says. Can a decaying internet be fertilizer for something better? It’s a rosy notion, but speaking as a perennially failed composter—it’s just too gross, and I’m too lazy—I have my doubts about whether enough hardy, patient gardeners can be mobilized to make our digital landscape bloom once more.
Then again, as West’s book sought to remind me, I am destined to die as well. Maybe I’ll be mixed in with the soil.

Popcorn bucket innovation is at an all-time low and the Dune: Part Three 'Double Sandworm' is proof
Where is the imagination?
Collectible popcorn buckets have become a fixture of movie theaters' post-pandemic recovery, and if hawking plastic helps them keep the lights on, so be it. But if we are going to submit ourselves to the Funko Pop-ification of food receptacles, shouldn't they at least be interesting?
Two years after Dune: Part Two's Sandworm popcorn bucket went viral, AMC Theatres made the obvious decision to double down for Dune: Part Three. The theater chain is selling two themed buckets for the film's release, the "Sandworm Thumper" and "Double Sandworm," each with a worm-shaped hand hole (the Double, naturally, has two).
An epic conclusion calls for legendary collectibles. See DUNE: PART THREE and seize control of your collection, including AMC Theatres exclusives on 12/17. Take a sneak peek now. 👀 https://t.co/XIUIke0xaZ pic.twitter.com/h0xjF4WwWS
— AMC Theatres (@AMCTheatres) October 29, 2026
Adding a second hole solves one of the original bucket's problems by letting two people reach for popcorn at the same time, while underlining the sexual innuendo many people found implicit in the original bucket's orifice. It's also completely uninspired.
You can get a lot of mileage out of serving popcorn out of an unusually shaped box. AMC was right to think it would be funny to eat out of a handbag while watching The Devil Wears Prada 2. It's hard not to love the Trojan Horse bucket sold for The Odyssey. Even the "Guile Hair" wearable popcorn bucket the company sold alongside Street Fighter has some charm. But those are the exceptions, and novelty can only take you so far.
Is it actually fun to reach on top of your head for popcorn more than once? Is adding a second hole the best AMC could come up with to capture the spirit of one of the more visually striking blockbuster franchises in recent memory? Should anyone in their right mind pay $35 for a bowl with a lumpy hand in it that says "Clayface" on the side? I don't think so.
One reason the original Sandworm bucket might have connected is that its creators somehow didn't anticipate people would immediately see it as a sex toy. It was weird, seemingly by accident. Most popcorn buckets released since don't appear to be made with that same level of childlike naivete, and they're worse for it.

An immunization worker gets set up to receive her wages on her mobile wallet in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Credit: WHO
Campaigns in Africa to stop polio and other diseases have a more stable, better-motivated workforce thanks to WHO’s collaboration with countries and partners to pay frontline health workers through their mobile phones instead of in cash.
“Over 80 percent of workers are saying they prefer the digital payments,” said Ahmed Hamani Djibo, head of WHO’s Digital Finance Team.
WHO has been leading among international organizations in moving away from the unwieldy, less-secure practice of disbursing salaries in cash. Over the past few years, the Organization launched its Digital Finance Team and joined the Better Than Cash Alliance, an 80-member United Nations partnership with a mandate to develop the digitization of payments and expand financial inclusion – activities that support the UN Sustainable Development Goals.
Since it was established in 2020, WHO’s Digital Finance Team has designed and implemented digital payment solutions in 24 countries in Africa, including, last year, in Benin, Botswana, Madagascar, Rwanda, Togo and Zimbabwe.
“WHO has successfully digitized payments for more than two million health workers across Africa,” said Tidhar Wald, Managing Director, a.i., at the Better Than Cash Alliance. “With these inspiring results, WHO is taking a clear leadership role in accelerating the digital transformation in the provision of health outcomes globally.”
A polio immunization team on the job in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Credit: WHO
“A really big difference in speed”
Workers surveyed in Côte d’Ivoire, Liberia and Tanzania said they appreciated the security of not carrying cash, the convenience of no longer having to travel to a disbursement site to receive their wages, and above all, the speed of payment – as short as half an hour after finishing work compared to waits of weeks or even months.
The surveys, funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, linked timely compensation to better morale and worker retention.
“There is really a big difference in speed,” said Jean-Luc, a health worker interviewed in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) at the end of a polio immunization campaign. “We finished the campaign mop-up yesterday and received a text notification the next evening. I’m going to pay my child’s school fees. Now we can relax.”
Digital payments also save time and money for health campaign organizers, including the burden and expense of transporting large sums of cash and completing documentation.
“When you have 300 to 500 volunteers to pay, doing accounts and signing receipts takes a lot of time,” said Saïdi, a polio team leader in DRC.
WHO first used the new digital payments in polio immunization campaigns in Côte d’Ivoire. Although outbreaks of vaccine-derived polio were on the rise, vaccination campaigns were having trouble getting off the ground. In the first quarter of 2020, almost half the polio campaigns in WHO’s African Region were postponed, saw workers drop out, or suffered other detrimental effects stemming from delays in cash disbursements.
As WHO and partners worked to develop the nuts-and-bolts aspects of a digital payment ecosystem (registering workers into a database, verifying their profiles with the mobile network operator and more) the benefits of a cashless approach became more apparent.
"There is substantial evidence that digitizing payments can support people, especially women, to gain access to financial services and increase control over their earnings,” said Maria May, Senior Program Officer, Inclusive Financial Systems, at the Gates Foundation. “Over the past four years, the World Health Organization has utilized the growing presence of mobile money across Africa to ensure that the courageous frontline vaccinators in polio outbreak campaigns are paid completely, quickly, and securely.”
Alain Labrique, director of WHO’s Department of Digital Health and Innovation, said that “digital payments are one of the key pillars of Digital Health Public Infrastructure currently strongly encouraged within WHO’s guidance to member-states on Digital Transformation.” WHO views digital payments as a foundation for many more digital development activities, together with Data Exchange and Digital ID Infrastructure. He added “we are delighted to work with partners in the digital space and add our voice to this celebration of WHO's joining the Better Than Cash Alliance”.

Why Hurts played with blood clot and what it means for NFL
- Published
News that Jalen Hurts played a game hours after being diagnosed with a blood clot had already shocked the NFL world.
The Philadelphia Eagles then said their star quarterback will probably miss the rest of the season after multiple blood clots were found in his lungs - a life-threatening condition if not treated quickly.
It raised questions over the NFL's handling of the matter and its general approach to player health and safety, partly because the game in question was part of the league's international series.
Hurts' initial diagnosis was in London, before the Eagles played at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on 11 October, and he flew back with the team that evening.
What do we know about what happened? Why was Hurts allowed to play and then fly home straight after? And what does it mean for him, the Eagles and the NFL?
What happened?
Sunday, 4 October: Another player stepped on Hurts' left calf during Philadelphia's defeat by the Los Angeles Rams, although he completed the game.
Thursday, 8 October: Hurts first reported an issue to the team. He trained in full all week and had treatment on Thursday and Friday.
Saturday, 10 October: The Eagles arrived in London in the morning and Hurts visited the Cleveland Clinic that evening. An ultrasound showed he had a superficial blood clot (vein thrombosis) in his calf but he was cleared to play on Sunday.
Sunday, 11 October: Hurts returned to the team hotel at about 3am before playing the full game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. A follow-up ultrasound was recommended within 72 hours and Hurts was cleared for the flight home.
Wednesday, 14 October: After receiving daily treatment, Hurts had another ultrasound, which showed the clot had moved, and he was ruled out of the next game.
Monday, 19 October: Joint statement by the Eagles and Hurts' agent said further tests showed he now has deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli (multiple blood clots in both lungs).
His treatment will involve blood-thinning medicine and he should make a full recovery but is expected to miss the rest of the season.
What has the NFL said?
Some of the initial reports said that Hurts did not sleep for 36 hours before playing in London, but his agent later confirmed that he slept after returning to the hotel and also at the stadium.
Dr Allen Sills, the NFL's chief medical officer, was in London that weekend and arranged for Hurts to be evaluated at the Cleveland Clinic, an American-owned private hospital which is an official supplier of sports medicine services for the NFL's London games.
The NFL has protocols in place for concussions, emergency preparedness and extreme heat, for games in the US and overseas.
But, speaking at a news conference last Tuesday, Sills explained the league does not have a protocol for situations such as this.
Nevertheless, Sills said that those who dealt with Hurts were "incredibly conservative" and that he had "complete confidence" in how the Eagles handled the situation.
Later that day, the NFL Players Association (NFLPA) called for a full investigation, adding that the NFL "previously informed the union that it did not plan to review the care [Hurts] received".
However, on Sunday the league and NFLPA released a joint statement saying they are "working together to review the matter".
Was anything done wrong?
The NFL's next international game is in Madrid on 8 November and the local medical co-ordinator is Real Madrid's chief medical officer, Dr Niko Mihic.
Dr Mihic told BBC Sport that blood clots among athletes are "not that common" and remembers in a previous role it took three visits for a baseball player to be diagnosed with a blood clot, because it is not something immediately associated with sports injuries.
Medical advice on whether to sleep and/or stay active is decided case by case. The same goes for whether it is safe to board a long-haul flight with a blood clot, as Hurts was allowed to do.
"It's not as simple as some people think," said Dr Mihic. "There's an amount of judgement that goes into this. It's like you're stuck between a rock and a hard place, but then you make your call."
As he and the NFL finalise their medical preparations for the Madrid game, Dr Mihic expects them to discuss scenarios such as that involving Hurts.
Asked what the NFL can learn from Hurts ultimately getting blood clots in his lungs, the league's Dr Sills replied: "I don't think you can take that outcome and say there was something flawed about the process.
"Sometimes in medicine we do all the right things and other things develop... but we have a committee that looks at all these cases."

  - Published5 October 2023
What does it mean?
Whatever the outcome of the NFL's joint review with the NFLPA, the league will face greater scrutiny over how they handle players around games played overseas.
Players had a 16-hour flight for Australia's first NFL game in September, while the NFLPA's executive director JC Tretter expressed safety concerns over the quality of the field for the game in Brazil.
There are a record nine international games this year and, although the NFL ultimately wants 16 per season, Tretter added that "the goal has to be growing the game while maintaining the standards our players deserve".
Only Hurts knows how he feels about the way he was treated by his team and the NFL's doctors, but even before this issue there had been talk of the 2025 Super Bowl MVP leaving the Eagles.
Even if he does make a full recovery and returns to action, the 28-year-old will always have to bear blood clots in mind.
"The worst risk factor for recurrent embolisms is having had one previously," said Dr Mihic.
As for Philadelphia, they do not have an experienced quarterback in reserve and back-up Tanner McKee could not prevent them suffering a fifth straight defeat on Monday.
They were beaten 38-21 at home by the Dallas Cowboys to extend their longest losing streak under coach Nick Sirianni, so this could be a long season for the injury-hit Eagles.
Or with the trade deadline two weeks away, this could be the start of a rebuild for a team that reached two of the past four Super Bowls.

The move is reportedly aimed at seeking an edge in financial markets where Trump's statements can trigger movements. The API enables subscribers to receive Trump’s posts faster than any human could by manually checking the platform. The service is said to give subscribers a timing advantage. It is reported to be ahead around 50 milliseconds, according to Trump Media officials. That difference might seem insignificant but can matter to high-frequency trading firms, especially those who rely on algorithmic and automated strategies to respond to market movement. Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Adam Schiff asked the US Securities and Exchange Commission in July to investigate whether the service violated securities laws and called it a “shocking abuse” of office by a president for personal gain. VRChat says it's not adding AI labels despite user survey showing people want that
Trying to make everyone happy could make no one happy.
VRChat has published a support post explaining the results from a survey of users regarding artificial intelligence on the platform. Despite 95 percent of its respondents stating that they want some form of label to designate AI usage, the company said that at this time, it will not be implementing any tags in that vein. VRChat is an app for creating and sharing virtual worlds for hosting social interactions.
The post says that VRChat will continue weighing the addition of a label for "Human-authored" content as well as a "Tools used" field, but it has not adopted a definitive stance yet. Similarly, it will not add a tag for labeling AI-generated content or for filtering it out of search results.
"While we think some creators would honestly label their content, we think others would try to pass off generative or assisted work as completely authored by hand," the game's creators said. "Likewise, we could see this creating 'sleuthing' behavior, where folks would attempt to sniff out 'AI' content or might harass other creators, even if they are genuinely not using any AI tools in their workflow."
The language in the post seems to want to make people with many different attitudes toward AI all happy, rather than accepting that it might adopt a policy that could be unpopular with any particular group. Instead, the platform said it would adopt some changes that had "alignment across the community," which included accurate thumbnails, better discovery tools and "quality as a core metric."
VRChat has displayed the potential for creating some genuinely cool things. It's being used in filmmaking and to create safe communities for transgender people. On the flip side, the platform has also been accused of hosting toxic and predatory behavior.

The U.S. health regulator has accepted Merck’s experimental targeted drug for a priority review based on data from a late-stage trial where it extended survival in women with an advanced form of endometrial cancer.
The drug, sacituzumab tirumotecan, also known as sac-TMT, delivers a cancer-killing payload to cells that carry a protein called TROP2, which is common in endometrial tumors.
The trial enrolled 776 patients whose cancer had returned or progressed after earlier treatment. Patients were randomly assigned to sac-TMT or to a chemotherapy their doctor chose, either doxorubicin or paclitaxel.
Results showed sac-TMT reduced the risk of death by 32%, with patients living a median of 19 months compared with 12.1 months on standard chemotherapy.
The treatment also reduced the risk of cancer progression or death by 41%, with patients remaining progression-free for a median of 7.2 months compared with 3.9 months on chemotherapy.
In addition, about 35% of sac-TMT patients saw their tumors shrink, compared with 17% on chemotherapy.
A regulatory decision is expected by June 2027, Merck said. The trial data was presented at the ESMO medical congress.
“Based on discussions with the FDA, the company is hopeful for an approval before the PDUFA date to bring sac-TMT to patients as quickly as possible,” said Dean Y. Li, president, Merck Research Laboratories.
Severe treatment-related side effects were more frequent with sac-TMT, affecting about 54% of patients compared with 41% on chemotherapy. About 3% of patients stopped treatment due to side effects.
About 68,000 cases of endometrial cancer are expected to be diagnosed in the United States in 2026, with over 14,000 deaths, according to the American Cancer Society.
Jefferies analysts project peak sales of roughly $900 million in endometrial cancer for the drug and $9 billion across all potential indications.
Merck is developing the drug with Chinese biotech firm Kelun-Biotech, which discovered the therapy.

Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said.
Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer.
But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India.
When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries.
Alexander’s comments show how much Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, who called this week for a “serious dialogue” on the UK’s relations with the EU, including possible re-entry, has shifted the government’s position.
Speaking to the Guardian from a trade delegation to India, Alexander welcomed the progress made since the Indian agreement came into force earlier this year, since when the price of scotch whisky in India has fallen by 10-15%.
But he said the economic benefits of trading agreements with the EU would be greater.
“In trade policy, geography still matters,” he said. “The Channel is just 21 miles wide. Our largest trading partner is and will remain the European Union in the years to come. We trade almost twice the amount with the European Union that we do with the United States, the largest single-country trading partner.”
He said: “It’s no secret that I was not a supporter of leaving the European Union, and I called out early as trade minister what I described as the ‘post-imperial delusions’ of the Brexiteers. Back in 2016, they promised a world of Britain as a buccaneering free trade nation in a world where barriers were coming down. Sadly, what we’ve witnessed in the year since is a more protectionist, more regionalised world in which barriers have been going up.
“At the time we joined the Pacific trade grouping, the CPTPP [Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership] – which undoubtedly makes a lot of sense geopolitically for the UK – our own analysis made clear that the long-term boost to UK GDP from membership is less than a tenth of 1%. If you compare that with estimates of the structural damage to the UK economy from Brexit, you get a sense of just how important Europe remains to our future trade and prosperity.
“We’re already paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours who, with almost half of total UK trade, remain easily our largest trading partners.”
Alexander was speaking in Mumbai, where he was joined by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, as well as a group of mayors from northern England. He made it clear he did not support any particular method of achieving closer relations with the EU.
The ministers spent much of their time in meetings with Indian officials as they attempt to iron out what they say have been “teething problems” with the early implementation, especially for smaller businesses.
“There are always teething problems,” Alexander said. “We’re also having a conversation at the level of regulation to see how do we overcome non-tariff barriers that can prove to be an inhibitor to the kind of progress we want to see unless they’re addressed.”
Many in the government say a bigger prize will be to reach an agreement at next month’s EU summit, where Burnham hopes to sign new trading deals for emissions, electricity and agricultural products.
One hurdle to delivering that is the UK’s desire to discuss the protectionist “Made in Europe” policy, which British manufacturers fear will shut them out of a key market. EU leaders say they are willing to discuss British entry into that scheme, though they are also pushing for the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, without which they fear the UK will become a back door into the European market.
Reynolds told the Guardian this week he would not impose tariffs simply because of pressure from Brussels.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration published draft guidance that would streamline approvals of some individualized gene therapies, a win for rare disease advocates who have criticized the agency approach to these treatments, STAT says. The FDA has continued to require companies to submit separate drug approval applications for each patient’s customized gene therapy, even when they use fundamentally the same approach to target different genes. Advocates argue this creates a prohibitively expensive regulatory burden. The new draft guidance formalizes a “plausible mechanism pathway,” and offers more specific rules for licensing and updating gene editing treatments.
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway warned Eli Lilly to discontinue its practice of requiring hospitals to provide claims data to receive discounted medicines under a federal program, a sign that more states are pushing back against such moves by drugmakers, STAT notes. The US ambassador has suggested Canada could be blamed if Republicans perform poorly in next week’s midterm elections, the latest intervention from a controversial figure who has been accused of inflaming a bitter dispute that has angered and baffled residents of both countries.
On Wednesday, CTV news reported that Pete Hoekstra told business leaders at a closed door meeting that if a number of swing races – including Maine and Michigan – go to the Democrats, it could make things harder for Canada because Donald Trump might try to blame the loss on it.
“That’s an interesting way of framing it,” the prime minister, Mark Carney, told reporters when asked about the allegations.
For months, Canada and the US have been locked in a bitter tariff war, with Ottawa retaliating against illegal US tariffs and targeting goods in states that rely heavily on trade with Canada.
Carney said that Canada “will pursue” such a deal if it presents itself, but that Ottawa’s trade negotiators are “not in that position right now”.
Hoekstra is a deeply polarizing figure in Canada, particular for his response to Trump’s rhetoric about making Canada the 51st US state. Speaking to a Michigan radio station last year, he described the threats as a “sign of affection” and questioned why Canadians were offended by what he characterized as a “generous offer”. He had previously described Canada’s 2025 federal election as “anti-American”.
This year a House of Commons petition signed by more than 225,000 Canadians called for his expulsion, suggesting his statements violated diplomatic protocols, including the prohibition on diplomats interfering in the internal affairs of a host country.
More recently, Hoekstra has accused Canadian officials of interfering in US elections, pointing to Canadian politicians who have criticized the tariffs in US media, and the province of Ontario’s anti-tariff advertisement that ran on US television.
“We see all of that. We are monitoring it. We are evaluating it. And if some of it becomes election interference, America will respond to it,” Hoekstra, who comes from Michigan, recently told a Canadian podcast, adding that Canadians should “keep your nose out of American politics”.
Canada’s industry minister, Mélanie Joly, who was a target of Hoekstra’s comments, told reporters in Ottawa that her country “would never do that” and said Canada would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada”.
Carney, while in Turkey, told reporters there was “no merit” to the claims of interference and that he was “disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions”.
Roland Paris, the director of the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs at the University of Ottawa and a foreign affairs adviser to the former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, said the remarks were an “extraordinary thing” for a US ambassador to say about his host country and looked like an effort to “manufacture a pretext for the Trump administration’s own political difficulties”.
“The job of an ambassador is to represent the interests of his country, but it’s also to maintain channels of communication and build relationships and manage disagreements,” he said.
“His comments have repeatedly aggravated tensions instead of helping to manage them. I don’t think that he’s serving American interests very well. I’m not even sure that he’s serving the interests of his president.”
Paris points to polling in the US that shows voters have increasingly linked tariffs, the war and cost of living. There is also widespread confusion over why the White House has chosen to treat Canada as a trade adversary.
“It’s certainly not working in Canada. It’s on the contrary. It seems that every time Mr Hoekstra opens his mouth, the Canadians are more determined than before to stand up to the bullying of the Trump administration,” he said. “That’s not serving American interests.”
The US embassy denied Hoekstra said Canada would face blame for a poor Republican showing, suggesting the remarks were “grossly taken out of context” from a broader discussion.
“The ambassador has consistently said that the Canadian media is attempting to overstate the relevance of Canadian issues in American elections. As we have previously stated, Americans will decide American elections based on issues that are important to them,” the embassy said in a statement.
At a Canadian American Business event last year, Hoekstra delivered what witnesses say was an expletive-laden tirade at Ontario’s trade representative after the province ran a series of anti-tariff ads in the US that featured Ronald Reagan. Ontario’s premier called the outburst “absolutely unacceptable” and “unbecoming of an ambassador”.
Last week, Barack Obama noted the unusual choice to attack a longtime ally while speaking at a Democratic campaign rally in Detroit, mocking Trump’s fixation on Canada and jokingly referring to his northern neighbor as a “well-known evil empire”.
“That historical adversary of ours: Canada,” the former US president said. “It’s your neighbor! It’s a few minutes drive over the bridge. These are the people who gave us Martin Short … and maple syrup. They are the nicest people. And somehow we’ve gotten them so mad.”

Delhi Metro trains to operate till midnight on Oct 30 for Diljit Dosanjh concert at JLN Stadium
The restrictions will remain in force from 1 pm to midnight on October 30.
The Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) said on Thursday it will extend train services until midnight on October 30 to help spectators travel to and from Jawaharlal Nehru (JLN) Stadium, where singer Diljit Dosanjh is scheduled to perform as part of his “Aura India Tour 2026”.
The move comes as the concert is expected to draw approximately 70,000 spectators, many of whom are likely to rely on the metro to reach the venue and return home after the event.
Metro services on all lines, except the Airport Express Line and Rapid Metro in Gurugram, will be extended beyond their normal operating hours on Friday, the DMRC said on its X handle.
Additional train trips will be operated across the network to manage the rush after the concert, while standby trains will be kept ready to handle any unexpected surge in passenger traffic.
The timings for QR ticket purchases through the Delhi Metro Sarthi mobile app will also be extended by an hour in view of the revised service timings.

'No sugar-coating it': NDP ex-ministers admit frustration at snap election blunder
Both Ravi Parmar and Niki Sharma leave door open to NDP leadership run
Two prominent figures in British Columbia's outgoing NDP government have spoken out about the scale of the mistake made in calling last weekend's election that resulted in the party's crushing defeat.
Niki Sharma and Ravi Parmar are both leaving open the possibility they may seek party leadership in the wake of the resignation of outgoing Premier David Eby, as the decimated NDP caucus meets at the legislature.
Sharma, who was previously attorney general, says Eby apologized for calling the snap election at a meeting of the outgoing caucus on Wednesday, and he "took full responsibility."
She says she's not seeking the interim leadership of the party, a position that is being discussed at today's meeting of the incoming caucus, but was non-committal on the permanent leadership.
Parmar, the outgoing forests minister, says the party and Eby clearly made the wrong decision to call the election that resulted in a two-thirds majority of 63 seats for the B.C. Conservatives, while the NDP ranks have been reduced from 47 to 28, according to the preliminary count.
Parmar says the party "got it wrong" and owes British Columbians an apology for calling the election, while adding that it's too early to say if he'll seek leadership.
"The premier made a decision, we all stood by him … clearly we made the wrong decision calling the election, and that's something that we're all going to live by," he said before the start of the caucus meeting.
Asked to rate the level of frustration at the election call, Parmar said it was "about 10, absolutely."
"I'm disappointed, I'm frustrated, but that disappointment and frustration can't last four years, it can only last a few days," he said.
Sharma said that Wednesday's outgoing caucus meeting was an emotional affair, as colleagues bid farewell to each other.
"There's no sugar-coating it. It was a tough day. We had to say goodbye to MLAs that were excellent, that really served their community well," she said.
"So we were reflective, and I think there's a resolve within that reflectiveness to figure out how we do the job that British Columbia has elected us to do now, which is as official Opposition."

The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.
As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.
“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said.
“Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.
“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.
Kaseya said leaders around the world should realise that although the brunt of the health crisis is affecting Africa at the moment, the situation could change. “We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”
This outbreak, the 17th in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history.
Ebola is a highly contagious, severe, and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies, such as during funeral preparations.
On 15 May, DR Congo’s health ministry declared an outbreak in Ituri province, though sequencing shows it had begun in February. It has now spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last week, in west Africa, Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.
France is the only non-African country to have confirmed a case of Ebola so far – a doctor who had returned from DR Congo – in June.
The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way. The results should be available in three to six months, said Kaseya.
Of the total 10,091 cases, 10,060 have occurred in DR Congo, with 4,887 deaths. Two people have died in Uganda, and two in Kenya.
The response to the crisis has been hampered by inadequate protective equipment and unpaid health worker wages, leading to strikes. Conflict in DR Congo as well as mistrust towards officials in affected areas, misinformation and global aid cuts have further complicated the situation.
Kaseya will convene a meeting of African health ministers on Wednesday to urge greater cross-border cooperation. He wants governments to introduce screening and testing for people coming from affected regions at points of entry and exit.
“The main message to ministers is that they have to understand they could be affected, and we don’t want them to be surprised by what could happen,” he said.
At a meeting in November with African heads of state, Kaseya will call for a “corridor of peace” in conflict areas. “Currently, we have colleagues in Ituri who want to go and support the population, but they cannot because of insecurity,” he said. “I have to say to leaders, this outbreak is not for rebels, it’s not for the official army, it’s for everyone. Ebola can affect everyone … We need to come together to have a kind of agreement on how to protect each other.”
Kaseya called for a global effort to fund the response. He said governments had pledged $3bn (£2.3bn), but that more than $2bn was still outstanding. African countries had committed $120m, he said, while the rest is meant to come from international donors including the US, the UK and the EU.
“We need this money now,” he said. “We must understand that failure to provide funding now to African countries [will result in more being spent] because the outbreak will continue to move. If we have other countries affected we’ll be talking about trillions of dollars because it will require a lot of support to stop this outbreak.”

How to Publish Your Portfolio Website for Free
To publish your portfolio site, there are plenty of options, but in this guide, I will show you two free, reliable options: Netlify Drop and GitHub Pages.
Method 1: Publish Your Portfolio Website Using Netlify Drop
Step 1: Create a free Netlify account. First, go to netlify.com and sign up with your email. You can also sign up using Google or GitHub.
Step 2: Go to app.netlify.com/drop and drop the index.html you created using Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Google AI Studio from your downloads folder, or click the file and select it.
Step 3: Next, it automatically creates a free address. After a few minutes, your project shows as published with a random address such as sunny-tulip-tf52.netlify.app in my case. You can also click on that link to see the live site.
Step 4: However, if you think it can have a better name, open the project settings and change the project name to something short, such as meera-ai. Your address becomes meera-iyer.netlify.app. Make sure your site name is unique, since there will be hundreds of free Netlify sites out there.
Step 5: Once you have hosted the site successfully, you can share your link. Your portfolio is now live for anyone on any device to access it.
Method 2: Publish Your Portfolio Website Using GitHub Pages
Now let’s look at how to publish it for free using GitHub Pages.
GitHub also lets you host a simple website for free, and you can do everything on the GitHub website without installing anything. However, it takes a few more clicks than the Netlify Drop process.
Step 1: First, create a GitHub account. To do that, sign in to your free account at github.com, then go to github.com/new and create a new repository. For example, you can create ramesh.portfolio and set it to public. Remember that free accounts need a public repository for Pages to work. Turn on “Add a README” and finally tap on Create repository options.
Step 2: Once done, you can upload a file to the repository. Click Choose your files or drag and drop the index.html file, and at the bottom type a short message such as “Add portfolio website” and click on the Commit changes button.
Step 3: Once done, open the repository and go to Settings. Then click Pages in the left sidebar. Under Build and deployment, set Source to Deploy from a branch, pick main and / (root), and click Save.
Step 4: Now wait until GitHub says the changes can take up to 10 minutes. Wait for your site to go public, refresh the page, and wait for it to update. Once it’s done, click Visit site.
That’s it. GitHub will create your page under your name using a GitHub subdomain.
Final Thoughts
This is how you can use free AI tools to create free portfolio websites. Whether you are a beginner and have never written code before, you can follow this simple step-by-step process to create your first portfolio website.
If you have never built one and don’t even have an idea of creating profile sites, you can simply upload your resume into the AI tool and ask it to convert it into a portfolio website and generate an index.html page. Alaska's all-important Senate race is roiled by a report on alleged spoiler candidate
Alaska's governor is ordering an investigation after a New York Times report on the state's toss-up U.S. Senate race, which could determine which party controls the chamber next year.
That story detailed efforts by Democratic campaign operatives to recruit what Republicans have long alleged is a spoiler candidate whose presence on the ballot could confuse voters and siphon support from the GOP incumbent. The two candidates share the name Dan Sullivan.
NPR hasn't independently confirmed the Times' reporting, but it's roiled the Senate race just days before Election Day. Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, is hoping to flip the seat for her party.
The Times' story is based on interviews and communications among Peltola's attorneys and advisers, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.
Democrats have long denied involvement in the non-incumbent Sullivan's candidacy, and both the Peltola campaign and the DSCC reiterated those denials after the Times story published.
While campaigning Wednesday, Peltola called the story a distraction, according to Alaska Public Media, and the non-incumbent Sullivan did not respond to Alaska Public Media's requests for comment. He has previously said it was his decision to run for Senate.
Republicans have pounced on the news.
"Mary Peltola and her campaign have spent months gaslighting Alaskans, denying a scheme they were running all along," Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan, said in a statement. President Trump called it "Voter Fraud at the Highest Level," in an online post.
Trump's Justice Department had already sought to intervene in the Senate race, asking a court last week to delay certification if the incumbent Sullivan loses by a small margin. The legal effort cited potential voter confusion stemming from the second Sullivan on the ballot.
Election law experts had broadly criticized the DOJ's case as weak, in part because the Constitution grants states control over elections.
The Sullivan candidacies had already been probed by state officials, but the Alaska Supreme Court ruled in June that the non-incumbent Sullivan could appear on the general election ballot.
Justice Department officials said Thursday the Times' story expands its options for investigating the Senate race, and it filed an amended complaint citing the new reporting.
And in the wake of the Times story, Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy said Wednesday night that he is directing the state's Department of Public Safety to "investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted."
It's unclear what laws could have been violated.
Trickery has been fairly common in politics, and it can be difficult to write laws that prevent shenanigans, according to Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution who's co-authored a book on dirty tricks in campaigns.
"There's just a lot of tricks," Kamarck told NPR. "There's old ones. There's new ones. In this day and age, the internet makes it really easy to get the word out, both on a trick or, frankly, on a correction to a trick. But it's pretty standard fare for campaigns."
At times major-party advisers will seek to boost third-party candidates, in an effort to undercut the other major-party's candidate. Some voters who spoke with Alaska Public Media compared the new reporting about the Sullivan case to Republican groups' spending in support of a Democrat who's a federal prisoner in New York but who's on Alaska's U.S. House ballot.
The second, non-incumbent Sullivan advanced to the general election after Alaska's nonpartisan primary that sends the top four vote-getters to the fall ballot.
Alaska Public Media found mixed reactions to the Times' reporting, with some residents frustrated that it's drawing attention from other issues, and others expressing skepticism that voters would be confused. The ballot notes which Sullivan is the Republican incumbent.
Some experts have pointed out that all the news about the second Sullivan's candidacy could reduce any voter confusion. And because the state has a ranked-choice voting system for the general election, if voters are confused, they could rank both Sullivans and not rank Peltola.
Whether voters want to keep the state's unique election system is also on the general election ballot.
NPR's Hansi Lo Wang and Ryan Lucas contributed reporting.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

The number of registered medical practitioners (RMP) in Keralam has crossed one-lakh mark, and 32.75% of them got their registrations between 2021 and 2025, data collected from the Kerala State Medical Councils (KSMC) till October 8, 2026, show.
According to RTI data collected from the KSMC, there are 1,13,023 RMPs in the State. As many as 31,446 doctors were registered between 2021 and 2025. A total of 5,981 doctors got registered in 2021, 5,734 in 2022, 5,283 in 2023, 7,065 in 2024, and 7,383 in 2025. As many as 2,695 doctors registered with the KSMC till October 8 this year.
K.V. Babu, Kannur-based ophthalmologist and public health activist, who gathered the information, says that 95,993 doctors were added to the list in the last 27 years. “Keralam’s population is around 3.62 crore. Among the above-mentioned doctors, at least some may have migrated to other States or abroad seeking better opportunities. However, if at least 80,000 of them are here, there is one MBBS doctor for a population of 450 people already,” he says. Dr. Babu claims that the consequences of this trend could be unemployment among medical graduates and commercialisation of health care.
Seats fall vacant
“According to reports, hundreds of MBBS seats have fallen vacant in [deemed-to-be universities] in Tamil Nadu this year [after the final round of counselling for the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test for undergraduate medical courses]. A similar phenomenon could happen in Keralam as well. The government should study this issue before giving permission for new medical colleges,” he says.
M.N. Menon, president, Indian Medical Association (IMA), Kerala State branch, says around 5,000 graduates are coming out of medical colleges in the State every year. “Another 2,000 are passing out from other States and countries. Unemployment among new medical graduates is already high. Instead of granting sanction for new medical colleges, the government should improve the infrastructure in the existing ones and deploy qualified faculty members. Also, we are seeing shortage of doctors and faculty members in government hospitals and government medical colleges. The focus should also be on appointing necessary staff there,” Dr. Menon adds.

These Are the Best Kindles You Can Buy
Featured in this article
There’s a lot for readers to love about a Kindle. These Amazon-powered ebook readers let you bring thousands of books anywhere and typically give a month of battery life per charge. You can subscribe to get unlimited books from Amazon or use the device to access free books via your local library. But how are you supposed to know which model to buy, given the many options available?
I’ve owned all kinds of Kindles, including the newest Kindle Aluminum and a seasoned hand-me-down device that lacks a front light. Between all of my testing, I've found that many options offer great value for specific uses.

While you're at it, check out my other buying guides for readers, including the Best Kindle Accessories, Best E-Readers, Best Digital Notebooks, and Best Gifts for Book Lovers.
Updated October 2026: I’ve added the newest Kindle (2026, 12th Gen) as my affordable Kindle pick if the previous Kindle (2024, 11th Gen) isn’t on sale. I’ve also added notes on the Kindle Aluminum and ensured up-to-date pricing.

What Are the Newest Kindles?
Amazon recently announced a whole new generation of Kindles is coming, with every model getting a new version. I'll update this guide with thoughts as I review each new model. Here are the current details:
- Kindle (2026, 12th Generation) for $150: This is the new version of the base Kindle. Many features will sound familiar (a 6-inch screen, six weeks of battery life, and 16 GB of storage), but it comes with a new flush-front design for the screen and a lighter weight. It also shares a $150 price tag with the older base Kindle, which became more expensive as of August. You can upgrade to the Aluminum version that has a more premium feel and additional color options, plus 32 GB of storage. Both versions are available now, and I've included them in my notes above.
- Kindle Paperwhite (2026, 13th Generation) for $200: The 2026 Kindle Paperwhite will still pack a waterproof design and 12 weeks of battery life (my favorite part!), but its updated display is the largest yet among Paperwhite devices, and with a higher contrast ratio. The Signature Edition has aluminum backing and also packs dock charging with pogo pins on the back and a double-tap capability to turn pages. The regular Paperwhite is available for preorder and retails for $200 (same as the old model) with 16 GB of storage and comes in only black. The Paperwhite Signature Edition is on preorder for $250 and comes in two colors with 32 GB of storage. Preorder is available on a rolling basis in various regions, so if you're not able to reserve your model yet, check again soon.
- Kindle Colorsoft (2026, 2nd Generation) for $290: The Kindle Colorsoft's second-generation model has an updated display and edge-to-edge color that promises a richer look than what the first generation offered. The update also gets a flush-front design, similar to the other new Kindle models, and is available in a Signature Edition that has aluminum backing, an auto-adjusting front light, pogo points for charging, and the double-tap page-turning capability. The new Colorsoft is available for preorder at $290 with 16 GB of storage, and the new Colorsoft Signature Edition is available for preorder at $320 with 32 GB of storage and two device colors to choose from. Similar to the Paperwhite, the preorder availability is rolling steadily, so keep an eye out if you can't buy yours yet.
- Kindle Kids models starting at $180: All three of the above models have a Kids version that will include kid-friendly covers and up to 12 months of Amazon Kids+ content. The base Kindle Kids is available now, while others are on preorder in certain regions.
Kindle is also releasing a handful of new accessories, including the Kindle Click ($35) Bluetooth remote that will work with Kindle models as early as 2024, a Page Turn Cover ($80) that will only work with the Paperwhite and Colorsoft Signature Editions, a Charging Dock ($60) designed to work with the pogo pins on the Signature Editions, and new Kindle covers in a variety of colors and textures. I’m most excited about the remote; I will update this guide and our Best Kindle Accessories guide with my notes as I test.
Why Are Kindles More Expensive Now?
Amazon raised its prices across its product categories, including Kindle devices. The price increases hit several current Kindle models, leaving only Kindle Scribe models with their original price tags. Amazon declined to comment to WIRED, but a spokesperson told CNET the price hikes were due to rising costs in memory and storage components. Interestingly, none of the more powerful Scribe models needed a price update, but it’s also a relief since all three of those models are significantly more expensive than a regular Kindle.
Here are all the increases, including for the Signature versions:
