Carney hosts EU leaders as Trump pushes Canada toward Europe, but membership label faces resistance
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has called Canada “the most European of non-European countries” early in President Donald Trump’s trade war
TORONTO -- Prime Minister Mark Carney called Canada “the most European of non-European countries” early in U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war. Now, he’s hosting European leaders to pursue an unprecedented alliance, but the proposed EU “associate member” designation faces resistance even as the EU’s top official champions it.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa will join Carney in Montreal on Thursday for a two-day summit aimed at deepening trade, defense and economic ties as Canada and Europe seek to reduce their dependence on Washington in a changing world order.
European Union officials who briefed reporters ahead of the summit said the proposed partnership could bring Canada closer to the bloc than any previous arrangement with a non-European country. But its structure and even its name remain unsettled, with some member states questioning the “associate member” designation proposed last month by von der Leyen.
Arriving in Montreal, von der Leyen showed no sign of abandoning the proposal, posting on social media that Europe wanted to bring Canada closer than ever before “as Associate Member of the EU.”
Anand Sundar, a special adviser at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said France and Germany are among the countries unhappy with the designation and that it may not survive the summit.
Carney said Tuesday the summit would launch further negotiations over the next year.
“It doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference that it will make to lives of Canadians, young Canadians in terms of opportunities to study, work and travel, our Canadian businesses in terms of new opportunities, Canadian researchers in terms of depths of opportunity, and Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation, so we can live our lives as we choose.”
Carney has ruled out formally joining the EU, which would require Canada to align its laws and regulations with the bloc’s. Canadian officials said Canada would not assume the EU’s membership-related budget obligations, although it could contribute to specific programs. Carney has said any enhanced partnership would face a vote in Canada’s Parliament.
The summit puts Carney’s vision for a new global order to the test. At the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January, he warned that the U.S.-led international order was breaking down and urged middle powers to unite against economic coercion.
Trump has suggested Canada’s proposed EU arrangement could be a “hostile act” and threatened tariffs on Europe if he considered it unfriendly. Asked Wednesday about possible retaliation, a senior Canadian government official told reporters the closer relationship was not directed against the United States but reflected longstanding shared interests.
The summit is expected to launch an “Alliance for the Future,” a framework for closer cooperation on trade, defense, critical minerals, technology and research. Von der Leyen said the alliance would help Canada and Europe respond together to a world of growing rivalries.
The proposed relationship could include regular meetings between Canadian ministers and European commissioners and expanded opportunities for students through the EU’s Erasmus+ program, which supports international study and educational exchanges.
European commissioners and Canadian Cabinet ministers will hold sector-specific meetings, beginning with a business forum Thursday before formal leaders’ talks Friday. Officials hope to develop the broader partnership for possible endorsement in 2027.
Tobias Gehrke, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said the disagreement over terminology was unlikely to derail closer cooperation.
“There is no magic shortcut to rapidly reducing Europe’s and Canada’s reliance on the U.S. economy and military — not least since Washington might retaliate,” Gehrke said. “But the political window is now wide open to take a much bigger step than was previously conceivable.”
Canada has long looked to Europe to reduce its dependence on its much larger southern neighbor.
“It was the idea of not being alone with the Americans that drove it,” said Robert Bothwell, a University of Toronto historian.
Carney has deep personal ties to Europe. The former Bank of Canada governor led the Bank of England from 2013 to 2020. He chose Paris and London for his first foreign trip as prime minister rather than Washington, a break with tradition. He said the countries reflected Canada’s founding Indigenous, French and British peoples.
Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal, said Trump’s policies are accelerating Canada’s efforts to strengthen ties beyond the United States.
“The policies and rhetoric of the Trump administration are clearly pushing both Canada and the EU to imagine a world without strong U.S. leadership and to act accordingly,” Béland said.
Ottawa is reviewing plans to buy 72 additional American-made F-35 fighter jets and considering Sweden’s Saab Gripen as an alternative. Canada has committed to an initial 16 F-35s.
Canada is the only non-European country participating in the EU’s 150-billion-euro ($167-billion) SAFE defense procurement program, allowing Canadian companies to take part in joint European military purchases.
But deeper defense cooperation faces obstacles. Sundar said France is pushing for strict “Made in Europe” rules that could limit Canadian companies’ access to future EU defense spending, while Germany favors broader participation by countries outside the bloc. He said negotiations over the EU’s next seven-year budget could matter more to Canada than anything announced in Montreal.
The two sides already have a sweeping free trade agreement, known as CETA, that eliminated most tariffs. Most provisions have been in force since 2017, although some EU member states have yet to ratify it.
The United States accounted for 71.7% of Canada’s merchandise exports in 2025. Carney wants to double exports to other countries over the next decade.
Canada and the EU are pursuing closer cooperation on digital trade and critical minerals, including possible European Investment Bank financing. Canadian officials said Wednesday they were exploring ways to stabilize mineral prices and encourage investment.
Gehrke said Europe’s growing trade confrontation with China is driving demand for Canadian critical minerals. Canada has the resources and mining expertise Europe needs, while Europe offers industrial demand, technology and capital.
Sundar said the shifting international order presents Europe with an opportunity to become a more influential global power.
“Trump’s predatory behavior is allowing the EU to position itself as an alternative geopolitical anchor,” he said.

Climate change must be declared a "global health emergency" to shape governments' policies after heat caused three million deaths between 2016 and 2023, a report in The Lancet said Wednesday.
Published by the British medical journal ahead of the COP 31 climate summit in November, the 10th edition of the report brought together 146 researchers from 30 countries to assess the impact of climate change on the health of the world's population.
It said there were a record 710,000 heat-related deaths in 2023 with more than 70% of that toll linked to human-caused climate change.
Marina Romanello, the executive director of the health and climate research project Lancet Countdown, said there were "three million heat-related deaths globally in an eight-year span since the Paris Agreement" of 2015.
"That's roughly equivalent to the entire population of Wales being wiped out in the space of eight years due to heat," she told a news conference.
And "68% of those deaths are directly attributable to climate change."
The legally binding international climate treaty adopted in the French capital aimed to limit global warming to well below 2C and pursue efforts to keep it to 1.5C compared to pre-industrial levels.
Climate change impact
Romanello said the global health emergency due to climate change should have "an integrated approach so that we're not responding to emergency after emergency".
Instead she called for "a cohesive long-term response that builds resilience, builds capacities, and builds the possibilities of countries to avoid further emergencies moving forward".
To determine the share of deaths attributable to warming caused by human activity, the researchers compiled the number of heat-related deaths recorded by states, then subtracted those that would have occurred in the absence of climate change, said Professor Ollie Jay of the University of Sydney.
Jay said the intensity and frequency of periods of intense heat were amplified by climate change, pointing out that last year an extreme drought affected more than half of the world's land surface for at least one month.
Economic cost
By reducing worker productivity, warming has cost the global economy more than one trillion dollars per year over the past three years, the researchers said.
Southeast Asia and Africa, the hardest-hit regions, are estimated to have lost the equivalent of 3.9 percent and 3.2 percent of their GDP, compared with 0.2 percent for Europe and 1.5 percent for the Americas.
However there has been concrete progress in some areas.
Since 2016, 56 of the WHO's 194 member states have adapted their health and early-warning systems to anticipate extreme events.
Investment in clean energy reached $2.1 trillion in 2025 -- double that of the amount invested in fossil fuels, which cause climate change.
However fossil fuels still account for 80 percent of global energy, causing air pollution that results in 2.73 million deaths per year, the study said.
Meanwhile, roughly 323,000 deaths have been avoided in "at least" 77 countries where air pollution from fossil fuels has fallen since 2016, according to the report.
Although funding for climate-related medical research has increased sevenfold to reach $316 million in 2024, 84% of these funds go to researchers in wealthy countries, even though the least developed nations are the most affected by the growing climate-related health threats.
Romanello said this year for the first time the researchers' work was complicated by the disappearance of certain data sources, particularly from the United States, such as fossil fuel subsidies, which have not been made public by the US authorities.
And for the past two years, global geopolitical instability has pushed global warming and its health impact into the background, she said, stressing that inaction was exacerbating the situation.

The company behind the successful Hello Kitty franchise has apologised and ended its commercial tie-up with a Japanese TV drama after Chinese state media and netizens condemned the show’s “deliberate smears” against China.
Sanrio, a Japanese firm whose characters are popular around the world, said in a post on the Chinese social media site Weibo that it had decided to end its association with the TV drama Vivant after concluding that it “contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio’s core values”.
In the second season of the popular spy thriller, produced by the Japanese TBS network, Masato Sakai plays a salaryman who is drawn into a web of international crime and espionage.
The backlash began this week when Chinese state media blasted the portrayal of Chinese agents using “ruthless violence” to torture members of a secret unit of Japan’s self-defence forces, calling it a “deliberate smear” against Beijing.
Chinese media said that some of the torture methods were similar to those Japanese troops used against Chinese civilians during the second world war.
The state-run tabloid Global Times said the acts shown in the episode “bear striking similarities to the torture inflicted on Chinese nationals by invading Japanese troops” during the war, adding that the drama “distorts the truth by attributing these atrocities to modern Chinese characters”.
In the 4 October episode, a Chinese agent is seen cutting off the fingers of the Japanese intelligence officer and stabbing him in the abdomen.
Sanrio said in a statement: “Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people.
“We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects.”
The drama’s first season, set in a fictional central Asian country, avoided controversy, but its latest season is being shown at a time of increasingly fractious relations between Beijing and Tokyo.
Japan’s conservative prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, set off a diplomatic row in November last year when she told MPs that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger the deployment of her country’s self-defence forces if the conflict posed an existential threat to Japan.
Takaichi said earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and hoped to watch them over the year-end and new year holidays.
China is a crucial overseas market for Sanrio, whose cast of characters includes My Melody and Cinnamoroll – both featured in Vivant-themed merchandise.
The Tokyo-based company racked up 781m yuan ($117m) in revenue from the Chinese market in the first half of this year, according to Chinese media, up more than 40% from the same period last year.
The backlash against Sanrio comes days after the French international footballer Kylian Mbappé was dropped by several Chinese brands after he jokingly referred to Mao Zedong as a “dictator”. The Real Madrid forward, who is nicknamed the “dictator” for his influence on the game, later apologised for his “ill-judged” remarks.

Zverev seals world number one spot after win
- Published
Alexander Zverev will replace Jannik Sinner as the men’s world number one at his earliest opportunity after reaching the quarter-finals in Vienna.
He was already guaranteed to finish 2026 as the ATP’s leading player, but made sure he will rise to the summit on Monday with a 6-4 7-5 win over Tallon Griekspoor at the Erste Bank Open.
Zverev, 29, is the second German to reach the pinnacle of the men's tour after Boris Becker in 1991.
The achievement is a testament to his body of work this year, having won two Grand Slam titles and 64 of his 80 matches.
"It's been a wait but sometimes you have to wait for the best things in life," said Zverev, who is the second oldest man to top the rankings for the first time.
"I'm super happy, super thrilled - I have no words for this year."
At the start of the year it seemed unthinkable that anybody other than Sinner or Carlos Alcaraz would become world number one.
But the dominant duo have missed large chunks of this season through injury, opening the door for Zverev - who won the French Open and US Open titles with at least one of the pair absent - to take over.
Going into 2026, Alcaraz led the rankings with 12,050 points, closely followed by Sinner on 11,500.
The pair's duopoly - splitting all of the eight Grand Slam titles in 2024 and 2025 between them - was illustrated by the huge gap to the rest of the field.
Third-ranked Zverev had 5,110 points - closer numerically to the 2,221st player in the world than the top two.
Both his major triumphs came without having to face Sinner or Alcaraz, and he did not face a top-10 player until beating Ben Shelton in the New York final.
As the season entered its final stretch, Zverev achieved what many thought was impossible by securing the year-end number one ranking when Alcaraz lost in Shanghai on 12 October.
Zverev knew he still could not overtake Sinner until 2 November at the earliest, but beat Griekspoor to become the first man other than Sinner and Alcaraz to top the rankings since Novak Djokovic in June 2024.
Zverev conceded he would "maybe not" be the world's best player if both his rivals were "healthy and at the top of their game".
But he has efficiently beaten what has been in front of him, recording the greatest season of a career which had threatened to fall short of the lofty expectations placed on him since emerging as a teenage prodigy.
Fery continues to prove himself - and faces Zverev next
Zverev goes on to face British number one Arthur Fery in the quarter-finals - a repeat of their Wimbledon semi-final.
Fery, 24, made an unexpected run to the SW19 last four in July, but continued to prove he belongs among the world's best with a 6-4 5-7 6-4 win over Italy's Lorenzo Musetti in Vienna.
Trailing 4-2 in the decider, Fery showed his mental fortitude by breaking straight back and then overcoming what seemed to be cramp to serve out an impressive victory.
It is easy to forget Fery is still inexperienced at the elite level following his Wimbledon heroics.
Beating former world number five Musetti - now ranked 26th after injury - represents his biggest win by ranking on the regular ATP Tour and provides another opportunity to test himself against the very best.

However, Cameron Norrie fell short of his best victory of the season when world number five Daniil Medvedev saved match point to win their last-16 match.
A frustrating year has seen Norrie drop to 41st in the world rankings and exit each of the past three Grand Slam tournaments in the first round.
But the 31-year-old showed his key attributes - tenacity, athleticism and controlled aggression - to threaten a huge upset against Medvedev.
Third seed Medvedev, fresh from winning the Almaty title last week, was left angrily punching the surface when he fell a break down in the deciding set.
Norrie served for the match at 5-3 40-30, but Medvedev picked off his opponent's serve-volley attempt and fought back to win 4-6 6-3 7-6 (7-1).
Second seed Alcaraz also progressed with a 6-1 7-6 (13-11) win over Georgia's Nikoloz Basilashvili.
Meanwhile, Novak Djokovic's hopes of qualifying for the ATP Finals were harmed by a second-round defeat at the Swiss Indoors event in Basel.
The 24-time major champion, 39, lost 7-6 (7-4) 5-7 6-7 (5-7) to Germany's Jan-Lennard Struff, who produced some inspired tennis to beat the Serb for the first time in nine attempts.

Scientists at the ICAR-Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI) have developed a new potato variety called ‘kufri jamunia’ that has higher levels of anthocyanins, vitamin C, and certain micronutrients than regular potatoes. The Central government has been promoting it of late as a means to address hidden hunger, i.e. when people consume enough calories but still do not receive the necessary nutrients.
Usually, experts who fortify foods, focus on items like rice and iodised salt, which a large number of people in India consume, often throughout the year, thus ensuring the added nutrients are delivered to a significant chunk of the population. Kufri jamunia is however a potato, which people in India generally consume much less consistently than rice or salt, and the micronutrient intake depends on preparation methods and how the body absorbs them.
What makes it different
Kufri jamunia offers nutritional advantages, but they are substantial in some aspects more than others. Questions also linger about its ability to resist disease and retain nutrients through different Indian cooking methods.
The variety reportedly has a mealy texture. In one CPRI assessment involving 64 people, 95% rated its overall acceptability ‘good to excellent’ and 56% said its taste was very good. This study cohort, though, is too small to generalise the results. CPRI researchers themselves have proposed that kufri jamunia can be used in curries, parathas, soups, baked goods, and dehydrated flours.
Importantly, kufri jamunia potatoes also have purple skin and flesh, which could affect consumer interest. Research on other biofortified foods has already shown that while people are generally willing to pay modest premiums — the national average cost of ordinary potatoes purchased wholesale is around ₹17/kg — whether they accept a new variety depends on its appearance, their awareness, taste, and of course local preferences.
How was is developed
The CPRI team developed the kufri jamunia variety by crossing two potato lines, MS/8-1148 and CP4242, in 2015. MS/8-1148 is high in vitamin C whereas CP4242 had purple skin and flesh. The result, formally called MSP/16-307, could naturally accumulate higher concentrations of specific nutrients as it grew. The team then conducted trials, including multi-location testing, in 2021-2023.
Based on the trial data, the Central Sub-Committee on Crop Standards, Notification and Release of Varieties for Horticultural Crops approved the variety in mid-2024 and the government notified it in November that year. The variety’s plants produce 10-12 medium to large tubers each and mature in around 90 days. The purple colour comes from anthocyanins — organic compounds also found in jamun and blueberries.
According to the Press Information Bureau, 100 g of kufri jamunia flesh contains around 42.75 mg of vitamin C (versus 23.15 mg in regular potatoes), 42.05 mg of anthocyanins, 2.28 mg of zinc (versus 0.28 mg), 3.22 mg of iron (versus 0.57 mg), and 161 micrograms of carotenoids. And per the CPRI team’s findings themselves, published in Potato Journal in 2025, 100 g of kufri jamunia was found to have a range of carotenoid levels, from 15.6 micrograms in Kanpur to 298.4 micrograms in Raipur, during the multi-location trials. Kufri jamunia also contains slightly less zinc than kufri neelkanth and slightly less iron than kufri manik; the latter are other coloured potato varieties developed at the Institute.
Anthocyanins are known to have antioxidant properties, although whether the same benefits will accrue when delivered by kufri jamunia potatoes is not known. And in the absence of similar studies, the same caveat goes for iron and zinc.
A 2016 study in Food Chemistry examined purple-fleshed potatoes and reported that steaming and microwaving generally preserved more of the nutritional substances than stir-frying did. However, again, research specific to kufri jamunia is not available.
Cultivation factors
Nutrient availability and delivery constitutes one half of a biofortification programme; the other half is determined by cultivation.
At the Modipuram research station, according to the Potato Journal paper, the team recorded an average yield of 49.01 tonnes per hectare after three months, across three seasons, whereas subsequent multi-location trials, including at Modipuram, recorded an overall mean of 31.96 tonnes per hectare across north (36.77 tonnes), central (33.79 tonnes), and eastern (25.91 tonnes) India.
On the other hand, at these locations, kufri manik yielded 31.52 tonnes per hectare and kufri neelkanth 36.61 tonnes per hectare. Further, kufri jamunia could moderately resist late blight, a disease caused by the water mould Phytophthera infestans, in laboratory conditions but has been reported as ‘susceptible’ in the field. Late blight is a devastator of potato crops and the CPRI team has already recommended that farmers apply fungicide.
Next, the multi-location trials also produced 29.19 tonnes of marketable potatoes per hectare, versus 33.48 tonnes for kufri neelkanth. So if the costs of cultivation were equal, kufri jamunia farmers could need a 15% premium on the selling price to attain the same gross revenue. (A study published by a CPRI in Indian Horticulture in 2020 estimated that, for regular potatoes, the seed material accounted for 40-50% of the production costs vis-a-vis regular potatoes, with a per-hectare seed cost of around ₹60,000-75,000 per hectare.)
Many unknowns
Taken together, there are many unknowns about kufri jamunia at this point to assess its overall cost-benefit ratio, including the cost of seeds and disease management, pricing, its uptake in the market, and how efficaciously it will deliver iron and zinc to the population. It would be premature as a result to deem kufri jamunia to be a proven solution to address India’s hidden hunger.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.
Some really excellent stories today, including Anil Oza’s profile of Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and the next installment in Bob Herman’s “Out of Pocket, Out of Reach” series.
Also, Andrew Joseph and Adam Feuerstein go live at 10:00am EDT to break down the latest news coming out of Europe’s big cancer conference. You can tune in here.
Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed: RFK Jr. is the ‘most incompetent HHS secretary ever’
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is known for his comical social media videos, his advocacy of “Medicare for All,” and his controversial stance on U.S. policy toward Israel.
One thing that’s been overlooked? El-Sayed would be the Senate’s first epidemiologist. And he plans to use his decades of experience in public health to “grill” health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who he called the “most incompetent HHS secretary ever” during an interview with STAT’s Anil Oza.
El-Sayed is a man with big dreams for how to overhaul the U.S. health care system so it can better serve vulnerable Americans. He has also become a target for many conservative politicians in recent months, including Kennedy, who told a crowd in Michigan earlier this week that “there’s 500 million Arabs in the world and yet they don’t produce science.”
Read more from Anil’s excellent profile, which also dives into El-Sayed’s personal motivations for reducing health disparities and his work to rebuild Detroit’s health system.
Great news, peptide fans…
… federal health officials just made it easier to compound some unapproved peptides.
The Department of Health and Human Services released a policy yesterday that will temporarily allow compounding pharmacies to manufacture some peptide products, increasing access to the experimental wellness therapies embraced by many in the MAHA movement.
The move comes as the Food and Drug Administration weighs broader approval of these compounds. In July, an FDA advisory panel voted to recommend that these pharmacies be cleared to manufacture six of these substances, even though agency scientists cautioned against the move due to the lack of clinical safety or efficacy data.
Read more from STAT’s Margaret Manto.
Martin Kulldorff critiques scientific gatekeepers at NIH lecture
Should academic journals decide what science should be published? Martin Kulldorff, the biostatistician known for co-authoring the Great Barrington Declaration, which advocated against Covid lockdowns, raised that question Wednesday in a lecture on rebuilding trust in science. “Why have journals decide what can be published or not?” Kuldorff, who now serves in a top role at HHS, asked.
Kulldorff made the remarks as part of a larger critique on how gatekeeping in scientific stifles trust. But he did not address the ways that unvetted scientific research, even when debunked after publishing, can sow distrust as well. Numerous polls show, for example, that Americans’ belief that vaccines cause autism has only increased in recent years, despite the fact that the major research making this claim was retracted back in 2010.
During his talk, Kulldorff also insisted that the rise in measles cases being experienced in the United States is the result of missed doctors appointments caused by Covid-19 lockdowns, despite the fact that that claim has been disputed by public health experts. – Nicholas Florko
How employer health care costs are shaping midterm elections
Multiple polls show that Americans are fixated on the high cost of health care even as prices for gas, groceries, and other necessities soar. Voters are asking for the government to intervene and lower prices, and their anger is casting a pall over the midterm elections.
STAT’s Bob Herman is back with the sixth installment of Out of Pocket, Out of Reach, where he has been investigating why health care costs are skyrocketing, even for American workers who get their insurance through their job. As the health care industry sucks up more and more cash, employers are shifting these costs to their workers.
Read more from Bob, or brush up on the rest of the series.
75%
How do you figure out the prevalence of a disease if you can only study it post mortem?
Researchers have struggled for years to suss out an accurate rate for chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a neurodegenerative disease that afflicts National Football League players and other people after repeated head trauma. But a study published yesterday of 2,362 former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 found that 74.5% had CTE, which can lead to worrisome cognitive and behavioral changes.
What does this estimate mean for the quarterbacks and wide receivers who line up every weekend to compete in America’s most popular sport? The researchers are careful to say that this estimate cannot be extended to current players. They suggest the rate could be lower — but it also could be higher.
While the jury’s still out on what these data mean for today’s athletes, I hope Roger Goodell reads Morning Rounds. Here’s the study, if you want to take a look at the data yourself.
The research gap facing trans women and breast cancer risk
The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends cisgender women get regularly screened for breast cancer starting at 40. But what about trans women?
A great story from Rewire News dives into the research gap on this topic, as the most authoritative study on the subject finds only that trans women face less risk than cis women, but more risk than men. That’s 1 in 8 versus 1 in 775.
The few existing guidelines for trans women are based on basically zero data, which is tough to come by for this population. Trans people — including the roughly 700,000 trans women in the U.S. — routinely face discrimination and mistreatment in clinics and hospitals.
My grandmother died of breast cancer at 67. I’m a 33-year-old trans woman. When should I get my first mammogram? For now, science has no answer to that question.

A group of Sasquatch hunters has been investigating Bigfoot sightings in New Jersey, with the hope of solving a mystery that has bewildered many for decades.
While Bigfoot, the big and hairy bipedal, is more tied to the Pacific Northwest, Sasquatch hunter Mike Familant believes there is more to discover on the opposite coast.
Mike Familant, who documents his investigations into reported Bigfoot sightings on his online series, In the Shadow of Big Red Eye, has mentioned forests around High Point State Park, Stokes State Forest, and the Delaware Water Gap as some of New Jersey’s hotspots.
The Bigfoot hunter recently told NJ.com about a bizarre sound his team recorded in 2022 after mimicking a barrel owl call at High Point.
A military linguist “came back with a report that said it was outside of human vocal range and wasn’t any known animal from northwestern New Jersey,” Familant said.
The Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization has listed 79 reported Bigfoot sightings in New Jersey on its website, including 18 in Sussex County, 16 in Burlington County and 11 in Ocean County.
Outdoorsman Jacob Korbel, an investigator for the research organization, was initially a Bigfoot skeptic.
In 2021, he joined an expedition in the Pine Barrens to check out the organization’s work.
“About 100 yards away in front of us, there’s this whoop response,” Korbel told NJ.com. “And right away, I’m like, that’s nothing that I’ve ever heard before. That’s not an owl, that’s not a coyote, fox.”
“And you could hear it slowly getting closer to our position, like it was coming in to check us out. Like we were almost getting flanked,” he recalled.
With no solid evidence of the Sasquatch, it remains unclear whether Bigfoot is simply elusive or just bogus.
While public polling on the matter is scant, a 2012 Angus Reid Public Opinion survey found that 29 percent of Americans believed Bigfoot is “definitely” or “probably” real.

UP tightens government job verification rules, says political ideology alone cannot disqualify candidates
A government order states that political ideology alone cannot be grounds for denying employment.
The Uttar Pradesh government has introduced a consolidated policy specifying offences—ranging from murder to association with outfits that use violence to overthrow the ‘established system’—that can disqualify candidates from government jobs.
A government order issued by principal secretary (appointments) M Devraj on Wednesday states that the policy supersedes orders dating back to 1958 and lays down uniform criteria for verifying candidates’ antecedents. It states that political ideology alone cannot be grounds for denying employment.
“Political ideology won't serve as ground for disqualification”
“[One's) political ideology won't serve as a ground for disqualification… [those] associated with organisations whose purpose is to force a change in the existing through violent means will be considered ineligible,” the order said.
Also read | 'Secretly happy about PDA's victory': Akhilesh Yadav's dig at UP deputy CM Keshav Maurya after MLC polls
The policy identifies rape, kidnapping, human trafficking, terrorism, cybercrime and document forgery among the offences that will lead to a candidate being unsuitable for public employment. It also covers offences under specified special laws, including the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act Prevention of Corruption Act, the Prevention of Money Laundering Act.
The revised policy follows Allahabad High Court directions in two cases on antecedent verification, asking the state to frame guidelines in line with the CRPF’s February 1, 2012, guidelines.
The earlier framework comprised a 1958 order governing character verification, followed by orders issued in 1978, 1985 and 2013 prescribing timelines for completing the process. A 2021 order subsequently permitted provisional appointments after candidates submitted prescribed verification forms and self-declarations. The new policy brings these provisions together while defining disqualification criteria and streamlining recruitment-related checks.
An FIR, complaint, ongoing investigation or chargesheet will not, by itself, lead to disqualification if a competent court has not framed charges, subject to specific provisions for certain offences, it states. The policy also provides exceptions for cases involving final acquittal or discharge, legally recognised compromises, government withdrawal, quashing by the high court or Supreme Court, and certain minor offences.
Existing state government employees will not require fresh character verifications, though necessary service records may be requisitioned from their previous parent departments, it said.

In July, as supporters of the Cockroach movement took to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, incensed over exam-paper leaks and demanding the resignation of India’s education minister, the rest of the nation realised that for the first time since the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) came to power in 2014, the curse of inertia and the grip of fear had been smashed irrevocably. Prime minister Narendra Modi’s image of invincibility has been punctured.
People in India have been conditioned to believe in an idea of intense slow-burn protests that eventually bring change – but the Cockroaches have shown us that the revolution can be fast-tracked.
This time the Cockroaches are demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, following reports in the Indian Express in late September that he had pushed through a purge of voter rolls. Round one of the Cockroach protests came to an end because the BJP was willing to sacrifice the education minister. Round two does not allow for such scapegoating. If Kumar goes, Modi must go too – it would be an open admission that the electoral system has been compromised.
The response of the BJP so far has been hysterical. The repressive apparatus of the state was out in full force: detentions and arrests of journalists, protesters being roughed up and beaten, an internet blackout in the capital. The Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke’s bravado in announcing his protest plans paid unexpected dividends the first time around. The second time, the continual broadcasting on social media by the three Cockroach leaders seemed like a lack of experience in organising and strategic thinking. Police forces detained them on touchdown at Delhi airport on the morning of the protest. They alleged that thousands of their members faced preventive detention or were not allowed to reach the capital city.
So at protests on 10 October, the CJP leaders were conspicuous by their absence. Only leftwing and Congress-allied student organisations, prominent gutsy young activists (Neha Bora, Aishe Ghosh, Gurmehar Kaur) and their elected political representatives held the ground and faced the worst of the police brutality.
The absence of the Cockroach leadership on the ground notwithstanding, the protests continued in pockets, eventually reaching a crescendo on 12 October. Heeding a call by Rahul Gandhi on behalf of the Congress-led opposition bloc, the streets of Delhi were filled in an act of defiance the like of which I have not witnessed in my lifetime. The state, however, seemed to have got the memo beforehand. The Delhi police and security forces numbered 90,000, 45 metro stations were closed in the inner city and trains to Delhi were cancelled. Student activists travelling to the capital were picked up en route from their railway carriages.
The following day, a small group of Cockroaches were arrested entering Jantar Mantar, which the Delhi police had banned from being used as a protest site. Two of the group’s leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained and subsequently sent to jail for five days.
Despite the high-handed approach of the police, the people are still clamouring for battle on the streets. Every screengrab, every video, every reel reinforces the feeling that we are witnessing a carnivalisation of the protests. The songs, the slogans, the sudden bursts of dancing, the satirical placards, the sheer joy of the crowds: this is Mikhail Bakhtin’s carnivalesque. What is the cause for such celebration? This: the state is evidently in retreat. People have begun to treat power as something to be ridiculed.
One of the most popular slogans has been Jab jab Modi darta hai, police ko aage karta hai (“Whenever Modi is afraid, he pushes the police forward”). The regime’s undiluted dread was most visible at Connaught Place in central Delhi on 16 October, when the CJP had called on people to gather at Central Park for a flag-waving celebration. The New Delhi Municipal Council shut down the park for two days and an elaborate fortification followed. The park was cordoned off, security personnel formed a human chain along the metal railings and 220 companies of the Central Armed Police Forces were deployed alongside the Rapid Action Force and the Delhi police.
Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke and communist student leader Neha Bora were both detained as they made their way towards Connaught Place. Neither was allowed to contact lawyers until late into the night, and lack of knowledge about their whereabouts caused panic online. Neha was released from detention the following morning, and Abhijeet could walk free on conditional bail.
For over a decade, the regime crushed students and dissenters by branding them anti-national and punishing them under the draconian Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. The genius of the Cockroach protest lay in something very simple – how could the state frame the waving of the Indian national flag as an anti-national activity? We now have a government that is not confident of its own legitimacy; it views the tricolour as a weapon when it is in the hands of its citizens.
The powerlessness of the state could also be seen in its desperation to police the online space: it summoned Meta officials over the summer and imposed an internet shutdown earlier this month. For a party that coasted to power with post-truth propaganda on WhatsApp, its undisputed dominance on X and heavy investment in keeping social media influencers on its payroll, the algorithms (or their oligarch owners) may well have turned. It is impossible to capture the entire social media ecosystem with threats and purchasing power alone.
For the regime, it is a losing battle against the newfound visual grammar that has defined a wave of protests around the world: nothing is as seductive as young women defiantly clashing with uniformed police, or an opposition leader who climbs the barricades and waves the national flag. The German philosopher Walter Benjamin wrote about the tendency for fascism to lean into the aestheticisation of politics – today, looking at Delhi, he would be pleased to report back that the aesthetic can also be snatched back by the masses.
On 12 October, after the mass mobilisation, Gandhi addressed the media by saying: “This is tandav, Lord Shiva’s dance. There is no planning here”, and “This is the wedding procession of Shiva, anyone can join in”. These references to Shiva are a calculated manoeuvre. It is a nod to India’s majority Hindus who, time and time again, have been sold the lie that their sole protector is Modi.
Modi recently went Bhajan clubbing – a kind of rave setup with remixed Hindu devotional music – in a desperate attempt to establish his gen Z connections. But he may find the rug pulled from beneath his feet. Modi’s base rewarding the BJP election after election for weaponising their faith did not secure jobs for the next generation. And now it is their own children who are at the receiving end of the state’s violence.
Saving India cannot happen without pulling Hindus out from the vicious grip of extremist Hindutva. This is one unforeseen outcome of this protest and the wider movement. Whether it topples the government or not, it has shown it can unite people against the divisive force that is the BJP.
- Meena Kandasamy is a poet and writer based in Chennai

Delhi's Jamia University agrees to students’ demands, sets timeline for union polls
The Jamia university administration has directed that the students' union constitution be completed by May 15, 2027.
Delhi's Jamia Millia Islamia on Thursday agreed to key demands raised by protesting students, including setting a timeline for the implementation of the Students' Union constitution and revoking disciplinary action linked to the protests.
Offline classes are set to resume on Monday, November 2. The university administration directed that the students' union constitution be completed by May 15, 2027, with elections to be held within six weeks of the commencement of the academic session on July 16, 2027.
All disciplinary actions, show-cause notices, suspensions and campus bans linked to students' participation in the protests will also be revoked.
The development comes as the agitation over the restoration of an elected Jamia Millia Islamia Students’ Union (JMISU) entered its 18th day. The union has remained defunct since 2006, and students have been demanding a time-bound plan for holding elections.
Students mark Foundation Day with ‘Inquilabi Mela’
Protesting students marked the university’s 106th Foundation Day on Thursday by organising an ‘Inquilabi Mela’ near Gate No. 7, boycotting the official celebrations, PTI reported earlier. The gathering was held at Gulistan-e-Ghalib, where five students were on hunger strike demanding the restoration of the elected students’ union.
The students -- Ebin Basil, Rehan Khan, Ritik, Altaf and Abuzar -- said the event reflected Jamia’s founding ideals of democratic participation, freedom of expression and respect for dissent. The protesters had also demanded the withdrawal of disciplinary measures against those involved in the agitation, the release of students placed in judicial custody and a clear deadline for resuming regular academic activities.
Students oppose online classes
The university’s decision to extend online classes until November 24 and conduct odd-semester examinations online had triggered further opposition. The administration had cited concerns over the campus situation and the safety and security of students.
Students from the Department of Commerce and Business Studies, through their subject association, submitted a memorandum opposing the move. They said the lack of a firm date for resuming physical classes had created uncertainty over their studies and access to university facilities.
The students argued that those enrolled in regular courses needed classroom discussions, peer interaction and practical exposure, which online teaching could not fully provide. They also highlighted the financial burden on students who had relocated or arranged accommodation near the campus.
A student group claimed that students from more than 100 classes had approached their teachers seeking the restoration of offline classes and examinations. Protesters had also announced a boycott of online classes until the campus reopened.
Under the earlier schedule, online practical, fieldwork, project, viva and minor project examinations were to be held from November 25 to 30, followed by theory examinations from December 1 to 24. Winter vacation was scheduled from December 25 to January 12, with even-semester classes set to begin on January 13.
The administration had initially extended online classes until November 8 before issuing the October 28 order extending the arrangement until November 24.
Disciplinary action adds to tensions
The university’s action against students had become another major point of contention. A show-cause notice dated October 27 was issued to a resident of Begum Hazrat Mahal girls’ hostel over allegations that she had obtained emergency leave on misleading grounds before taking part in the protests.
The hostel’s provost asked her to submit a written explanation within 24 hours, warning that an unsatisfactory response could lead to disciplinary action.
A notice circulated by the hostel’s discipline committee also said residents had been asked to take compulsory leave by November 1 because of the online academic schedule. However, a university official said no official notification directing students to vacate hostels had been issued.

Patrick Stewart, a perceptive patriarch in 'Star Trek' and 'X-Men,' dies at 86
Sir Patrick Stewart's most famous characters tackled concepts such as honor, morality and courage. He played Professor X in the X-Men franchise and Jean-Luc Picard, captain of the starship USS Enterprise, on the show Star Trek: The Next Generation and its later spinoff, Picard.
Stewart died Wednesday at 86. A post on his Facebook and Instagram pages said he died at home in Los Angeles after a "brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia."
Although he was beloved for playing compassionate father figures who united families of misfits, Stewart's own upbringing in Yorkshire, England, was harsh. He remembered his father as alcoholic and abusive. He found solace in school and, eventually, in Shakespeare. He joined the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966 and debuted on Broadway in 1970 in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
"To stand in the middle of an empty stage in an empty theater and feel that I was at home was everything," he told NPR in 2023. "But it took a while for me to get there."
Stewart played alongside some of the best Shakespeareans of his time, including Judi Dench and Ian McKellen. He was lecturing on Shakespeare at UCLA when his name came up for the lead in a new series of Star Trek.
"Don't do this, Patrick," he remembered McKellen advising him. "You're a very good stage actor. That's where you ought to be. Don't do it."
But Stewart's agent had reassured him that the show was unlikely to make it past the first season. As the actor recalled to NPR, he was encouraged to take what he believed to be a quick and easy job. "'Do six months' work. Make some money for the first time in your life and get well known. Get a suntan, and go home.' And I thought, 'Yeah, that doesn't sound too bad. I could live with that.'"
But Star Trek: The Next Generation was a tremendous hit. It aired for seven seasons, from 1987 to 1994. Stewart was embraced by fans, who adored the character's penchant for Earl Grey tea and cool-headed leadership, with such signature phrases as "Engage!" and "Make it so!"
But success on the starship Enterprise came at a cost. Throughout his career, Stewart portrayed only a handful of Shakespeare's leading men. He put some of that character energy into an award-winning, one-man version of Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol, in which Stewart played more than 40 roles.
By the beginning of the 21st century, Stewart had reestablished himself on stage while also lending his voice to numerous big-budget animated films. He went on to dominate another blockbuster franchise, the X-Men, beginning in 2000. He'll appear for the last time in his role as Professor Charles Xavier in the upcoming movie Avengers: Doomsday.
As for his signature role, Stewart thought he was done playing Picard. But a team of producers — including writer Michael Chabon — had different ideas. They pitched him a new show, Star Trek: Picard, that began streaming on the CBS service now called Paramount+ in 2020.
"I would've been happy just shaking Patrick Stewart's hand and telling him how much I loved him on Star Trek," Chabon told NPR. "But to be able to actually write words that he will speak and act is — it's incredible."
In the show, Picard is struggling with the psychological damage that led to leaving Starfleet. The performance is vintage Stewart. His character is keen-eyed, haunted, weary, yet joyful. While this Picard was trapped in the past, Patrick Stewart spent his career charting the future.

Just yesterday, Apple refreshed its 14-inch MacBook Pro with the new M6 chip inside, and it’s currently available for preorder. This is the first MacBook to get the chip (but certainly not the last), and I look forward to testing this thing out myself. But I do already have a good sense of how well it’ll perform, as I already tested this same chip in the latest Mac Mini. And it points to an issue with the current state of the Mac lineup.
The 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro currently costs $1,999. That gets you 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. Even for as good as these laptops are, that feels like too much money for those specs. Apple raised prices across all Macs earlier this year, but the base 14-inch MacBook Pro got hit the hardest, with a $300 bump. It was already an awkward configuration, as it used the same M5 chip as the much cheaper MacBook Air models. It was such bad pricing that it ended up on my “do not buy” list. The addition of the M6 seems like it’ll add some value, especially with the improvements to GPU performance I saw in the M6 Mac Mini. It also has the dual Neural Engine, which can speed up certain AI tasks in creative applications, especially for content creators. I won’t pretend to make a final evaluation until I’ve thoroughly tested the machine myself.
The Smarter Buy
But consider this. The M6 Mac Mini is on sale for $779 right now, $120 off its retail price. The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air is similarly $150 off its retail price right now. You could buy both for the same price as one M6 MacBook Pro. That’s kind of insane when you think about it. You miss out on the MacBook Pro’s excellent Mini-LED display and powerful speakers, but to me, it’s a tempting alternative for a $2,000 budget.
It’s even more compelling when you consider how many people are using Mac Minis these days—more as always-on AI agent boxes that you can control remotely with any old MacBook. Pairing the M6 Mac Mini and M5 MacBook air together is a recipe for AI goodness (especially if you configure the Mac Mini up to 32 GB or 64 GB of memory).
Another alternative is the M5 MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro chip inside for only $200 more. It looks identical on the outside, and has better performance on the inside.
I’m still interested to see how the new M6 MacBook Pro performs, but the price alone makes me wonder if there aren’t better ways of spending your money—even while staying within the Mac lineup.

Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack
- Published
Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public.
The leak includes names, work addresses and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work they do for each agency.
Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks that a government agency has been targeted by leaks or hacks.
A DHS spokesperson said the agency is "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively."
"We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected," the spokesperson added.
"We will update the public when more information is available."
The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was made public online. A group called the Department of Peace accessed the information from DHS, while journalist and cybersecurity researcher maia crimew alongside the website Distributed Denial of Secrets put it online.
The information was put in a database named Icepick.
Most of the agents included, more than 21,000 of them, work for CBP, according to the data. Nearly 6,600 work for ICE.
Other records show agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and even people working for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.
The leaked information also included dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents that led and worked on those operations, and some of the technology they used in their work, including tech provided by Cellbrite and Palantir.
The groups wrote in an online statement that the the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets.
"The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in its simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added.
BlueLeaks refers to a massive leak of US police data in 2020, data from which DDoSecrets also hosted.
A spokesperson for the Department of Peace pointed directly at actions by ICE agents for the group's work to hack DHS records.
"On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat'. This is what happens to ICE when you do that," the spokesperson wrote on Wednesday.
Mullin in March became Secretary of Homeland Security.
The Department of Peace said it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta.
Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them.
A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised."
Last month, the FBI was hacked by a group called ShinyHunters, which took personal information about thousands of agents.
In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt.
Public backlash to US immigration enforcement has been building as the Trump Administration has pushed a huge increase in arrests and deportations of people suspected of being in the country illegally.
Immigration operations this year have repeatedly turned violent, external, with ICE agents shooting at more than two dozen people and killing at least nine people.
Those killings include the high profile deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, both of whom were shot and killed by ICE agents this year in Minnesota, despite not being the targets of arrests.
Often, ICE agents carry out enforcement actions while their faces are covered by masks and sunglasses. Immigration agents rarely identify themselves, despite being required by law to do so, and US politicians have publicly demanded, external DHS enforces the requirement.
Since President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, the US has enacted nearly 1 million deportations, external, according to data from the Migration Policy Institute. More than 70% of the deportations have been of people with no criminal record.

A jet carrying the far-right Brazilian senator Flávio Bolsonaro has left Guayaquil in Ecuador and is on its way to Miami, Florida, where it is expected to arrive mid-morning on Wednesday.
After losing Sunday night’s election to the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Bolsonaro disappeared for more than 24 hours, until Argentina’s migration authorities said he had entered the country by land on Tuesday night.
There, he boarded a Gulfstream IV registered as LV-JQW. The aircraft had been parked at Puerto Iguazú airport since the early hours of the previous morning, when the first reports emerged in Argentinian media that he intended to flee on it.
Bolsonaro, the son of the jailed former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, boarded the jet with his wife and two daughters at about 11.30pm, bound for Guayaquil, reportedly to avoid Brazilian airspace. They made a brief stop in Ecuador, and have continued to the Miami-Opa Locka executive airport. The senator is expected to hold a press conference in the US at some point on Wednesday.
A senior US state department official told media outlets that visas would be granted to Bolsonaro and his family, and on Tuesday night the US president said he would approve their move to the country.
“They’re fine people. The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible,” Donald Trump said, as he returned from a campaign event in Texas. “I didn’t take sides, you know. I know them both. I know Lula. I know Flavio a little bit. I know the father very well.”
Lula called Bolsonaro’s flight “shameful”. “This is what the Bolsonaro family are like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as they’ve become accustomed to doing,” he said at an event celebrating his 81st birthday in Brasília.
Some in the Brazilian government suspected Bolsonaro allies had spent Tuesday privately telling the press he was already on his way to the US to distract from his real plan through Argentina. The federal police are facing criticism for failing to prevent him leaving the country.
There is a gap between the last time he was seen by allies at about 6pm on Monday and the moment he entered Argentina late on Tuesday. It remains unclear how or when he travelled to the border, or where he was during that time.
Footage from a television channel there shows two vans crossing the border checkpoint and then being escorted by airport security officers to the airport.
Shortly after the election result, police asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s passport to be retained over concerns he could flee, citing an interview given last Friday by his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro.
Speaking on a podcast in the US, where he is in self-imposed exile and lobbying the Trump administration against Lula, Eduardo said if his brother were to lose the election, he should not concede and should go to the US.
O Globo newspaper reported that the escape had been planned for weeks as a contingency in case he lost, and that Eduardo had been its main organiser, holding talks with US officials about receiving the senator.

Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso has doubled down on his criticism of "low level" Formula 1 drivers who have a "lack of talent" following his collision with Williams' Alex Albon in Austin.

Post-race, Alonso stated the quality of the drivers in the bottom third of F1's grid is "very low" and he had not changed his stance in Thursday's media day ahead of this weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix.
"I think it's simply a very low level of driving and lack of talent," he told Sky Sports F1.
"When you make repeated mistakes throughout the season and have crashes and 50 per cent of your race is in Lap 1, if I was the team principal I would not be happy but if they are happy, I'm OK with that.
"When I see Max [Verstappen], Lewis [Hamilton] starting at the back when they change the engine or whatever, Kimi in Monza, they still win the races. Lap 1 is not the end of the world when you have your confidence and the talent to wait for one or two more laps."
Alonso says he will not bring up the issue in Friday's drivers' meeting as "it's part of the game" and it is down to Aston Martin to start higher up the grid to "get out of that part of the field".
"Some teams cannot score points. It's the same for us this year. You go into the races knowing you need eight DNFs to score points, so it's more about driving the best race to the finish line," he added.
"Probably if you're not having a good season, being beaten by your team-mate, whatever is in your head it brings extra frustration but other drivers and teams should not pay for that."
'Not nice to hear that' - Albon reacts to Alonso comments
Albon was told about Alonso's comments in the FIA press conference and argued the grid is as strong as it has been "for a while".
"I'll double down with what I said as well. I have a huge respect for Fernando. I looked up to him a lot growing up as a kid," said the Williams driver.
"It's not nice to hear those comments in many ways. You're racing someone that you look up to, but at the same time, I don't agree. It's as simple as that.
"I think level is strong up and down the grid. I think 10, 15 years ago, the back half the grid wasn't the way it is now. We don't have pay drivers anymore. It is what it is. Hopefully, we don't cross corners or cross paths in the race this weekend!"
However, Alonso had pointed out his comments would be the same at any point in his career since he made his F1 debut in 2001.
"It's the same over the years. When you are at the back of the grid, the cars are difficult to drive, more difficult to drive - they have less grip so mistakes are coming more often because you don't have an environment which is under control and the car is not welcoming you in a nice way, so you make more mistakes.
"But I don't feel all the incidents in Lap 1 and the touches, the front wings that fly around, all these things are not necessary, especially when you are fighting for nothing at the back of the grid and there is the cost cap, adding to this problem.
"There are teams that are happy with the cost cap and breaking things every race. They can pay for them."
Gasly and Bearman back Albon
Alpine's Pierre Gasly and Haas' Oliver Bearman were sat alongside Albon in the press conference and were asked about Alonso's comments, given they often race in the midfield.
"You have to love Fernando for the statements he makes out there. I have so much respect for the driver he is, and at the same time, he's very vocal," said Gasly.
"I haven't seen his race. I'm not too sure what he referred to. But I think I would agree [with Albon]. I will say that the level on the grid is probably one of the highest, considering all the drivers we have now, from what I've seen over maybe nine years. I've seen some wild driving approaches when I joined compared to what I see now."
Bearman added: "I think that's a slightly harsh conclusion [from Alonso] because I agree with Pierre that the level is very high on this current grid. With the gaps that we face this year, you have to be very opportunistic at times, and that can end in disaster, like it did for me last week with myself and Pierre.
"I wouldn't say it's a question of quality. It's a question of trying your very best and trying to make something happen, which is very challenging when the top eight positions are pretty much all filled by the top four teams."

Dozens are dead in a high-speed train crash in Spain
URDA, Spain (AP) — A high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks in Spain Wednesday, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens in the second deadly rail collision this year.
The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers searched the wreckage through the day for survivors and bodies.
The collision came just nine months after another deadly crash involving high-speed trains operated by the same two companies in southern Spain in January.
"Today all of Spain is grieving," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of national mourning.
Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride.
"It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year," said Sánchez, who faces a national election on Nov. 29.
Spain's rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the central province of Toledo, involving two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading south in the same direction from Madrid to Seville.
A train operated by the state-owned RENFE company struck the rear of another train operated by private company IRYO that was stopped. The collision derailed two carriages on the tail of the IRYO train and the front of the RENFE train.
Samy Paul, a British tourist, described the shock of the impact to The Associated Press after being rescued from the RENFE train.
"Suddenly, everything started falling apart. Bang! We fell down," he said. "We realized carriage two, carriage one, all gone, all smashed. There was blood all over."
David Gómez, a construction worker, was working nearby when he heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El País.
"People were trying to get out through the windows ... We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought until emergency services arrived," he said. "As I was trying to pull a young woman out, there was a piece of a leg."
Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Transport minister says crash was due to "inexplicable" decision
Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said that the crash was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command center for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Authorities were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph (124 mph) for that stretch of the track, Puente said.
"I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts," Puente said.
Everything went flying when the trains collided, a passenger said
The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left carriages shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.
"We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact," he said. "The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook."
Authorities said 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.
Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while unscathed survivors were put on buses. A military emergency brigade was deployed to help.
Spain's King Felipe VI also visited the crash site.
"We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected," Spain's royals said in a statement.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said "My heart goes out to the victims' families and loved ones. Today, Europe mourns with you."
Spain's soccer federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled on Wednesday.
Spain already suffered a devastating train crash this year
The wreckage of Wednesday's crash reminded many of the aftermath of another train collision in January, when 46 people died in southern Spain when an IRYO train jumped the track and hit an oncoming RENFE train. That sent the first two cars of the impacted train plummeting down a four-meter (13-foot) slope.
That crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people.
Before this year, there had been no fatal crash on Spain's dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992.
Spain is a leader in high-speed rail
Over recent decades, Spain has invested heavily in high-speed rail — which the country's railway union defines as rails for trains going 250 kph (155 mph) and over — turning it into a world leader.
Spain has laid some 3,900 kilometers (2,400 miles) of such tracks over more than three decades for its 49 million residents. Only China, with 45,000 kilometers (28,000 miles) for its 1.4 billion people, has more high-speed track, according to the International Union of Railways.
Only recently did Spain open its rail network to private companies to compete against RENFE. The Italian-owned IRYO started operating in Spain in 2022.
A spokesperson for Spain's train workers' union, Joan Rodríguez, said increased traffic brought by privatization has put extra strain on rail infrastructure.
"We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines," Rodríguez told TVE on Wednesday. "I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind."

Madih Talal has been a man on the move since he set foot in India three seasons ago. After impressing with Punjab FC in its debut ISL season, he journeyed across the Eastern belt, spending a campaign each with East Bengal and Jamshedpur FC.
And now, as the Indian Super League enters a new era, the French attacking midfielder has found a new home in the South of the country with Chennaiyin FC.
“I feel comfortable (in India). You know, in my country sometimes we say the grass is not greener somewhere else. (But) I feel happy, I like the league and the football is good,” Talal told Sportstar during an exclusive chat.
But it has not exactly been smooth sailing for the 29-year-old, who suffered an anterior cruciate ligament injury (ACL) while with East Bengal. The blow left him off the pitch for several months, and he was eventually released by the club at the end of the 2024-25 season.
“It was not easy. You feel alone, like the world has stopped because we only play football. So, when you remove football, it’s like nothing is there,” Talal recalled about that period in his life.
ALSO READ | Tough times never last, only tough people do: Edmund aims to take next leap in Indian football
When he recovered and signed for Jamshedpur, the league was in financial crisis that ended up postponing his return to the pitch.
“I came back from injury, and I was ready to play even during the summer. So, after that, it was difficult because we didn’t know if the league would start or not,” he said, adding, “That was not easy not only for me but for everyone. I hope this will never happen again.”
Then another setback followed, with Tata Steel deciding to withdraw Jamshedpur from the league ahead of this season, news that Talal admitted left him “totally shocked.”
But when one door closed, several others opened, and Chennaiyin was the one that Talal eventually decided to walk through.
“I had a great introduction to the club. Owen Coyle (his coach at Jamshedpur and former Chennaiyin head coach) told me a bit about it, and so far it has been good,” he said.
Pulling the strings in attack
His time in the ISL will be especially valuable to the two-time champion, considering it recruited 15 new players over the summer after a poor last season, where it finished 13th out of 14 teams.
Meanwhile, Chennaiyin has had a challenging start to its campaign, drawing 1-1 with FC Goa in the opener before facing defeats against Bengaluru FC (0-2) and Mohun Bagan Super Giant (0-1).
The shortage of goals will be particularly concerning as Chennaiyin was the only side, apart from the relegated Mohammedan SC, to not hit double figures in goals scored last season. And Talal knows that he will have to get his gears running as soon as possible, especially considering the three words he used to describe his playing style were: offensive, creative and technical.
In the last edition, Talal created 39 chances in nine appearances – the third-highest in the league – and led the charts for chances created per 90 with 4.33. His progression across the three games this season, although, has been encouraging.
After coming off the bench against FC Goa, Talal started the next two games, largely running Chennaiyin’s attack, especially against Mohun Bagan. He often linked up with Serbian Nikola Stojanovic to find space in the final third and then release the forward players. A couple of those releases could have resulted in a goal if not for some sloppy finishing and timely saves from Vishal Kaith.
And while Chennaiyin has gathered just one point so far, Talal is cautiously optimistic about what’s coming up.
“Now we have a new team, and we don’t need to compare with last season. The club is building a new project with the young and experienced players. So, it takes time. If you compare the first game and the last game, it’s completely different. We are getting better. I think we just need to continue to work like that and be more clinical in front,” Talal noted.
