Despite significant economic progress and sustained public health efforts, anaemia — driven significantly by iron deficiency — continues to be one of India’s most pressing public health challenges. Affecting over half of Indian women and almost three-fourths of children, anaemia contributes to maternal mortality, an intergenerational cycle of malnutrition, impaired cognitive development, reduced productivity and substantial economic losses. The Government of India’s 7X7X7 Anaemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategy, which was launched recently, rightly recognises the multifactorial nature of anaemia through a comprehensive approach spanning prevention, screening, treatment, dietary diversification and behaviour change. Yet, one proven preventive intervention remains significantly underutilised.
The promise of fortification
That intervention is Double Fortified Salt (DFS) — salt fortified with both iodine and iron. Salt offers an unparalleled opportunity to address iron deficiency. Consumed daily by virtually every household across India, in predictable quantities regardless of income or geography, it is uniquely suited to deliver a preventive nutrition intervention at population scale. DFS also addresses one of the fundamental challenges of anaemia control — sustained compliance.
Delivering iron through an everyday food complements interventions such as iron supplementation and dietary diversification, whose effectiveness depends on regular adherence. India already has one of the world’s most successful public health platforms in Universal Salt Iodisation, with around 95% of households consuming iodised salt. Building on this existing infrastructure, DFS is already distributed to an estimated 76 million people across four States through government safety-net programmes. Global and Indian evidence strongly support DFS. A global review has shown that DFS can reduce anaemia by up to 21%. Randomised controlled trials in Bengaluru, Darjeeling, and Punjab, along with large-scale implementation in Uttar Pradesh, have shown improvements in iron status and confirmed that, when manufactured to validated specifications, DFS is acceptable to consumers, reduces iron deficiency, and is highly cost-effective. A DFS standard has been issued by the Government of India’s Food Safety and Standards Authority (FSSAI), and the Government of India actually mandates DFS’ inclusion in the national school feeding programme (PM POSHAN and the national early childhood development programme- Integrated Child Development Scheme, or ICDS).
At an estimated cost of ₹14-₹20 per person annually, DFS represents one of the most affordable population-level nutrition interventions available, with a benefit-cost ratio of 4.2:1 for national DFS introduction, primarily driven by improved health outcomes and subsequent increases in labour productivity. India also possesses the manufacturing capacity to produce high-quality DFS at scale. Established fortification technologies, centralised salt production and existing laboratory infrastructure make quality assurance and regulatory monitoring simpler than for many other fortified foods.
What the barriers are
What has limited DFS from wider adoption? The barriers are now primarily institutional rather than technical. The next imperative is to accelerate its nationwide adoption and ensure last-mile access, particularly the Public Distribution System apart from social safety-net programmes, across all States through a central flagship scheme. Although DFS is recommended under PM POSHAN and ICDS, its integration into the largest safety net programme i.e., the Public Distribution System (PDS) — which reaches around 800 million beneficiaries — remains uneven because implementation depends largely on State governments. Greater policy commitment, dedicated financing, stronger quality assurance, wider commercial availability and consumer awareness are now needed to accelerate nationwide scale-up. These are implementation challenges — not technological ones — and are well within India’s capacity to address.
Like all public health nutrition interventions, DFS should be implemented within a robust regulatory framework. It should complement existing strategies under Anaemia Mukt Bharat, align with India’s sodium reduction goals, and continue to be accompanied by screening for haemoglobinopathies such as thalassaemia and sickle cell disease. These safeguards are well recognised through experience of rice fortification programme and can be readily integrated into implementation and monitoring systems.
The launch of the revised AMB strategy provides renewed momentum to strengthen the preventive pillar of India’s anaemia response and advance the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.
Potential to be a global model
India has already shown the world how science, policy, public systems, and public awareness can transform nutrition through Universal Salt Iodisation. By scaling DFS nationally, India can not only accelerate progress towards Anaemia Mukt Bharat but also contribute to global efforts to reduce iron deficiency by demonstrating an affordable, scalable model for other low- and middle-income countries.

Trump cancels final Kansas and Iowa rallies before Election Day — and unloads on reporters asking about it
The president appears to be abruptly ending a blitz of campaign-trail appearances as polls show dim prospects for GOP candidates

President Donald Trump has canceled two campaign-trail appearances scheduled for the weekend before Election Day, opting instead for a series of telerallies amid dimming chances of Republican victories in midterms.
The president unloaded on a reporter who questioned why he canceled a Saturday appearance at a Kansas rally, one of last appearances on the road following two weeks of near nightly events. Hours later, the president pulled out of Sunday’s rally in Iowa.
Trump, who appeared to be sweating as he briefly addressed reporters following his remarks at a campaign rally in South Carolina, called a reporter with Reuters “way out of shape” and mocked him for asking whether the president was “feeling well.”
“You know what the reason is? I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas,” Trump told reporters Thursday. “He said, ‘You’re not going to Kansas, sir, are you feeling well?’ You’ve been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect.”
He then called the reporter “disgusting.”
“Put yourself in shape,” he said. “You look like hell.”
The president will instead participate in a series of 20 virtual rallies.
Trump was scheduled to appear at Salina Regional Airport to support embattled Republican incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall, who is polling closely in a race for re-election against Democratic candidate and pastor Adam Hamilton. The last time voters in the state elected a Democratic U.S. senator was in 1939.
Pieter Miller, executive director of the Salina Airport Authority, said “all Salina events are cancelled” due to the president’s schedule.
Trump’s Sunday rally at Five Flags Event Center in Dubuque, Iowa was also canceled on Thursday.
“With Republicans in a strong position in Kansas and Iowa, previously planned in-person rallies in those states will no longer take place as scheduled,” officials announced.
Protesters repeatedly interrupted the president’s last appearance in Kansas, which Trump falsely claimed were “paid” to be there. At least 11 people were escorted from the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City that night.
It was at that event where the president invoked the antisemitic slur “shylock” while defending Marshall’s history of suing former patients for failing to pay medical debt when he worked as an OB-GYN.
“And they made it like, oh, he was some kind of a shylock-type guy. And if he didn’t make these requests, he would be breaking the law,” Trump said at the Kansas rally earlier this month. “He would have been breaking a very strong criminal law, and he would be subject to criminal arrest and liability. And he didn’t do it. He has a law firm that did it.”
Kansas GOP Chair Danedri Herbert told The Kansas City Star that she heard about the president’s plans to scrap the event through the Republican National Committee.
“That’s all they told me that it was canceled and we’d get more information,” she said. “They are going to do a series of telerallies but I don’t have any information about those.”
Rob Fillion, executive director for the Kansas Republican Party, told Wichita’s CBS affiliate KWCH that “Salina and Kansas are very important to our nation, but there are a lot of other races that are in play.”
Trump being able to speak at “multiple locations at the same time is probably more valuable for his time,” Fillion said.
The White House said the president will “continue connecting directly with Americans nationwide through more than 20 telerallies before election day.”
“Telerallies give him the opportunity to highlight his accomplishments and expand his reach across the country,” the White House added.
Kansas is among several states where Democrats appear to be in striking distance to reclaim a Senate majority and tip the balance of power in Congress, according to polling data.
The results of a recent CNN/SSRS poll published Thursday show Hamilton leading among likely voters at 49 percent to Marshall’s 45 percent. Marshall’s favorability rating among likely voters is only 36 percent to Hamilton’s 41 percent.

It’s a bright day in Cupertino. Apple’s new CEO strolls to an outdoor seating area within the company’s otherworldly ring-shaped headquarters and pulls up a chair. An employee notes the angle and asks if he minds the sun. John Ternus doesn’t mind at all.
Nearly two months into his tenure, he’s been busy. While the tech world buzzes about AI agents and the upcoming IPO of a company reporting spectacular losses, Ternus’ leadership of a ridiculously profitable firm has so far been defined by a sequence of significant launches—the long-awaited foldable iPhone, a household device that can control digital appliances, new Mac Minis, and AirPods. Intentionally or not, all that activity sends a message that, even as AI dominates the public imagination, hardware products still rule.
Ternus doesn’t endorse that take, but he doesn’t object when I suggest it. “We’ve been working on these products for quite some time,” he says. “It feels like everyone here is just kind of riding high right now, enjoying it.”
I ask if Apple is about to break a long-imposed taboo and introduce a Macintosh with a touch screen.
Ternus beams. “Who knew?”
We are referring to the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display that Apple is releasing today at an event in Los Angeles. It’s got a mighty M5 Pro or M5 Max chip and a show-stopping tandem OLED screen. (A tandem screen has multiple light-emitting layers, producing more dramatic contrasts.) But its most conspicuous feature is one that’s been deeply woven into iPhones, iPads, and even Apple Watches for years but not Apple’s laptops: a touch display. After years of resistance, a Mac screen has finally gone digital. As in fingers.
This turnaround is a big deal to Apple fans. Ternus shrugs off the drama. “The Mac is first and foremost an indirect input device, built around the trackpad and keyboard. But I think there’s times when it’s comfortable and handy to have touch.”
Ternus and Apple want to make sure that the Mac faithful don’t panic that the 42-year-old franchise is losing its identity to Apple’s gangbusters mobile products. “We needed to get to a point where adding touch didn’t make the product lesser in any way. It didn’t make it heavier. It didn’t make it thicker. That came together with the OLED screen, the best display we’ve ever put into a Mac,” Ternus told me. “All of these things, and, oh yeah, it has touch as well.”
Apple has a long history of refusing to implement certain desirable features, only to pivot when it feels the time is right. Steve Jobs once proclaimed iPods would never do video, until they did. He also once said “no one’s going to buy” a jumbo-size phone—and then Apple released a supersized iPhone 6. Then there was that time Jobs declared styluses inappropriate for tablets. Now the Apple Pencil works with iPads and the brand-new Duo.
The 2026 MacBook Pro instantly qualifies as the canonical example of this switcheroo. Apple executives had been on record regarding touch on PCs as a misbegotten idea. Never mind that just about every PC maker not headquartered in Cupertino has implemented touch on their laptops. And customers of Microsoft, Dell, Acer, Lenovo, and HP have snapped them up. Clearly, people wanted touch on their laptop displays. Even toddlers knew it—put some rug rats in front of a computer and their little arms shoot straight to the screen in futile attempts to swipe and scroll as they do on their iPads. People were baffled why Apple—the pioneer in touch displays since the iPhone—was so steadfast in its rejection.
In 2015, while doing a story about a new iMac, I pressed Phil Schiller, then the senior vice president of worldwide product marketing, on this very question. Usually, top Apple executives field such queries with cryptic remarks. In this case, Schiller began a filibuster. “I’m going to get a little bit philosophical,” he said, then launched into what I later described as the Grand Unified Theory of Apple Hardware.
He explained that every Apple hardware product—the Watch, iPad, iMac, MacBook—is basically a computer and a piece of glass. Each one has a specific function. And each one has an interface appropriate to the hardware. Multitouch is fine for products like the iPhone, he said—but not the Macintosh. He provided two reasons: ergonomics and the software interface.
“From the ergonomic standpoint, we have studied this pretty extensively, and we believe that on a desktop scenario, where you have a fixed keyboard, having to reach up to do touch interfaces is uncomfortable,” he told me.
As for the interface, Schiller argued that Apple’s two main operating systems were built on different design principles. The iPhone and iPad’s iOS was multitouch from the get-go, and didn’t use macOS conventions that require precision, such as cursors and tiny boxes to close windows. “These two worlds are different on purpose, and that’s a good thing—we can optimize around the best experience for each of those and not try to mesh them together into a least-common-denominator experience,” he told me.
A year later, when Apple introduced a MacBook Pro with the ill-fated “touch bar”—a dynamic strip of virtual function keys above the keyboard’s top row—Schiller doubled down on the view that touch should never find its way into a Mac display. He said that such a move would mean totally redesigning the menu bar for fingers, and that would clash with the experience of pointer devices like a touchpad or mouse. “You can’t optimize for both,” he said.
To double-check this assumption, Apple conducted user tests with touchscreens on Mac. “What the heck, we could be wrong,” Schiller told me then. “We’ve absolutely come away with the belief that it isn’t the right thing to do. Our instincts were correct.”
When I met with Apple executives Johny Srouji and Greg Joswiak this week to discuss the touchscreen MacBook Pro, you bet I invoked Schiller’s list of concerns. (Apple’s reps chose not to make Schiller, who now holds the title of “Apple Fellow,” available for an interview. In fact, they laughed when I asked.) It wasn’t only Schiller drawing a red line. In 2021, Ternus told journalist Joanna Stern, “The Mac is totally optimized for indirect input. We haven’t really felt a reason to change that.”
“Ten years is a very, very long time,” says Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer. “Many things have changed, whether it's the display technology, the custom silicon, et cetera.” Eventually, he told me, the confluence of chips, display tech, and software architecture “met our bar.” “I like my engineers to be gated by physics, not imagination or timelines,” he says.
Joswiak, who holds Schiller’s old title of SVP of worldwide marketing, concedes that touch was overdue, at least for users with sophisticated needs. Its pro customers—engineers, scientists, software developers, and media creators—were impatient with Apple for its failure to let them interact directly with the screen. “Most pros own an iPad, and almost every pro owns an iPhone,” Joswiak says. “So this is something that they’re natural with. There’s a generation of young creators and young people using our MacBook Pros that expect to touch.”
Between the lines, Srouji and Joswiak seem to consider their competitors’ touchscreen implementations shabby and lazy. The Apple ethos, as every one of its executives will happily explain to anyone who asks, is an expectation of quality that’s sky-high. “If you’re working on something easy, you’re wasting your time,” says Srouji, who has been at Apple since 2008 and has pretty much driven its innovation by spearheading the company’s charge to custom-build silicon.
“The easy things, I want to outsource,” he continues. “So the custom silicon is hard. The touch is hard. The display is hard. Everything we build is hard.” This swaggering philosophy dates from the Steve Jobs days and, in 2026, stands in contrast to the endgame of the ascendant AI industry, which hopes to turn over the toughest parts of industrial production to superintelligent entities.
Srouji presents Mac touch as a suite of innovations, starting with that screen that Ternus described as the Mac’s best ever. It also involves custom silicon and a rearchitected thermal system to prevent the display from feeling hot when people pinch, stretch, and swipe on it. Srouji contends that current touchscreen laptops suffer from “wobble” when fingers make contact with the display; to minimize this effect, Apple has redesigned the hinge on the MacBook Pro screen to stabilize it.
When I get a demo of the 16-inch version (as with previous Pros, it’s also available in a 14-inch version), I see what they mean about the display. It’s noticeably dense and bright, and the obsidian blacks are the deepest I’ve seen on a computer screen. In part because the OLED screen doesn’t require backlighting, this MacBook weighs less than its predecessor.
As a pair of Apple managers take the MacBook through its paces, I see how Apple has addressed some of Schiller’s decade-old concerns, like having to redesign the menu bar for fingers. While it looks the same, when you move a finger over a menu item, it expands to allow you to select your choice with precision. Some of the objects on the screen, like the traffic-light buttons that close or hide windows, also get bigger when you touch them.
They show me how the touch tech can handle precision tasks, like color grading in the video editing software DaVinci Resolve, or tweaking a soundtrack on Logic Pro, Apple’s high-end audio workstation. One innovation, not just for pros, is a new gesture to pull down the “Dynamic Island,” that black oval hosting ongoing tasks that has made its way to Mac from iPhone. An expanded version floats on the screen like a widget, enabling easy access to Siri responses and Spotlight search.
But what about greasy fingers messing up the screen? I was told that the new display has an anti-reflective outer coating that will require no more cleaning than your normal non-interactive screen.
Apple clearly hopes that the MacBook Pro launch puts an exclamation point on the burst of product announcements that Apple customers are still absorbing. For the foldable Duo, some customers are impatiently waiting for delivery dates that stretch into January. (Lines were long at Apple stores last Friday, when the device went on sale, and Joswiak personally greeted those who queued up at Apple’s Fifth Avenue store in New York City.)
I ask Srouji whether Apple is making a statement with its armada of new products, maybe as a way to say that in a year dominated by AI obsession, Apple is still here. He responds much as his new boss did, contending that Apple is simply sticking to its game plan. “We’re here to build the most amazing products in the world, and we want to ship them when we believe it’s ready and complete,” says Srouji. “That’s the statement we’re making. I think everyone knows we’re here.”
While longtime users will be happy to hear that a Macintosh now has a touchscreen, those with limited budgets will be disappointed. Apple’s current stance—that touch-on-a-Mac display is most appropriate to the “pro” crowd—rationalizes an astronomical price tag: The new MacBook Pro starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch version and $3,399 for the 16-inch model. Financial analyst Neil Cybart, who got an early MacBook Pro briefing, thinks that serious professionals will pay up. “People are in search of value, and that means going for products that leverage technology to improve what they’re doing,” he says.
When I ask Ternus about the timeline, or even the possibility, of seeing touch displays on less exorbitantly priced MacBook Airs and iMacs, he shakes his head. “You’ve been doing this a long time,” he says. “You know I will never tell you anything about our future.”
I don’t know why I bothered to ask. If Ternus said that touch would never happen on a MacBook Air, who would believe him? I’d be back at The Ring a year later, hearing that Apple had finally figured out a way to do it right.

Australian court says mushroom poison murderer should never be released from prison
Erin Patterson poisoned estranged husband, his relatives with death cap mushrooms
An Australian appeals court on Friday ordered triple-murderer Erin Patterson to never be released from prison because of the "shocking criminality" involved in poisoning four of her estranged husband's relatives with death cap mushrooms.
The three judges of the Victoria state Court of Appeal dismissed Patterson's appeal of her convictions and upheld prosecutors' challenge to the leniency of her 33-year non-parole sentence, meaning she will spend the rest of her life behind bars. Beforehand, she would have been 82 years old when she could be considered for release.
"This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms," Justice Stephen McLeish said on behalf of all three judges.
"In all the circumstances after anxious consideration, we have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period," McLeish added.
The convictions stemmed from a family meal she hosted at her rural home in Leongatha in July 2023.
Death cap mushrooms are seen in this undated handout by the B.C. Centre for Disease Control. (BC Centre for Disease Control/The Canadian Press)
She can apply to Australia's High Court to overturn the verdicts on her sentence and her convictions. The High Court is her last appeal option.
Patterson insisted she added death cap mushrooms to the beef Wellington pastry dishes accidentally.
She was sentenced last year to three life sentences for murder and 25 years for attempted murder.
Murders attract global attention
The deaths of Patterson's parents-in-law Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister, Heather Wilkinson, within days of having lunch immediately attracted an extraordinary level of global media attention.
The case has also inspired podcasts, books and screen adaptations.
Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson survived the lunch after spending weeks in hospital. Erin Patterson was convicted of his attempted murder.
Prosecutors argued at an appeal hearing in August that she should never become eligible for parole.
They argued the minimum period behind bars did not reflect the "calculated criminality" of the case.
McLeish said Patterson's intent to murder all four was sustained for almost three weeks from when she invited them to lunch.
Her crimes involved an "elaborate series of deceptions" including falsely claiming a cancer diagnosis to explain the absences of her two children from the lunch, the judge said.
The only survivor, Ian Wilkinson, testified that Erin Patterson had told her guests she wanted their advice about what to tell the children about her diagnosis.
Destroyed evidence, false claims
McLeish noted Erin Patterson had destroyed evidence, denied foraging for mushrooms and repeatedly made false claims about where the mushrooms had come from.
"The offending was carefully planned and deliberate. It represented a cruel breach of trust," McLeish said.
Patterson opted not to attend court and watched the verdicts by video link from prison.
In a supplied court sketch, Erin Patterson is depicted on a video link, as seen in the Victorian Court of Appeal in Melbourne, Australia, on Aug. 19. (Anita Lester/Australian Associated Press/The Associated Press)
Because of her notoriety, Patterson is held in the high-security Gordon Unit of Melbourne's Dame Phyllis Frost Centre women's prison. The unit is for prisoners assessed as being at high risk from other inmates.
In sentencing her in September 2025, trial judge Christopher Bale said there was a "substantial chance" that Patterson could be held in "solitary confinement for years to come."
Patterson's estranged husband, Simon Patterson, was invited to the lunch but declined the day before.
After her conviction, pretrial evidence was released that detailed the husband's suspicion that Erin Patterson had previously attempted to kill him.
Simon Patterson testified at a pretrial hearing that he had declined the lunch invitation out of fear.

Amgen's Imdelltra used in combination with AstraZeneca's immunotherapy Imfinzi reduced the risk of death by 58% compared to the Astra drug alone in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, according to data from a study presented at a major medical meeting on Saturday.
Imfinzi is currently the standard of care following chemotherapy for patients with this very aggressive and hard-to-treat disease whose cancer does not worsen after initial chemotherapy.
The study found that those given both drugs lived for a median of 21.1 months, compared with 12.7 months for those treated only with Imfinzi.
"If you give Imdelltra earlier and earlier, you get bigger clinical benefit," said Paul Burton, chief medical officer at California-based Amgen. He called the results "unprecedented in advancing the treatment of extensive-stage small cell lung cancer."
Imdelltra's U.S. list price is about $30,000 per cycle, or over $390,000 a year. Wall Street analysts have estimated annual sales reaching more than $2.5 billion by 2030, according to LSEG data.
The Amgen drug is currently approved for adults in the advanced stages of small cell lung cancer that has worsened despite chemotherapy, based on data showing that Imdelltra reduced the risk of death by 40%.
Full results of the 563-patient trial were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology meeting in Madrid and published in the New England Journal of Medicine. Amgen had previously announced that the Phase 3 study was successful.
Imdelltra belongs to a dual-target class of drugs called bispecific antibodies designed to pull immune system T cells into contact with cancer cells to destroy them. Imfinzi is an older type of immunotherapy that essentially blocks the mechanism tumors use to hide from immune-system assault.
Most lung cancer cases are non-small cell, while up to 15% are the small cell variety targeted by Imdelltra. About 250,000 new cases are diagnosed worldwide each year, according to the U.S. National Institutes of Health.
Very few people diagnosed with small cell lung cancer are candidates for surgery, and most are initially given radiotherapy and chemotherapy, Burton said.
Survival rates depend on when the cancer is diagnosed, but the overall 5-year rate is only around 9%, according to the American Cancer Society.
Amgen said that nearly 80% of trial patients treated with the combination were alive after one year, compared with 53% of those on Imfinzi alone, as patient follow-up continues.
Serious side effects, including low white blood cell counts, occurred in 20.9% of patients on the dual therapy and 10.8% with the single therapy. A potentially dangerous condition known as cytokine release syndrome, an aggressive inflammatory response, was reported in 49.6% of patients who received Imdelltra. But only one case was serious and there were no CRS-related deaths.
Adverse events led to discontinuation of the combination therapy in 5.7% of trial patients and 5.8% of patients given only Imfinzi.

Stanford researcher Chuyue Sun and her fellow computer scientists developed an AI tool that completed an engineering project in less than half a day for under $500, compared to the five months it took three highly skilled experts to do the same work manually. The dramatic reduction in time and cost, which Sun reported in a recent paper, is among the early results that are awakening an obscure field of coding and mathematics known as formal verification.
For decades, developers have envisioned using math to prove that their software is bug-free. This process is long and laborious, requiring engineers to write precise statements about the goals of their software and convert their code into formulas that can be validated. While companies already run sophisticated tests to identify as many flaws in their software as possible, they rarely shell out for formal verification, which can catch even more erratic behavior.
Now, a wave of startups is betting that generative AI will make formal software verification both practical and essential. Among them is &Truth, which Sun joined in August and publicly launched on Thursday. Sun’s research demonstrated the technology’s potential by using AI to verify part of the code that encrypts conversations in the messaging app Signal.
“Bridges, buildings, they don’t collapse because people did math before constructing them,” says Ilya Sergey, &Truth’s chief science officer. “Why don’t we do the same for code? The technology to mathematically reason was all there, just difficult to scale.”
&Truth has raised $70 million from investors and aims to eventually verify any programming language. Rival Harmonic, which was cofounded by Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev and has received $295 million in funding, announced this week that its math-focused AI agent Aristotle supports verifying software written in C and hardware designs in Verilog. It is evaluating the technology with potential users, including chipmakers Tensordyne and Nvidia, whose venture capital arm is one of the startup’s investors.
And just last week, Anthropic and the verification startup Theorem jointly announced they had used AI to assist in finding bugs in open source software that trillions of tests had failed to detect. They also introduced an add-on for Claude to help other developers with verification. Costs of the initial project were not disclosed.
The big promise is a future where software runs more reliably with fewer security headaches. But whether AI can bring formal verification beyond the most critical systems at organizations like NASA and Apple and into widespread use remains an open question.
The technology is still in the prototyping stage. Though demand is high, it's unclear how much customers are willing to pay and how they prefer to adopt the technology. Formal verification relies on making assumptions about how computers and people interact with software, and some experts are skeptical about its ability to catch bugs stemming from user error and hardware breakdowns.
Will Wilson, who runs the bug-hunting AI software startup Antithesis, calls formal verification “a trap” for math nerds like himself. Antithesis spent millions of dollars to formally verify some of its cybersecurity defenses, a process Wilson describes as a “pain in the ass.” Yet the startup still uncovered additional errors using its own tool, and Antithesis has also found bugs in software that several of its customers had formally verified. “It can give you some assurance, but only robust exhaustive testing can prove your assurance is true,” Wilson says.
Or as Vitalik Buterin, the engineer known for creating the Ethereum cryptocurrency, put it in a blog post earlier this year, “formal verification is not a panacea.” But he and other proponents of the approach still believe it will be an important defense against AI systems launching cyberattacks and wreaking havoc.
Core Security
Boeing planes, Amazon servers, and more than 2.5 billion active Apple devices contain at least some formally verified software, according to company disclosures. The code in question is typically security-related, and vulnerabilities in it could cause serious harm if exploited.
Byron Cook, a distinguished scientist and vice president at Amazon Web Services, says formal verification has eased customer concerns about cloud security and helped internal teams move faster by squashing big bugs early on.
But several midsized tech companies tell WIRED they have typically verified only one key feature of their products, if any at all. They cite a lack of verification engineers, costs that outweigh the potential risks, and, perhaps most importantly, concerns that waiting weeks for code to be formally verified could slow innovation.
Earlier this year, Apple’s security team said that some of the issues formal verification uncovered in its “corecrypto” library, which is used for encryption, could not have been found any other way. But the company added that it has to be “conservative” when adding new code to corecrypto to ensure it can keep pace with reviewing it.
Two cybersecurity executives at major companies that haven’t formally verified any code say they aren’t sure whether automation will make it worthwhile. But the executives, who weren’t authorized to speak publicly, say they could imagine paying major AI labs for “verified” AI-generated code.
Developers of open source software projects, which are the bedrock of many apps, are increasingly experimenting with AI-aided verification. The nonprofit Beneficial AI Foundation used a grant from Anthropic to validate the same encryption code this year as Sun did at Stanford. Michael Rosenberg, a maintainer of the library known as curve25519-dalek, hopes sustainable funding emerges for ongoing verification efforts. “I have no ideas as to how that’s going to happen, though, and we certainly shouldn’t rely on the goodwill of the AI companies,” he says.
Some of the startups eager to expand verification also aren’t sure whether to deploy their tools directly to customers or through intermediaries like Anthropic. Their general plan is to use AI to automate much of the work involved in defining how a program is supposed to behave. For example, specifications for a data table might require that it contain the same items before and after sorting, just in a different order. Further automation efforts, which may not involve AI, would translate that code into a format that math tools like Lean, Rocq, and Isabelle can use to check whether the code works as intended.
Another recent entrant to the formal verification field is Madan Musuvathi, who left Microsoft Research after more than 20 years to found the startup Truidic. After incidents like the OpenAI hack of Hugging Face, he felt there was an urgent need to commercialize his studies. “AI in the hands of attackers can be extremely powerful,” Musuvathi says, but verification can “make AI safe and secure for everyone, everywhere.”
Proofcraft, one of the few companies that has long offered traditional verification, says growing excitement about the process is translating into a flood of inquiries from potential customers. June Andronick, the company’s CEO, and Gerwin Klein, its chief scientist, say interest easily outpaces what they and their competition can provide.
But both worry that AI-generated specifications could inspire “unjustified trust” in the results. Verifiers are also eager to preserve the joy their work brings them. Klein calls it “pretty addictive, like a puzzle game.” If all goes well, he’ll be doing more solving than ever.

Families hold out hope for loved ones missing after deadly Spain train crash
Families are desperately searching for missing loved ones after two high-speed trains collided in central Spain
TOLEDO, Spain -- Families desperately searched for missing loved ones Thursday, more than 24 hours after two high-speed trains collided in central Spain, killing at least 69 and injuring dozens of others.
“I have my father, and I don’t know where he is. I hope to find him, oh my Lord," said César Vicente, an actor who traveled 495 kilometers (307 miles) from his native Seville to Toledo in search of his father. He spent the night with many other families at a religious center converted into a base for those affected by the disaster.
Vicente was with his mother and his aunt, all of whom were looking for César Vicente, who was sitting in seat 13A on the RENFE train that struck another operated by the private company Iryo, which had stopped on the tracks. The family was among those who braved the cold to take a short walk on a chilly morning.
“I don’t want this to happen to anyone. This is unbearable,” he added. “This is hell.”
Online, relatives and friends flooded social media with desperate appeals for information on the whereabouts of their loved ones, posting photos or describing the clothes they were wearing when they boarded the trains bound for Seville and details about their physical appearance or the seat in which they were traveling.
In a post Wednesday on Instagram, Alejandra Marroquín told her followers that her sister Adriana, who was wearing dark blue clothes, was traveling in car 8 of the RENFE train and that they had been unable to contact her.
“We’re still praying, we don’t know anything,” Marroquín said in a post Thursday morning, as search teams with sniffer dogs continued to look for victims.
“The entire government is working to respond to the victims’ families, shed light on the tragedy, and strengthen security so that this never happens again,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told reporters on Thursday morning.
This was the second high-speed rail disaster this year. In January, 46 people died after one train jumped the track and slammed into the side of another going the opposite way in southern Spain.
The high-speed rail network has been considered one of Spain’s crowning achievements. It is the world’s second-largest, after China’s. Until this year, it had not experienced a deadly crash since coming into service over three decades ago.
Life in Urda, a small town of about 2,500 people south of Madrid, was turned upside down early Wednesday.
Residents rushed to help in any way they could: from assisting the injured to preparing sandwiches for the unharmed passengers, many of whom they even carried from the tracks to a nearby sports pavilion in their cars.
David Gómez, a construction worker, was working with his brother and another colleague nearby when they heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El País.
“People were trying to get out through the windows ... We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought until emergency services arrived," he said.
With 180 people injured, including 110 taken to hospitals, authorities issued a call for blood donations.
The response was immediate: in Castilla-La Mancha alone, the region where the collision occurred, more than 2,000 people volunteered in the aftermath.
“I want to express my personal and very sincere gratitude to everyone who has stepped up, starting with the all-time record number of donations,” said the region’s president, Emiliano García-Page, who also thanked the 1,300 emergency service personnel who were mobilized.

Are you an organ donor? Here are some rule changes you may want to know
Organ donation conversations are changing. Critics worry families may feel pressured
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
The U.S. organ transplant system is making a controversial change to a long-standing rule that was designed to protect potential donors. The revision aims to boost donations and reduce errors. But critics worry that the move may endanger patient care.
Under the change, the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network, which runs the transplant system, will relax a strict firewall between the doctors and nurses trying to save patients in the hospital and the transplantation team standing by to procure patients' organs.
Previously, no one from that team was even supposed to talk to family members until after they had made the heart-wrenching decision to let a loved one go. The rule was intended to prevent pressure that could change the care patients receive. It was also in place to dispel any doubts that doctors aren't doing everything they can to save patients.
But the board of directors for the transplant system voted Aug. 20 to modify that rule as part of a new set of guidelines governing donation following circulatory death. That occurs after life-sustaining care has been withdrawn and now accounts for about half of organ donations.
The new rules, which go into effect Nov. 18, "allow discussions for organ donation to take place once end of life discussions are taking place with the potential deceased donor's agent," according to the new policy.
Why is the firewall previously barring these conversations coming down?
"I think the best way to think about it is that insisting on a bright line without focusing on what's happening on either side of that line is a false sense of security," Dr. Raymond Lynch, the director of transplantation at the Health Resources & Services Administration, the federal agency that oversees the organ network, told NPR in an interview.
The new rules aim to prevent disturbing mistakes that have occurred in the past. Those errors have included patients being wheeled into operating rooms to remove their organs when they were still alive.
"That specific line in the policy is part of a suite of improvements to the coordination and communication between the organ procurement organizations and the healthcare team that is caring for these patients in hospitals and the families of the patients themselves. And that really is a marked improvement over the policy that was in place before," Lynch says.
A balance of safety and speed
In addition to allowing donation teams to approach families sooner, the new policies include making it easier to pause organ retrieval if anyone becomes concerned that something is amiss and standardizing other patient protections, including testing for determining death.
"Documentation, clear coordination, deference to the primary healthcare team and consequences — that's what keeps patients safe," says Lynch.
The change in policy is also designed to make sure the organ retrieval team isn't brought in too late to conduct the tests and preparation necessary for families to honor their loved one's desire to be a donor.
When that happens, "the family loses out on that memory" of helping their loved one donate their organs, "the patient loses out on the choice that they made, and the people on the waiting list lose out on the chance to receive a lifesaving organ," Lynch says.
More than 109,000 Americans are waiting for an organ transplant, according to the Health Resources & Services Administration. About 12 die every day because of a chronic organ shortage.
Does the change cross an ethical line?
Critics, however, say the change is dangerous. It could subtly pressure families and caregivers to discontinue care and create confusion about who's in the intensive care unit to try to save their loved one and who's there to obtain their organs, which could deepen distrust in the organ donation system.
"It's a very important bright line," says Dr. Lainie Ross, a bioethicist at the University of Rochester. "Our primary responsibility is that patient's well-being and care. And we need a bright line. That's where our focus is, and we're not even going to start thinking about whether those organs are usable until death is inevitable and imminent."
She adds: "When my family member is in that hospital bed, I want to know that we're all on Team Mom and not worried the reason the doctor's really suggesting the treatments aren't working is because they want your organs for someone else."
Ross says she's "horrified to think that families will feel pressured. They'll feel manipulated."
Others also see problems with the change.
"I don't disagree with the desire to have more transplantable organs. I think transplants provide great benefit to many, many people," says Dr. Claire Morgan, a transplant surgeon who serves on the transplant network's Patient Affairs Committee. "But people may be pressured to make that decision too quickly. I don't want to interfere with a family's grieving process, and I don't want to interfere with a family's ability to make a decision for their family member at a time when it's correct for them."
Some critics say the change is the latest worrisome development for organ donors.
"This is part of a number of things that are going on in organ donation that are blurring lines," says Lois Shepherd, a professor of law and bioethics at the University of Virginia who opposed the change as a member of the working group that developed the new guidelines. "A lot of safeguards for patients are weakening. And that's a concern to me."
But the change was endorsed by the Association of Organ Procurement Organizations (AOPO), a trade group.
"Families/agents who are considering [withdrawing life support] must be informed about donation and how the donor evaluation process may affect the timing of the [withdrawal of life support]," the group said in its public comments. "Many families have expressed frustration with learning about this timing impact after planning for other family members to be present at the time of [withdrawing life support]. Waiting until the family has made the decision is too late."
The AOPO declined to make someone available for an interview with NPR. But AOPO President Allison Erickson said in a written statement: "Donation depends on public trust, and it is our responsibility to respect and maintain it. Any time there is confusion or concern, [organ procurement organizations] clarify and improve the process. Donor families deserve to fully understand each stage of the end-of-life and donation processes, as well as that their loved ones are cared for by all involved."

Ukraine-Russia war latest: Kyiv ‘pauses oil strikes’ under pressure from Trump even as Putin keeps up attacks
Pause on strikes targeting Russia's oil infrastructure could reportedly last deeper into November

Ukraine's military has reportedly paused its strikes on Russian oil refineries until after the US midterms, following weeks of pressure from Donald Trump.
The pause could last deeper into November, sources told the Wall St Journal, and comes despite the fact that Russia continues to target energy and civilian infrastructure in Ukraine.
Ukrainian strikes targeting Russia's oil infrastructure have in part contributed to a sharp downturn in relations between Trump and Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky, with the former blaming them for diesel prices hitting record highs.
Earlier, a Russian drone attack killed 14 people at the main railway station in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, hitting a platform crowded with people boarding a train, officials said.
And both Russia and Ukraine said on Thursday that demining operations around the Russian-held town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine had been completed and that an operation to bring aid and allow residents to leave was ready to begin.
Efforts have been underway for several weeks to organise a relief operation for the acutely deprived town's residents, which Russian forces seized soon after Moscow's February 2022 invasion of its smaller neighbour.
Residents given deadline to return to Ukraine-controlled territory
Residents wishing to leave and return to territory controlled by the Ukrainian government are expected to exit via Russia-controlled Crimea before crossing into southern Russia and being flown to Belarus from where they will be able to cross the border into Ukraine.
By the middle of Thursday, neither Ukraine nor Russia had reported violations of the ceasefire, due to last until Sunday.
Putin says aid is reaching Oleshky civilians due to ceasefire
President Vladimir Putin told a gathering with African nations in Moscow that relief supplies would begin reaching Oleshky civilians on Thursday and Friday, "with the support, incidentally, of the first lady of the United States".
The truce applies only to Oleshky and the wider Kherson region, which has suffered years of near-daily drone and artillery attacks. Some 1,500 of the town's prewar population of 24,000 people are believed to live among the ruins, under regular shellfire amid severe shortages of food and medicine.
Ukraine has long accused Russia of refusing to let aid in or people out. Russia says it is Ukrainian mines on the approach roads and Ukrainian shelling that have prevented the delivery of aid or the safe evacuation of residents.
Ukraine pauses strikes on Russian refineries after pressure from Trump – reports
Ukraine has halted its strikes on Russian oil refineries after pressure from US president Donald Trump, the Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday, citing people with knowledge of the operations.
Ukrainian units carrying out long-range strikes were told in mid-October that the campaign against refineries was effectively on hold once missions already in motion were completed, the Journal reported.
The unofficial pause is expected to last until after the US midterm elections and potentially deeper into November, it added. Russia has meanwhile stepped up attacks on Ukrainian energy and civilian infrastructure.
The news of a pause comes amid renewed efforts to revive US-backed peace talks to end Europe's deadliest conflict since World War Two.
Relations between Trump and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky have taken a sharp downward turn in recent weeks, with Trump growing increasingly frustrated over Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure as diesel prices hit record highs.
Ukraine had refused to halt the strikes, saying its long-range drone campaign is its only viable response to years of Russian bombardment.
That prompted Trump to announce a deal to buy diesel from Moscow and waive sanctions on Moscow authorised by a bill he signed into law in September.
Russia, Ukraine say Oleshky demining operations complete, humanitarian operation to proceed
Russia and Ukraine said on Thursday that demining operations around the Russian-held town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine had been completed and that an operation to bring aid and allow residents to leave was ready to begin.
Efforts have been underway for several weeks to organise a relief operation for the acutely deprived town's residents, which Russian forces seized soon after Moscow's February 2022 invasion of its smaller neighbour.
Both sides have praised US first lady Melania Trump for helping broker a truce in a town where at least one resident who escaped said those remaining feared death by starvation.
"Demining operations of routes have been completed for the humanitarian mission in Oleshky," the two sides said in virtually identical statements issued by Yana Lantratova, Russia's human rights commissioner, and Dmytro Lubinets, her Ukrainian counterpart.
"The humanitarian convoy is ready for departure."
The convoy would head for the district hospital and residents wishing to leave would be permitted to go within a specific time frame. Aid packages would then be distributed, the statements said.
The operation aims to address a crisis in a town marooned inside a war zone since 2022. But it is also part of a diplomatic dance where both sides want to show US President Donald Trump that they back his peace efforts, albeit for different reasons.
Lantratova, Russian human rights commissioner, said she was taking four journalists from the conservative US outlet Newsmax to the area. Lubinets made no reference to specific reporters.
Aid mission set to enter Oleshky as a localized Russia-Ukraine truce holds for a third day
Humanitarian aid is poised to roll into the stricken city of Oleshky, negotiators said Thursday, as a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine stretched into a third day and military units cleared landmines.
Moscow and Kyiv have observed the truce in and around the devastated southern Ukrainian city since Tuesday, but remain otherwise locked in the war that began with Russia’s full-scale invasion more than four years ago. Previous ceasefire talks either failed or the truces quickly fell apart.
“Demining of the designated routes has been completed, and the humanitarian convoy has been assembled and is ready,” ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, who heads Ukraine's negotiating team, said Thursday. He said aid deliveries were due to begin Friday.
Elsewhere, deadly attacks continued and Ukraine's central bank warned that damage to industrial targets could push the country into a recession.
The planned six-day ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky has brought a rare and welcome stillness for civilians in the nearby city of Kherson, which is held by Ukraine and has also been wracked by the war.
Russian and Ukrainian officials head to Oleshky for aid delivery
Both sides thanked Melania Trump for what the White House called her help in brokering the ceasefire so food and medical supplies can be delivered to about 2,000 people trapped in Oleshky. Pope Leo XIV also pressed for a truce.

The recent protests called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), and helmed by Opposition parties, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar have exposed a chink in journalists’ armour. The crackdown on journalists, especially freelancers and independent journalists, during the October 10 protests, has rekindled the debate on who has the right to be recognised as a journalist and about who decides who is a journalist.
One has seen how during the CJP protests, both in July over the NEET paper leak and in October over the demand for the CEC’s removal, freelancers and independent journalists, and content creators descended in hordes at the protest venue already bulging at the seams with reporters from registered media houses. However, during the second round of protests on October 10, phalanxes of riot police removed them from the protest site and sent them to detention centres. Only journalists with the Press Information Bureau (PIB) or Directorate of Information and Publicity (DIP) accreditation were allowed to cover the protests.
A Bench comprising Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi, while hearing a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) which seeks the protection of the right to freedom of expression by freelance journalists and content creators, wondered whether the right to freedom of expression empowered every citizen of this country to be a journalist. “If everyone starts becoming a journalist, it will create problems for every other person,” the CJI said. During the hearing, senior advocate Indira Jaisingh said that there must be a national protocol for police not to obstruct the professional work of any journalist who has an identity card from the employer. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta said that in the present era, any person with a mobile phone could claim to be an independent or freelance journalist when he/she would, in fact, be making reels only to garner popularity on social media to earn money by either presenting one-sided stories or sensationalising events.
Recognising journalists
These developments have put the focus back on the question of who recognises journalists. As per the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, a working journalist is a person whose principal avocation is journalism and who is employed in a newspaper, electronic media or digital media. This definition excludes people employed in a managerial or administrative capacity. Further, Central and State governments provide accreditation to working journalists, freelance journalists, camerapersons and technicians. Accreditation recognises working journalists and others and gives them access to designated official sources of information. For journalists in Delhi-NCR, accreditation is provided by the PIB for covering the Central government while the DIP accreditation gives them the right to cover the Delhi State government. Media accreditation guidelines of the PIB and DIP define the eligibility criteria for all those seeking accreditation. However, one of the major issues with government accreditation is that it has a quota depending upon circulation (for newspapers, periodicals and magazines), subscribers (for news agencies), licence under uplinking and downlinking guidelines (for private satellite TV channels), and unique visitors (for digital news publishers). Therefore, all journalists in recognised media organisations don’t get accreditation. This leads us to the question on how all working journalists can be recognised.
One solution could be a national media council or commission. Just like there is the Bar Council of India for lawyers and an Institute of Chartered Accountants of India for chartered accountants, the media council can recognise all working journalists, freelance journalists, camerapersons and technicians. Just like you need a law degree to practise law, a medical degree to become a doctor, the media council may mandate a degree or diploma in journalism and mass communication while applying for a licence.
A few years ago, the Press Club of India drafted a Media Transparency (and Accountability) Bill, which mandated the formation of a national media council, among other things. Recently, some other journalists’ bodies have also submitted a memorandum to the government with the same demand. As more and more people with a camera claim to be freelance journalists, it may be high time for the government to give some serious thought to the idea of such a council.
Rakesh Goswami is Professor of Journalism at Indian Institute of Mass Communication, New Delhi

- Versions of a post claiming to state a list of "facts" about the history of Social Security have circulated online for over a decade.
- This supposed list of facts is so pervasive, the Social Security Administration debunked the claims within it on the administration's website.
- We have rated this list overall as mostly false because every claim is largely or entirely inaccurate, except for two.
- Former President Franklin D. Roosevelt — who signed the law creating Social Security — did, in fact, put the program's money in a trust fund separate from the government's general budget. However, claims that former President Lyndon B. Johnson reversed that decision are inaccurate. Social Security has always been in a separate, independent fund and still is as of this writing.
- Democrats did, in fact, increase taxes on Social Security annuities under former President Bill Clinton, but only for higher earners.
In late 2026, readers asked us about posts claiming to share a long list of "facts" about the history of Social Security, including five supposedly broken "promises" about the program and a Q&A section about the Democratic Party's supposed impact on the public benefits program.
Snopes readers referenced posts on LinkedIn and Facebook. These posts claimed that when former President Franklin D. Roosevelt introduced the public benefits program, he allegedly promised voluntary participation, far lower tax rates, tax deductible-eligibility and a Social Security fund separate from the general government budget.
The Q&A section of the posts blamed the Democratic Party for supposedly breaking these promises and providing benefits to immigrants.
Here's one example: 
HISTORY LESSON ON YOUR SOCIAL SECURITY CARD:
Just in case some of you young whippersnappers (& some older ones) didn't know this. It's easy to check out, if you don't believe it. Be sure and show it to your family and friends. They need a little history lesson on what's what and it doesn't matter whether you are Democrat or Republican. Facts are FACTS.
Up until the 1980's, Social Security cards expressly stated the number and card were not to be used for identification purposes.
Since nearly everyone in the United States now has a number, it became convenient to use it anyway and the "NOT FOR IDENTIFICATION" message was removed.
Franklin Roosevelt, a Democrat, introduced the Social Security (FICA) Program. His promises are in black, with updates in brackets.
1.) That participation in the Program would be completely voluntary [No longer voluntary],
2.) That the participants would only have to pay 1% of the first $1,400 of their annual Incomes into the Program [Now 7.65% on the first $90,000, and 15% on the first $90,000 if you're self-employed],
3.) That the money the participants elected to put into the Program would be deductible from their income for tax purposes each year [No longer tax deductible],
4.) That the money the participants put into the independent 'Trust Fund' rather than into the general operating fund, and therefore, would only be used to fund the Social Security Retirement Program, and no other Government program [Under Johnson the money was moved to the General Fund and spent], and
5.) That the annuity payments to the retirees would never be taxed as income [Under Clinton & Gore up to 85% of your Social Security can be taxed].
Since many of us have paid into FICA for years and are now receiving a Social Security check every month — and then finding that we are getting taxed on 85% of the money we paid to the Federal government to 'put away' — you may be interested in the following:
Q: Which Political Party took Social Security from the independent 'Trust Fund' and put it into the general fund so that Congress could spend it?
A: It was Lyndon Johnson and the democratically controlled House and Senate.
Q: Which Political Party eliminated the income tax deduction for Social Security (FICA) withholding? 
A: The Democratic Party.
Q: Which Political Party started taxing Social Security annuities? 
A: The Democratic Party, with Al Gore casting the 'tie-breaking' deciding vote as President of the Senate, while he was Vice President of the US
Q: Which Political Party decided to start giving annuity payments to immigrants? 
A: That's right! Jimmy Carter and the Democratic Party. Immigrants moved into this country, and at age 65, began to receive Social Security payments! The Democratic Party gave these payments to them, even though they never paid a dime into it! 
Different versions of this copypasta — copied-and-pasted text shared online — have spread for years. The claims within have been debunked not only by independent fact-checkers, but by the Social Security Administration itself. In fact, these claims contain so many inaccurate details that our peers at FactCheck.org said in 2009 that they believed a near-identical version of the post circulating online "must be an intentional and malicious effort at disinformation."
Given that almost every single supposed "fact" in the above post is largely inaccurate — but there are a few details based in varying levels of truth — we have rated the overall post as mostly false. 
Below, we broke down each claim made in the post and gave each its own rating, primarily relying on the Social Security Administration and the original Social Security Act of 1935 that Roosevelt signed into law.
(For further reading, we also previously looked into a list of supposed Social Security "fun facts.")
Roosevelt's supposed promises
CLAIM: Roosevelt promised that participation in Social Security would be completely voluntary.
RATING: Mostly False
All employees who are covered by Social Security are subject to the Federal Insurance Contributions Act tax, or the FICA payroll tax, which funds Social Security and Medicare.
"Like all taxes, this has never been voluntary," said the Social Security Administration. "From the first days of the program to the present, anyone working on a job covered by Social Security has been obligated to pay their payroll taxes."
According to the Social Security Administration, however, when Roosevelt passed the law, "only about half the jobs in the economy were covered by Social Security." As such, people could technically choose to work a job that did not pay FICA taxes, which would make them ineligible for Social Security benefits. Nevertheless, there's no record of Roosevelt promising that participation in the program would be "completely voluntary," contrary to claims.
As of 2026, an estimated 94% of workers are covered under Social Security.
There are several exceptions to mandatory participation in Social Security, such as for some employees of state and local governments, who might be able to voluntarily choose Social Security coverage under certain conditions.
CLAIM: Roosevelt promised participants would only have to pay 1% of the first $1,400 of their annual incomes into the program.
RATING: Mostly False
The tax rate on employees is listed in the Social Security Act of 1935 as 1% on the first $3,000 of earnings from 1937 to 1939. The rate then would increase on a regular schedule up until the end of 1948, when it was 3% on the first $3,000 of earnings.
Section 801 clearly lays out the tax rates:
INCOME TAX ON EMPLOYEES
SECTION 801. In addition to other taxes, there shall be levied, collected, and paid upon the income of every individual a tax equal to the following percentages of the wages (as defined in section 811) received by him after December 31, 1936, with respect to employment (as defined in section 811) after such date:
(1) With respect to employment during the calendar years 1937, 1938, and 1939, the rate shall be 1 per centum.
(2) With respect to employment during the calendar years 1940, 1941, and 1942, the rate shall 1 1/2 per centum.
(3) With respect to employment during the calendar years 1943, 1944, and 1945, the rate shall be 2 per centum.
(4) With respect to employment during the calendar years 1946, 1947, and 1948, the rate shall be 2 1/2 per centum.
(5) With respect to employment after December 31, 1948, the rate shall be 3 per centum.
Meanwhile, Section 811 defines "wages" as everything paid to an individual up to $3,000.
We have rated this claim as mostly false because the 1% tax rate figure in the claim was somewhat accurate for the program's early years — even though the maximum taxable amount claimed in the rumor is inaccurate. Furthermore, Roosevelt did not expressly promise a permanent 1% tax rate, per the law.
CLAIM: Roosevelt promised the money the participants elected to put into the program would be deductible for income tax purposes.
RATING: False
In truth, Section 803, Title VIII of the original 1935 law that Roosevelt signed expressly forbids making employees' Social Security payments tax deductible (emphasis ours):
SEC. 803. For the purposes of the income tax imposed by Title I of the Revenue Act of 1934 or by any Act of Congress in substitution therefor, the tax imposed by section 801 shall not be allowed as a deduction to the taxpayer in computing his net income for the year in which such tax is deducted from his wages.
Since the claim made is the opposite of the truth in this instance, we have rated it as false.
CLAIM: Roosevelt promised the money participants paid would be put in an account independent from the general government fund.
RATING: Mostly True (but misleading)
The Social Security Administration called this idea "basically correct."
However, the list of "facts" in question claims that this was a broken promise and that under former President Lyndon B. Johnson, "the money was moved to the General Fund and spent." Below, we rate that claim, which shows up in the Q&A section of the post, as false.
That's because the government's independent Social Security trust fund has never been "put into the general fund of the government," the Social Security Administration said.
CLAIM: Roosevelt promised Social Security annuity payments to retirees would never be taxed as income.
RATING: Mostly False
According to the Social Security Administration, while Social Security benefits were not originally taxable income, that had nothing to do with the Social Security Act of 1935, "nor anything that President Roosevelt did or could have 'promised.'"
In truth, Treasury Department issued a series of administrative rulings after the law already passed determining that Social Security benefits would initially not be taxable income.
In 1983, under former President Ronald Reagan, a Republican, Congress changed the law to authorize the taxation of Social Security benefits (see the section titled "TAX TREATMENT" for a detailed explanation from the Social Security Administration about how the Social Security Amendments of 1983 changed U.S. tax code).
Since Roosevelt was president when the Treasury Department's administrative rulings went into effect — but he made no such promise about taxable income, nor did he personally sign such a rule into law — we have rated this claim as mostly false.
Evaluating more of the post's claims
CLAIM: Former President Lyndon B. Johnson and the Democratic Party took Social Security payments from the program's independent trust fund and put the money into the general fund so Congress could spend it.
RATING: False
As we previously stated, the Social Security Trust Fund has always been a separate, independent account.
This claim likely comes from confusion about how the Social Security Trust Fund is treated in federal budget accounting, the Social Security Administration said.
In 1968, the Johnson administration changed the way the federal government presents its budget by creating a "unified budget." This was simply a framework for presenting all of the federal government's finances together in order to make the budget less confusing.
Presenting everything as a unified budget did not actually change the operations of the Social Security trust fund. The way Social Security is presented in relation to the federal government's budget has undergone changes since Johnson's time, but it ultimately doesn't change how the federal government actually deposits or withdraws money from the fund.
We have rated this claim as false because Johnson did not take money from Social Security's independent trust fund, nor did he put it in the general fund so Congress could spend it.
CLAIM: The Democratic Party eliminated an income tax deduction for Social Security (FICA) withholding.
RATING: False
As stated above, Section 803, Title VIII of the original Social Security Act prohibited income tax deductions for Social Security (FICA) withholding. As such, there was no income tax deduction for the Democratic Party to eliminate.
CLAIM: The Democratic Party enacted taxes on Social Security annuities.
RATING: Mostly False
Taxes on Social Security benefits began in 1984 under Reagan, who signed the Social Security Amendments of 1983.
Those amendments, which were aimed at saving the Social Security program from insolvency, passed on a bipartisan vote and came from a bipartisan commission's recommendations. (Reagan even praised the "bipartisan spirit" in which the amendments were passed.)
"The basic rule put in place was that up to 50% of Social Security benefits could be added to taxable income, if the taxpayer's total income exceeded certain thresholds," the Social Security Administration said.
At the time, Reagan presented the amendments and the new taxes as a compromise to ensure the Social Security system continued: 
Time and again, benefits were increased far beyond the taxes and wages that were supposed to support them. In this compromise we have struck the best possible balance between the taxes we pay and the benefits paid back. Any more in taxes would be an unfair burden on working Americans and could seriously weaken our economy. Any less would threaten the commitment already made to this generation of retirees and to their children.
Since Democrats were involved in the efforts to save Social Security in the 1980s by taxing annuities — but these taxes happened under Reagan and were overwhelmingly bipartisan — we have rated this claim as mostly false.
CLAIM: The Democratic Party increased taxes on Social Security annuities, with former Vice President Al Gore casting a "tie-breaking" vote in the Senate.
RATING: Mostly True 
In 1993, Congress increased taxes on Social Security benefits through a single provision in a massive budget bill called the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act, which former President Bill Clinton, a Democrat, signed into law.
Section 13215 of the bill increased the taxes from the 1983 amendments from 50% to 85% for "higher income" beneficiaries (see Page 164 of the bill).
After its passage, Clinton said the act "created real fairness" in the U.S. tax code by placing more tax burden on higher earners and implementing tax cuts on low-income working families.
As vice president, Gore did, in fact, cast the tie-breaking vote, given that Republicans were universally against this legislation at the time (as were a few Democrats).
CLAIM: The Democratic Party and former President Jimmy Carter passed a law giving Social Security annuity payments to immigrants, who don't pay into the program.
RATING: False 
Noncitizens in the United States who have Social Security-covered jobs — in other words, almost every job in the country — must pay Social Security payroll taxes.
That even includes people who are working in the U.S. without authorization or those working in the country temporarily.
In fact, a 2013 report from the Social Security Administration found that immigrants in the country illegally paid a net $10 billion to the Social Security trust fund in 2010. More recently, an independent report from the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy found "undocumented immigrants paid $25.7 billion in Social Security taxes" in 2022. (It is worth noting that some immigrants are also in the country legally but cannot legally work in the United States.)
Immigrants who become citizens or legal residents can qualify for Social Security only to the extent that they have worked and paid into the system — the same as for citizens.
When the Social Security program began, there were no restrictions on payments to noncitizens, according to a Congressional Research Service report. Restrictions for certain groups of noncitizens came later.
It's unclear where the claim about Carter came from. The Social Security Administration said this claim likely confuses the Supplemental Security Income (SSI) program with Social Security. SSI is a federal welfare program that some immigrants can qualify for, but it was an initiative of former President Richard Nixon, a Republican, not Carter.
