The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi has been allowed to speak to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.
“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook on Thursday.
Aung San Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.
Images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show Aris, who lives in the UK, standing outside the Myanmar embassy in London.
“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” he said in the post. “But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”
Myanmar’s military has held the Nobel peace prize laureate in almost total seclusion since the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy. But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life”.
On Monday, authorities said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch. Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.
Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.
After ruling Myanmar as military chief since the coup, Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year.
Analysts described the election that put him in office as a charade, and said he could be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in an attempt to court international legitimacy.

Los Angeles: Veteran English actor Patrick Stewart passed away at the age of 96 at his Los Angeles home. The “Star Trek” and “X-Men” star was surrounded by family and friends in his final moments.
His estate took to his X, formerly Twitter, and shared the news. They wrote, “We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia. He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all. We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace”.
They further mentioned, “A son of Mirfield in the West Riding of Yorkshire, he travelled from the Royal Shakespeare Company to an equally acclaimed career spanning 6 decades on Broadway, the silver screen and television”.
The actor is survived by his third wife, singer Sunny Ozell and Daniel and Sophia, children from his first marriage from actor Sheila Falconer. Tributes poured as soon as the news of his death broke. Hollywood superstar Hugh Jackman, who played Wolverine in the X-Men film franchise, took to his Instagram, and wrote, “We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days”.
Patrick Stewart's last cinematic appearance will be Avengers: Doomsday, which is set to be released in India on December 17, 2026.

Orissa HC issues notice to BJD MLAs over alleged cross-voting in Rajya Sabha polls
Justice MS Sahoo directed suspended MLAs Arvind Mohapatra, Sanatan Mahakud, Chakramani Kanhar, Souvic Biswal and Subasini Jena to file their replies by December 4
The Orissa high court on Thursday issued notices to five Biju Janata Dal (BJD) MLAs in connection with petitions filed by the party seeking their disqualification over allegations of cross voting in the March 16 Rajya Sabha elections.
Justice MS Sahoo directed suspended MLAs Arvind Mohapatra, Sanatan Mahakud, Chakramani Kanhar, Souvic Biswal and Subasini Jena to file their replies by December 4. The court scheduled the matter for hearing on January 11 next year.
The BJD had alleged that eight of its MLAs voted in favour of Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-supported independent candidate Dilip Ray instead of the BJD-Congress joint nominee Datteswar Hota in the Rajya Sabha poll. Though Ray and Hota got 23 first preference votes each, the former was elected to Rajya Sabha after counting of second preference votes.
Also Read: Rajya Sabha polls: Cross-voting set to take centre stage in Uttar Pradesh, ‘extra votes’ key
Subsequently, the party approached legislative assembly speaker Surama Padhi, seeking cancellation of their membership. However, the speaker dismissed all eight disqualification petitions in June, citing procedural deficiencies.
Also Read: Disciplinary action against cross-voters has begun: BJP
Challenging the speaker’s decision, BJD chief whip Pramila Mallik moved the high court, filing eight writ petitions against the order. Five of these petitions came up for hearing on Thursday.
The BJD contended that the speaker had dismissed its petitions without giving the party an adequate opportunity to present its case.
Appearing on behalf of the speaker, advocate general Pitambar Acharya submitted that the petitions had been rejected in June through a detailed order.

Politics is his core areas of expertise as he closely tracks Odisha's political landscape, including the rise and transformation of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the Biju Janata Dal (BJD), the two principal political parties in Odisha. His long association with the state's political establishment enables him to write on contemporary developments in a larger political context. Mohanty takes a deep interest in writing human interest stories, environmental issues and documenting the impact of cyclones, floods, heatwaves, and other climate-related events in one of the most disaster-prone states. His coverage extends to public health, governance reforms and stories on accountability of government institutions. Before joining Hindustan Times, Mohanty worked with The Indian Express, Mail Today, and The Telegraph, where he covered at least six general elections and as many assembly elections. Lost your spark? The "silent sister" of depression, and a quiz to spot her
Some people with clinical depression can't get out of bed. But what about those who exhibit other signs of depression who never stop moving, and may double down on their work?
Psychiatrist Dr. Judith Joseph says the second group often goes unnoticed, even by the people living it. She calls it "high-functioning depression": people who keep meeting their obligations at work and at home while quietly losing the ability to feel pleasure.
"When you are joyful, you have better physical health, you have better relationships, you have better productivity at work," Joseph said in an interview for the Your Turn podcast. "So why don't we prioritize it?"
At the center of Joseph's work is anhedonia: a reduced ability to feel joy, pleasure or interest in things that once brought those feelings. Joseph describes it as "the silent sister" of depression.
"One sister is depressed, and crying, and not getting out of bed, and getting all the attention," she says. "The other one is quiet and numb." Anhedonia may not seem like a crisis in the classic sense, Joseph says. "But it is an existential crisis, and it's not something to ignore."
What the research shows
In a peer-reviewed study published in the journal Cureus, Joseph and colleagues interviewed adults using a set of questionnaires designed to assess high-functioning depression, trauma and anhedonia.
The results supported the researchers' hypothesis that people with high-functioning depression have increased levels of anhedonia and trauma. Participants with higher anhedonia scores also had higher high-functioning depression scores.
Parents and caregivers had the highest anhedonia and high-functioning depression scores in the study.
The authors note that high-functioning depression is not an official diagnosis in the DSM-5, the manual clinicians use to diagnose mental health conditions. They say that is part of the problem: people who keep functioning may not recognize their symptoms or seek treatment until they reach burnout.
'Something's gonna give'
Joseph says she often sees the pattern in women who are the steady presence for everyone around them. They are so focused on their responsibilities at work and at home that they don't realize they are burned out, or close to it.
"But eventually something's gonna give," she said. "Either they do break down and they have a clinical depression and they lose their functioning, they go into distress or crisis, or they physically break down."
She said she has seen patients end up in the emergency room without understanding why, only to learn they had been carrying unresolved emotional pain.
Joseph said the pattern is common in professions that discourage vulnerability, including her own. In medicine, she said, crying after a patient died was seen as weakness.
"In medicine, we focus on the crisis," Joseph said. "You're [taught] to look for the mania, for the psychosis." She believes there should be more focus on anhedonia, the loss of sense of joy.
A self-assessment
Joseph developed an anhedonia quiz based on the Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale, a measure of the capacity to feel pleasure that was published in the British Journal of Psychiatry.
The questionnaire asks about everyday experiences, such as whether you have trouble enjoying praise, whether you savor your meals or other small pleasures, and whether you struggle to enjoy your work or accomplishments because they never feel good enough.
The quiz is not a diagnostic tool. It's an invitation to take stock of what might be standing in the way of a fuller, more joyful life. If you'd like to take the quiz, you'll be asked to share your email to see the results.
Five V's
In her book, "High Functioning: Overcome Your Hidden Depression and Reclaim Your Joy," Joseph also outlines a framework she calls the Five V's:
- Validation: naming and accepting what you feel.
- Venting: expressing emotions, through talking, writing, creative expression or maybe a good cry.
- Values: making time for what matters most.
- Vision: having something to look forward to.
- Vitals: caring for your whole self (mind + body) through sleep, nutrition and movement.
Joseph says anhedonia appears across many conditions, in many people in midlife and other times, too. "It's something that we need to learn how to detect," she said, because it can be a silent problem.
If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988, to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline

Quick Answer
To stop Google from using your Gmail, Drive, and Photos data for personalized ads, visit google.com/search-personalization, open Connected Content Apps, and disconnect Google Workspace and Photos. Then turn off personalized ads at myadcenter.google.com. You can also delete past activity at activity.google.com.
It’s not hyperbole to say AI agents are genuinely helpful. The big tech companies aren’t stupid to be investing billions of dollars to build these AI agents, but they need more than your money to help you – your data. Google is best placed to play this smart answers game considering it owns some of the most widely used services in the world – Search, Gmail, Chrome, Photos, and Android.
If you’ve let Google’s AI look at your Gmail or Google Photos for smarter answers, there’s a catch. As of October 16, 2026, Google’s privacy policy says data from those apps can also help personalize ads. Google is also testing ads in AI Mode for people who have connected their apps.
Here’s what changed, what it does and doesn’t mean, and how to turn it off.
Table of Contents
What changed
Since 2021, Google’s privacy policy has said that it doesn’t use your Gmail, Drive, or Photos content for personalized ads. According to Ars Technica and Google’s own archive, the old line read: “We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos.”
The current policy, effective October 16, 2026, adds a condition:
We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos, unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.
A new passage in the same section spells out how this happens:
You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive… For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.
You “choose” this through Personal Intelligence, the opt-in feature that lets AI Mode and other Search tools draw on your Gmail, Calendar, and Photos. Calendar is US and English only for now, Photos isn’t available in every region, and Drive, though named in the policy, isn’t currently one of the apps you can connect to Search.
The ads side is already live as a test.
What it means for you
It’s easy to overstate this, so here’s what Google actually says.
What Google says won’t happen:
- In its Search help page, Google says: “Ads will not be based directly on your Gmail inbox or your Google Photos library.“
- Advertisers don’t get access to your connected apps, and Google doesn’t share your name or email with them.
- Google says it won’t personalize ads on sensitive categories such as race, religion, sexual orientation or health.
What can happen:
The same help page says Search “may reference summaries, excerpts and inferences” from your connected apps, and “that same info may be used to show you ads.” The policy gives an example of personalizing answers: ask Search about a recent hotel booking, and it may use booking details from an email. The ads link comes from the help page: that same kind of info may now be used to show you ads.
Search vs. Gemini:
The ad test is in AI Mode in Search. Google’s Gemini Apps Privacy Hub says “Your Gemini Apps chats are not being used to show you ads.” The policy still lists “Gemini Apps” among services you can connect your data to.
Beyond AI Mode:
When you connect your apps, Google says all Search services can access them, including Search, Discover, Maps, Shopping, Flights, Hotels, Translate, and News. The same page says human reviewers may see some of that data.
Where this applies:
Connecting content apps to Search is available to adults in a long list of countries, including the US and India. The UK and EU countries don’t appear on that list. Personal Intelligence in Gemini is not available in the European Economic Area, Switzerland, Nigeria, or the UK. Google hasn’t said where the ads test is running, and the policy wording is global. What we think is, since Google doesn’t offer either feature in the UK yet, UK readers look largely unaffected for now.
How to opt out of Search Personalization
Disconnect Gmail and Photos from Search (web, Android, iPhone)
As per Google’s help pages, the steps are the same on the web, Android, and iPhone:
- Open your Google Account and go to Data & privacy > Personalization settings > Personalized Recommendations in Search services. Or you can click this if you are already signed in: google.com/search-personalization.
- Under Additional Personal Intelligence, open Connected Content Apps.
- Disconnect Google Workspace and Google Photos.
To go further, turn off Personalized Recommendations on the same page. Google says it’s updating these settings, so labels may differ.
Disconnect apps in Gemini
- Gemini mobile app (Android/iPhone): tap Menu > your profile picture > Personal Intelligence > Connected Apps.
- Web (gemini.google.com): select Menu > Settings & help > Personal Intelligence > Connected Apps.
Turn off Google Workspace and Google Photos, plus any other apps you don’t want connected.
Turn off personalized ads in My Ad Center
Go to My Ad Center, select On or Off next to Personalized ads, choose Off, and confirm.
Google says it will then stop using your saved account info and activity for ads, and will show ads based on general factors like the topic you’re viewing. You’ll still see ads; they just won’t be tailored to you. This doesn’t stop connected-app data from being used for AI answers.
Clean up what’s already saved
Disconnecting doesn’t delete your Search Services History, which can still be used for product improvement. Review and delete it at activity.google.com. In Gemini, disconnecting doesn’t delete your Gemini Apps Activity either.
Should you disconnect?
Personal Intelligence is genuinely useful: asking about your trip without pasting in your booking is the whole point, and Google says advertisers don’t get access to your connected apps.
But helping you and choosing your ads are different uses, and the ads part was added after Personal Intelligence launched. If that bothers you, disconnect. A middle path is to keep Personal Intelligence on and turn off personalized ads in My Ad Center. Your data still feeds Google’s AI answers, and Search Services History can be used for product improvement, including AI model training.
The bottom line
While you’d see a lot of noise around these changes on social media, know that this change doesn’t touch everyone’s inbox, because it’s opt-in. But if you connected Gmail or Photos to its AI, what that AI learns can now help pick your ads, starting with a test in AI Mode. If that trade isn’t for you, the switches above take minutes.
FAQs about Search Personalization
1. Is Google reading my emails to target ads?
Not directly, according to Google. It says ads aren’t based “directly” on your inbox, but summaries, excerpts, and inferences Search draws from connected apps can be used for ads.
2. I never turned on Personal Intelligence. Am I affected?
As per the policy, Gmail, Drive, and Photos content isn’t used for ads unless you make it available to other services. It’s opt-in, but worth checking the settings above in case you connected and forgot.
3. Does this apply to Gemini chats?
Google says Gemini chats aren’t used to show you ads right now. The ad test is in AI Mode in Search.
4. Does disconnecting erase what Google already has?
No. Delete your Search Services History at activity.google.com and your Gemini Apps Activity separately, as we described earlier in this article.

Even birds get jet lagged, study shows
New research shows that humans are not the only species to get jet lag: Some birds appear to experience it too.
A study published in the journal Science found that a type of seabird known as the Manx shearwater appears to become slightly disoriented during long flights across the Atlantic Ocean. That disorientation, the authors say, is due to the bird's internal clock falling out of sync with the sun's position in the sky.
Manx shearwaters are a common bird in the British Isles. They look a little like seagulls, but "they're actually very closely related to an albatross," said Patrick Lewin, a behavioral ecologist at the University of Oxford.
Shearwaters mate for life, and when they breed, a couple lays just one egg.
Then they take turns incubating it: "One partner will sit on the egg nonstop while the other one goes out to sea," Lewin said.
For up to two weeks the hunting partners scour the North Atlantic for fish and squid, often travelling hundreds of miles from their nests.
Once these birds' bellies are full "they absolutely bomb it back to their colony," Lewin said. Often they make the long journey home in just a day or so.
Which raised an interesting question: Do Manx shearwaters feel jet lag (or perhaps more aptly, flap lag)?
To see if these little birds really did feel the effects of flying through time zones like humans do, Lewin used a remarkable tool – for 20 years, his colleagues had been tagging birds with GPS trackers and collecting data on their flights out to the Atlantic and back.
He figured he could see the jet lag in their flights. That's because the Manx shearwaters are believed to use the sun to navigate.
"To use the sun as a compass you have to know what time of day it is," Lewin said.
In the morning, the sun is in the east, at midday it's slightly to the south (if you're in the northern hemisphere) and then in the evening it's in the west. If the shearwaters had the wrong time of day, they would fly the wrong way.
That's exactly what Lewin and his colleagues saw. As the birds rushed back to their partners and eggs, they veered ever-so-slightly off course. It wasn't much: A seven-degree error, the maximum deviation observed, only took a bird out of its way by about three miles on a 600-mile journey. "It's a really small addition," he said.
"This paper is so cool," said Alice Boyle, a biologist at the Centre for Animals on the Move at Western University in Ontario, Canada who was not part of the study.
Boyle said pretty much every creature on the planet, from corals to chipmunks, has to navigate its environment, yet it's rare to see a study showing navigation decisions in action. That's what makes this type of GPS work so valuable.
"It's using these wild birds that travel to completely remote places and we're able to learn so much about how they do that," she said.

The Ebola outbreak in Congo passed a grim milestone this week — 10,000 confirmed cases — and spurred questions about whether health authorities are losing their ability to contain it.
Nearly half the infected people in this outbreak have died, and some experts say there are reasons to worry this could grow into the worst Ebola outbreak in history. Others don't think it will reach that level. Researchers are currently working on updated projections.
Current circumstances suggest it's unlikely to spark significant problems in most other countries, some researchers said. But about 30 confirmed cases have already popped up in other nations. And the risk that more will appear outside Congo will grow if the outbreak isn't tamed, said Justin Lessler, a University of North Carolina researcher who studies the dynamics of infectious disease outbreaks.
Experts also are hopeful that a vaccine will become available next year that could help control it.
At a virtual summit of African health ministers on Wednesday, Africa CDC Director-General Dr. Jean Kaseya said the continent is “not winning” the fight against Ebola and needs to do more after it spread to multiple African countries. “Together, we agreed to prepare every country, coordinate across our borders and keep those borders open while watching them closely,” Kaseya wrote on X.
Steady case numbers raise concerns about spread beyond Congo
About 400 to 500 new confirmed cases have been reported in Congo each week, and that number seems to be holding steady. It's good news that “cases are not rising exponentially,” at least for the moment, said Dr. Boghuma Titanji, an Emory University infectious disease specialist.
“But they're not coming down, either," she said. "It's at a plateau. And the plateau is at a very, very high set point."
A major challenge in Congo is limited contact tracing and collaboration with affected communities; health workers sometimes spend more time trying to convince locals to work with them than giving care.
Fewer than a quarter of new cases are coming from people known to have been in contact with an infected person, showing there are ongoing chains of transmission that health authorities are not aware of.
As cases mount, the likelihood grows that more infected people travel to other countries, Titanji and other experts said. France, Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda also have reported cases tied to the Congo outbreak.
Travel restrictions, like those imposed by the US, can make it harder for the virus to leave Africa. And in many places where a traveller's infection may surface, health officials should be able to quickly isolate an infected person and find any contacts, experts say.
“The direct risk it poses to the US at this point, I'd say, is very close to zero,” Lessler said.
But Ebola could flare in poor and conflict-stricken places with weakened health systems — like South Sudan, for example, Lessler said.
Viruses that cause Ebola disease spread through contact with bodily fluids such as vomit, blood and semen.
Second largest outbreak
Dozens of Ebola outbreaks have been reported since the disease was first discovered in 1976. The largest and deadliest occurred in West Africa in 2014 to 2016, with 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.
The current outbreak already ranks second, and has had at least three times the number of cases and deaths in the time since it was declared compared with the West Africa outbreak. Health officials declared the outbreak in May, but medical evidence suggests infections were occurring months earlier.
One reason is that past outbreaks were almost all caused by the Ebola virus. Initial testing was geared toward that virus — not the related, but different, Bundibugyo virus that was actually causing illnesses.
A series of other challenges have hurt the response, including armed conflict in some outbreak areas, gaps in the health system, mistrust and misinformation, and global aid cuts, experts say.
Conditions vary in Congo, which explains why cases can be stable or falling in some places but can be trending up in others, researchers and response workers say.
“Testing, care and contact tracing only work if we work with communities, going door to door, village by village to break the chain of transmission and stop this deadly escalation,” said Katie Thomas-Canfield, the International Rescue Committee's Ebola response director, in a statement.
Dr. Wendy Armstrong, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America, said she thinks the situation is going to get worse.
“This is very far from being controlled,” she said.
Updating projections
Experts expect the outbreak will continue through the end of the year, but Titanji is hopeful about 2027. That's because vaccines are being tested against the Bundibugyo virus, and she is optimistic an effective shot will become available in the next 12 months.
She noted no vaccines were available early in the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak.
Forecasting the outbreak is difficult, of course, but scientists have been trying.
In May, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention published a range of scenarios generated by computer models. At the time, the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention was reporting 400 confirmed cases. The US CDC models estimated the growth in cases over three months could run from 10,000 to more than 20,000.
The CDC is updating its modeling work. But the agency declined to let The Associated Press interview staff scientists about how the outbreak is trending.
Alessandro Vespignani, a Northeastern University disease modeler, has been monitoring trends with US and international health officials.
There's not been the kind of “decay in the number of cases weekly that we need to see the light at the end of the tunnel,” he said.

Right now, millions of workers are choosing their health plans for next year. The average family premium for employer coverage hit $28,303 in 2026, up 28% in the last five years. While employers appear to cover most of that premium, workers ultimately bear the full cost of those benefits through lower wages. Yet no one is really pushing back.
The industry’s major players have little appetite for change. Insurers record higher earnings when premiums rise. Insurance brokers and benefits consultants get a piece of those premiums. Large hospital systems use their bargaining leverage to demand high prices with little fear of losing patients. Physicians, who are commonly paid fee-for-service, earn more by doing more. Drugmakers, with patent protection, largely set their own prices. Each has good reasons to keep things as they are.
The most telling signal is health care prices: For the same service, prices vary enormously, even within the same market. An MRI or a knee replacement can cost several times as much at one hospital as at another across town, with little evidence that the higher-priced hospital provides higher quality care.
This violates a fundamental economic principle: the law of one price. In functioning market settings, price discovery and competition ensure this tendency. But in health care markets, such forces are obscured. Patients have little ability or incentive to shop for lower cost care, and insurers are content to pass on higher prices through as higher premiums.
Employers should be the natural check on this process, but few are engaged health care purchasers. They focus on the premium, while most benefit-design decisions are outsourced to insurers, brokers, and benefits consultants. Employers understandably worry that narrowing health benefits will anger workers. The result is a peculiar situation in which the employers paying the bill on behalf of employees rarely tell an expensive hospital, “No thanks. We’ll go somewhere else.”
A few purchasers have gone a different direction. They do the shopping ahead of time on behalf of their workers and reward them for following their advice.
Walmart offers employees with serious conditions treatment at designated centers of excellence, including the Mayo Clinic. Employees pay nothing out of pocket, and Walmart covers travel and lodging for the patient and a caregiver. This has had some unexpected benefits. Walmart reports that many workers referred for spine surgery ended up not needing it.
In 2011 CalPERS, California’s public employee plan, set a reference price for hip and knee replacements. Members who chose a hospital above that price paid the difference. The goal wasn’t to punish patients but to discipline hospitals, and it worked: High priced hospitals cut their prices sharply.
For two decades, consumer-driven health care mostly meant higher deductibles: When patients had “skin in the game,” the argument went, they would become savvy shoppers. But we know deductibles stop mattering once they are met, and for major surgery that happens almost immediately. Walmart and CalPERS turn the idea around. Instead, the sophisticated purchaser shops ahead of time, then tells employees where to go for high-quality, high-value care.
Small employers lack the heft of Walmart and CalPERS, but innovative solutions are available to them too. Self Fund Health brings the Walmart model to small firms in Wisconsin, where hospital prices are high. The company says it can be cheaper to fly patients to Johns Hopkins than to treat them locally. Members still have access to a broad network of doctors, but care from a preferred tier of low cost providers is free.
A plan doesn’t need to dominate a market to affect prices. When a hospital loses 10 lucrative cardiac cases to an out-of-state center, it notices. For example, CalPERS didn’t get all its members to change hospitals, but moving some patients made the threat credible. The key is to reintroduce price discovery by giving patients curated price information. This is how workers can be activated to vote with their feet.
The question remains: Why do so few employers use these methods? There are many reasons, but three seem most relevant.
First, the tax code is a huge obstacle. Because employer-provided health insurance benefits are excluded from workers’ taxable income, a dollar of health benefits costs employees less than a dollar of wages.
The result is a dulled incentive to save money on health care. While the Affordable Care Act’s “Cadillac tax” on high cost health plans was repeatedly delayed and eventually repealed in 2019, it was the only serious effort to limit the tax exclusion, albeit in a clunky way. It died because major beneficiaries of high spending pushed back, with an assist from public- and private-sector unions whose members often enjoy richly negotiated health benefits.
However, given that the current tax code is littered with caps and phase-outs of preferential tax advantages (think retirement benefits, mortgage interest, and the child tax credit), it doesn’t seem so outlandish to apply similar logic to the health insurance tax exclusion.
Second, small employers rely on brokers to help with plan selection and benefit design. But commissions influence their recommendations in complex ways. At a minimum, employers should proactively question their brokers about the commissions they earn; indeed, federal law requires brokers to disclose them.
Finally, big hospital systems can fight back even when engaged employers try to steer patients to cheaper providers. Recently, North Carolina’s State Health Plan built a tiered network that charges members more to use high-priced systems. Atrium Health didn’t like being placed in the costly tier, so it fought back by waiving cost-sharing requirements at its facilities, effectively neutralizing the tiering effort while keeping the plan’s high prices.
The answer is not to ban this behavior but to steer at enrollment rather than at the point of care. The employer can offer a lower premium that includes only lower-priced providers and let workers who want Atrium pay the premium difference. A hospital can waive copays, but it can’t pay your premium.
Workers are paying the bill for this largesse, and most would rather see that money in their paychecks than spent on bloated health care prices.
Anthony T. Lo Sasso, Ph.D., is a health economist and the Robert F. and Sylvia T. Wagner professor of public affairs in the La Follette School of Public Affairs at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

In a few days, judge Geoffrey Vos will retire as Master of the Rolls, the most senior position in England’s civil justice system. As one of his final acts, he’s trying to stoke a debate about whether—and how—judges should be using artificial intelligence.
Under the latest guidance, judges in England are advised to confine their use of AI to administrative tasks, and Vos tells WIRED he uses Microsoft Copilot all the time to locate far-flung documents and summarize large bodies of text. But recently, he visited a court in Shenzhen, China, where civil disputes are already being decided by judges with heavy assistance from AI. Impressed by what he saw, Vos believes that courts across the globe should consider following.
That road is littered with pitfalls. Multiple lawyers have been caught citing case law hallucinated by AI, and in a first for the UK, somebody recently lost their license to practice in part because they misused the technology. Meanwhile, with chatbots as their legal counsel, litigants are flooding the courts with an unprecedented number of claims, some of them bogus.
Yet Vos remains convinced that AI will someday help resolve civil disputes more rapidly and in ways that cost far less. While complicated commercial disputes and sensitive family cases might require a human judge, he believes that personal injury claims, low-value professional negligence cases, and the like could easily be adjudicated by AI.
“What most people desperately want in civil disputes is resolution,” Vos tells WIRED. “The question is, where is the line to be drawn?”
Given his impending retirement, the debate for Vos is largely a philosophical one. But for everyone else in the profession—and for coders, cybersecurity experts, math professors, and a whole host of others—the rules are changing fast.
In October, WIRED met with Vos at his office at the Royal Courts of Justice, London. We discussed the ways that AI is spilling into the courts, the practical and ethical issues it raises, and how the justice system might adapt to serve a new generation raised alongside the technology.
This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
WIRED: You’re just a few days away from retirement. How do you feel about leaving the post at this particular juncture, as AI begins to reshape how law is practiced and justice administered?
GEOFFREY VOS: When I started as a lawyer, we had foolscap paper, typists, and Tipp-Ex. We moved rapidly into word processors, faxes, and eventually computers.
Lawyers are conservative with a lowercase c. But that doesn’t mean that they should be backward-looking or retrogressive. It means they should be adopting change cautiously, with their eyes open.
The legal system is for the people of this country. You can’t be effective in providing access to justice if you’re not on the same technological wavelength. But it’s time to leave it to a new generation of leadership judges.
How have you built AI into your practice to date?
I don’t use it for writing judgments, but I use it for finding things out, navigating large quantities of material, and checking things. It saves me time. I have 11 meetings a day. I know there’s a document created years ago that’s relevant to my meeting—and Copilot finds it in seconds. I do that every day.
In law, isn’t the devil always in the details? Doesn’t confidence in the legal system depend on the understanding that a judge will review and consider every inch of every court submission?
I’m a little more cautious about using it to read papers for my cases, but that’s because I do the most important cases in the system.
People have confidence in our justice system because they believe that our judges have absolute integrity. In order not to lose that integrity, you have to explain how you’re adopting technology and achieve a broad consensus that it is appropriate.
How is AI spilling into the courts right now? Is it changing how litigants and legal professionals behave? What issues is it throwing up?
It’s changing everything remarkably quickly. We see a 10 percent rise in the number of county court cases started every year—and it looks as if this may increase. That’s because everybody who has a legal problem now puts it into Gemini, ChatGPT, or Claude. Ask it to create a particulars of claim, a case, a claim form—it can.
What proportion of these claims are based on sound legal principles, though? How often are people led by a chatbot to mistakenly believe they have a claim?
We don’t have the data. But I think it’s a mistake to assume that just because a claim is created by AI, it’s totally frivolous.
In a way it’s a good problem, because it shows there’s greater access to justice because of technology. One of the problems with justice in the past is that it’s only been available to rich people.
If people have a problem sufficient to bother ChatGPT, they probably genuinely think they have a claim. When you explore their problem in detail, you might find it is actually a bit different, but it may still be a legal problem and may still be reasonable for them to have wanted to bring it to attention.
People are not generally time wasters. They’re not generally trying to make trouble.
What about the opportunity for AI to fabricate evidence on which judges have previously been able to rely—images, video, voice recordings? Where does that leave the courts?
Often, judges have to decide whether a person is telling the truth. That is the most difficult thing to do, because humans are not bad at lying. But judges make these decisions every day. There’s absolutely no difference—in scale or qualitatively—in somebody producing a false image created by AI.
The only reason we’re all getting so excited about deepfakes is because they are so new. But actually, that is the stuff of judging.
But we’re talking about a whole category of evidence that’s now somewhat compromised. Doesn’t that affect a judge’s ability to decide whether somebody is lying?
It was always thus. We always had to decide whether wills were forged, because people used to do that. It’s exactly the same with voice recordings, and video. It’s just an extension of the type of false information that is produced to the court.
People will find out when they produce fake images to the court that they are committing perjury and they will go to prison, just as if they’d forged a will.
I think we need to be cautious about predicting disaster. I’m very optimistic.
You’ve previously described an “inevitable” future where simpler civil cases are adjudicated entirely by AI. Why are you confident that’s where we’re headed?
You need to find a way to deliver justice that is within the cultural grain. That doesn’t mean you just conduct all your cases on TikTok. But if you don’t understand that people are asking LLMs for the answer to almost every question under the sun, including legal questions, you’re likely to get it wrong when you try to devise a process fit for the 21st century.
It’s all about consensus. It will only be possible to ask people to accept algorithmic decision-making if they consent to the process in a particular case, or if society decides through legislation.
When people go to court and get an adverse outcome, even if they regard the outcome as idiosyncratic or even wrong, when it’s delivered in a human way, it can be accepted over time. With AI, we have to be careful; it may be less easy for people to accept an adverse machine-driven decision.
I very much want to see a very open, international discussion about how we should resolve disputes.
I suspect part of the reason people object to trial by AI is because we can’t know precisely how a model has arrived at a decision. What’s to be done about this problem of explainability?
I don’t think it’s about reasoning; it’s about outcomes. The AI can produce very plausible reasoning. You can’t see how it produced that reasoning, but you can see the reasoning it produced, and you can judge the plausibility.
I don’t think you’ll ever do away with human judges. There’s something almost biblical about the human judge; it’s in the human psyche to want to be judged by their fellow man. But that does not mean that in some situations people wouldn’t rather have a quick outcome—even if it’s not a human outcome.
Where would you draw the line?
I don’t think judges are yet in the position to say. It’s a question for society, politicians, and legislation to resolve. That debate is really important.
I think that custody and family cases are one of the areas where essentially human judgment is expected, even by the younger generation. In complex commercial cases, I think that’s also the case. But I think we will whittle away at how commercial cases are decided by using AI to collate information to make the decision-making process better and easier.
We will allow more people access to justice more cheaply and more quickly using technology. That will be an overall good for the economy and for the people we serve.

What's gone up even faster than gas or rent? The cost of caregiving
As prices have ticked up in recent years, the cost to caregivers has skyrocketed. A study, released Wednesday by AARP, finds that family caregivers — people helping out disabled, chronically ill or elderly adults — now spend an average $11,508 out of pocket each year. That's roughly 60% more than just five years ago, and adds up to 31% of a caregiver's income, on average.
The increase during those years is more than twice the overall rate of inflation of 24%, as measured by the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price Index.
What's driving the ramp-up? Food, housing and medical expenses are the biggest chunk, finds the study, which queried 2,538 family caregivers.
In other words, just the basics.
The bump in costs comes as family caregivers take on more care and more complicated medical responsibilities at home, says Megan O'Reilly, vice president of governmental affairs at AARP. "The more care that's needed, the more it costs."
And increased spending is only part of the story. The demands of caregiving often require people to reduce their working hours or quit work entirely, the survey finds. It's a double whammy: increased costs on top of lost income.
Increasing demands, falling income
Meghan Maher has seen that first-hand. Just seven weeks after the birth of her first baby, her mother was diagnosed with advanced cancer. Suddenly, Maher was a "sandwich" caregiver — parent and child needing her at the same time.
At first, she tried to manage it all. She returned to her career in cancer research after maternity leave, but keeping up with the demands of work, her mom and her newborn son was too much.
She shrank her hours to part time. But even that wasn't manageable. There was no way to attend all her mother's appointments, coordinate her care, and also be available for big deadlines on the job.
She quit, and the family's income fell by half. Because her husband had a good job, they weren't struggling, but "it was definitely scary," she says now. As her mom got sicker her parents moved in, increasing the household expenses.
Soon after her mother's death in 2017, her father had a series of major complications from abdominal surgery and was critically ill for months. Maher needed to be by his side during hospital stays, advocating for him on a moment's notice, so now the family also needed to pay for child care. She estimates the cost at about $10,000 a year.
Her father eventually recovered, and the family was able to manage despite the difficulties. Many aren't so lucky.
About half of all family caregivers say they've made major financial sacrifices, according to the AARP report: Working more hours, cutting savings, or even drawing down on money put away for retirement.
More family caregivers, bigger bills
Many Americans deal with the cost of care, and more will in the future. About 63 million people now provide ongoing help for a family member or friend — roughly 1 in 4 adults. The need will likely grow: An estimated 70 percent of the people turning 65 today will need some form of help as they age.
Medicare does not pay for routine help either at home or in a facility, and that care is expensive. In 2025, 40 hours of in-home caregiving help a week ran about $72,792 a year, according to the insurance company Genworth, which conducts annual surveys of the cost of care. Skilled nursing costs an average of $115,000 per year for a shared room.
When Maher returned to work, she became a professional death doula. That means she helps clients with the emotional and practical challenges at the end of life. She's self-employed, so she can control her own schedule and limit the number of clients she serves. It allows her the flexibility to help her father as he ages. But her income is half what it would have been in her old career.
With the clients she helps, she sees other ways that care costs pile up. In Florida where she lives, it's routine for chronically ill people to hire an attorney in order to qualify for Medicaid, which unlike Medicare does foot the bill for long-term care. Even though they are eligible for the benefits, the paperwork is so complex that they wind up paying for legal help to navigate it. In Florida, she says, that runs about $6,000.
What she has seen and experienced motivates her to call attention to the caregiving crunch. In April, Maher testified before Congress at a special Senate committee on aging. "Caregiving has also reshaped my professional life," she said on the Senate floor. "The flexibility of self-employment comes with real financial and professional tradeoffs." She was invited by Daughterhood, an organization that offers support and resources for caregivers.
Family caregivers can access some public money, depending on where they live. All states pay some types of family caregivers through Medicaid. In California, for instance, more than 800,000 caregivers earn between $16.90 and $25 an hour for in-home work. Funds for these programs are likely to dwindle due to President Trump's big budget bill that cut nearly $1 trillion out of Medicaid funding over the next decade.
If the person who needs care is eligible for Veterans Administration benefits, they may also be entitled to financial help to cover the cost of caregiving. Like Medicaid, the rules are complex, and many family caregivers hire advocates to advise on eligibility and the application procedure.
More support on the horizon?
The cost of care hasn't been as visible as the cost of gasoline, food and healthcare, says AARP executive vice president Nancy LeaMond. She believes that will change. "When you see the number of people paying this kind of money, I think that'll be an impetus for action in the legislative arena."
In the last few years, Congress has introduced various proposals that could put some money back into the pockets of caregivers, such as allowing caregivers to spend money from their tax-sheltered health savings accounts on their parents' medical expenses. In some states, new rules are already a reality.
Six states now offer tax credits to family caregivers for expenses like retrofitting a home with grab bars or railings, usually between $1,000 and $5,000 a year. Two other states have more limited programs. Last year, two U.S. Senators introduced a bipartisan bill that would establish a similar $5,000 tax credit nationwide.
In 14 states and the District of Columbia, most employers are required to offer paid family and medical leave. Those policies include time off for caregiving for a family member. Another bill introduced into Congress would convert that into a national policy that would require up to 12 weeks of partly paid leave for some workers.
A third proposed federal law would protect the Social Security benefits of caregivers. Under current rules, a person who stops working in order to care full-time for family sees their future Social Security check shrink, because they are no longer earning credits toward retirement. This bill would change the law to continue awarding points to full-time caregivers.
"We spend a lot of time talking to members of Congress, and you can't raise this issue in a meeting without being interrupted by someone telling their own story," says LeaMond. "In time, I believe that will coalesce to support family caregiving."
Kat McGowan is an independent journalist covering adult caregiving who reports the series "What It Takes" for NPR.

China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
- Published
Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said.
Official data released in the last week, external show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%.
The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole.
The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say.
China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children.
The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population.
At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under.
No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy.
The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said.
"It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying.
The demographic shift is "symbolic" and could suggest more public spending will move from families and schools to pensions and healthcare, said Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.
It may also pose a challenge to the country's ambitions, as it could limit its economic growth as well as people's spending power, said National University of Singapore sociology lecturer Mu Zheng.
China's ageing population has been driven by a mix of factors, including rapid urbanisation and the effects of the controversial one-child policy, which was in place from 1980 to the end of 2015.
The strategy, designed to keep China's rapid population growth under control, is estimated by the country's government to have prevented about 400 million births since it began, though this number has been contested.
The policy played a key role in shrinking the population and means there are fewer younger people to support a growing number of elderly relatives, Mu said.
But despite easing restrictions on the size of families, Beijing has struggled to persuade couples to have more children, with birth rates hitting historic lows.
Other contributing factors include changing gender roles, rising living costs and higher education levels that have put pressure on fertility rates, Mu said.
Beijing made further support for older people a part of the measures in its five-year economic blueprint that was announced earlier this year.
Financial help for pensioners has been a growing part of Chinese government spending. More than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior citizen allowances and subsidies by the end of 2025, according to official figures.
The Global Times noted that many people entering old age who were born between the 1950s and the 1970s have generally higher incomes compared to previous generations, stronger purchasing power and are healthier.
The dependency ratio is widely-used to measure ageing populations but it has also been questioned by some experts who argue that its scope is too limited.
Gietel-Basten said the use of the statistics risks "taking agency away" from older people - many of whom he says have been misrepresented as dependants.
It also does not take into account improvements to healthcare, he added.

Keralam Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan’s recent remarks questioning “unnecessary” angioplasty procedures have drawn objections from medical organisations concerned that it could undermine public confidence in doctors. But the Chief Minister’s remarks demand more than a reflex response; it requires a thoughtful, honest response built on up-to-date evidence based on clinical and research studies.
Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI), by balloon angioplasty and stent placement, has transformed cardiovascular care. During an acute heart attack caused by a suddenly blocked coronary artery, prompt angioplasty and stents can restore blood flow, save heart muscle and improve survival. There is no debate about this approach and second opinions are unnecessary as time is of essence in such an emergency. Stents also offer substantial relief to selected patients with persistent activity-limiting angina (chest pain caused by lack of oxygen-rich blood).
There is a crucial distinction between stenting as a life-saving measure in the above situations to medical treatment via stenting because a narrowing of blood vessels is seen on an angiogram. A coronary angiogram shows the anatomy of the arteries; it does not, by itself, establish that a narrowing requires intervention. The decision to intervene and how to intervene must take account of the patient’s symptoms, the severity of the blockage, its effect on blood flow, the overall pattern of coronary disease and the expected benefit of intervention.
The landmark ISCHEMIA trial, published in The New England Journal of Medicine in 2020, enrolled 5,179 patients at 320 sites in 37 countries with stable coronary artery disease and moderate to severe ischemia (restricted blood flow to the heart). The patients were assigned either to an initial invasive strategy — angiography followed by angioplasty or coronary bypass surgery — or to a conservative strategy of optimal medical treatment, with revascularisation reserved for those who had an acute event or angina. After a median follow-up of 3.2 years, there was no significant difference between the two groups in composite outcomes (cardiac arrests, hospitalisation for unstable angina or heart failure) and all-cause and cardiovascular mortality were similar. After a follow-up of 5 years, there was still no significant difference between the two groups in composite outcome or mortality. The core lesson is that most patients with stable coronary artery disease with ischemia on optimal medical treatment would do as well as those who undergo stenting or bypass surgery.
Concerning scale
The growing scale of PCI in India deserves careful examination. National Interventional Council figures show that annual PCI procedures rose from approximately 1,13,000 in 2008 to more than 7,26,000 in 2024 — an increase of more than six-fold. In contrast, PCI procedures in the U.S. fell by about 40% between 2003 and 2016, reflecting progress in prevention and treatment.
These figures do not by themselves prove that stents are overused in India considering its large population, the substantial burden of premature coronary disease, the socio-economic progress in the past decades and the improved access to cardiac care centres. Nevertheless, the divergence in trends between the two countries raises an important question: how much of the increase in PCI is a reflection of fulfilling a genuine clinical need, and how much of it is a reflection of differences in practice patterns, financial incentives and gaps in knowledge on the efficacy of optimal medical treatment?
Optimal medical therapy, based on evidence-based guidelines, is the foundation of care for all coronary artery disease patients. The elements of optimal therapy include LDL-cholesterol lowering, appropriate anti-platelet treatment, blood-pressure control, evidence-based diabetes management and lifestyle changes. A coronary stent treats a specific narrowing; it does not cure the underlying disease of atherosclerosis or eliminate the risk of future heart attacks. Patients remain vulnerable to disease elsewhere in the coronary arteries and must continue preventive treatment.
The way forward is neither condemnation of cardiologists nor unquestioning acceptance of every recommendation for angioplasty. Most doctors strive to act in their patients’ best interests, but no profession is immune to inappropriate practice. The ultimate test of healthcare is not how many procedures are performed, but how many lives are saved and whether patients receive the right treatment at the right time at an affordable cost.
Dr. Enas A. Enas is Preventive Cardiologist and Physician-Scientist, Founding President of the CADI Research Foundation USA; Dr. Basil Varkey is Professor Emeritus of medicine

Hacker may have stolen millions in a malware attack against online poker players
Wired has the story of a superuser cheating scandal.
Professional poker is the latest community to reckon with the impact of a high-profile cyberattack. Wired reports that hundreds of online poker players have allegedly been targeted in a malware attack that allowed a cheater to see their screens.
Cases where a player manages to cheat by getting unfair access to another person's cards is known as the "superuser" strategy, and it has popped up from time to time in the poker scene over the years. This most recent attack appears to have been a long-term campaign that may have seen millions of dollars stolen from across major online poker platforms. The Wired story claims that the hacker exploited third-party tools allowing people to run multiple poker games at once to install a malware program called MeshAgent on specific players' computers.
Different online poker platforms reportedly displayed a range of responses, which is especially surprising since the hacker's real name is known by the community. Wired did not publish the cheater's identity since they have not been charged with a crime, and the individual did not respond to the publication's requests for comment.
One service had banned the cheater before the MeshAgent hack was publicly uncovered based on the account having an anomalously high win rate and play tendencies. Others released tools to help players check if their machines had been compromised after the malware was found. But one company not only allowed the cheater to remain active despite complaints made by other players, but further claimed that it found no evidence of compromised game outcomes and would not refund players for their losses.
The entire Wired profile is a fascinating read for cybersecurity and poker fans alike. It's also just the latest reminder to take basic protective actions to keep you and your hardware safe.

- The claim that the U.S. Postal Service hired a private security company to station 1,000 armed guards at post offices in "blue" states ahead of the 2026 midterm elections is unproven.
- The rumor stems from reporting by the independent newsroom RawStory. The outlet reported in early October that Prosegur, an international security company, had deployed "nearly 1,000" armed security officers to at least 55 post offices ahead of the 2026 elections as part of a contract with the Postal Service.
- A spokesperson for the U.S. Postal Inspection Service said in a statement that it had deployed "a mix of unarmed and armed contract security officers to key USPS facilities" but that this deployment started in 2025 and had "absolutely nothing to do with elections." According to Postal Service policy, the deployment of security officers to mail facilities is based on the number of employees, not political leanings in any given location.
- Neither the Postal Inspection Service nor Prosegur confirmed how many officers had been contracted or where. The president of the union that represents postal police officers said RawStory's "nearly 1,000" estimate was based on the union's tally of approved work hours for contracted guards rather than the number of contracts.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We asked Prosegur to confirm its contract with the Postal Service and to respond to RawStory's allegations that it had "a history of alleged human rights abuses and price fixing." We await replies to our queries.
In October, a claim circulated that the U.S. Postal Service hired a private security company to station 1,000 armed guards at post offices in Democratic-leaning states ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
For example, one X user wrote (archived): "USPS has hired security company Prosegur to station 1,000 armed guards at post offices primarily in blue states. Prosegur has a history of human rights violations in Brazil."
Similar claims also circulated elsewhere on X (archived) and Facebook (archived). Snopes readers contacted us asking about the claim.
The claim stemmed from investigative reporting by the independent newsroom RawStory. The outlet reported in early October that Prosegur, an international security company, had deployed "nearly 1,000" armed security officers to at least 55 post office locations ahead of the 2026 midterm elections as part of a contract with the Postal Service.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, which is the federal law enforcement arm of the Postal Service, said in a statement on Oct. 28:
The U.S. Postal Inspection Service's deployment of a mix of unarmed and armed contract security officers to key USPS facilities has absolutely nothing to do with elections. These deployments have been ongoing since last year, under supervision, and represent a supplemental staffing to our career employee Postal Police Officer complement.
The statement said the Postal Service could not confirm where it stationed armed or unarmed guards in order to "maintain operational security." For that reason, we could not confirm the claim that the service stationed additional security in Democrat-led areas. The service's own policy on security staffing said deployments were based on staff numbers at a given facility.
Because the claim is unproven, we leave it without a rating.
The Postal Inspection Service's statement did not confirm that the Postal Service contracted specifically with Prosegur or how many armed security officers the company had deployed. We asked Prosegur to confirm its contract with the service and to respond to RawStory's allegations that it had "a history of alleged human rights abuses and price fixing." We await replies to our queries.
Speaking to RawStory, a spokesperson for Prosegur reportedly said that the company had a "USPS account" that they were not able to discuss the details of.
USPS contracted guards since 2025, not connected to elections
Cathy K. Purcell, a senior public relations representative for the Postal Service, reportedly told The New Republic in October that the service had deployed armed security officers "since last year."
The Postal Inspection Service told Snopes in a written statement that the deployment of armed and unarmed officers was "part of our overall security plan" and repeated Purcell's reported timeline for the deployment, which it also said had "absolutely nothing to do with elections."
Frank Albergo, executive director of the Postal Police Officers Association, which represents officers who are part of the service's uniformed force, also told Snopes that wider deployment of armed security officers within the Postal Service began after October 2025. He added that "claims that the guards were brought in to meddle with the election are not supported by the information we have."
The Postal Service security staffing policy (Page 3) shared by Albergo in September showed the service allocated security officers — contracted or non-contracted, armed or unarmed — to locations based on how many employees were at a facility, not the political leaning of the state in which it was located. RawStory reported that the service had deployed armed security officials to seven cities in the U.S., all of which were in or near Postal Inspection Service divisions.
USPIS hired security through Prosegur from 2019
According to a 2022 report (Page 3) by the Postal Inspection Service Office of the Inspector General, which audits the service, the Postal Inspection Service has contracted security officers through Prosegur since at least 2019, when Prosegur took over another company that the Postal Inspection Service had contracted with since 2014.
Albergo said Prosegur was the only company that provided security officers to the Postal Inspection Service in 2026.
The inspector general's report said the Postal Service contracted additional security officers to provide "perimeter and building security at assigned postal facilities" alongside the service's own postal police officers. According to the Postal Inspection Service, this was still the case in 2026, as a spokesperson described the deployment of armed and unarmed guards as "supplemental staffing" to existing postal police officers.
There were several key differences between postal police officers and contracted security officers. Most importantly, the inspector general's report said (Page 3), postal police officers could "conduct investigations, and make arrests" while contracted security officers could not. Both types of security officers could carry firearms, though Alebergo told Snopes that the security officers Prosegur and its predecessor supplied before October 2025 generally were not armed.
Albergo said the Postal Inspection Service employed 440 postal police officers in October 2026. By comparison, he said the Postal Service had approved 39,587 contract guard-hours per week — the approximate equivalent of 990 full-time positions. Though neither Albergo, the Postal Inspection Service nor Prosegur had confirmed exactly how many contracted security officers it hired using the approved hours, Albergo's comparison suggested that contracted security officers far outnumbered postal police officers.
Reporting questioned Prosegur's labor and human rights record
Though the Postal Service had contracted with Prosegur for several years by 2026, it didn't appear the cooperation had always been easy. The 2022 inspector general's report (Page 4) found that 35 of the 115 security officers reviewed by inspectors during fiscal year 2021 — around one in three — worked on the contract without proper security clearance. Inspectors were also unable to verify the duration and nature of any training the Prosegur security officials had undertaken before working on post office sites.
According to the report, the service did not adequately track the quantity or quality of the Prosegur security officials' work, meaning Prosegur could have overbilled the service for work carried out under its contract. According to the inspector general's report, the estimated total cost of the potentially 10-year contract with Prosegur was $250 million (Page 3). The report did not present any evidence that Prosegur actually overbilled the Postal Service during the contract in question.
Snopes could not independently confirm the value of any newer contracts between the Postal Service and Prosegur because the former does not report (Page 6) its spending to the federal USAspending.gov database.
RawStory's reports on the service's contracts with Prosegur raised additional labor and human rights issues relating to Prosegur's work in the U.S. and abroad.
For example, the Charlotte, North Carolina-area branch of the American Postal Workers Union reportedly requested that the Postal Service replace contracted security officers with postal police officers at one site after a contracted security officer allegedly punched a postal worker and pushed her to the ground in April 2024. The Postal Service reportedly denied the request.
Miriam Bell, the general president of the Charlotte-area branch of the union, reportedly told RawStory that the Postal Service hired contracted security officials in an attempt at "union busting," which is when a company's management attempts to stop employees from unionizing.
Bell told RawStory that two post office employees in the Charlotte area had been fired or attempted fired as a result of speaking up against contracted security officers. Snopes has not independently verified the details of Bell's accounts to RawStory.
RawStory's reporting described Prosegur as "a multinational private contractor with a history of alleged human rights abuses and price fixing." In particular, the reporting highlighted a 2024 recommendation by the Norwegian Council on Ethics to exclude Prosegur from investment by the country's government pension fund due to "an unacceptable risk that the company is contributing to serious human rights abuses."
The Norwegian Council on Ethics research found that Prosegur's subsidiary in Brazil had been involved in "severe acts of violence and abuse of tribal people's rights." It added that Prosegur continued to operate in "numerous countries in which there are land disputes and serious antagonism between commercial companies and local populations."
Prosegur said in a joint account of "labor controversies" from 2013 to 2020 that it believed at least one union that had accused it of human rights abuses had "misused" the concept (Page 8).
The company had not returned a request for comment on RawStory's allegations at the time of this writing.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether election volunteers were training to confront voter intimidation by federal agents at the polls. Follow our wider coverage of claims related to the 2026 midterm elections here.

Aga banned for fake prescription from family member
- Published
Ethiopian marathon runner Ruti Aga has been handed a six-year ban after she attempted to explain a positive test for a banned substance using a prescription from a non-existent clinic, issued by a doctor who turned out to be a family member.
Aga, who won the 2019 Tokyo Marathon, tested positive for methylprednisolone after winning a half marathon in China in March.
She received a two-year ban for testing positive for the prohibited steroid - used to reduce inflammation and classed as performance enhancing by the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada).
The 32-year-old was given a further four-year ban for tampering with evidence and misleading investigators during an interview.
"Aga attributed her positive test to treatment for a knee injury, submitting a prescription from a clinic that did not exist, issued by a 'doctor' who turned out to be a family member with no medical registration with the relevant authority," the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said on Thursday.
"When questioned, the family member claimed to have used an old prescription pad from a former workplace. But that clinic confirmed the individual had never worked there and the prescription was not theirs."
Aga, who has finished second three times at World Marathon Majors, has been provisionally suspended since 10 September and the ban will run from that date.

Reddit is announcing a huge shift: It’s going to start requiring users to log in.
Reddit will force everyone to log in
Reddit is becoming a ‘logged-in-only experience,’ says CEO Steve Huffman.
Right now, you can browse Reddit without having an account, and the site is generally a great resource for crowdsourced information on a whole range of topics. I know I’m not the only person who appends “reddit” to a lot of Google searches to find answers to things written by actual humans instead of robots. But that openness has made it a target for scraping and automated traffic, leading Reddit to file lawsuits over alleged unauthorized access of its data and make product changes like limiting access to “Old Reddit.”
There’s no definitive timeline on when this change will roll out to all users, or how the site will work if you’re logged out. (If I send my friend a link to a thread and they aren’t logged in, what will they see?) To start, Reddit will test the logged-in requirement in “select markets outside the US” in the “coming months,” according to CEO Steve Huffman. “We’ll look at the impact on the user experience, on our business, and on the whole Reddit ecosystem, figure out where the right boundaries are, and go from there.” Reddit has also rebuilt and is rereleasing the Reddit app’s incognito mode.
Huffman claims the login requirement is better for Reddit’s user experience and its ads business and is “more protective of Reddit data.” The “vast majority” of unauthorized Reddit access happens “through our logged-out experiences,” though the company will still strike licensing deals of its data with companies, like the deals it made with OpenAI and Google in 2024. Huffman notes that Reddit does not need to know a logged-in user’s identity — “Honestly, we don’t want to know” — just that the user is logged in at all. And he says that more logged-in users lets the company deliver “more relevant ads.”
“This is a big change for Reddit, where we’ve allowed logged-out access to basically all of Reddit for the last two decades,” Huffman says. “And I don’t know about you, but as someone whose life has been defined by the open internet, it’s a big change for me. But I’ve come to the conclusion that this is the right decision for our platform and the right decision for our business.”
Reddit is making this announcement alongside its Q3 2026 earnings, which were released today. Search traffic was “down meaningfully” in Q3, Huffman says in the company’s shareholder letter, with logged-out traffic and web traffic being the most heavily impacted. “During October, we have seen that search traffic has dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week,” Huffman says.
However, Huffman notes that app and logged-in daily active unique users make up “over 80% of the monetization on Reddit,” which he says “speaks to the strength of Reddit as a destination and the impact of our ongoing product work.”

The Indian Council of Medical Research has funded a four-year study to investigate the genetic and immunological mechanisms underlying autoimmune diseases by studying families with multiple affected members, AIIMS doctors said on Thursday, appealing to SLE patients to get enrolled in the study.
The project titled ‘Genomic Profiling and Identification of Targetable Shared Immunopathogenic Events in Multiplex Families with Autoimmune Diseases’ has been awarded to Dipyaman Ganguly of Ashoka University, Sonipat, Haryana, and Ranjan Gupta, additional professor in the Department of Rheumatology, AIIMS, Delhi.
The study aims to build a nationwide cohort of 200 families in which multiple members are affected by autoimmune diseases. Each participating family must have at least one member diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), commonly known as lupus, Gupta said.
The researchers will conduct genetic and immunological assessments of the enrolled patients and their family members to identify shared biological mechanisms that contribute to the development of these conditions.
The findings could help scientists better understand the disease processes involved and identify potential targets for developing new therapies, he said.
Autoimmune diseases occur when the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own tissues. A family history of such conditions is associated with an increased risk of developing them, highlighting the importance of investigating genetic and shared immunological factors, Gupta said.
The four-year project will involve clinical centres at AIIMS Delhi; AIIMS Bibinagar, Telangana; Sanjay Gandhi Postgraduate Institute of Medical Sciences (SGPGIMS), Lucknow; St John's Hospital, Bengaluru; Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences, Hyderabad; and the Kolkata Medical College. These centres will contribute clinical data and biological samples for the study.
Patients diagnosed with lupus and residing in Delhi-NCR can contact the centre at AIIMS Delhi to check their eligibility for participation, Gupta said.
Participation will be subject to eligibility assessment and the study's enrolment requirements.
