Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

An Indian court has ordered the release of two leaders of India’s Cockroach movement, who were jailed last week amid a mounting state crackdown on youth-led protests.
The two leaders of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, had spent a week in Delhi’s Tihar jail after being arrested by Delhi police last week.
On Wednesday, a special magistrate ordered that Das and Ranka be released, despite efforts by police to keep them in prison. They were made to sign a bond pledging no further breach of peace.
Their arrest came after a draconian police crackdown on a CJP march held in the capital two weeks ago, to protest alleged manipulation of the country’s electoral roll, led to the barricading of central Delhi and thousands of young people being detained.
Das and Ranka were taken into custody for a second time days later after they jumped police barricades and held up an Indian flag at a site in central Delhi that police had cordoned off.
The pair were charged with trespass and violating the peace and sent to jail for five days, which was then extended by two further days. Their detention had provoked outrage among leaders and supporters of the youth movement, who accused the government of “cowardice” for jailing CJP leaders for holding a peaceful protest.
After the magistrate’s ruling on Wednesday evening, Das said that “truth has triumphed”.
The release of the two leaders is likely to come as a blow to the ruling Narendra Modi government, which has implemented an unforgiving crackdown on recent protests that have erupted across India.
The CJP, alongside the opposition alliance, student groups and civil society, have been calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of the electoral roll that benefits Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) and has led to more than 130 million names being deleted from the voter register. The BJP has denied any interference.
The CJP began as an online satire earlier this year, but has since grown into a fully fledged political movement, challenging the powerful Modi government. Over the summer, it was Cockroach-led protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister after sustained demonstrations.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP movement, vowed over the weekend that the Modi regime and threat of jail would not intimidate the Cockroaches. Dipke was also detained on Friday after he called for a peaceful demonstration in central Delhi where CJP supporters would gather and wave the Indian flag in solidarity with Das and Ranka.
He had said that, once his fellow Cockroach leaders were released, they would “gather, re-strategise, and determine how to move forward”.
“The illegal arrests and detentions we have witnessed over the past few days indicate an attempt to intimidate us,” said Dipke. “But we will not be cowed down or retreat. This is a long battle and we are prepared for it.”

In Summary
- Earclip-style earbuds are getting very popular these days, with the likes of Sennheiser and Samsung also launching buds in this style.
- While they are more stable than conventional earbuds and are designed to let ambient sound in, earclip-style buds have their own pros and cons.
- If you are thinking of grabbing a pair of earclip-style buds for yourself, here are some important points to keep in mind about these buds, which make them very different from traditional, ‘normal’ earbuds.
Sony has released its first. Sennheiser has released its first one too. And so has Samsung. And many others – including Apple and Google – are believed to be readying theirs. We are talking about the clip-style or clip-on earbuds that are now becoming increasingly popular in the personal audio market. As their name indicates, these earbuds are shaped like clips and are attached to your outer ear, rather than inserted into your ear canal. They generally comprise two tiny cylinders, one of which is a speaker and the other of which is a battery, connected with a band, and they are designed to clip onto your ear.
Although they were first seen on the market a couple of years ago, most notably from Huawei and Bose, and were released by many budget-friendly brands, clip-style earbuds are now taking their place in the audio tech spotlight. But what makes these relatively new totally wireless earbuds different from other TWS earbuds, and should you be thinking of getting one for yourself?
Well, here are thirteen points we think you need to know about clip-style earbuds before you clip a pair to your own ears:
Table of Contents
They are on-ear and “open” and generally more comfortable
Clip-style earbuds are on-ear buds, and clip on to the outer ear like an ear cuff. This means that they lie on top of or near the ear canal, and do not go inside it, like many other earbuds. This makes them more comfortable to wear for most users – you do not feel something is inside your ear or just dangling near your earlobe.
They are light
In terms of weight, clip-style earbuds are about the same weight as general buds – about 5-7 grams, based on the design and materials used. For instance, the Sony LinkBuds Clip are about 6.4 grams each, while the Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5 are 7 grams each, and the AirPods are about 5 grams.
They are incredibly stable and almost NEVER fall off
Clip-style earbuds are among the most stable wireless earbuds. This is because they actually “clip” on to the user’s ear, gently pressing it between a speaker and battery cylinder or sphere. As a result, they are actually attached to your ear on both ends. You can shake your head violently, and they still won’t fall off. In our book, they are as stable as earbuds with hooks that go around your ears.
No ear tip options – one size fits all
As clip-style earbuds do not go into the ear canal, there are almost always no earbud options to let you adjust for a better fit. It is pretty much a one-size-for-everyone rule out there. This can cause a few problems, as the next point will show.
The size of your ear could affect your experience
The fact that there are no size adjustment options available at all in most clip-style earbuds and that they are basically clipped onto your ear means that your experience of them could depend on the size of your ear. Those with relatively large ears might find the speaker end of the buds lying farther away from their ear canal, while those with small ears might find the speaker end coming right on top of their ear canal. There is unfortunately no cure for this, other than making the connecting band on these earbuds adjustable or flexible, which no brand is doing so far.
They come with bigger drivers…
Most clip-style earbuds come with slightly larger drivers than those seen on most TWS. While most TWS have drivers of the size of 5 mm to 8 mm, most clip-style earbuds have drivers that are 10 mm or larger. For instance, the Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless have 7 mm drivers, and the AirPods are believed to have 7.5 mm drivers, while the Sony LinkBuds Clip have 10 mm drivers, and the Moto Buds Loop have 12 mm drivers.
…but are not the loudest
The interesting part, however, is that even though they have larger drivers, most clip-style earbuds are not as loud as other TWS. This is because the larger drivers push sound towards the ear, often going past pockets of air that lie between the buds and the ear canal. Some of the sound inevitably gets lost in this, resulting in lower volume levels.
Love bass? These are not great options
We are going to be up front about it – clip-style earbuds, and in fact most ‘open’ earbuds are not for those who love audio with plenty of bass. The open fit of these buds is not ideal for bass, which sounds best in a packed setup, allowing for reverberations and rumble. Many brands attempt to tune their buds to accent the bass and even use larger drivers, but the result is seldom close to what we get from in-ear earbuds.
External noise comes in…too much external noise sometimes
One of the biggest attractions of clip-style earbuds is that they allow external or ambient sounds to come in too, and do not seal you away from the outside world. However, this is a bit of a mixed blessing, as too much external noise, combined with the lower volumes of these ear clips, can drown out audio. We would not recommend using them in very noisy conditions like traffic jams, or even in gyms with loud noises – those sounds will come right in.
And there is no ANC either, but ENC exists
As they are “open” in design terms, and are actually made in a manner to allow external sounds to come in, clip-style earbuds do not have any active noise cancellation. The microphones on them – for phone calls – do come with some environmental noise cancellation, so call quality on many of these buds can actually be quite good.
Controls can be…challenging
Thanks to their design, which makes them very small, clip-style earbuds almost always have touch controls – there is hardly any room for buttons on them. And as the buds themselves tend to be small, these can be difficult to use and get used to. One inevitably figures out a way to get them working, but they are never quite as comfortable as those on other TWS and earbuds, especially those with stems. These are best controlled from the connected device.
Perfect for those times when you need to listen to your surroundings too (offices, large families, outdoor runs, etc.)
The fact that they are light, stay securely attached to your ear, and allow some ambient noise to come in makes the clip-style earbuds perfect for those places where you need to be aware of sounds around you. They are great for offices in which you need to keep your ears open for queries and remarks from colleagues or even for ringing phones, and even for those who stay in large families and need to keep their ears open, even while listening to music. And of course, we think they are perfect for those who love to go on outdoor runs and rides, as they stay in place and give one access to one’s phone and audio (when allowed) and also keep one aware of traffic and people around one.
Not for audiophiles, gamers, or for intense listening sessions
No matter what the brands tell you, clip-style earbuds are not for those who are very serious about their audio. They seldom deliver the kind of detail and audio quality that one gets from other TWS at their price points. At the most, one can hope for a reasonable level of clarity and a relatively balanced audio signature. While equalizers can make a difference to different frequencies, clip-on style earbuds are not really for audio purists or for those who like to listen very intensely to their music. Their relative lack of volume and limited bass also mean they are not the best option for gaming or even watching films, even though some of them do come with spatial audio. They are, however, excellent for podcasts and live streaming audio, absolutely super for audiobooks, and more than adequate for casual listening.
And one more thing…
They have a special ring carrying mode
One of the biggest problems with most TWS is putting them back in their cases. You need to find the case, open it, take them out of your ears, put them back in the case, and snap it shut. All of which can take some time, especially when you are in a hurry (say, when you want to talk to someone, or get on or off the Metro). Well, that can be avoided with clip-style earbuds. Thanks to their shape, you can simply wrap a clip-style earbud around one of your fingers. Just like a ring. Don’t worry, it won’t fall off easily. No need to fiddle around trying to find their case immediately.

Cyclone Arnab made landfall along the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts on 28 October 2026, bringing heavy rainfall and strong winds. Authorities evacuated more than 1.8 lakh people from vulnerable areas in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha ahead of the cyclone. As of 29 October 2026, the storm had weakened into a deep depression, but heavy rainfall and flash-flood risks persisted across parts of eastern India. In Andhra Pradesh, seven people were reported killed in cyclone-related incidents, while flooding, uprooted trees, and infrastructure damage disrupted power supplies and transport. The India Meteorological Department has forecast further heavy rainfall in several states over the coming days.
Amid this incident, several visuals are being shared on social media (here, here, here, here, and here) with the claim that they show Cyclone Arnab and the conditions during its landfall. Times Now (archived) and BBC News Telugu (archived) also shared some of these videos in their Instagram posts about Cyclone Arnab. Let’s verify the truth behind these videos in this article.
Claim: The videos show visuals of Cyclone Arnab and the conditions during its landfall.
Fact: None of the videos show Cyclone Arnab or the conditions during its landfall in October 2026. The first video shows a tornado in Bihar’s Vaishali district on 26 September 2026, the second shows a tornado in the US Virgin Islands on 6 July 2026, the third shows a severe storm in Antalya, Turkey, reported on 27 October 2026, and the fourth shows a tornado in Odisha on 15 March 2026. The origin of the fifth video could not be independently verified; however, it has been available online since at least 29 May 2026, predating Cyclone Arnab’s landfall on 28 October 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1
In our investigation, we found that the same video has been available on the internet since at least 27 September 2026, confirming that it predates Cyclone Arnab and is unrelated to it. The video is reported to show a tornado in Mahisaur village in Bihar’s Vaishali district.
We also found that the same footage was published on TheWeather.net under the headline “A tornado wreaks havoc in the village of Mahisaur, India.” According to the description, the weather phenomenon caught residents off guard, with strong winds lifting objects, damaging structures, and causing destruction. The video was also shared in a Facebook reel by Digital Bihar Live on 27 September 2026, with the caption stating that it was from Mahisaur in Jandaha block of Vaishali district, Bihar.
According to local news reports (here, here), a strong tornado struck the Mahisaur village area in Bihar’s Vaishali district on 26 September 2026, damaging trees, crops, and the roofs of houses.
Video 2
In our investigation, we found that the video shows a tornado that struck the US Virgin Islands on 06 July 2026. The same footage was featured in media reports published in July 2026 (here, here), confirming that it predates Cyclone Arnab and is unrelated to it.
Video 3
In our investigation, we found that the video shows (here, here) a severe storm that struck a construction site in the Kepez district of Antalya, Turkey. The same footage was featured in several media reports (here, here) published on 27 October 2026, reporting that a devastating storm had overturned workers’ accommodation containers and caused a crane to topple. According to local authorities and media reports, four construction workers died, and several others were injured in the incident.
Video 4
In our investigation, we found that the same video has been available on the internet since at least 16 March 2026, confirming that it predates Cyclone Arnab and is unrelated to it. The video reportedly shows a tornado with wind speeds of 170 km/h that struck Odisha.
According to reports (here, here), a tornado triggered by a nor’wester struck four villages in the Karanjia block of Mayurbhanj district, Odisha, on 15 March 2026, killing two people, injuring 29 others, and damaging more than 100 houses.
Video 5
In our investigation, we found that the same video has been available on the internet since at least 29 May 2026, confirming that it predates Cyclone Arnab and is unrelated to it. However, we could not independently verify where the video was filmed or the context in which it was recorded. The available evidence confirms that the video is unrelated to Cyclone Arnab in October 2026.
To sum up, these viral videos are unrelated to Cyclone Arnab’s landfall.

- A rumor circulated in October that some popular chocolate brands have switched to using lab-grown chocolate, also referred to as cell-based chocolate or cultured chocolate.
- The rumor stems from information published by a variety of unreliable outlets that cite no sources, such as investment firms giving advice on investing in lab-grown cocoa, holistic food blogs or alternative lifestyle blogs.
- Snopes bases its ratings on direct and verifiable primary evidence. In the absence of such evidence in this instance, we've left this claim unrated. Most of the companies named in examples of the claim have denied using lab-grown cocoa in current products. One has admitted to investing in the research of lab-grown cocoa but not actively using it in products. Another has a product with a sunflower-seed-based cocoa alternative that is different from cultured chocolate. Two of the companies have not responded as of this writing.
Ahead of the candy-fueled Halloween season in October, a rumor spread that some popular chocolate brands have switched to using lab-grown chocolate, also referred to as cell-based chocolate or cultured chocolate.
Cell-based chocolate has been billed as a possible sustainability solution for harvesting cocoa, an industry faced with supply, environmental and labor issues.
Essentially, the goal of cell-based chocolate is to create an environmentally and ethically sustainable alternative to farming cocoa beans, the fermented seed of the cacao tree that is the basis of making chocolate.
Critics of such technology claim some of the leading chocolate brands are "quietly pulling off a massive corporate bait-and-switch ... to flood retail shelves with lab-grown chocolate alternatives." One popular social media video asserts that specific brands are "spending billions of dollars into biotech startups that are making the switch from real cocoa to lab-grown," including:
- Kinder (a brand of Ferrero)
- Lindt & Sprüngli
- Snickers & M&Ms (brands of Mars)
- Kit Kat (a brand of Nestlé)
- Hershey
- Cadbury (a brand of Hershey)
The rumor appears to stem from a variety of unreliable outlets — such as investment firms giving advice on investing in lab-grown cocoa, holistic food blogs or alternative lifestyle blogs — the latter of which claims "climate change is a hoax" and therefore people should not "let corporations replace real chocolate with lab experiments."
Crucially, none of these outlets provide sources when making iterations of this claim. We reached out to each outlet, asking for any evidence they have to support their claims and if they would share their sources. We will update this article if we receive responses.
As Snopes bases its ratings on direct and verifiable evidence, we have left this claim unrated. It is important to note that most of the companies named in examples of the claim have denied using lab-grown cocoa, while one admitted to investing in researching lab-grown cocoa but not actively using it in products. Two have not responded as of this writing.
The Hershey Company and Cadbury
A Hershey spokesperson said via email, "Hershey has no active research and development or product commercialization work on cocoa substitutes, such as lab-grown cocoa or alternatives, underway or planned in the future."
Hershey's FAQ section on its ingredients webpage directly addresses the question of using lab-grown chocolate, using identical language to the above statement.
The company's sustainability webpage says it made a $500 million investment in Cocoa For Good, a strategy aiming to "improve farmer livelihoods, support children's well-being [and] protect the environments in which cocoa grows."
The company also notes the struggles within the cocoa industry, such as child labor, and points to Cocoa for Good as a way of "contributing to a cocoa supply chain where farmers and their families can prosper."
Further, Hershey's website notes that it has produced the Cadbury brand in the U.S. since 1988.
In February 2026, a descendent of the inventor of Reese's Peanut Butter Cups, a brand Hershey's now owns, reportedly accused the company of cutting corners and using inferior ingredients, but did not mention lab-grown chocolate.
Nestlé and Kit Kat
A Nestlé spokesperson said via email, "We are not developing lab-grown chocolate."'
They added, "While we keep an eye on emerging technologies and ingredient innovations, our primary focus remains on cocoa. It is at the heart of our confectionery business and will continue to be the core ingredient in our chocolate portfolio."
Nestlé's corporate website highlights The Nestlé Cocoa Plan, an initiative launched in 2009 and billed as an effort to help its farmers and improve the quality of ingredients.
The spokesperson focused on those efforts in their email:
Our research efforts concentrate on strengthening the resilience and sustainability of cocoa production, including supporting the development of climate-resilient cocoa varieties.
At the same time, we remain strongly committed to supporting cocoa-farming communities through initiatives such as the Nestlé Cocoa Plan and our Nestlé Income Accelerator Program, which aim to improve farmer livelihoods and strengthen the long-term sustainability of the cocoa supply chain (for example through cash incentives, training or agroforestry support that promote good farming practices and help reach higher crop productivity).
In 2025, the company announced that its research and development division had devised a "novel technique that uses up to 30% more of the cocoa fruit."
Nestlé does produce a product in Europe called Choco Crossies that is made with ChoViva, a chocolate alternative made from sunflower seeds — a different process to cultured chocolate — that German company Planet A Foods produces.
Planet A Foods describes ChoViva as a "cocoa-free chocolate alternative [proving] that chocolatey indulgence doesn't have to depend on cocoa: it can be produced at scale from an independent supply chain."
Lindt & Sprüngli
Best known for its Lindt brand of chocolates, as well as owning the Russell Stover and Ghirardelli brands, a Lindt & Sprüngli spokesperson said via email that claims the company is "using 'lab‑grown' or 'artificial' cocoa in its products are not correct." They added: "All Lindt chocolates available on the market today are made with cocoa beans sourced in the traditional way. All ingredients are clearly labeled on the packaging."
The company's sustainability webpage, like Hershey's and Nestlé's, cites similar issues in the cocoa industry, including child labor practices and forest conservation.
However, the Lindt & Sprüngli spokesperson said the company "continuously explores innovation in cocoa cultivation and chocolate production as part of its long‑term commitment to quality and sustainability," and, as a result, "made an investment in Food Brewer, a Swiss company researching cocoa ingredients based on natural cocoa plant cell cultures. "
The company added: "This collaboration is research‑focused and at an early stage ... Lindt & Sprüngli remains fully committed to exceptional quality and taste. Traditional chocolate made from natural cocoa beans will always remain at the heart of our portfolio."
Food Brewer posted about Lindt & Sprüngli's investment via LinkedIn, saying, "The profound knowledge of this global chocolate player will help us in accelerating our go-to-market strategy and further develop our delicious cocoa products."
Other brands in the claim
Snopes contacted Mars (which operates the Snickers and M&M's brands) and Ferrero (which operates the Kinder brand) but we had not received responses prior to publication. Both companies have sustainability webpages similar to the other companies mentioned in the claim.
Ferrero's says its goals involve "protecting the environment and sourcing ingredients sustainably," as well as "promoting responsible consumption and empowering people."
For its part, Mars describes its sustainability program as "transforming the way we work – from how we source raw materials like palm oil and cocoa, to how we fish the oceans for our pet food ingredients – to ensure every part of our operations and extended supply chains help people and the planet thrive."
We will update this article if we receive further comment from Mars, Ferrero, or the outlets who reported their alleged investments.

Windows 11 Home is ideal for everyday tasks like browsing, gaming, and office work. Windows 11 Pro adds BitLocker encryption, Remote Desktop hosting, Hyper-V, and advanced management tools. Pro suits professionals and businesses, while Home is enough for most users. You can upgrade from Home to Pro without reinstalling Windows.
Unlike macOS, Windows comes in different versions. Windows 11 Home is the most common version designed for everyday use, while Windows 11 Pro is for professionals and business users who want maximum security and useful remote features.
Most PCs and laptops mostly come with Windows 11 Home out of the box. It is enough for most users. However, if you need specific features for enhanced device security and remote access, Windows 11 Pro is a strong option, especially for professionals who handle sensitive information and for businesses that need to access devices remotely when staff are away from home.
If you are a beginner, choosing between Windows 11 Home and Pro can be confusing, especially since they look almost identical and it’s hard to tell them apart at first. In this guide, you will learn the differences between Home and Pro and which one you should choose.
What do Windows 11 Home and Pro have in common?
Windows 11 Pro is basically an extension of Windows 11 Home. Compared to Windows 11 Home, it adds a few extra features designed for business and professionals. However, both versions share most basic, everyday features.
Starting with the interface, both look and feel similar and support the same core Windows features, everyday apps, and software. Both also support Windows Hello, Secure Boot, Find My Device, and receive frequent Windows security updates.
For security, both Windows 11 Home and Windows 11 Pro include a firewall and network protection, support Windows Hello sign-in options, and support Secure Boot on compatible hardware.
Microsoft also offers basic device encryption in Windows 11 Home on supported PCs. However, full BitLocker management is only available on Windows 11 Pro, which you can learn about in the next section.
Since every major core feature of Windows is the same, and every app runs without any issues, and both versions have support for everyday apps and software, you won’t find much difference between them if your main activities include: accessing Windows core features, browsing, video calls, editing videos, documents, streaming, browsing, and gaming. However, keep in mind that while Windows 11 Home and Pro offer the basics for everyday users, performance depends on your PC hardware, including the processor, memory, and graphics card.
Even if you initially choose Windows 11 Home, you can upgrade to Windows 11 Pro without extra hardware.
The Pro features that can change your decision
Windows 11 Pro is designed for people who care about security and want to control their PC when they are away from home. The biggest difference is BitLocker encryption: Windows 11 Home offers only basic device encryption on supported PCs, while Windows 11 Pro offers full BitLocker management, so if you lose your PC and someone accesses your encrypted storage without authorization, they can’t easily retrieve your data.
This is especially useful for businesses with confidential information, so Windows 11 Pro makes more sense. Windows 11 Pro offers BitLocker encryption and supports Remote Desktop hosting, which isn’t available in Windows 11 Home. A Windows 11 Pro-supported PC can act as a Remote Desktop host, so you can connect to it from another device when you are away from home. This is especially useful when you are away from home and want to access an important file or use an important application that’s installed on your device.
Another Windows 11 Pro-exclusive feature is Windows Sandbox, which lets you run a temporary, isolated Windows environment on your computer, especially useful for running risky applications that may contain malware and could damage or access sensitive files on your device.
Windows 11 Pro also supports Hyper-V virtual machines, where you can install another version of Windows on your laptop and test your software.
This is especially useful for developers testing your app on various Windows versions. Another major difference is the Group Policy Editor, which lets Windows 11 Pro users access admin controls and advanced Windows settings.
It is not just software; Windows 11 Pro also extends your hardware capabilities. For instance, Windows 11 Home supports up to 128 GB of memory, while Pro supports up to 2 TB. Another big difference is price; Pro costs more because of these extra features.
Checking your edition before you set up or upgrade
The best part of Windows 11 Pro is that you can upgrade from Windows 11 Home. Even if you are currently using Windows 11 Home or chose Windows 11 when buying a new laptop or computer, you can easily upgrade to Windows 11 Pro later.
To check which version of Windows you are using, go to Settings > System > About and look under Windows specifications. Then open System > Activation to check its activation status. If you are on Windows 11, you can compare the features. Nerdused carries Windows 11 product keys, and this Windows 11 Home vs Pro guide can help you review the differences as you decide.
Upgrading from Home to Pro without a clean reinstall
As I said before, you can also upgrade from Windows 11 Home to Pro without losing your files or reinstalling Windows. First, make sure Windows 11 Home is activated.
For safety, I highly recommend backing up your important files and installing all available Windows updates.
Once done, open Settings, go to System, then Activation. From there, click Change next to Change product key. Enter a valid Windows 11 product key, then follow the on-screen instructions to upgrade.
If you don’t have the key, select Upgrade your Windows, open the Store, purchase one from the Microsoft Store, then restart and follow the on-screen instructions, restarting the PC if prompted. Then return to Settings > System > Activation and confirm your device is running Windows 11 Pro.
To summarise, choose Windows 11 Home if you mainly use your device for browsing, gaming, video editing, office work, and other everyday tasks.
However, choose Windows 11 Pro if you are a professional or want advanced security features such as BitLocker encryption and remote control of your device while you are away from home. You can test different Windows versions and install one inside your current Windows. Support for features such as Remote Desktop hosting, Hyper-V, and business management tools.

Gajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear the azaan, the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.
The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.
He is also excited because the mosque has been funded almost entirely by the Sikhs and Hindus living in his village of Jakhiwal, in Fatehgarh Sahib district. Even though he fondly remembers how Sikh neighbours sheltered him and his brothers when brutal sectarian violence erupted during partition in 1947, he never expected a house of worship to be rebuilt for the 18 Muslim families who remain in the village.
“This was my maternal home. My parents sent my two brothers and me here to save us from the bloodshed – they were killed back in our village,” says Khan. “Sikhs hid us from the patrols of men with sticks and burning torches.”
Khan reserves his deepest gratitude for Bibi Rajinder Kaur, 77, a Sikh villager who persuaded her grandson to donate a parcel of their farmland to build a mosque. She did so, she says, because every other faith had a place to gather, while local Muslims had none.
“There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,” Kaur says. “Also, it felt like we needed to appease God for the blood this land had seen. The Muslims in our village had to travel 4km [2.5 miles] to another village just to pray.”
During the partition of British India, the border severed Punjab in two, unleashing catastrophic communal blood-letting and forced migrations that virtually emptied the eastern, Indian side of the region of its Muslim population. Hundreds of village mosques were abandoned, desecrated or turned into cattle sheds and storage units.
But over the past decade, several rural Sikh and Hindu communities have quietly stepped forward to restore these places of worship. Even in villages without a Muslim population, people have invited Muslim farmhands and clerics from nearby districts to pray in these newly revived mosques.
About 50 miles fromJakhiwal, in Sangrur district’s Punawal village, Jaspal Sharma, who comes from a family of Hindu priests, donated his land for the construction of a new mosque and hosted a feast for the entire village at its inauguration in February.
Sharma, 48, says the donation was about neighbourly duty. The village has 550 households, of which just a very small proportion are Muslim.
“It’s right opposite our house, so the sound of prayers five times a day creates a lively atmosphere. We like it,” says Sharma. “And it wasn’t just us; everyone in the village, Hindus and Sikhs together, contributed what they could. Some gave money; others donated bricks and cement.”
For Sukhjinder Singh Pandher and his brother, restoring a local shrine in Malerkotla’s Umarpura village was an act of filial reverence. Their grandfather fled west Punjab during partition to settle in India.
“Nobody is treated as different here,” says Pandher, sharing a cup of tea with his Muslim neighbours on the bare floor of the restored mosque. “Eid and Gurpurab [Sikhs’ most holy festival] are celebrated by both communities with the same fervour.
“We live as one and no matter what happens in the rest of the country, the mood here is that of love and unity. Punjab’s conscience cannot tolerate cruelty against a being, irrespective of caste and religion,” he says.
Pandher points to the syncretic traditions and blending of cultures that are deeply rooted in Punjabi history, noting the popular belief that the 16th-century Sufi saint Hazrat Mian Mir was invited to lay the foundation stone of Sikhism’s holiest site, the Harmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple, in Amritsar.
Inspired by the former shahi, or chief, imam of Punjab, Maulana Habib-ur-Rehman Sani Ludhianvi, non-Muslim villagers have contributed to more than 165 such mosques in the past nine years.
“Partition tore at the natural fabric of Punjab,” says the current shahi imam, Maulana Muhammad Usman Rehmani Ludhianvi, who succeeded his father in 2021. “This state itself is an inquilab [revolution]. Online, there is immense polarisation, but on the ground in our villages, ordinary people are still choosing to protect each other.”

US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by a Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to a new report by the New York Times.
Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
In the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he’s developed with Trump, according to the New York Times.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
In a statement to the New York Times, Nvidia said there was nothing out of the ordinary about the Nvidia CEO’s interactions with Alice Huang.
“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in a statement. Megaspeed and customers like it “receive ordinary business information – not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets – and zero information relevant to national security”.

The Trump administration is trying to stop Utah from enforcing its gambling ban against Kalshi, making Utah the 10th state sued by the US government agency that regulates prediction markets.
Utah, which prohibits gambling, sued Kalshi in a state court last week. Utah’s lawsuit seeks an order prohibiting Kalshi from offering bets on sports, elections, politics, and other events.
“Kalshi runs an online casino in Utah and calls it a prediction market. That violates Utah law,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, a Republican, said last week. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution. For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.”
Utah already defeated Kalshi in federal court after the prediction market filed a preemptive lawsuit that sought to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling laws. Now that Utah is moving ahead in its attempt to shut down Kalshi, it must defend against a lawsuit filed by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).
Trump admin claims sole authority
The CFTC “has filed a lawsuit against Utah to block the state’s efforts to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets using state laws,” the commission said yesterday. “The lawsuit follows Utah’s decision to file civil enforcement actions in state court against CFTC-regulated markets and other businesses. Utah’s effort to restrict the functioning of CFTC-registered exchanges obstructs Congress’s decision to federally preempt state law.”
If Utah can shut down Kalshi, that could spell trouble for Kalshi’s chief prediction-market rival, Polymarket, and for sports betting sites like DraftKings and FanDuel. DraftKings and FanDuel advertise availability in all US states via a mix of products, including prediction-market platforms in states like Utah. Both are registered with the CFTC.

Britain’s medicines regulator on Friday approved Johnson & Johnson’s daily pill for adults and teenagers with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, a skin condition causing red, scaly and often itchy or painful patches.
The Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) approved the oral drug Icotyde for people aged 12 and older who weigh at least 40 kg. The approval was based on four late-stage trials in 2,500 people with the disease, including 72 teenagers aged 12 to under 18. In all four studies, patients who took the drug saw better results after 16 weeks than those given a placebo, the regulator said.
Icotyde was approved in the U.S. earlier this year for the same condition — its first approved indication. The drug is made in collaboration with Protagonist Therapeutics. J&J is also studying the drug, chemically known as icotrokinra, for ulcerative colitis, psoriatic arthritis and Crohn’s disease.
The company expects the treatment to bring in $5 billion in peak sales across multiple indications. The drug competes with established psoriasis treatments such as Bristol Myers Squibb’s Sotyktu and AbbVie’s blockbuster Skyrizi.

What killed 500-plus penguins? How scientists solved the mystery
Sailing toward the Danger Islands, Dr. Ralph Vanstreels had a good idea of what he might find: A lot of dead Adélie penguins.
It was March 2024 and a virus had been sweeping through the area, leaving deceased birds in its wake.
Vanstreels got the crime right but the culprit wrong. There were dead penguins but a virus was not to blame.
As his vessel pulled up to a landing ramp on one of the islands — located just off the Antarctic Peninsula — Vanstreels and his fellow researchers immediately noticed bumps in the snow.
"Was each bump a rock or was it a carcass? We had to do quite a bit of intensive searching [through the snow]," says Vanstreels, who is based in Argentina and is a wildlife veterinarian with the University of California, Davis.
The team ultimately found more than 537 penguin carcasses on just the ramp, which he estimates was about the size of an airport runway.
There were many more carcasses elsewhere on the Danger Islands, which are home to two mega colonies for penguins. The researchers estimate there were thousands of dead Adélie penguins and other species of birds. But they had to work quickly and couldn't do a complete count, Vanstreels says.
"You cannot stay there very long because you might be locked down with an iceberg blocking your way out," he says.
As the team has pieced together this tragic penguin mystery, Vanstreels says, the case holds broader lessons for tracking the spread of diseases globally.
The only continent to dodge the virus — until now
Now let's time jump to Australia a few months ago for another bird disease conundrum.
In June, H5N1 — high pathogenicity avian influenza also known as bird flu — arrived in mainland Australia. Up until that point, Australia had been the only continent to dodge the virus which has traversed the globe, leaving a trail of carcasses in its path.
Since late 2021, the virus has led to the death of nearly 300 million poultry birds. Either the virus killed them or they were culled as a preventive measure to stop the spread of the disease, according to the World Animal Health Information System. Further, bird flu is estimated to have killed millions of wild animals and marine mammals, although it's hard to get an exact figure.
Researchers were amazed that Australia could stay bird-flu-free for six years. And the virus didn't take the path that scientists expected.
"We have a lot of migration of birds between Australia and Southeast Asia, so for the first few years, we're like: That's where the virus is coming from," says Dr. Amandine Gamble, an assistant professor at Cornell University in the Department of Public and Ecosystem Health.
The way bird flu eventually got there was from the other direction. It came from Antarctica likely via migrating birds.
"This is a virus that's not assisted by airplanes," Michelle Wille, senior research fellow at the Center for Pathogen Genomics at the University of Melbourne, told NPR in 2025. "This is a virus that's traveling by mass mortality after mass mortality after mass mortality after mass mortality."
"The virus loads are low"
So when Vanstreels set sail to check on the penguins, he assumed bird flu would be the culprit.
Bird flu arrived in Antarctica in late 2023 and early 2024. Vanstreels and his colleagues rapidly arranged for a trip to try to figure out exactly what was happening.
"The expedition was initially fully set up to look for bird flu because that was the panic," he explains, adding that ongoing fear of a continuing global panzootic — or pandemic among animals — is justified.
In several layers of warm clothes covered by protective gear — double gloves, coveralls, glasses and masks — Vanstreels and the team started taking samples of the penguin corpses they found.
"We looked a little bit stiff when walking — like a penguin walking almost — because of all the gear," he says. "We had very strict biosafety standards."
They brought samples from the deceased penguins back to a mini-lab on their boat. By evening, they had early results. But not the results they expected.
"There is bird flu here, but the virus loads are low," he recalls. "That was a little bit puzzling."
The carcasses were not very old, so Vanstreels would have expected to find far more bird flu virus if that had killed the birds. Perhaps something else was the main driver? "We were unsure what was happening," he recalls.
What the microscope revealed
So what killed the 500-plus penguins on the landing ramp and the many others on the island?
Back on land several months after the voyage, in the Netherlands, Vanstreels' colleagues did more investigation. "Under the microscope, you can see that there's bacteria in the tissues," he says — not virus.
They discovered a different disease, a bacterial disease that causes avian cholera (which is distinct from human cholera).
Vanstreels and his team's findings were published in October in the journal the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.
So how worried are they about avian cholera?
The disease is not considered a major threat to humans since the strain that is specialized to birds is distinct from the strain specialized to mammals. "The risk for human infection is not really that high when you see an outbreak on birds," Vanstreels says. But, it does kill birds worldwide — especially in cold environments where the bacteria thrives.
While there's not enough research to know exactly how common avian cholera is, the disease has been on the radar of scientists for decades. However, it's not exactly top of mind. The last time researchers looked for it in the Antarctic Peninsula was 25 years ago.
"One could be misled to think that: Well, that was a unique thing that happened back in 2001, and nothing's happened ever since," says Vanstreels. Instead, it is possible that avian cholera die-offs could be occurring regularly, only scientists haven't been checking.
One of his big takeaways from this bird-flu-that-turned-out-to-be-avian-cholera event?
"Yes, there is a big thing with bird flu. But we still want to keep checking for the other diseases because they might be mixing up in the middle," Vanstreels says.
Antarctica isn't as remote as it seems
Like any good mystery, the case of the cholera-stricken penguins has got scientists wondering: Whodunit?
There's a theory that avian cholera might have been introduced to Antarctica decades ago from researchers who brought poultry from the U.S., Vanstreels says.
Gamble, of Cornell University, adds that the strain of avian cholera found in penguins in Antarctica is "very close" to the strain found 5,000 miles away on Île Amsterdam in the Southern Indian Ocean.
"Antarctica is way more connected to the rest of the world than we think it is," she says.
It's hard to track diseases in Antarctica but, she says, it's turning out to be an important piece in the global pathogen puzzle.
The work of keeping tabs on what's happening has fallen to a number of different countries since Antarctica is not governed by any one government. It was designated as a continent of peace and science by the mid 20th-century Antarctic Treaty, which now has 58 parties — among them are the U.S., France, Japan and Russia. Many nations have research stations and team up on scientific undertakings, including tracking pathogens — be it bird flu or avian cholera — that travel great distances and don't respect borders.
"So this Avian cholera outbreak is just showing this is not a unique event," says Gamble. "We really need international collaboration."

Star Trek actor Patrick Stewart dead at 86
Stewart's career spanned six decades, from Shakespeare to Broadway
Patrick Stewart, British stage actor who found fame as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek, has died. He was 86 years old.
His death was announced in a statement on his official social media account, which said he died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles after "a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia."
Stewart's career spanned six decades, from the Royal Shakespeare Company in Stratford-upon-Avon to Broadway to film and television.
He was best known as Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the Star Trek: The Next Generation series and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film franchise.
Marvel Studios is remembering Stewart as an actor who brought his X-Men character to life with "extraordinary grace, intelligence and humanity." It calls him a "singular talent, generous collaborator and true gentleman."
Hugh Jackman, who starred as Wolverine in the X-Men films, also paid tribute to Stewart on Instagram, calling him "a tremendous friend and man."
Star Trek actor Jonathan Frakes, who played Picard's No. 1, Commander William Riker, was among the first of Stewart's colleagues to post a tribute to him online, simply saying, "Rest in peace my friend," on his Instagram stories.
William Shatner, who played Picard's predecessor aboard the USS Enterprise, Captain Kirk, called this a heartbreaking week, making reference to the death of his co-star Walter Koenig on Monday. Shatner said he was filled with admiration for Stewart.
"From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him," said Shatner on social media.
George Takei, who portrayed physicist Hikaru Sulu in the original Star Trek series, said his heart was heavy.
"Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before, and he inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity," Takei wrote on Threads.
Stewart spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise.
Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of A Christmas Carol and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter's No Man's Land and Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot in repertoire with long-time friend and X-Men co-star Ian McKellen.
Early years and advocacy
Stewart was raised in Mirfield in Yorkshire, a working class corner of northern England, and grew up without a bathroom in his house.
At age 12, he joined an amateur drama group and memorized Shakespeare for fun as a teen. He won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, launching a career as a character actor.
He was bald since he was 19 — alopecia runs in his family.
His father, a former regimental sergeant major in the British Army, was prone to outbursts of "repeated violence against my mother," as Stewart wrote in the Guardian.
"Violence is always a choice a man makes and he alone is responsible for it."
Stewart would later became a patron for Refuge, an organization that provides shelter for domestic abuse victims.
"Some years ago, I woke up to the reality that there were other conditions attached to celebrity status, and those conditions provided the opportunity to speak about things I really cared about other than show business," he told CBC News in 2015.
Sonnets to lift spirits
In 2013, Stewart married Brooklyn songwriter and singer Sunny Ozell, with McKellen officiating.
He said it was his wife's idea to start sharing his love of Shakespeare with the public during the COVID-19 pandemic.
When people were locked down at home, he posted one sonnet a day on his social media accounts, to help lift spirits.
Stewart is also survived by two children, a daughter, Sophia, and a son, Daniel.
The statement on Stewart's social media said "he has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all.
"We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace."
In lieu of flowers, the statement requests donations be made to Johns Hopkins Alzheimer's Disease Research Center Fund or Alzheimer's Foundation of America Caregiver Resources.
Fans mourn
The death of Stewart is being felt keenly by X-Men fans and Trekkies alike.
"I believe generations to come, they will look back at this absolutely remarkable, this treasure of a person, this knight of the realm, this genius of acting that was Patrick Stewart," editor-in-chief of thatshelf.com Jason Gorber told CBC News.
"Patrick Stewart's voice was one of those that was so exquisite, so luscious, so captivating, that it simply brought us in whatever he was saying."
Family Guy creator Seth MacFarlane was one of those who benefitted from his work as a voice actor.
"He was that rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful," MacFarlane wrote on X, saying Stewart will be deeply missed "by the entire planet."

Hyron Andrews - the former Sale second row found dead at his new team's hotel base before a Champions Cup match in France on Saturday - died of natural causes, an autopsy has found.
The 31-year-old, who joined the Johannesburg-based Lions this summer, suffered a tear in the aorta, an artery which carries blood from the heart to the rest of the body.
The rupture led to blood filling the muscle sac surrounding his heart.
Andrews was found unconscious in a shower cubicle, with investigators working on the theory that he had either suffered a fall, a heart attack or, as transpired, an aneurysm, where a bulging blood vessel breaks.
A tear in the aorta is a rare and dangerous medical condition, which can be caused by undetected high blood pressure or a birth defect.
His body is yet to be returned to his native South Africa.
Andrews' wife Maighlin, with whom he had two young sons, has asked for "respect, privacy and patience during this difficult time as the repatriation process begins", according to a statement from the Lions., external

Delhi residents can now book liquor bottles online through the Delhi Liquor Booking app, developed by the Delhi State Industrial and Infrastructure Development Corporation (DSIIDC). The facility allows eligible customers to browse available brands, select bottle sizes and quantities, pay online and collect their orders from a designated retail outlet.
However, the service does not offer home delivery. Customers must visit the selected liquor shop to collect their orders within 48 hours of booking and making the online payment.
Under the applicable excise rules, an individual can purchase up to nine litres of whisky and 18 litres of beer. The app is available to customers aged 25 and above, in line with Delhi's eligibility requirements.
How to book liquor online in Delhi
The Delhi Liquor Booking app allows users to select their preferred liquor and arrange collection from a participating store. Here is how the process works:
Download the app: Install the Delhi Liquor Booking app on your Android phone.
Register: Open the app, accept the statutory warning and register using your mobile phone number.
Choose your liquor: Browse the available brands and select the liquor you want to purchase.
Select the quantity: Choose the bottle size and the number of bottles, subject to the applicable purchase limits.
Select a store: Choose a participating liquor outlet operated by DSIIDC.
Pay online: Review the order details and complete the online payment.
Save the QR code: Keep the booking confirmation and QR code generated after the transaction.
Collect your order: Visit the selected outlet within 48 hours and show the QR code to the store staff to collect your purchase.
Where do customers collect their orders?
Despite enabling online bookings and payments, the service requires customers to collect their liquor in person. Orders must be picked up from the specific DSIIDC-operated outlet selected during booking.
The facility is not available at every liquor shop in Delhi. It is currently restricted to the 208 retail outlets operated by DSIIDC across the capital.
The corporation has introduced the service with the aim of reducing queues and congestion at liquor shops, particularly around payment counters. It also allows customers to check available brands before visiting a store.
Can you cancel a liquor booking?
Customers can cancel their bookings before collecting their orders. However, there is no provision for returning liquor after it has been sold or collected.
Customers should therefore check their order details and selected outlet before completing the booking.

For WeWork's CEO, Fridays are for sneakers. Sometimes.
At Business Insider's The Long Play event on Thursday, John Santora told Deputy News Chief Cadie Thompson that he rebuilt WeWork in part by establishing a sense of trust and decorum among employees.
In pursuit of that goal, Santora instituted a dress code for employees, but also gave them one day a week to work from home.
"I didn't have the ability to go watch my son play a 3 o'clock baseball game," Santora said, adding, "We have to give our employees that flexibility to do all that."
Santora, formerly the chief operating officer at Cushman & Wakefield, a real estate firm, became WeWork's CEO in 2024 as the once-buzzy office startup emerged from a disastrous Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing.
Santora had a short time to decide whether to join the faltering company, he recalled. And it wasn't exactly an easy choice.
"I was kind of at that point of, 'Should I retire?'" he said. "My daughter Nancy said, 'Dad, you know we love you, but when you have too much time on your hands, you're a pain in the ass.'"
Since those deeply red days in 2019 when WeWork's valuation plummeted from $47 billion to roughly $8 billion before it was bailed out, the company has stabilized. It posted eight quarters of EBITDA profitability and expects a fourth straight quarter of cash-flow profitability.
In 2025, it reported about $2.3 billion in revenue.
Though it hasn't hit the valuation it once had, the fact that the company could be revived at all is remarkable. WeWork, founded in 2010, rents out office space, spruces it up, and parcels it out to freelancers, startups, and other businesses.
Its first CEO and founder, Adam Neumann, made bold pronouncements that WeWork would "change the world" and "elevate the world's consciousness" by renting out office space to startups.
But after a bungled IPO, it became clear to the new stakeholders that a different type of leader was sorely needed.
As it turned out, Santora was that leader.
Having worked for 47 years at Cushman & Wakefield, Santora had the real estate experience that Neumann lacked, albeit without the magnetism of a Silicon Valley whiz kid.
"From a leadership standpoint, I'm a very structured, disciplined person," he said. "I'm a suit and tie, buttoned-up real estate person."
Santora recalled an early trip to one of the offices, where he discovered employees wearing jeans, pajamas, slippers, and shorts.
"I grabbed my head of HR," he said. "See that? I don't want to see it anymore."
Santora, who at one point described himself as an "old chubby guy from Staten Island," didn't just force employees to wear sports coats to important meetings. In his words, there was some "give and take."
"I don't look at what time they leave, what time they come in," he said of his employees. "As long as they're getting their work done and they're keeping their clients happy."
And Santora allows himself one exception to his suit-and-tie persona.
"Fridays, I'll actually sometimes wear sneakers, depending on what my schedule is," he said.

Scottish football could pave way for 3pm TV blackout to end
- Published
The first tentative steps to end the 3pm television blackout have been taken by Scottish football as it seeks offers for the next broadcast cycle.
The SPFL has said that it is "flexible about the number of games" that will form part of the new deal, which will kick in from the 2029-30 season.
BBC Sport understands this includes the possibility that broadcasters could bid to show all matches live - including those shown on a Saturday afternoon.
The SPFL has created a tender with the greatest flexibility on the basis that the broadcaster does not seek to impose Article 48 of the Uefa Statutes.
Article 48 allows leagues to set specific times when matches are banned from being shown live on television. It can only be enforced when 50% of matches in a country's top two divisions are played at the same time.
While other parts of Europe have experimented with a blackout, it is now only present in the UK between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on a Saturday.
Other leagues now tend to stagger kick-off times so the top divisions do not all play at the same time, meaning the blackout could not be applied.
In the UK, 3pm remains the traditional, default kick-off time for all leagues from the very top down through non-league.
It was introduced due to fears that televised games at 3pm could affect attendances, not just at the clubs involved but at those down the divisions too.
But as streaming has grown in popularity, critics have argued that it hinders the ability of clubs to exploit this revenue stream.
This is especially the case in the lower levels, which have had to adhere to the blackout and not show any of their games online.
The Cymru Premier, the top division of football in Wales which has a mixture of professional and semi-professional clubs, removed the blackout in the summer in favour of a streaming model for all matches.
In August, Premier League chief executive Richard Masters indicated the direction of travel was to end the blackout, but any decision would be 18 months away and taken in consultation with the EFL and the FA.
The upcoming broadcast cycle provides a unique opportunity for all leagues to come together and reach a consensus, as the rights deals for the Premier League, EFL and SPFL all end in 2028-29.
While the possibility to take all games is on the table in Scotland, it is by no means certain the option will be taken up.
Under the current terms, Sky Sports can show up to 60 Premiership matches a season, with Premier Sports showing up to 22.
In total, there are 228 games in the top flight, meaning only 36% of matches are shown live under the current broadcast deal.
The tender allows broadcasters to present any proposition for live coverage they see fit.
Any decision would then be up to the Premiership's 12 member clubs, with eight votes required to approve a deal.
Clubs could potentially opt to reject an offer which would include the Saturday 3pm games.
Scotland ending the 3pm blackout would not automatically mean English (plus Welsh clubs in the pyramid) and Northern Irish football follows suit.

A top nine finish for Antonelli, or Russell or Lewis Hamilton failing to win Sunday's Mexico City Grand Prix, would secure the title for the Italian, who would be the youngest champion in F1 history at 20 years old.
Russell came into 2026 as favourite after dominating Antonelli last year but has won just three races to his team-mate's nine, regularly being outperformed throughout the season.

"I've probably learned more about myself this year than I would have liked to in all honesty. The highs and lows you go through in sport are immense. That's because we all care so much for what we're doing," said Russell.
"I remind myself I'm 28 years old. I see Lewis still competing extremely well at 41 and Fernando at 44. Lewis won the majority of his titles in his 30s.
"This year is absolutely not going to define my career as a whole. It's not going to break me. If anything, it's going to make me stronger."
Russell pointed to an unusual trend where he's generally bounced back strongly from poor weekends or misfortune, including an underwhelming race in Madrid where Antonelli won, before a dominant performance on his way to pole and victory at the next race in Baku.
"I've been pretty proud of my resilience and how I've bounced back from very tough moments," he explained.
"Actually through my lowest points of this season, I've generally bounced back really, really strong then I had another bad race, after the good one, so maybe it's something I need to analyse as well because I always perform best after my worst races, which is maybe just a coincidence, maybe there's something in it.
"I've been racing more years of my life than I haven't. I've had more successful years than relative failures, and I don't think any athlete, no matter how great, has every single year of their career performing at their highest level.
"Unfortunately, this year for me has come at maybe the time when I needed it most. But it's by no means the end of my journey. I've still got a good 12 to 15 years left in me."
Russell: Antonelli has been at a higher level than me
Antonelli's title-winning campaign is a big surprise after his challenging rookie season in 2025 as he has completely turned the tables in the Mercedes head-to-head battle.
Russell finished eighth last time out in Austin while Antonelli won and the British driver says "it's important to find some consistency" and admits his team-mate has been getting more out of the car.
"On a personal level, Kimi is obviously a great guy with lots of energy. We've had no reason this year not to continue a good relationship," he said.
"I think a lot of these rivalries start because of on-track incidents or actions. The truth is he's been at a higher level than me this year, so we've not really been in that situation too often.
"We've had one or two races, and when it comes to the race itself, we sort of keep ourselves to ourselves and work with our individual engineers to try and get the most out of it."
Antonelli missed Thursday's media day at the Mexico City Grand Prix due to a viral illness but is expected to be fit enough to drive in Friday's practice sessions.
He told Sky Sports F1 in Austin: "The perfect way would be to finish off in style and enjoy the rest of the season.
"I'm very well aware it's very close but the mindset hasn't changed. I want to finish the season on a high in order to have high hopes in 2027.
"First we focus and worry about finishing this [season] well and we will see."

Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.
She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.
Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.
The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.
It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.
Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.
Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.
So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?
More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.
Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.
It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.
Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.
The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."
Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.
"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."
And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".
Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.
Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.
Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.
Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.
Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".
In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".
The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.
She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.
When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.
"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.
This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.
More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.
Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.
Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.
The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning
Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title
Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.
Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.
For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.
Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.
The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.
"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.
Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.
Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.
Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.
She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.
Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.
More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.
It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.
In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.
The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.
The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.
Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.
In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.
Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".
Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".
She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.
