India’s development story over the past decade has been one of infrastructure: highways, metro lines, electrification and digital public platforms, each treated as a foundation for growth that requires public investment and planning. One foundation on which every household and economy depends has not received the same attention: care.
Everyone needs care at some point in life. How care is organised shapes people’s opportunities, well-being and participation in society and the economy. When services are absent, families, and women most of all, bear the cost in unpaid work, lost earnings, and narrower opportunities.
In the Periodic Labour Force Survey 2025, 44.4% of women outside the labour force cited childcare and homemaking as the main reason for staying out of the labour force. India’s Time Use Survey 2024 found that 41% of women aged 15–59 provided unpaid care, spending an average of 140 minutes a day on it. Expanding access to affordable, quality care services can give women greater freedom to pursue employment, leisure and participation in public life. With an ageing population, the need for accessible care services will only grow.
Yet care rarely features in India’s growth strategy. For a Viksit Bharat 2047, the question is not only how to expand women’s economic participation, but how to build the care system that makes such participation possible. The Anganwadi network, strengthened through Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0, anchors early childhood care and nutrition. Palna, under Mission Shakti, supports crèches, while Mission Vatsalya, social security and provisions for persons with disabilities and senior citizens address other needs. The challenge is architecture, not ambition. Four gaps stand out.
First, fragmentation. Care is split across multiple Ministries, from women and child development to housing and urban affairs. Each runs valuable programmes, but without a common framework. This can leave gaps such as crèches that close before factory shifts end or eldercare needs that fall outside of existing schemes.
Second, coverage. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) estimates that 9–10 million women in low-income urban households need childcare. Similarly for eldercare, 24% of older persons face limitations in daily activities, while national data on service availability and coverage remain limited.
Third, the workforce. Care depends on frontline workers; from Anganwadi workers to home-based caregivers and domestic workers — many of whom remain inadequately remunerated or engaged on an honorary basis. Building on NITI Aayog’s proposals, clear standards, certification, decent working conditions, social protection and career pathways would recognise care as skilled and paid work.
Finally, financing and norms. Care is still budgeted as welfare rather than investment, and workplace policies assume that caregiving is women’s work. The Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister (EAC-PM) recommends statutory paid paternity leave in the private sector.
Comparable economies are building their own care ecosystems. Colombia’s 2025 National Care Policy brings 34 government entities under one framework. Brazil’s 2024 National Care Policy and 2025 National Care Plan set up inter-Ministerial committees to steer implementation. In Nepal, care mapping was used to fund care pilots.
The way forward
In India, NITI Aayog’s Reimagining Care: Strategies for Empowering Caregivers in Viksit Bharat@2047 report proposes a National Caregiving Council to strengthen coordination. The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is consulting States and Union Territories; its May 2026 national workshop discussed a National Care Economy Mission with inter-Ministerial governance, aligned financing and shared data. State-level care roadmaps can make this practical. States can map needs, services and demographic trends, identify gaps in childcare, eldercare and disability support, and prepare costed plans with clear responsibilities.
Building on UNDP’s research and lessons from UN Women’s TransformCare initiative in more than 50 countries, the two agencies are supporting this agenda under government leadership, from mapping care services and skilling care workers to backing women-led childcare enterprises with the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs and Women Entrepreneurship Platform.
India has the programmes, policy vision and evidence. On this International Day of Care and Support, the task is to connect them, finance them and hold them to account: to build care the way India builds infrastructure.
Shoko Ishikawa is Country Representative, UN Women India; Angela Lusigi is Resident Representative, UNDP India

China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering, which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.
Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.
The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.
“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X.
The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. But in recent years the campaign has intensified, taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.
Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey”.
A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin.
Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.
The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress which happens every five years and, is expected to be held in the second half of 2027. Xi is expected to secure a fourth term as leader of the party, making him the longest ruler of Communist China since Mao Zedong.
The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo will be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

Early voting in the U.S. midterm elections is underway. Voters are deciding which party will control Congress, as well as numerous state legislatures and governors' offices. Snopes' fact-checkers are flagging rumors surrounding the election, debunking false statements by candidates and suspicious voter fraud claims with nonpartisan research and expert sources. Join our effort to keep this election fact-focused by becoming a Snopes member.
- A long-standing, unproven voter fraud theory claims that some voters receive multiple ballots, allowing them to vote more than once.
- The theory is not supported by evidence. We found no documented examples of voters receiving multiple ballots and casting multiple votes on a large-enough scale to skew election results.
- There can be legitimate reasons why voters receive or turn in multiple ballots in a single election, and it is not uncommon for voters to receive more than one ballot both as a result of a mistake or on purpose. In cases where extra ballots mistakenly get sent to voters, elections officials have multiple ways to ensure they count only one vote per person.
- Ballots are also extremely difficult to copy, meaning large-scale fraud using copied ballots would be near-impossible to carry out. Election officials would likely catch attempts at fraud during the canvassing process if the number of returned ballots was higher than the number of registered voters.
- Tammy Patrick, the chief programs officer at the National Association of Election Officials, an association that trains and certifies election and voter registration officials, encouraged voters with doubts about how officials certify and count ballots to engage with the system to understand how its many safeguards work.
In October, Tulare County, California, said on Facebook (archived) that some voters may have received "duplicate vote-by-mail packets" for the Nov. 3 midterm election.
The Sacramento Bee — citing Michelle Baldwin, the county's registrar of voters — reported that a printing vendor had mistakenly printed and sent extra ballots to 7,791 voters.
The incident in Tulare County appeared to play into a long-standing theory of fraud: namely, that some voters receive multiple ballots, allowing them to vote multiple times in the same election and skew results in favor of a particular party or candidate.
One X user reacting to news about voters in California receiving extra ballots wrote (archived): "Shocker… We've been talking about receiving multiple ballots every election cycle since 2018 and how big a problem it is, only to be told we're wrong or lying by internet 'fact checkers.'"
The X user above was correct that voters receiving multiple ballots is a known election phenomenon. In the run-up to the 2026 midterms, election officials in Michigan and California addressed the issue in local media. The Bipartisan Policy Center, a nonprofit organization, discussed the issue in a February report on voting by mail.
However, we found no documented examples of voters receiving multiple ballots and casting multiple votes on a large-enough scale to skew election results. There can be legitimate reasons why voters receive or turn in multiple ballots in a single election. Some incidents, such as the one in Tulare County, can be attributed to human error. Other times, election officials might send a second ballot if the first contained an error. Either way, officials have well-established safeguards in place that prevent voters from voting more than once.
Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer at the National Association of Election Officials, an association that trains and certifies election and voter registration officials, told Snopes the data does not support claims that fraudsters are using multiple ballots per voter to skew election results, mainly because it would be extremely difficult to pull off such a scheme. Patrick said:
There's a saying, "Is the juice worth the squeeze?" And in this case, it isn't. When we think about voters being able to vote multiple times because, that is what it comes down to here: Is there anyone who is being able to vote more than once in a jurisdiction because they got more than one ballot? That does not happen.
Because there was no documented proof of fraudsters skewing elections by issuing multiple ballots to individual voters, we leave this claim unrated.
Tracking 'extra' ballots in 2026 cycle
Using the National Association of Election Officials' "Electionline" project, which collects news articles on various topics related to elections, we found at least 10 reports across eight states of voters receiving more than one ballot ahead of the 2026 midterms where election officials did not intend to send the extra ballot.
- Local media in California reported on Oct. 24 that at least 15,000 voters in Fresno County could have received an extra ballot. The county's registrar of voters, James Kus, reportedly said sending out extra ballots was a "common issue" that often happened after voters updated their information on the voting register.
- In Tulare County, California, 7,791 voters received an extra ballot. Officials said this was due to a vendor error.
- Local media in Kane County, Illinois, on the outskirts of Chicago, reported that elections officials had sent "about 2,000" extra ballots to voters due to "processing issues" with the clerk's ballot-printing machine.
- In Athens-Clarke County, Georgia, 1,154 voters received extra ballots as a result of "an error in a mailing list."
- More than 600 voters in Warren County, Iowa, reportedly received an extra ballot. Election officials had not given a reason why at the time of this writing.
- Officials in Weber County, Utah, reportedly sent up to 167 voters an extra ballot due to a "miscalibrated envelope stuffing machine."
- Officials in Imperial County, California, said around 160 voters were affected by a "mailing error" that issued them an extra ballot.
- Local media in Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, reported that due to "a communication issue between the county and state while files were prepared," 157 voters received an extra ballot.
- Election officials in Pueblo County, Colorado, said that some homeowners received more than one ballot to vote on a special tax issue. Officials said anyone who received more than one ballot should call the elections office as they may not have received them in error.
- Officials in Pleasant Prairie, Wisconsin, said Oct. 27 that some voters may have received extra ballots due to an error by a village employee helping to prepare absentee ballots.
While the instances of officials sending extra ballots to voters recorded above were almost all the result of mistakes, there were also legitimate reasons why a voter might receive an extra ballot.
For example, Patrick said that election officials might send out a second ballot if the first contained a mistake. She said it was then up to election officials "to make sure that the security protocols are there and are followed" so voters who received more than one ballot got only one vote.
'Extra' ballot does not mean extra vote
In all the cases above, officials emphasized that safeguards during the vote-counting process mean that just because a voter received an extra ballot did not mean they got an extra vote.
For example, the elections-focused nonprofit news organization Votebeat reported in May that election officials in Wisconsin and other states print individual barcodes on ballots that tie them to a particular voter. If an official scans a barcode tied to a voter who has already voted, the vote-counting system will reject the second ballot.
In Pennsylvania, Westmoreland County Commissioner Doug Chew reportedly told the Latrobe Bulletin that officials would use a barcode system to ensure that their vote-counting system would reject a potential second ballot from the same voter.
Patrick told Snopes that other protections such as signature verification keep voters from submitting an absentee ballot and also voting in person. Election officials use those same protections to ensure that the system counts only one absentee ballot per person.
In addition to barcodes and signature verification, Patrick said the ballots themselves were very specific and individualized, meaning fraudulent attempts to mass-copy ballots and sway elections would be extremely difficult to pull off. She said:
The ballots themselves have pretty specific card stock, they have very specific timing marks down the side that allow for them to be tabulated. It's not the case that there's one ballot that everybody gets. In Maricopa County, they literally have upwards of 10,000 different ballot styles. So, knowing which ballot style each individual voter gets is tied to the ballot style, it's very specific, so even if you were to go out and take your sample ballot and duplicate it somehow, it doesn't matter, that's not an official ballot, it's not going to go through the tabulator. It's never going to get to that point in the process because it has to first be authenticated before it even makes it that far into the building.
Aside from ballots being difficult to copy, adding a significant number of ballots to a count would not go unnoticed. As part of the election certification process, officials will canvass — meaning count — absentee ballots and compare them with the known number of voters. A significantly higher number of returned ballots than voters would raise the alarm on fraud.
Patrick warned against automatically assuming election fraud if one person turned in multiple ballots at a polling station or drop box. According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, at least 35 states allowed voters to nominate a person other than themselves to turn in their ballot, meaning some voters might legitimately hand in more than one ballot.
Engage with system to quell concerns, expert says
Despite there being no documented incidents of election fraud via illegal ballot duplication, prominent politicians such as U.S. President Donald Trump have shared the unproven theory. However, as we outlined above, election officials have multiple safeguards in place that are effective at ensuring that any one voter gets only one vote.
Patrick suggested that the best thing worried voters could do was to engage with the system.
It's important to understand all the safeguards that are in place all along the path. To talk to your neighbors that work at the elections office, or who are poll workers. To go down and take a tour the next time there is a town hall and ask questions and see how it actually works.
She said, "When you have questions, elections officials are there with the answers and they want you to understand your process and your elections and to have confidence in it," but added that voters should not "try and 'test the system'" by submitting more than one ballot if they received multiple, "because that's criminal and you'll get caught, so you don't want to do that!"
For further reading, Snopes has covered a number of claims related to the 2026 elections.

Google's Gemini 4 Carbon promises 'significant leap' in AI coding and cybersecurity
The company's new frontier model tops Claude Opus 5.5 in several key benchmarks.
OpenAI and Anthropic's frontier models have been trading blows of late, with each claiming bragging rights in different categories. Now, Google has barged in with its latest Gemini 4 Carbon model, boasting of top benchmark scores in key areas like cybersecurity and coding. "Building on Gemini 4 Argon, which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we're pushing the frontier forward," the company wrote in a blog post.
The company's benchmarks show Gemini 4 Carbon hitting the highest AA Index v5.0 score (a general AI benchmark) at 59, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. Google also claims a near sweep across categories including agentic coding, computer use, knowledge work, science and math, and others. Google especially highlighted Carbon's domination in cybersecurity, where it bested other models by fairly wide margins.
In that category, Google claims that Gemini 4 Carbon excels in finding and prioritizing vulnerabilities, as well as patching them at the root cause. The company said that it also advances frontier model safety and security by reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation, boosting transparency and honesty (yes, there's a test for "unsupported claims"), resisting prompt injection, improving collaboration and "following through without overstepping." It's also twice as likely to generate secure code compared to Argon.
As we've seen with previous frontier models, Carbon will only be released to select cybersecurity defense companies at first, to allow for pre-release model testing. Google will eventually allow access to additional trusted partners through the company's Fairwind Program, before releasing it widely. That's exactly what Google did with Gemini 4 Argon, which is now available in the Gemini app and AI search mode.

Delhi police have again obstructed protests in India’s capital as thousands of people returned to the streets, led by opposition leaders, to demand the resignation of the election commissioner.
After mass unrest in the capital over the weekend, when thousands were detained and harassed by police as they attempted to take part in a protest led by the gen Z Cockroach movement, on Monday the main opposition leaders led another procession through Delhi, this time to the supreme court.
The leader of India’s opposition alliance, Rahul Gandhi, alongside other opposition figures and student groups, had declared their intention to march to the court and submit a petition calling for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down.
Kumar has become a deeply controversial figure for his role in an exercise to verify and “purify” India’s electoral rolls, which has led to more than 130m names – more than the population of Japan – being deleted from voter lists since last year.
Opposition parties and civil society groups allege Kumar implemented this special intensive revision (SIR) to help entrench the power of Narendra Modi’s government and his Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Muslim voters and other minorities who are traditionally not BJP voters have allegedly been disproportionately affected by the deletions.
The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters could re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Several metro stations were closed on Monday in central Delhi and police barricades prevented thousands of protesters getting within 600m of the supreme court, forcing them to turn back.
However, lawyers confirmed they had submitted the petition on Gandhi’s behalf and by late evening, Gandhi had broken through the barricades and reached the court gates.
In a press conference before the march, Gandhi reiterated his allegation that the Modi government was using the commission to commit “vote chori” (cheating) and accused Kumar of being a “thief”.
Gandhi expressed support for the mass uprising of young people, led by the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and student groups, who had tried to protest over the weekend but were met with police brutality and mass detentions.
“Till the constitution is upheld, till the chief election commissioner is removed, till the system of elections is revamped, till justice is served for India, the youth won’t stop,” he said.
The SIR and calls for Kumar’s resignation have galvanised support for beleaguered opposition parties, who are seen to have flailed in the face of the BJP’s electoral power. Gandhi was detained twice last week after the police refused to let him and other opposition leaders reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in central Delhi.
Mahua Moitra, an opposition MP who was marching after being detained last week, alleged that in her constituency in West Bengal more than 10,000 voters had been unjustly removed from the electoral rolls.
“There’s no going back now. People know that their votes have been stolen and this government is finished,” Moitra said. “The police can detain us, they can use brute force and crack our skulls, but we are not going to get off the streets until Gyanesh Kumar resigns and this government is gone. If we don’t stand up to this, then there will be nothing left of our country.”
Moitra accused the supreme court of helping to validate the SIR process and disenfranchise millions of Indians. “When the history of this dark chapter of India is written, the supreme court will be the most disgraced,” she said. “It was the supreme court who put a stamp of approval on every illegality of this government.”
Gandhi has spent months accusing the BJP of fraudulently influencing elections, but his claims have been largely ignored. The issue exploded last month after the Indian Express newspaper reported multiple irregularities in the SIR process that had been pushed through by Kumar.
The protests are likely to continue this week. On Monday, leaders of the CJP approached the Delhi police to seek a date to be allowed to hold a protest without obstruction. They said that if the police refused to comply, their supporters would take to the streets again.

President Donald Trump has made it through another Halloween event at the White House — this time without going viral for putting candy on the head of a child dressed as a short yellow henchman from the Minions movie franchise -- or anything else too silly.
During his first term in 2019, a child, dressed in an inflatable Minions costume, went up to Trump and First Lady Melania for some sweets, but instead of putting the candy bar in the child’s bag, he plopped it on their head. Trump did the same thing last Halloween, placing a candy bar on top of a child’s light-up mask.
This year’s event was fairly tame. The Trumps handed out candy, this time putting it in children’s bags in an event that lasted about an hour. Members of Trump’s administration, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, joined in on the fun with their families Thursday evening.
While there were no notable Minions costumes greeting the Trumps at the White House, which was decked out with pumpkins and fall leaves, there were a few Trick-or-Treaters dressed up as the henchmen’s favorite treat — a banana.
There were also kids dressed up as Barbie, racecar drivers, Toy Story characters, dinosaurs and animals from Winnie the Pooh.
But Trump was most impressed with costumes close to his interests, such as himself.
One older kid took a photo with Trump and Melania dressed in a “Make America Great Again” red hat, a white long-sleeve shirt with the number 47 — for the 47th president — on it and red flannel pajama pants with the phrase “MAGA for life.”
Other kids dressed as soldiers, police officers, Secret Service members, Uncle Sam and Rosie the Riveter. There were also a few little ones dressed as the Founding Fathers with white wigs and colonel-style clothing.
To complete the spooky vibe, the Air Force Strolling Strings played Halloween music from the Ghostbusters theme song to the Rocky Horror Picture Show’s iconic song, Time Warp.
Earlier Thursday, Trump was in South Carolina campaigning for Republican Senator Darline Graham, who is running for a full term after being appointed to finish out her brother Lindsey Graham’s term after his sudden death in July.
Trump ranted about Graham’s Democratic opponent Annie Andrews, with whom she’s in a surprisingly tight race, and he raved about the attractiveness of college golf players whom he invited on stage.
But the president decided not to insult Barack Obama amid a feud over the former president’s jab comparing the White House to a Cheesecake Factory restaurant.
Obama had joked that Trump’s renovations left the White House “looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory” at a recent rally in Ohio. This angered Trump’s base, which accused Obama of “elitism,” but the Democrat laughed off the uproar, saying the Cheesecake Factory was actually his “jam.”
While Trump may have been busy Thursday, he just cleared out his weekend rally schedule. The president was supposed to travel to Kansas on Saturday and Iowa on Sunday, but he canceled both visits, according to reports.

An Egyptian man who firebombed a Jewish group at a demonstration in Boulder last year has pleaded guilty to federal hate crimes and other charges.
Mohamed Soliman is already serving life in prison after pleading guilty to state charges last spring in connection with the deadly June 2025 attack that targeted elderly activists. He yelled “Free Palestine!” and threw two Molotov cocktails at demonstrators who were marching in support of hostages taken in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel.
Soliman used a “makeshift flamethrower and threw an incendiary device” into the crowd, the FBI said.
Federal prosecutors accused Soliman of attacking the group because they were Jewish. The flames badly burned Karen Diamond, 82, and injured a dozen others. Diamond died three weeks later and her family said she suffered “indescribable pain.”
The charges Soliman pleaded guilty to in federal court in Denver included nine counts of hate crimes, two of using fire or an explosive to commit a felony and one of carrying an explosive while committing a felony. They are punishable by life in prison after federal prosecutors declined to seek the death penalty.
Plea hearing
Soliman spoke through an interpreter at a hearing Thursday and said little besides “yes” and “no” responses to the judge’s questioning as he was asked whether he understood the consequences of pleading guilty. Soliman was led out of court in handcuffs and shackles without looking at the victims in the courtroom.
In all, Soliman pleaded guilty to nine federal counts of hate crimes, including one resulting in Diamond’s death and eight for attempting to kill other demonstrators. Three additional counts were federal weapon charges.
“The defendant violently used the explosives to cause permanent and life-threatening injuries to several of these victims and cause the death of Karen Diamond,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Melissa Hindman said in court shortly before Soliman pleaded guilty.
A group of victims sat stoically in the courtroom, some taking notes as the judge asked Soliman if he understood the proceedings. Several victims intended to make statements at Soliman’s sentencing but declined to do so in court Thursday.
Colorado U.S. District Judge John Kane said he would review sentencing guidelines before deciding whether to accept or reject prosecutors’ sentencing recommendation. He noted the guidelines are not binding.
“I have not made up my mind about the sentence,” Kane said. “Sometimes I follow that advice and sometimes I don’t.”
Soliman's federal sentencing was set for Jan. 7.
Boulder shaken by the attack
Boulder residents, particularly the Jewish community, described being unnerved by the attack in their city northwest of Denver that’s home to the University of Colorado. The group “Run for Their Lives” had been demonstrating weekly downtown.
Soliman got near the demonstration on Pearl Street, a pedestrian mall lined with shops and restaurants, by posing as a gardener.
Federal authorities say Soliman planned the attack for a year. After his arrest, he told police he sought “to kill all Zionist people,” a reference to the movement to establish and protect a Jewish state in Israel, according to an FBI affidavit.
Federal officials said he was in the U.S. illegally. He entered in 2022 on a tourist visa that expired the following year, then filed for asylum. He was granted work authorization, but it too expired, federal officials said
Soliman was living with his wife and their five children in an apartment in Colorado Springs at the time of the attack and worked a series of low-paying jobs. The couple divorced in April and Soliman recently dropped his opposition to removing his family from the U.S.
Prosecutors in Soliman’s state case argued he planned for more harm than he carried out and tried twice to buy a gun but was denied. He brought 18 Molotov cocktails — bottles filled with flammable liquid that are lit, thrown and burst into flames when they shatter — to the demonstration in a box, but only two were thrown.
Of the 29 attack victims identified by state prosecutors, 13 were physically injured. Prosecutors considered the rest victims because they could have been hurt and an injured dog led to a state animal cruelty charge.
While in court to plead guilty to the state charges in May, Soliman said he has known and respected Jewish people but questioned the deaths of innocent people in Israeli attacks on Gaza.
“Yes, I am against Israel and I can’t deny that. And that is my right,” Soliman said.

India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.
Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday.
Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians.
Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential.
On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday.
Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing last week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares.
The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share.
At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company.
However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer.
It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year.
Jio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. It gained 16 million subscribers in the first month, and topped 100 million subscribers within 170 days, according to Reliance Industries. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable, by triggering a price war. The company intends to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure.
Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director, told investors last week that the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working.
“What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”

On 22 October 2026, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur acknowledged that face-offs with Chinese forces had occurred at multiple locations along the Arunachal Pradesh border. On 23 October 2026, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal stated that the situation along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) becomes “disturbed” when Chinese troops deviate from established patrolling patterns.
Amid these developments, several videos are being circulated on social media (here, here, and here), purportedly showing clashes between Indian and Chinese troops along the Arunachal Pradesh border, including claims of an Indian soldier’s capture and alleged attempts by Chinese troops to cross the border. Let’s verify the claims made in these posts in this article.
Claim: The videos show clashes between Indian and Chinese troops along the Arunachal Pradesh border in October 2026.
Fact: None of the viral videos shows the reported India–China border face-offs in October 2026. The first and third videos were circulating on social media by December 2025, while the second features footage filmed on 28 September 2021, as reported by CNN. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1
During our investigation, we found several social media posts (here, here, and here) featuring the same visuals dating back to December 2025. This confirms that the viral video predates the reported India–China border tensions in October 2026 and is unrelated to the recent developments. These posts allege that an Indian soldier suffering from diabetes and altitude-related health complications fainted while on duty near the Line of Actual Control (LAC). Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) personnel provided him with first aid and medical assistance before safely handing him over to his own unit. The posts portray the incident as a humanitarian gesture amid India–China border tensions.
A News18 Hindi report published on 16 December 2025, featuring a screenshot of the viral video, claimed that Chinese soldiers had assisted an unconscious Indian soldier. While highlighting the humanitarian aspect, the report also noted scepticism over the video, particularly why the soldier’s legs appeared to be tied, raising questions about whether the incident was a genuine humanitarian gesture or an attempt by China to improve its image.
However, we could not independently verify the video’s origin or the context in which it was recorded. The available evidence indicates that the video predates the October 2026 border face-offs. At the time of writing, the Indian Army had issued no statement confirming the capture of any Indian soldier during these incidents.
Video 2
During our investigation, we found that the viral video predates the reported India–China border tensions in October 2026 and is unrelated to the recent developments. The video has been online at least since December 2022.
A CNN report published on 15 December 2022 featuring the same visuals stated that the footage was filmed on 28 September 2021. According to CNN, a serving Indian military officer familiar with clashes along the India–China border confirmed that the video was recorded in Arunachal Pradesh, near the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto border between the two countries.
Video 3
During our investigation, we found several social media posts (here, here, and here) featuring the same visuals dating back to December 2025. This confirms that the viral video predates the reported India–China border tensions in October 2026 and is unrelated to the recent developments. These posts claimed that the video shows Indian soldiers beating Chinese troops allegedly attempting to infiltrate Arunachal Pradesh, describing it as an old border clash.
An X post by the Indian Army’s Fact Check Unit debunking the viral video stated that the footage was unauthenticated and was falsely presented as a recent October 2026 confrontation, creating rumours and confusion about the situation along the LAC. It also warned that old videos are often circulated as recent incidents and urged citizens to avoid sharing unverified footage and rely on official sources for updates.
To sum up, none of these viral videos shows the India–China border face-offs in October 2026.

Delhi's Jantar Mantar added as venue for Indian Biennale 2026
Vivek Aggarwal, secretary, ministry of culture, told HT last month that the whole of Delhi will be a stage for the Biennale.
Jantar Mantar, one of the five astronomical observatories built by Maharaja Jai Singh II of Jaipur in the early 18th century, has been added as a venue for the upcoming India Biennale 2026, organised by the ministry of culture.
The India Biennale website was updated on Thursday to reflect the addition.
The 108-day art, architecture and design festival, which is to begin on December 4, will take place across 18 other venues in the capital city. This includes the lawns of the Lodhi Gardens, the Qutub Minar complex, the Agrasen ki Baoli, the Red Fort and the Safdarjung Tomb, as well as other galleries, embassy precincts and private cultural venues.
Also Read | Jantar Mantar: From the science of the stars to the politics of dissent
The ministry’s own exhibition is expected to be held at the 16th-century Purana Qila, which will serve as the hub of the Biennale.
Participants include architecture and design firms as well as public and private art and cultural institutions such as the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA), the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art, the Nita Mukesh Ambani Cultural Centre, the JSW Foundation, and DAG (formerly Delhi Art Gallery).
“We should make our monuments into live cultural spaces and open them up so that [visitors] can not only enjoy history but also get a glimpse of the contemporary art scene of India,” Vivek Aggarwal, secretary, ministry of culture, told HT last month. “The whole of Delhi will be a stage.”
The development follows the October 11 denotification of a stretch of Jantar Mantar Road as a designated protest site, against the backdrop of a series of major agitations against the Union government this year.
Police also identified three alternatives – Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground in north Delhi and CBD Ground in east Delhi as alternative protest venues.
The move also aligned with October 9 observations from a Supreme Court bench, led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, advocating for larger, better-equipped sites to balance public safety and the right to protest.

“If the public is drifting away from government hospitals and being pushed into the clutches of the corporate healthcare system, it is undeniably because politicians and governments lack genuine sincerity,” said 115 citizens and activists in an open letter to Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy and Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha.
The letter accused successive governments of failing to strengthen public healthcare, alleging that the lack of basic amenities in government hospitals is driving patients towards private healthcare.
Gaps in basic facilities
The letter highlights concerns over drinking water facilities, toilets, sanitation and the maintenance of infrastructure at major government hospitals in Hyderabad, including Osmania General Hospital, Gandhi Hospital, Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS), Niloufer Hospital and Petlaburj Maternity Hospital.
The signatories — comprising social activists, academics, writers, journalists, teachers and other citizens — questioned whether the government’s promises to improve public healthcare translated into better conditions for patients.
Is the problem a lack of medical expertise or basic facilities?
The signatories argued that the challenges confronting government hospitals cannot be viewed solely through the lens of shortages of doctors and other medical personnel. The signatories acknowledged that healthcare workers were already working under considerable pressure, but said the absence of basic amenities was adding to the difficulties faced by patients.
“Government hospitals have experienced doctors, medical staff and research capabilities, but inadequate facilities are undermining the healthcare experience,” they added.
Referring to Osmania, Gandhi, NIMS, Niloufer and Petlaburj hospitals, the signatories questioned why patients should have to endure difficult conditions to access treatment when the institutions were expected to provide essential public healthcare services.
When basic amenities become a question of dignity
They have identified clean drinking water, functional toilets and proper sanitation as among the most pressing requirements in public hospitals. Questioning the government’s responsibility for maintaining these facilities, the signatories asked whether patients should be held responsible for unhygienic conditions and unpleasant odours in hospital toilets, arguing that the responsibility for maintenance rested with the authorities.
They said patients who could afford private healthcare might choose to seek treatment elsewhere, but those unable to bear the additional expense were left with fewer options.
Should hospital maintenance be handed over to private entities?
The signatories also cautioned the government against transferring responsibility for maintaining basic hospital amenities to corporate entities under the banner of public participation as doing so would impose an additional financial burden on patients. They called for the government to take responsibility for improving existing infrastructure and ensuring that essential facilities were properly maintained.
They further questioned the emphasis placed on changing photographs on walls and ambulances after a government assumes office, arguing that the same attention should be directed towards providing basic amenities in hospitals.
A call for a Right to Health law
Beyond immediate improvements to hospital infrastructure, the signatories urged the Telangana government to introduce a strong Right to Health law through consultations with people’s organisations and public. They called for a broader effort to strengthen the public health and medical system so that ordinary citizens would not be compelled to abandon government hospitals because of inadequate facilities.

I have consulted my AI-powered crystal ball, and it’s telling me that frontier models are going to get a lot better at making predictions in the near future. Just ask my Premier League fantasy team.
A few weeks ago, I deployed a small horde of AI agents to craft and manage an experimental roster. Given the proliferation of AI agents into pretty much every aspect of our lives, I wanted to know if a swarm of bots could put together a winning team.
I first looked at the potential for AI here a few years ago, playing around with a tool from the UK’s Turing Institute that selected teams after modeling previous fantasy league data. Its suggestions were remarkably bonkers—it didn’t incorporate real-world information, like a player’s injury or a team’s change in management.
This time, while on a flight to visit family, I asked Codex for help. First, I fed the model a couple of relevant research papers. Then, I asked it to build a harness—instructions and code that guides different agents through various steps—that would check recent news and run a model to make predictions.
It quickly came up with a setup that seemed to collate and analyze way more information than I ever would have. And yet I was surprised by how dumb the initial team suggestions were. Leaving Erling Haaland on the bench? Really, Codex?
I then asked Codex to create a team of agents that did different things: several that read news and blog posts; others that analyzed recent results; more that ran models; and a bunch that critiqued suggestions. This seemed to significantly improve the suggestions. I tried increasing the number of agents to more than 100, hoping this would make the system smarter still, but it didn’t change much besides running up my API bill.
Still, the improvement from a few years ago was striking. According to Haifeng Xu, a computer scientist at the University of Chicago who studies the uses of AI in market situations, newer models may be even better at making predictions because they’re able to consume and analyze huge amounts of real-world information, and they’re able to orchestrate more complex systems for their guesses.
“AI is just getting smarter in understanding the world—I feel like that's the fundamental reason they’re improving,” Xu tells me.
Late last year, Xu was marveling at the growing popularity of prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket. He wondered how the best commercial models might fare on those markets, so alongside several colleagues, he began testing their forecasting skills.
They had models guess, for example, who would win the NBA Championship and who President Trump would meet with.
“Very quickly we started to realize that models did really well,” Xu tells me. The models were sometimes able to do better than the average person without any special instructions or guidance, he says. In their testing, GPT-5 was the best at making predictions, followed by Grok 4, Claude Sonnet, Gemini, and Llama.
The team went on to develop Prophet Arena, a benchmark that measures a model’s ability to make predictions. It’s one of a number of benchmarks designed to test AI’s future-gazing capabilities; another, Prediction Arena, from researchers at Harvard University and a company called Arcada Labs, recently gave frontier models $10,000 to wager on prediction markets over 57 days. The models consistently lost money in their experiment, but the researchers saw evidence of them improving consistently over time.
Xu tells me that AI can most effectively make predictions using a custom harness, and notes that having agents with unique tasks—reading the news, collecting other data, and analyzing the whole system, for instance—seems to be the most effective approach.
Interestingly, AI still often lags behind very skilled experts known as superforecasters. Xu explains that, although humans cannot consume as much information, their understanding of the real world—that is, of the dynamics behind a news story—is deeper.
That said, there’s growing evidence that the human superforecaster’s edge is eroding. A contest called the Metaculus Cup recently showed that AI can sometimes beat even the best human predictors. And a benchmark called ForecastBench could provide further evidence that AI can match human skills when the results of an ongoing contest conclude soon. In fact, I think we can expect the big labs to turn their attention to future-gazing as a powerful new way to measure progress in machine intelligence.
All of these predictive experiments seem to suggest that, like math, coding, and law, industries predicated on trading may soon be upended by AI. Perhaps the best human traders will take on a new kind of role: supervising and orchestrating AI agents capable of divining the future far better than they can.
For the time being, my AI’s suggestions still don’t seem all that impressive. Its team hasn’t outscored the average over the past weeks. I certainly won’t be using any of its suggestions in my own selections.
But AI will no doubt get better, perhaps making it all too easy to dominate fantasy league pretty soon. I’m kind of hoping it won’t, though, as it would spoil the fun of trying to earn bragging rights by winning all by yourself.

The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.

Several companies produce animal-free egg white protein in the U.S. Some of these products have been available since 2021. The EVERY Company made its OvoPro product available to consumers in March 2026. The FDA said in October 2023 that it had "no questions" regarding The EVERY Company's declaration that the protein ingredient in OvoPro was "generally recognized as safe."
We found no evidence that brands that used OvoPro were omitting it from their product ingredient lists. Federal law governs what must appear on ingredients labels. An OvoPro spokesperson said the EVERY Company had not sought an exemption from OvoPro being included in ingredients lists and provided guidance to companies about how to list it.
It was also unclear whether OvoPro and products like it that are grown using yeast qualify as "lab-grown." That classification usually describes products that grow actual animal cells, which OvoPro does not.
In October 2026, a claim (archived) circulated that U.S. consumers could buy federally approved "lab-grown" eggs that brands were secretly including in their products.
For example, one Facebook user shared a video about the alleged lab grown eggs in which two speakers said:
Lab-grown eggs are federally approved and Walmart, alongside Target, are already selling them. The protein is squeezed out of gene-edited mold and cloned on repeat because a steel tank costs less than a hen.
They're brewing eggs with no chicken in sight and slipping them onto your breakfast plate. That egg isn't real food, it's factory fungus, spliced with the gene for egg protein then dumped into giant fermenting vats and fed on sugar until it swells into a wet, moldy soup. And it gets worse: that cloudy sludge is blasted into dust, ton after ton, padded out with plant filler and passed off as egg white, then buried in packaged foods under labels that never say so. At Walmart, two or more of these lab egg products already sit on the shelf.
The video also circulated elsewhere on Facebook (archived, archived). It included shots of the packaging for OvoPro, an egg protein The EVERY Company produces. Snopes readers also contacted us about the claim, asking questions like, "Are there such a thing as Lab grown eggs being sold in secret?"
The claim was a mixture of true, false and undetermined elements.
Though it was true that egg proteins grown using yeast rather than chickens were available to U.S. consumers in October 2026, products like OvoPro were not new to the market. The EVERY Company, which produces OvoPro, also did not appear to be the only company selling animal-free egg protein to consumers in the U.S.
OvoPro was not FDA "cleared" or "approved" — the latter of which is generally a status reserved for drugs, not food. Rather, in October 2023, the FDA responded with a "no questions" letter to The EVERY Company's declaration that the egg-white protein in OvoPro was "generally recognized as safe."
We found no evidence that retailers could decide not to list the animal-free egg protein as an ingredient in products that contained it, as some claimed. Federal legislation governs what must appear on ingredients labels. A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said via email on Aug. 21 that the company had not sought to exempt OvoPro from ingredients lists.
Additionally, it was unclear whether OvoPro and other yeast-grown egg proteins could correctly be called "lab-grown," a classification that usually describes products grown from a small sample of the source, as seen with fish, poultry and meat. A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said:
OvoPro is made through precision fermentation: a yeast (Komagataella phaffii) is given the genetic instructions to produce egg-white protein, and it does so during fermentation. No animal cells, and no chicken, are involved at any point.
What is egg protein grown by yeast?
According to its website, The EVERY Company uses a patented method to produce ovalbumin, the dominant protein in egg whites, through precision fermentation.
The company described this process as "programming" yeast to produce egg protein through fermentation, a process familiar from beer brewing.
It said the process eventually results in "a pure, powdered protein that is tasteless, colorless, sugar-free, and can be used to replace the functionality of eggs and egg whites in a range of applications."
The EVERY Company received its patent for its method of precision fermentation in September 2024. The company, previously known as Clara Foods, has been working to develop animal-free egg protein since at least 2021.
It unveiled EVERY ClearEgg, a predecessor to OvoPro, in October 2021. The EVERY Company received a "no questions" letter in September 2021 in response to its GRAS (Generally Recognized as Safe) determination for ClearEgg.
The FDA's GRAS Notification program allows companies to submit documentation that they believe their product is "safe under the conditions of its intended use." In the case of ClearEgg, the FDA said in a letter on Sept. 9, 2021, that it had "no questions," meaning The EVERY Company could market ClearEgg as "Generally Recognized as Safe."
The EVERY Company got another "no questions" letter in response to a GRAS determination for an egg white protein produced by Komagataella phaffii, a species of yeast, in October 2023. A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said on Aug. 21, 2026, that this GRAS notice was for the egg-white protein in OvoPro.
Company sold animal-free eggs before 2026
OvoPro and related products have been available to consumers since at least 2021, meaning they were not new to the U.S. market in October 2026, as some claims appeared to suggest. For example, in November 2021, The Spoon, an outlet that reports on the food tech industry, reported that smoothies containing ClearEgg had hit the market.
The next year, The EVERY Company reportedly sold its EggWhite product in macarons and Every Protein (formerly ClearEgg) in juice. By January 2024, the New York Times wrote that The EVERY Company had showcased EveryEgg, a "yellow vegan plant-based liquid" that the paper said, "behaves astonishingly like a whole beaten egg."
It did not appear that The EVERY Company sold EveryEgg directly to consumers at that point, but rather distributed the product through restaurants.
The new development in 2026 appeared to be that The EVERY Company was selling OvoPro, a successor to EveryEgg, directly to consumers. The company announced on March 11, 2026, that the general public could buy OvoPro through Healthier Comforts, a food retailer, and Amazon.
The company said in June that same year that OvoPro was also available as an ingredient sold in Walmart and Target.
Brands not hiding use of animal-free egg protein
According to some claims, brands could allegedly decide for themselves whether to declare OvoPro as an ingredient in their products. The video above said that companies "buried" their "lab-grown" eggs in "packaged foods under labels that never say so"The EVERY Company's website page on OvoPro said, in reply to a frequently asked question about how the protein appears on ingredient declarations, that "Final labeling decisions are made by our customers, but we recommend labeling OvoPro™ as 'egg white protein (from fermentation),' 'egg white protein (from yeast),' or 'animal-free egg white protein.'"
That did not appear to mean that brands that used OvoPro in their products could avoid labeling them entirely. Federal law dictates that products must generally include an ingredients list, with ingredients listed in descending order according to how much of the product's weight they make up.
A spokesperson for The EVERY Company said that it had never sought to exempt OvoPro from being included in ingredients lists. Speaking via email, the spokesperson added:
"OvoPro" is the trade name we use with the manufacturers who buy the ingredient, so it typically won't appear on a retail pack — the same way most functional ingredients are listed by common name rather than by supplier brand. What appears on the label is the ingredient, named plainly.
Healthier Comforts listed OvoPro as an "animal-free egg white protein," one of The EVERY Company's suggested phrasings, on its branded version of the product.
In sum ...
Though the claims circulated in October 2026, OvoPro had actually been available to consumers since March of that year. The FDA told The EVERY Company in October 2023 that it had "no questions" regarding the company's declaration that the egg-white protein in OvoPro was GRAS.
That letter was not the same thing as FDA approval, which is a process whereby the administration approves drugs for consumer use. Rather, they showed that the company had documented to the FDA's satisfaction that the product in question was "safe under the conditions of its intended use."
We found no evidence that brands that used OvoPro were leaving it off product ingredients lists. This appeared to be a misinterpretation by some social media users of a statement by The EVERY Company that brands had leeway in how they described the product.
OvoPro is also not the only animal-free egg white protein product available to U.S. consumers.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether Quaker instant strawberries and cream oatmeal contained "beaver butt secretions" or whether McDonald's apple pies contained an ingredient derived from human hair.

With its playful design, versatility, and relatively affordable price, the Ikea Varmblixt quickly became one of my colleague Jennifer Pattison Tuohy’s new favorite smart light products when she tested it in April. Now, the donut-shaped lamp is on sale for $79.99 ($20 off) through November 11th at Ikea.

Hong Kong Leader Apologizes for Deadly Fire and Blames Construction Industry
John Lee, the city’s chief executive, said his housing secretary would step down, but he vehemently defended the government.
Hong Kong’s leader apologized on Thursday for a deadly fire last year and said his housing secretary had resigned, in an effort to offer accountability for a disaster that drew outrage and created a political challenge for his Beijing-backed government.
“The fire brought sadness and misery to us,” said John Lee, Hong Kong’s chief executive, at a news conference. Flanked by seven other officials, Mr. Lee bowed to the assembled media and added, “I apologize.”
The gesture was notable coming from a government that was quick to crack down on expression in the weeks after the deadly fire, which killed 168 people at the Wang Fuk Court housing complex in northern Hong Kong last November. But Mr. Lee also vehemently defended the government in a testy question-and-answer session on Thursday as he was asked, several times, about his own accountability.
The resignation of the housing secretary, Winnie Ho, was the first by a senior official following months of questions over the culpability of Hong Kong’s leaders. Mr. Lee stopped short of blaming her directly, adding that “the fire did not involve any personal wrongdoing by the secretary,” but said that she should “bear political responsibility.”
He primarily blamed collusion and corruption in the construction industry for the fire, saying that construction insiders with connections to organized crime groups known as triads had been responsible for shoddy repair work that led up to it. Mr. Lee said the government would hold criminally accountable anyone who was found guilty of rigging a construction bid.
The seven buildings that burned in the blaze had been undergoing government-mandated repairs and were shrouded in netting that was later found to be substandard. The authorities said the netting and polystyrene foam that was used to protect windows was responsible for the rapid spread of the fire, which burned with such intensity that it took thousands of firefighters two days to put out the blaze.

Alaska governor orders probe into Democratic campaign's alleged links to same-name candidate
- Published
The Republican governor of Alaska has ordered an investigation into an alleged "scheme" which led to two Dan Sullivans standing in the state's US Senate race.
Governor Mike Dunleavy said he was responding to a New York Times (NYT) story, external which said the team of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola worked with people who tried to recruit spoiler candidates in the Senate race.
The governor's post on X said he would investigate "whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws". He did not say which laws he had in mind.
Dan Sullivan, the incumbent Republican senator running for re-election, and allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters. Peltola's team deny any wrongdoing.
They say they did not encourage the second Dan Sullivan, a retired teacher who lives in a remote fishing village, to stand. He has denied any links with the Peltola campaign.
The Alaska race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest of the upcoming US midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress. Americans head to the polls across the country on Tuesday.
Dunleavy's statement, which did not name the Peltola campaign, said the NYT reporting had supported findings by the state Division of Elections earlier this year.
"I am therefore directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted," he wrote. "The evidence will determine what happens next."
The NYT report alleged that people connected to Peltola's campaign, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), worked to try to recruit Sullivan the schoolteacher to stand in the Senate race.
This was part of a broader effort to encourage other would-be "spoiler" candidates to enter the race and dilute the support of the sitting Republican senator, the newspaper reported.
The paper said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the NYT's reporting.
The DSCC did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Dunleavy's investigation.
The ballot paper is set to list the two men as Dan S Sullivan, who will be described as the incumbent Republican senator, and Daniel J Sullivan Jr.
Senator Dan Sullivan told Fox News on Wednesday night that Peltola should "come clean" and described it as a scandal of the highest order.
His fellow Republican senator in Alaska, Lisa Murkowksi, accused the Democratic campaign of engaging in a "pattern of lies". President Donald Trump has called for Peltola to be barred.
Previous efforts by the Republicans to remove the non-incumbent Sullivan from the ballot have already been rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court which found no state laws had been broken by him running in the race.
Though officials at the state and federal level have called for investigations in the wake of the New York Times reporting, election law experts said it was unlikely to dislodge the second Dan Sullivan from the ballot and it was unclear at this point if any state laws had been violated.
"It turns out that convincing somebody to run for office is not a crime, even if their name happens to be the same as an incumbent," said Justin Levitt, an election law expert at Loyola Law School and a former justice department official.
The non-incumbent Sullivan had a constitutional right to run and have his name on the ballot, added Ruth Greenwood, an election expert at Harvard Law School.
The Trump administration filed a federal lawsuit last week aimed at preventing the certification of the result if the Trump-backed Sullivan loses, arguing that the presence of both of them on the ballot could confuse voters.
Some legal experts expressed scepticism of the merits of the lawsuit, and their chances of success given Alaska's courts had already allowed the second Sullivan to remain on the ballot.
The actual legal arguments the justice department made were a "frivolous theory," Rick Pildes, an election law expert at New York University, told the BBC.
He noted the lawsuit did not cite a specific provision that the government wanted to enforce, merely a general preamble taken from a sweeping US voting law.
Alaska election officials asked a federal court to dismiss the lawsuit "because the complaint has no legal basis".
The justice department has pledged continued action in the wake of the New York Times' reporting.
"They are cheating, let's call it what it is," Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Fox News on Wednesday.
In a series of Truth Social posts, Trump too pointed to the report and made a variety of allegations against Peltola, who he argued should be removed from the ballot. He repeated his endorsement for Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican senator, writing: "Dan is a GREAT man, has ALWAYS delivered for Alaska."
Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box.
The battle threatens to delay the full picture of nationwide results following the midterm elections. The ultimate question of which party controls Congress will have a significant bearing on the remaining two years of Trump's presidency.
A statement from an Alaskans for Mary spokesperson, written prior to Dunleavy's call for an investigation, said: "Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any DC politician will keep her away from that fight.
"The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign."
In a statement given to US media, the DSCC likewise denied that it had been involved in any such scheme.
Peltola earlier this week paused campaigning activities in order to recover after she and her family sustained "minor injuries" in a car crash.

The Delhi Police had posted a video on their X handle on October 25, which urged citizens to not burn crackers this Diwali. Along with a meme video, the post was captioned: “This festive season, let tails wag, not tuck. Say NO to crackers, YES to a greener Diwali.”
Soon after the post was made, social media users had predicted that it would be removed soon. Incidentally, just within a few hours of the post being made, the Delhi Police removed it from X.
While Delhi Police did not issue any clarification as to why the post was taken down, several X users wondered whether the reason behind the post being taken down was perhaps the purported pressure from the BJP-led central government.
Alt News co-founder Mohammad Zubair had also remarked on Delhi Police’s post, before it was taken down, with the caption: “This tweet will soon be deleted due to political pressure.”
Another X user, Jeevansh Arya, shared a screen grab of the Delhi Police’s post and questioned whether it would be deleted.
@zoo_bear @DelhiPolice Tweet Deleted Now ?
Daro Mat 😂😂 https://t.co/q51PIYEFZG
— 𝐉𝐄𝐄𝐕𝐀𝐍𝐒𝐇 𝐀𝐑𝐘𝐀 🇮🇳 (@jeevansharya) October 25, 2026
After the post was deleted, many social media users posted that they expected something like this to happen.
Like most of us predicted, tweet deleted by @DelhiPolice
— Piyush Rai (@Benarasiyaa) October 25, 2026
The official handle of Indian Youth Congress also questioned the logic behind the retreat of the Delhi Police.
Administrative Indecision in The Past
This is, however, not the first time that the Delhi administration retracted its position during Diwali regarding firecrackers. Over the past two years, Delhi’s authorities and the courts have attempted to take a strong stance against firecrackers due to the city’s severe air pollution, but they have often backtracked on their decisions.
Ahead of Diwali 2024, the Delhi government imposed a complete ban on the manufacture, sale, storage and bursting of all firecrackers until January 1, 2025. The Supreme Court later criticised the poor enforcement of the ban and suggested that the government consider making it permanent. In December 2024, the Delhi government told the court that it had imposed a year-round ban on firecrackers.
However, the position changed soon. In April 2025, the Supreme Court refused to relax the ban, but in October it allowed green crackers to be sold and used in Delhi-NCR for a limited period during Diwali. The court said these crackers had to meet standards set by the National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI), and allowed their use only during specified hours. The Delhi government and the Centre supported the relaxation.
In effect, the authorities moved from a complete ban on firecrackers to allowing a limited category of green crackers, despite earlier court observations that even green crackers could not be considered a comprehensive solution to Delhi’s pollution problem.
Delhi Pays The Price
Delhi’s air quality worsened sharply during Diwali 2025, with the city’s AQI (Air Quality Index) reaching almost 500, falling under the hazardous category. Firecracker bursting was followed by a dramatic rise in PM2.5 and PM10 levels.
According to a Times of India report, between 9 pm and 10 pm on Diwali 2025, the PM 2.5 concentration of Delhi’s Nehru Nagar region saw a spike from 679 micrograms per cubic metre to 1,763µg/m³. The report also mentioned that the peak PM2.5 concentration was more than 29 times the national daily limit of 60 µg/m³ and around 118 times the World Health Organization’s recommended daily guideline.
Pollution Concerns Framed as Anti-Hindu
Following Diwali last year, Alt News had written about the Right-wing supporters in the country interpreting complaints on the detrimental environmental effects of bursting firecrackers as an “attack against Hindutva” itself.
YouTuber Dhruv Rathee had posted a video on his X page asking his audience to desist from burning firecrackers. Right-wing social media users immediately began sharing images of firecrackers that they had apparently hoarded. While some questioned Rathee’s stake in it, others indulged in whataboutery and asked whether he had shown environmental concerns on Bakrid. Certain users went to the extent of mockingly comparing the extreme pollution levels in India to the genocide in Gaza.
Similarly, when BJP leader Subramaniam Swamy wrote on X, “Exploding fire crackers after 10 pm today is a criminal offence. Police should crackdown on them”, Right-wing influencer Chandan Sharma (Hindutva Knight/@HPhobiaWatch) targeted Swamy’s daughter, The Hindu’s Diplomatic Editor, Suhasini Haidar, using obscene language for being married to a Muslim man.
Several Right-wing accounts, such as @NamitaBalyan, @AchAnkurArya, and @JaipurDialogues, posted photos showing the firecrackers and the knight sky shrouded in smog, ultimately dismissing grave environmental concerns under the garb of protecting Hindu festivals.

Bangladeshi author Taslima Nasrin, who is currently living in Kolkata, on October 20, Tuesday, wrote on Facebook that although Leftists in West Bengal organise bookstalls during Durga Puja, such stalls are absent during other ‘religious’ festivals such as Christmas and Eid. She questioned why Leftists choose not to sell books promoting ‘atheism’ during other religious festivals, but instead promote them only during a Hindu festival.
In her post, she wrote (translated from Bengali), “Someone asked, “Have you ever seen Leftists selling books on atheism to Muslims near an Eidgah on Eid? Have you ever seen them selling books by Richard Dawkins or Christopher Hitchens to people attending Christmas prayers on Christmas Day? Then, quite naturally, the question arises: why do they want to sell books on atheism specifically at Hindu Durga Puja pandals?” What answer do the Leftists of Kolkata have to this question?”
This post has garnered over 7,000 likes and 1,300 reshares, and garnered significant traction, although she had disabled the comment section of the Facebook post.
Nasrin, who has been in exile since leaving Bangladesh in 1994 amid death threats and protests over her writings critical of the ‘dogmas’ of Islam, was forced to leave Kolkata in 2007 following violent protests against her autobiography ‘Dwikhandito’ and pressure on the then CPI(M)-led Left Front government.
She remained unable to return to West Bengal for nearly 19 years, with successive CPI(M) and Trinamool Congress (TMC) governments in power. However, in July 2026, following the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) coming to power in the state, Nasrin returned to Kolkata and was publicly welcomed and celebrated by sections of the Right-wing BJP-RSS ecosystem.
Against this backdrop, her recent Facebook post questioned what she portrayed as the Left’s selective promotion of atheism. Moreover, her statement comes on the heels of state authorities demolishing and damaging certain bookstalls set up by Left parties near Jadavpur’s 8b bus stand on October 17.
Fact Check
Alt News found several social media posts and news reports that refute Nasrin’s claim that the bookstalls are exclusively set up during Durga Puja.
The Students’ Federation of India (SFI) and the Democratic Youth Federation of India (DYFI) have been organising a bookstall near Park Street, where Christmas is celebrated in Kolkata, for at least 10 years. Prominent Left leader Biman Bose has also visited the stall. The bookstall has been featured on the social media handles of SFI, DYFI, CPI(M) and other affliated organisations, and has also been covered by the media. The Telegraph reported the setting up of the bookstall at Park Street for the first time in 2016, Alt News also founds images of stalls from 2017, 2022, 2024.
